articles.title: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C
articles.context: The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component...
articles.full_text:
Read more about the wave of cyber-attacks on refrigeration control systems in Europe:

Major French Supermarket Chains Hit by Cyber-Attack, Food Stock Impacted

French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Cyber-Attack on Refrigeration Systems Hits Supermarkets Across Europe

Cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) were turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F) in a cyber-attack targeting temperature-controlled storage and refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld.

On November 3, French investigative weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported a new wave of attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France.

The outlet said unauthorized actors took control of some refrigeration controllers in EFS’s cold storage rooms in the night between November 1 and 2, notably in facilities in the Burgundy and Franche-Comté region, in east-central France.

These cold storage units host blood samples used for health monitoring but also plasma intended for transfusions. While they are typically kept at -30°C (-22°F), the newspaper reported some rooms hit up to 110°C (230°F). This does not mean the equipment or any blood samples reached these temperatures.

The refrigeration control systems of the affected EFS cold rooms are maintained by Coolworld, a Dutch temperature control rental company operating in France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands and the UK.

Coolword confirmed on November 4 it was "aware of the cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software used in refrigeration systems" and said it "responded promptly by implementing the appropriate measures," without sharing any details on those measures.

The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld."

No Operational Impact on Blood Samples

The French Ministry of Health sought to reassure the public and told Le Canard enchaîné that the incident had caused no operational disruption because it had been detected in time.

According to the EFS, an on-call technician noticed an abnormal rise in temperature in the cold storage rooms overnight, allowing the issue to be identified before it could affect operations.

Speaking to French national news channel BFMTV, EFS president Frédéric Pacoud said that while the EFS “could have lost samples or bags of plasma intended to treat patients,” the early warning meant “there was no compromise to the safety of blood products.”

The EFS also told French media it notified the country's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI). At this stage, nothing indicates that any EFS IT systems are impacted by the attack.

The EFS was approached for comment but had not responded at the time of publication.

articles.title: Impart uses AI to build virtual patches without putting models in the traffic path
articles.context: The launch comes as exploits increasingly outpace fixes
articles.full_text:
Impart Security has launched the Runtime Defense Harness, a controlled environment where AI agents write and test virtual patches for new vulnerabilities without putting AI in the traffic path. The launch comes as exploits increasingly outpace fixes.

In the harness, agents build each virtual patch against the customer’s own traffic, an engineer approves it, and Impart’s engine enforces it as deterministic code. Security teams get a tested virtual patch as soon as 60 minutes after disclosure, instead of waiting days for a vendor signature or weeks for a code fix.

When researchers disclosed the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in October, the first exploit attempt had come four days earlier. Nearly 80% of 4.38 million internet-facing PHP services run unsupported versions, so for many teams a patch release is not protection.

Most security teams have only a handful of people who can write and ship a custom rule. Everyone else waits on them, or on an edge vendor’s generic signature, which often ships in log-only mode.

“The old rhythm of security teams responding to a vulnerability, filing a ticket, and hoping for a patch a few weeks later is long gone. AI has compressed the timeline, so exploits can arrive before the fix. We built the Runtime Defense Harness with the controls first, so teams can move fast without risking production,” said Jonathan DiVincenzo, CEO of Impart.

The model helps write and test each rule but never sits in the live request path. Impart’s Layer 7 engine enforces approved rules inline as deterministic WebAssembly, so the same request gets the same decision every time, with no extra network hop or per-request inference.

The harness makes AI defense safe to run in production through three controls:

Scoped access and tiered autonomy: Agents get just-in-time access to only the traffic and systems each task needs. They investigate, draft, and test on their own, but block mode and live rule changes require an engineer’s approval.

Programmable enforcement: Every virtual patch is code that teams can version, test, and roll back in seconds.

Your model, full audit trail: Teams use Impart’s lightweight AI model or bring their own models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, or Google. Every agent action lands in an event timeline showing what the AI did, why, and what changed.

“The harness coordinates agents to do what a security engineer does when a new CVE lands: understand the attack, write the rule, test it, and hand it over for approval. Your engineers make the call. The harness makes sure everything in front of them is tested and auditable,” said Brian Joe, chief product officer of Impart.

The approach has held up under real disclosures. During a high-severity Node.js vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) that could allow remote code execution, Impart customers had a blocking virtual patch within 24 hours. A leading CDN’s rules arrived four days later, in log-only mode, against its own published five-day response target.

articles.title: AI-Linked Breaches Mount as WorkOS, Northflank, Trigger.dev Disclose Hacks
articles.context: While part of the same industry-wide trend, the attacks do not appear to be related, and initial access varies from compromised credentials to third-party dependencies and...
articles.full_text:
AI-related cyberattacks are surging, with hackers stealing AI access keys to monetize them and using AI tools to speed up their intrusions.

Over the past month, at least a dozen AI developer platforms were hit, with the most recent incidents involving CommandCode, Northflank, Trigger.dev, Chainstack, and WorkOS.

Across all incidents, the hackers appear to have been hunting for AI access tokens they could monetize, relying on AI agents to speed up and streamline their attacks.

While part of the same industry-wide trend, the attacks do not appear to be related, and initial access varies from compromised credentials to third-party dependencies and vulnerability exploitation.

The attackers hit Andromeda, Brev (NVIDIA), CommandCode, Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, Northflank, OpenCode, Railway, Trigger.dev, Warp, and Zeabur, mainly looking for stored customer secrets.

“Intruders are reaching AI provider credentials through the intermediary layer of hosting platforms, evaluation services, and developer consoles, and recent gateway compromises show the same interest in these secrets. Because that layer holds credentials on behalf of many downstream customers, a single intrusion can expose keys for many inference accounts at once,” Cloud Security Alliance pointed out.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Per Wiz’s analysis of the incidents, the surge is caused by the rise of LLM-jacking and LLM broker infrastructure, which make the stolen AI access tokens easily monetizable and will likely attract more threat actors to credential theft.

The cybersecurity outfit notes that this demand is also driven by distillation (training a cheaper model on the outputs of a more advanced one), “notably alleged against Chinese AI labs”.

Wiz says it has observed hackers abusing enterprise credentials compromised in these attacks, including two cases that “shared an identical first unauthorized activity, which happened within 30 minutes of the reported credential access within the vendor breach.”

The company observed multiple threat actors using the same compromised keys, which “suggests a robust market for this type of credential”.

Artex used to automate attacks

This week, blockchain infrastructure and Web3 services provider Chainstack and API platform for building enterprise applications WorkOS disclosed cyberattacks that relied on the open source AI penetration testing framework Artex for automation.

Multiple companies have linked attacks attributed to the Chinese APT Storm-0940 to the use of Artex, including a recent campaign targeting ConnectWise customers.

Chainstack was hit on October 26, and the attackers accessed a development environment and parts of the company’s production environment through a third-party component.

“The attacker accessed a database containing customer account information. Information that may have been exposed includes organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of your organization’s members on Chainstack, and password hashes,” the company said this week.

Node credentials might have been exposed as well, as the attackers had access to systems storing them, and Chainstack prompted customers to rotate those credentials.

On October 30, WorkOS says, the hackers compromised an internal application used by its sales team and accessed business contact details and summaries of customer communications.

The information includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, company affiliations, customer account histories, sales details, customer-relationship information, customer communications, and information about customers’ use of WorkOS products.

articles.title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
articles.context: The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly
articles.full_text:
Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent.

The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post.

The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly.

“Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said, adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign.

Fake installers used for real money

The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software, games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads.

The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software.

Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session.

The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates.

Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing.

A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization.

Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software

Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, and activation tools.

Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria.

For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear.

Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations.

Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said.

Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

articles.title: Canadian Extradited to US Over Cryptomining Hacks on University Supercomputers
articles.context: “These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials,” the DOJ explained
articles.full_text:
Two Canadian men face federal prosecution in New York after allegedly orchestrating a multi-year cyber incursion campaign that hijacked computing resources across American universities to secretly mine cryptocurrency.

A federal grand jury indicted Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario, on charges of conspiracy to obtain information and cause damage to protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional computer damage.

Roach was extradited from Canada on October 28, while extradition proceedings against Stubbings remain underway before Canadian courts.

According to the indictment, the intrusions spanned from June 2016 through December 2019, compromising systems at academic institutions in New York, Massachusetts, North Carolina, and Tennessee.

The two allegedly set up multi-country virtual private server infrastructure using fraudulent identities to manage the campaign. “These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials,” the DOJ explained.

The threat actors specifically singled out campuses maintaining supercomputers, using previously compromised machines as pivot points to conceal their origins.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Canadian court filings revealed that the hijacked university hardware was repurposed to mine a cryptocurrency called Electroneum.

“Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network,” prosecutors stated.

If convicted, the offenses carry a maximum statutory penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine on each count.

articles.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
articles.context: If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it
articles.full_text:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux. It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google.

Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38. It will become available on Google Play over the coming days.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look.

Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

CVE-2026-121229: Memory corruption in ANGLE, which could allow a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

ANGLE is Chrome’s graphics translation layer. A buffer overflow occurs when a program puts more data into an area of memory than it can hold, overwriting data in adjoining memory. An attacker can exploit this to make the vulnerable process run malicious code.

Chrome vulnerabilities that enable remote code execution outside the browser sandbox are particularly valuable to attackers because they can turn a visit to a malicious or compromised website into direct code running on the underlying operating system, often without requiring additional exploitation steps.

CVE-2026-121035: Use-after-free in Prerender.

Chrome’s Prerender component helps pages open faster by loading and preparing a page in the background before you navigate to it. If you then visit that page, Chrome can display the prepared version almost instantly instead of loading it from scratch.

This goes beyond just downloading content: Chrome also starts rendering the page and running its JavaScript.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

CVE-2026-121156: Buffer overflow in Dawn.

Dawn powers WebGPU in Chrome, allowing websites to use a device’s graphics processor for rendering and computational tasks. It checks and translates WebGPU instructions into commands that the device’s underlying graphics system can understand.

A buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to a block of memory than it can hold. This can cause a crash or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run code.

articles.title: CISA flags WordPress RCE flaw as actively exploited in attacks
articles.context: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress...
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned federal agencies that attackers have started exploiting a recently patched high-severity WordPress vulnerability in the wild.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, this high-severity WordPress Core flaw stems from a Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition and was reported by Picus Security researcher Umut Bayram.

Successful exploitation can let remote threat actors without privileges execute code on the server in high-complexity attacks due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades.

"A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window," the WordPress security team said on October 28 when it released WordPress 7.1.4 with patches to address this security issue. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately."

CISA confirmed CVE-2026-119977 active exploitation on Tuesday and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems by Friday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

"This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only US federal agencies, CISA urged all network defenders, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this vulnerability to protect their servers.

While CISA didn't provide more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-119977 in the wild, WordPress security firm Wordfence says in an advisory update over the weekend that it "blocked 13,095 attacks targeting this vulnerability in the past 24 hours."

In July, the WordPress security team also patched a critical vulnerability chain in WordPress Core (named wp2shell) that can be abused to deploy webshells and take over unpatched servers by exploiting a REST API batch-route confusion vulnerability (CVE-2026-63030) and an SQL injection flaw (CVE-2026-60137).

Public wp2shell exploits were released one day after the patches went live, and attackers began breaching unpatched servers a few days later to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins.

A Chinese-speaking threat actor also weaponized the wp2shell exploit chain in September to steal sensitive data from more than 18,500 records stored in backend databases belonging to small businesses and government organizations.

articles.title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
articles.context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
articles.full_text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

articles.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
articles.context: " Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs
articles.full_text:
Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0.

Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3.

All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523.

The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue.

The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions.

To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own.

XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host."

Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs.

Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports.

Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed.

Fixes and Restarts by Platform

These are the fixes published so far:

Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x.

Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024.

XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical.

Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19.

Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing.

XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

articles.title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
articles.context: With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat...
articles.full_text:
Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one.

One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel.

No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip.

The runtime is the application, not the pipe

The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model.

A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go.

Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing.

The inspection point is also a target

In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector.

None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure.

A millisecond verdict needs a memory

Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do.

Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist.

What real agent runtime looks like

Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block.

Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy.

Do not buy the end state

Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly.

What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime.

The first ninety days, in order

A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this.

Window

The work

How to know it is real

Weeks 1 to 2: get the number

Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic.

Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps.

Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations

Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first.

A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?"

Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path

Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults.

Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block.

The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance.

Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge.

Seven questions that sort vendors

Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists.

Ask

What a good answer looks like

Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO?

Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot.

For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain.

A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score.

Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents?

Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one.

When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain?

Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one.

What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict?

Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone.

What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised?

A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly.

How long until I see my real agent inventory?

Days. A quarter is a different product.

Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days.

Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.

The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days.

About Reco

Reco is the leader in Agent Security. The Reco Platform secures agents and their operating environments where applications, identities, permissions, and workflows intersect. It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. Security leaders at Fortune 500 enterprises choose Reco to bring order to agent proliferation and the chain reactions that follow. With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat detection together in one place. Learn more at reco.ai.
