articles.title: Poisoned cPGuard update hits thousands of web hosting servers
articles.context: Attackers now use AI tools to scan for weak points, read unfamiliar code and write custom tools in hours instead of weeks; the speed of this attack, from first probe to fake...
articles.full_text:
An attacker has compromised the update infrastructure of cPGuard, a security suite for Linux web hosting servers, and pushed out a malicious update to nearly 3,000 customer servers.

OPSShield, the company behind the security suite, also confirmed that the attacker made off with customer contact information and hashed passwords from the firm’s billing and licensing server.

How the attack unfolded

The attacker uploaded fake cPGuard updates – versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 – to OPSShield’s update storage on November 2, 2026, between 02:04 and 02:09, UTC.

For the next 70+ minutes, cPGuard agents installed the fake update on about 2,950 customer servers and ran it as root.

The fake update was a short script that collected sensitive files and sent them to a server controlled by the attacker. In an earlier report on the incident, OPSShield said that the latter was OPSSHIELD’s own licensing server, where the stolen info was stored under a compromised account for the attacker to retrieve later.

The collected and exfiltrated data includes password hashes, root SSH keys, the MySQL root password (where present), root shell history (which may include typed passwords and tokens), and cloud storage keys.

“[The script] also left two pieces behind: a hidden root shell at /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh with files in /var/tmp/.i93677/,” the company added.

According to OPSShield’s report, the day before the compromise of the update infrastructure the attacker probed OPSShield’s billing portal. They registered a customer account under a false identity, ordered a free cPGuard trial, and installed it to study how the agent talks to the licensing system.

An hour and a half later, the attacker sent crafted requests to the billing portal’s callback pages and, just minutes after that, gained the ability to run commands on the billing and licensing server, then started collecting client account records: the name, company, postal address, email, and bcrypt-hashed password of about 7,900 customers.

“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Attackers now use AI tools to scan for weak points, read unfamiliar code and write custom tools in hours instead of weeks; the speed of this attack, from first probe to fake update in about ten hours, reflects that,” OPSShield noted.

The attackers also made copies of three of the company’s cloud servers.

What OPSShield has done so far

OPSShield has yet to determine how the attacker got ahold of the access/update key that allowed them to upload the fake cPGuard updates. They also don’t know yet how the attacker managed to run commands on their billing and licensing server.

“Our logs do not record the exact request that gave them access, so we are reviewing that code, patched two possible entry points that we found and verify the related vendor components line by line. We have ruled out SSH, the control panel, FTP, API tokens, etc,” the company shared.

The investigation is still ongoing. In the meantime, OPSShield has cut off the attacker’s access to every system it knows was reached.

The company revoked the stolen update-storage key along with all cloud API tokens and access keys; removed the attacker’s SSH key, cloned servers and snapshots from its cloud account; and enabled stronger login protection.

For customers, it has released a clean update (v5.88.26) which removes the hidden root shell planted by the malicious update, and a follow-up update removes the i93677 scheduled task.

OPSShield has also replaced every SSH key and password across its own servers, reset all billing portal sessions, and rotated its billing system and reseller API keys. It is re-issuing all cPGuard license key pairs so that any copies held by the attacker become useless.

Finally, it is rebuilding billing, licensing and internal management servers from clean images with tighter PHP and web firewall settings and full request logging.

What should customers do?

First, they need to check whether a malicious cPGuard version has been installed on their servers. If it has, they need to:

Update to version 5.88.26 or later, confirm that the malicious scheduled task and root shell have been removed, and review their servers for any other signs of unauthorized changes: unfamiliar users, SSH keys, services and outbound connections, etc.

Reset passwords for root and all other password-enabled local Linux accounts from a trusted recovery environment.

Rotate affected database passwords, S3 access keys, DigitalOcean tokens, and password, API key or tokens recorded in root’s shell history, as well as any keys in /root/.s3cfg.

Replace SSH private keys stored under /root/.ssh and remove the corresponding old public keys from every system that trusts them.

Reset their OPSSHIELD billing portal password (as a precaution) and turn on two-factor login.

Because cPGuard checks for updates at intervals, not every customer server received the fake update. “If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update,” OPSShield said.

For customers it has contacted directly to confirm that the attacker logged in to their server by hand, the company recommends rebuilding the server from a clean backup taken before November 1.

OPSShield published a list of indicators of compromise that also include some found on their own servers, and offered to help customers go through the remediation process.

articles.title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
articles.context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
articles.full_text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

articles.title: Malicious cPGuard Updates Served in OpsShield Supply Chain Attack
articles.context: The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes
articles.full_text:
Indian IT security company OpsShield on Monday fell victim to a cyberattack that resulted in malicious versions of cPGuard being served to its customers.

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software, and cPGuard is its most notable product, designed for Linux web hosting servers.

According to the company’s incident notice, the attackers used compromised credentials to access its update distribution infrastructure (CDN) and distribute a malicious script via cPGuard’s update channel.

cPGuard versions 5.88.12–5.88.19 contained the malicious code. The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes.

The attackers first targeted the company’s billing and licensing server. They registered a customer account and ordered a free cPGuard trial to study its communication with the licensing system, then started sending crafted requests to the portal.

After obtaining command execution on the billing and licensing server, the hackers started collecting data and then uploaded a fake cPGuard update using a stolen access key, the company explains in an updated report.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The update was executed as root on the servers that polled OpsShield’s update infrastructure during the compromise window. At the same time, the attackers copied three of the company’s cloud servers.

The malicious script in the updates was designed to collect data and upload it to OpsShield’s licensing server under a compromised account. According to the company, the hackers retrieved 32 collected files from the data uploaded by the script, each from a different customer server.

Additionally, the script deployed a hidden root shell and certain files in the temp folder of customers’ servers.

OpsShield estimates that 2,950 servers executed the fake cPGuard updates, and that the attackers copied approximately 7,900 client account records containing names, company, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

All password hashes, root SSH keys, and MySQL root passwords, as well as shell history on the infected customer servers, should be considered compromised and rotated.

“If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update. You should still reset your billing portal password,” OpsShield says.

The company says it evicted the attackers from all servers they may have touched, reset secrets on its account, removed the attacker’s SSH key and cloned assets from its cloud account, and replaced all SSH keys and passwords across its servers.

Additionally, it started reissuing all cPGuard license private/public keys because the attackers compromised them, reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated associated API keys, and is rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers.

OpsShield also released cPGuard updates (version 5.88.25 and later) that remove the hidden root shell and the additional files left behind by the script, and published indicators of compromise (IoCs).

“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Our answer is to harden our own update and signing process first, and then to put what we learned here straight back into cPGuard for you,” the company notes.

articles.title: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist
articles.context: The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers
articles.full_text:
Binance says the hackers behind last week’s $6.34 billion theft reached its wallet signing systems after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers’ computers, one of them through a fake job interview.

The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3. Roughly $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said.

The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.

How the attack unfolded

According to Binance, the intrusion unfolded in stages and relied on fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company noted.

The campaign started in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while looking for a popular AI coding tool through a search engine.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance’s security team caught it, swapped out his device and reset the related credentials. Even so, the attackers had already gained insight into what he did and who he worked with on the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director. He was invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist.

During the first interview, the HR impostor shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to build rapport. The second took place over a chat app and ended with a request to download a coding “assignment” onto his work computer.

The assignment hid a malicious code repository that executed as soon as the engineer set it up. The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers.

“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time,” Binance said.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer’s system and a third wallet engineer’s system. The report does not explain how the AI tool was used.

The first engineer’s computer held a token that allowed container deployments. On October 29, the attackers signed into the third engineer’s computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and kicked off the attack with a malicious script.

Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets. The same service was used to abuse Ethereum’s EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under the attackers’ control partial execution rights over a hot wallet.

“However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure,” the company explained.

The hot wallet was secured with multi-party computation (MPC), which meant Binance had no single key it could use to cancel the delegation right away. The last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC, and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers’ credentials and tokens. It is engaging independent security firms to review the incident and is working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments.

The exchange also disclosed that it had detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year.

Other developments

North Korea has rejected the FBI’s attribution of the heist to its TraderTraitor hackers. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by state media.

[ Read: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea to Protest Binance Hack Claims ]

Binance has also completed a zero-knowledge proof for its October 31 reserves snapshot, which lets holders of 10 major tokens verify that their balances are backed at least 1:1. Co-CEO Richard Teng says 98% of the impacted tokens have now been replenished.

Teng also said on November 3 that withdrawals have broadly resumed. The exchange began reopening them in phases on November 1.

On the laundering front, Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, using automation but with no sign of AI agents making decisions. As of November 3, roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses. Separately, Chainalysis said an emergency pause at THORChain, triggered by an unrelated technical issue, had temporarily slowed the laundering.

articles.title: CVE-2026-58868: Critical Android Bug Could Let Attackers Run Remote Code
articles.context: Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17
articles.full_text:
Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17.

Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp. The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack.

“cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory. “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.”

Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin.

Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution.

Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction.

The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549.

MediaTek describes these six vulnerabilities as out-of-bounds write flaws caused by missing bounds checks, integer overflow or improper input validation. The company says it is not aware of any active exploitation in the wild.

The Qualcomm issue is tracked as CVE-2026-25285 and affects a closed-source component. Google does not provide further technical details in its bulletin.

One of the critical issues fixed by Google is CVE-2026-58882 (aka SMS of Death), which could allow attackers to remotely disable a phone by sending a specially crafted SMS message. The flaw affects decodeWapPdu, a function responsible for processing WAP Push messages, a type of content delivered through the SMS infrastructure.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning because exploitation reportedly requires no user interaction. An attacker only needs the victim’s phone number to send a malicious message. The message doesn’t appear in the SMS inbox, so the victim may have no indication of what caused the problem.

The issue also raises concerns about the reliability of mobile communications during an attack. According to a technical analysis published on October 29 by security researcher Mark B, a malformed WAP Push message can crash com.android.phone, the Android system component responsible for handling telephony functions. The crash can terminate ongoing calls, including emergency calls.

Tests on several Android phone models reportedly reproduced the crash consistently. The phone can also become stuck in a crash loop because Android retries processing the malicious message whenever the device starts. As a result, the device may continue crashing until the offending message is removed.

There is an important distinction, however. Google’s security bulletin and the CVE record identify the vulnerable decodeWapPdu function, but neither explicitly confirms that CVE-2026-58882 is the same issue described in the researcher’s SMS of Death report. The technical overlap is worth investigating, but the two reports shouldn’t be treated as definitively describing the same vulnerability without further confirmation.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-58868)

articles.title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
articles.context: Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

articles.title: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea as Pyongyang Protests Against US Claims on Binance Hack
articles.context: North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in...
articles.full_text:
North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance.

Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea.

Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang.

“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.

In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections.

Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser.

Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.

North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

articles.title: Meta Shares Top Muse Bug Bounty Findings as Payouts Reach $1.2 Million
articles.context: A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions
articles.full_text:
Meta has paid roughly $1.2 million in bug bounties for its Muse AI agent, including $300,000 for a pre-launch flaw that exposed data on internal test systems.

Muse is a personal AI agent that acts on a user’s behalf across their email, calendar, messaging and other accounts. Each user’s agent gets its own virtual machine.

The bug bounty program ran privately from April and went public at the agent’s September 8 launch, Meta’s David Singleton said in a blog post. Of the more than 630 reports received, 64 were valid.

The $300,000 reward was handed out four months before launch, while Muse was at an early internal testing stage. The researcher demonstrated access to conversations and tokens on pre-release VMs used by Meta staff to test the product.

“An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too,” Singleton explained.

Meta took the service offline, fixed the bug and stopped treating the local machine as trusted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A $90,000 bounty was paid for a report involving a malicious web page that, when Muse was asked to summarize it, mimicked status messages from the agent’s browsing tool. “It got the agent to execute some actions which should have been caught,” Singleton noted.

Meta has since added detection signals and changed how Muse treats tool output that looks suspicious. It says that, in testing, its classifiers now catch the attack and 100 variants.

Another $90,000 went to a report showing that specific formatting could slip one-time passcodes past Muse’s email redaction filters. Meta described it as one piece of an end-to-end attack.

A $50,000 reward went to an Android app flaw that let a malicious app pass a link to a privileged web view. “The link handler recognized a shared-page path without validating its host and loaded it,” Singleton wrote, allowing an attacker’s page to grab the web view’s credentials.

A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions.

Meta pays up to $300,000 per valid report, which it claims is several times more than the top rewards advertised by other leading AI developers. Prompt injection attacks affecting a single user can earn up to $130,000, while a fleetwide compromise can earn as much as $250,000.

articles.title: Russian Police Arrest 3 Suspected VasyGrek Hackers, Dismantle Criminal Infrastructure
articles.context: Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection
articles.full_text:
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure.

Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software."

In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware.

The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control.

"The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web."

The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value.

According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents.

Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities.

In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device.

The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors.

"The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said.

"The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis."

The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT.

While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf.

Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access.

"Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire.

"A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

articles.title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
articles.context: “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place
articles.full_text:
Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild.

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live.

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this.

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED.

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed.

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

This has been sort of ongoing over the last couple of weeks. Last week there was also some news that the U.S. military bases outside Europe were also affected by some of these hacks. The way these hacks work is that they typically connect to exposed control panels and then switch these refrigerators or freezers into defrost mode which ups the temperature in the 120-130 Fahrenheit or 50 Celsius range and of course leads to the spoilage of a lot of food. Well this is all bad of course and yes something that should be avoided. There wasn't much of an actionable part of this story. It wasn't quite clear how these systems got hacked. Lots of talk about weak default passwords in this case which is a typical IoT thing of course. Some people talked about fairly old exploits being used against these particular refrigerators and freezers. Well I have a little bit of another spin on this and that's why I want to tune our honeypots to actually look for what's actually going on there but in order to do so I need access to one of these refrigerators or thermostats in order to clone them. So if you know someone that has access to them please let me know and well maybe can get in touch and then get some data that helps us emulate these devices. And sticking here with an industrial control system and honeypot story there is evidence as presented by VulnCheck that the recently patched vulnerability in SIMATIC equipment that's running Node-RED which is essentially their admin API is being exploited now. So again this was patched in August but now is actively being exploited. The exploit here is I would say almost not so terribly spectacular in that they just run some standard Linux scripts and wget to download additional malware to the system to gain persistent remote access to these controllers. So definitely something to look out for and yes make sure your industrial control systems are patched and properly locked down. And in case you're running cPGuard, cPGuard is an endpoint protection anti-malware product that's often used sort of in shared hosting environments like if you're using cPanel I think it integrates quite well with that. Well OPSSHIELD, the company behind cPGuard, did announce that their update channel was compromised. So essentially the hacker was able to gain access to the server they stored their updates on, was able to add a malicious script and yes that script does off the usual credential exfiltration and the like. So definitely if you're running this product make sure that you didn't get caught by the bad update and OPSSHIELD has published a blog post with additional details indicators of compromise and some other assistance in how to detect and remove the malware. Well, security company Calif who is recently making a name for itself in the iOS exploit space has published a video that shows the successful exploitation of an iPhone 18. So essentially the just released version and reasonably recent even though not the latest iOS version running on the phone. This exploitation was successful even though Lockdown Mode was enabled in order to trigger the unspecified a virus. So if you consider yourself at risk enough in order to enable Lockdown Mode you probably shouldn't accept random AirDrop messages that pop up on your system and well better be sure who actually did send you that particular file. The compromise appeared to be pretty complete as in rooted they were able to essentially have some little animation running within the full screen of the iPhone on top of other applications. Well and that's it for today. So thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for subscribing. And I add a link to the Difference Maker Award vote to the show notes. So thanks and talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

articles.title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
articles.context: Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication
articles.full_text:
IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

articles.title: Hackers hijack cPGuard autoupdate to deploy backdoor, steal data
articles.context: ” cPGuard is a Linux web-server security suite offering malware scanning, firewalls, and attack protection
articles.full_text:
Attackers have compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script.

OpsShield, the cPGuard developer, published an alert earlier today saying the attack began on November 2 at 02:06 UTC and affected versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19.

The vendor says that it detected the compromise and stopped the malicious distribution within 12 hours after the attacker pushed the compromised cPGuard versions.

Although the company could not confirm, it said that some servers may have not received and run the malicious script due to update checks occurring at specific intervals.

The attacker leveraged legitimate credentials to gain initial access, although it remains unclear how they were obtained.

“On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OpsShield’s update distribution infrastructure (CDN),” OpsShield said.

“The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel.”

cPGuard is a Linux web-server security suite offering malware scanning, firewalls, and attack protection.

It is commonly used by hosting firms and server administrators alongside panels such as cPanel, DirectAdmin, and Plesk. Namecheap offers it on VPS and dedicated servers.

Users updating cPGuard during the compromise window received a script that targeted sensitive data on their machines:

Linux password hashes

Root database (MariaDB/MySQL) configuration

Root shell history

Root SSH authorization and known-hosts files

The stolen data was uploaded to OpsShield’s licensing server through a compromised account, which the attackers then used to retrieve it.

While OpsShield has not established what data was collected from each server, the company's evidence from the investigation shows that the threat actor retrieved 32 files from each customer.

System administrators are advised to update every cPGuard server to version 5.88.25 or later, reset passwords, and rotate database credentials, cloud secrets, and SSH keys.

OpsShield notes that updating to the latest cPGuard version removes the backdoor and staged files; however, stolen credentials must be invalidated as soon as possible.

The vendor also said that, as an extra precaution, it would release an update to remove previously installed OpsShield support-access keys.

BleepingComputer has contacted OpsShield to learn more about the attack, and a spokesperson told us that the incident has impacted nearly three thousand servers.

"We detected 2946 servers were affected and copied the information mentioned, and our billing system database was copied over as well. We are working on blocking all access, rebuilding the affected systems, and preparing for a public announcement at the earliest possible time," the company representative said.

The company also advises customers to follow the instructions and update cPGuard to version 5.88.25 or later, and reset or rotate credentials that may have been exposed on potentially compromised servers.

articles.title: Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit
Democracy without a safety net.
articles.context: Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028. Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day...
articles.full_text:
CISA scales back its Election Day role. Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet. The UK warns of AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure. German lawmakers face potential spyware threats. An AI-enabled infostealer ranks its victims. Ivanti patches more exploited zero-days. NATO launches cyber war games in Estonia. A Harvard breach exposes data linked to 850,000 email addresses. Our guest is Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, on protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Democracy is calling. And texting.

Today is Tuesday November 3rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA steps back from the midterms.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is taking a dramatically reduced role in today’s midterm elections, abandoning the coordinated national election security operation it has maintained since 2018, the New York Times reports.

Under the Trump administration, CISA has lost roughly a third of its workforce, scaled back intelligence sharing, and discontinued election-specific cybersecurity assessments. There will be no national election security war room or scheduled press briefings, leaving state and local officials with less federal support for responding to cyber threats, technical disruptions, and disinformation.

CISA insists it's fully prepared, pointing to regional teams available to assist election officials and hundreds of security-related engagements.

Former officials disagree, warning that the retreat leaves dangerous gaps in nationwide threat awareness and coordination.

States have significantly strengthened their election defenses since 2016, including expanded use of paper ballots. But experts say the federal government's ability to identify and communicate threats that cross state lines has substantially weakened.

Google dismantles a set-top-box botnet.

Google says it has dismantled a massive botnet built from more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes shipped with malware already installed.

The botnet, dubbed XCPE, allegedly originated with Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology, which Google says secretly turned customers' devices into residential proxies, renting their internet connections to third parties for activities including advertising fraud and other cybercrime.

Google severed ties with Videostrong and took legal action against the infrastructure controlling the botnet. Researchers say the disruption could also cut off access to more than 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware wasn't limited to streaming boxes. Researchers also found it on Android-based healthcare equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage.

Google says it has addressed the weakness that allowed the malware to activate during initial device setup. The case highlights a troubling supply-chain threat: devices compromised before customers even plug them in.

The UK’s NCSC warns of likely attacks on critical infrastructure.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028.

In its annual State of the Cyber Nation report, the NCSC also predicts Russia and China will routinely incorporate AI into their cyber operations.

Agency chief Richard Horne says the danger isn't necessarily new attack techniques, but AI's ability to discover and exploit existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.

He criticized organizations for running outdated systems, postponing security upgrades, and failing to monitor their networks.

The British government is responding with new investments in cyber defenses, AI security research, and vulnerability detection.

Horne warned that organizations face a choice: invest in resilience now, or risk serious disruptions to essential services later.

Warnings from Apple prompt German authorities to highlight potential spyware.

German authorities are warning lawmakers and prominent public figures about possible spyware attacks following a new round of threat notifications from Apple.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity agency, the BSI, confirmed that members of parliament and other notable individuals received alerts indicating they may have been targeted by sophisticated surveillance software.

Apple sent similar warnings to users in 99 countries. The company doesn't identify suspected attackers or confirm whether targeted devices were successfully compromised.

The spyware involved in these campaigns can potentially steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, sometimes exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction from victims.

German officials say they're taking the warnings seriously and advise recipients to assume their devices may be compromised.

It's unclear who's responsible for the latest campaign, or whether any German officials were successfully hacked.

A new infostealer uses AI to identify the most valuable victims.

Researchers at Cisco Talos have uncovered a new infostealer that uses artificial intelligence to analyze stolen data and identify the most valuable victims.

Dubbed Volta-Autodoxer, the malware collects passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, payment information, and cryptocurrency credentials. It also targets active sessions on platforms including Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox.

But Volta goes beyond simply stealing data. It conducts additional searches through victims' accounts, gathering information about their locations, habits, and purchases to build detailed personal profiles.

The malware then submits that information to commercial AI models, asking them to act as intelligence analysts and produce structured assessments that help attackers prioritize targets.

Volta defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallback options including Moonshot AI's Kimi and Google's Gemini.

Researchers haven't confirmed the malware has been deployed in the wild, but its design demonstrates how AI could make traditional credential theft more targeted and efficient.

Ivanti patches additional Connect Secure zero-days.

Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks since early October. Attackers chained a privilege escalation flaw and a file upload vulnerability with an authentication bypass bug patched last month, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution. Researchers at Volexity say the attackers avoided deploying malware, instead repeatedly exploiting devices to execute commands and tampering with logs to hide their activity. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch the authentication bypass vulnerability by Friday. More than 5,000 Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet.

NATO’s Crossed Swords cyber exercise kicks off in Estonia.

NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence has launched Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, bringing together more than 250 participants from over 40 countries.

The exercise focuses on coordinating offensive and defensive cyber operations with conventional military and special operations missions, where timing can be critical down to the minute.

This year's exercise introduces a dedicated AI agent track, allowing participants to build, deploy, and work alongside autonomous systems while maintaining human oversight. The training environment also incorporates OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense technology.

Military cyber operators, threat hunters, forensic specialists, and command staff are participating, alongside civilian partners helping integrate critical infrastructure protection into operational planning.

Crossed Swords has grown significantly since its beginnings in 2014, reflecting the increasing importance of coordinating cyber capabilities with traditional military operations.

A data breach at Harvard exposes more than 850,000 email addresses.

A data breach at Harvard University exposed personal information associated with more than 850,000 email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Attackers compromised Harvard's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025, stealing names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, dates of birth, donation details, and other biographical information.

Harvard says the affected systems did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or payment card information.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and published a 1.1-gigabyte archive of stolen data in February after Harvard reportedly refused to pay a ransom. Harvard has not publicly attributed the attack.

The incident was part of a broader series of university breaches, with Princeton and the University of Pennsylvania also reporting compromises involving donor information in November 2025.

Stick with us after the break, we are joined by Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, is talking about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. And….

Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, and I recently sat down to talk about protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Here is our conversation.

If you enjoyed this conversation, be sure to check out the full interview in the show notes.

Democracy is calling. And texting.

As Americans head to the polls for today's midterm elections, WIRED reporter Dhruv Mehrotra has a cautionary tale about the machinery behind political fundraising.

Since 2022, he's received more than 1,700 fundraising texts intended for a relative named John, whose modest donations to Democrats somehow got associated with Mehrotra's phone number.

Mehrotra replied STOP 49 times. The messages kept coming.

Investigating the deluge, he traced nearly half this year's messages to tracking codes apparently associated with Sterling Data Company, which uses AI and personal information to identify potential donors.

Sterling's CEO acknowledged that campaigns can rent the same contact records and that database mistakes happen, but didn't confirm responsibility.

His advice was to stop responding entirely.

So, on Election Day, a reminder that while Americans get one vote apiece, political fundraising texts apparently come with no such limits.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: WorkOS says attacker used ARTEX AI to breach internal sales app
articles.context: According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts
articles.full_text:
Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications.

According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected.

WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications.

According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify.

“On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert.

Data accessed by the attacker includes:

Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems)

Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health)

Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations)

Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship)

After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools.

The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact.

The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information.

ARTEX AI likely powering the attack

WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.

Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details, saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year.

Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security.

ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks, but several forks of its code are still available.

More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations.

Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September.

Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor.

The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes.

articles.title: Warning: Phishing Operations Are Impersonating Prediction Markets
articles.context: ” Recorded Future warns that attackers are now able to exploit current trends faster than ever before, as AI supercharges their development
articles.full_text:
Fraudsters are exploiting the increased public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi, according to researchers at Recorded Future. Criminal groups known as “traffers” are providing fellow crooks with “websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance” to target users of prediction markets.

“This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims,” Recorded Future says. “The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.”

The attackers are using AI tools to accelerate their operations by “reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events.” Recorded Future warns that attackers are now able to exploit current trends faster than ever before, as AI supercharges their development.

“The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities,” the researchers write. “Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.”

Recorded Future has the story: https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/prediction-markets-traffer-teams
