In this article

Fashion retailer Revolve said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen

Data at risk includes card numbers and expiration dates, customer names and addresses

Affected customers should watch their statements and consider asking issuers for new cards

Online fashion retailer Revolve Group said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen. In its customer notification letter filed with the Massachusetts Attorney General, Revolve told recipients the incident involved their names, addresses, and payment card details.

What was stolen?

The at-risk data includes customer names and contact information, payment card numbers, and card expiration dates. The breach only affected customers who had saved their payment card as a payment method in their Revolve account.

A filing on the Texas attorney general data breach website lists 127,200 affected Texans, but not a nationwide total. We found the figure of 1,515,073 in data returned by the site when searching for Revolve. That data labels it as the total number of people affected, but the figure isn’t displayed on the public listing. Other sites have repeated it, though they appear to rely on the same Texas record. The SEC filing did not give a number of affected people, and Revolve has not confirmed the total.

Revolve’s SEC filing does not mention card verification value (CVV) numbers. These three-digit security codes printed on the back of payment cards (four digits on the front for American Express cards) are an extra layer of security for card-not-present transactions.

It is also unclear whether the card numbers were fully visible or masked, or whether Revolve or a third-party payment processor held them.

Even without a CVV, card numbers and expiration dates may be enough to make purchases at some online stores. And scammers who know your real card details and contact information may be able to send more convincing phishing messages to trick you into revealing your CVV.

How did they get the data?

Revolve has not said how the attackers accessed the saved payment data. In its SEC filing, Revolve said it believes an unauthorized actor may have obtained the data “through automated means.” Records on the Texas attorney general’s site indicate that the incident happened on September 11 and was discovered on September 29.

No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the theft.

What Revolve customers can do now

Revolve said it has taken extra security measures following the breach, although didn’t say what those are.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

If you have saved payment information in your Revolve account, your details may have been among those stolen. Fraud can often begin within days of a breach. If you’re concerned about your card details being exposed:

Read your statements line by line to identify even small charges that you don’t recognize. Criminals will often make a small charge using stolen card details to see if the card works.

Look for unfamiliar merchant names on your statement.

Report unauthorized charges to the card issuer immediately.

Consider removing saved cards from shopping accounts. You could use a password manager instead, some of which will store autofill data for payment cards.

Ask your card issuer to cancel your card and reissue with a new number so that the old number becomes unusable.

Also, don’t immediately trust calls, texts, or emails about the incident. Scammers can use stolen information to make themselves sound convincing. If someone claims to be calling from your card issuer, call the number printed on your card to check.

If you’re unsure about a message or link, check it with Malwarebytes Scam Guard.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

articles.title: Red Hat Patches 9.8-Rated Linux TCP RCE Flaw While Ubuntu Releases Fixes for Testing
articles.context: Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its...
articles.full_text:
Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its three newest long-term-support releases remain in its opt-in testing channel with no date for a regular update.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, can be reached by a remote, unauthenticated attacker and can lead to remote code execution, Red Hat and Canonical said.

The Linux kernel's own CVE team rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Red Hat, which initially rated it Moderate at 5.9, has raised its score to 9.8 and now calls it Critical. The bug has been present since Linux 4.4, and the upstream fix landed in October.

What the Flaw Is

When a server accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, the kernel passes IP options from the incoming request to the new socket without copying them. If the client retransmits its connection request while another processor still reads those options, the kernel can read memory it has already freed.

An attacker triggers the race by sending connection requests that carry IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options to any listening TCP port. No login is needed. IPv6 is not affected on the main path.

Red Hat shipped RHSA-2026:93414 (RHEL 8), RHSA-2026:93412 (RHEL 9), and RHSA-2026:93413 (RHEL 10) on November 1. A reboot is needed after installing the update.

RHEL Version

Fixed Kernel

Errata

8.10

4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10

RHSA-2026:93414

9.8

5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8

RHSA-2026:93412

10.2

6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2

RHSA-2026:93413

Canonical said on November 2 that fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 26.04 LTS are in its -proposed pocket, an opt-in testing channel. Packages there do not install automatically.

Canonical tests kernel updates across more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before releasing them to the regular update channel, and no release date has been given.

Ubuntu Release

-proposed Kernel

Status

Administrators who need the fix before it reaches the regular channel can enable -proposed and install the kernel update by running:

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade sudo reboot

To check whether a system is running a fixed kernel, compare the output of uname -r against the versions in the tables above.

Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 have no fix yet. Older releases require Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro.

Cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernel variants for Ubuntu are listed as work in progress on the Ubuntu CVE page with target versions, but Canonical's blog post covers only the generic kernel.

Interim Mitigation

Red Hat published an nftables rule on October 30 that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. The rule blocks the known trigger for the race but cannot fully prevent exploitation and may break workloads that depend on IPv4 options, Red Hat said.

table inet cve_2026_98432 { chain input { type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept; ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop } }

The filter applies only to the host where it is loaded. Traffic between containers on the same host can bypass it, a member of the CIQ kernel team noted on the oss-security mailing list.

Several sources have recommended disabling Multipath TCP (MPTCP) as a workaround. The flaw is in the IPv4 TCP path, not in MPTCP, and that advice alone is not enough, Canonical said. "The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation."

Exploitation Status

No vendor, CERT, or the kernel CVE team has reported attacks using this flaw. It was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's October 30 release.

Anthropic said on October 27 that an unreleased, internal Claude research model wrote a remote root exploit for the flaw that works against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, with no credentials and no user interaction. In its proof of concept, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes and reaching a root shell took another 5 minutes. Anthropic has not published the exploit code.

Proof-only code that triggers the race and detects the kernel echoing freed memory in a SYN-ACK has appeared on GitHub. It does not implement code execution.

Amazon Linux scored the flaw 8.1 and rated it Important, saying the main outcome is a crash with possible memory corruption. Debian, Oracle Linux, and SUSE shipped fixes in October. Amazon Linux was fixed across all packages between October 24 and 30.

articles.title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
articles.context: Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will...
articles.full_text:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.

Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.

Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.

Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.

Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:

legacy metrics

compliance pressure, and

fragmented ownership

all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.

The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.

The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.

The four elements, and the question each one answers

Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.

Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:

An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.

The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.

Element 1: Threat Intelligence

Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.

The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.

Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality

An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.

This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.

Element 3: Exploitability Modeling

Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.

Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.

Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.

Element 4: Security Control Validation

This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.

An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.

Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.

How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop

The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.

Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.

Here’s how the platform maps to each element.

Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.

Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.

Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.

Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.

What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift

If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.

Here’s what our customers are reporting.

Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.

Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.

Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.

One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.

A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.

Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.

Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.

Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.

The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.

Ready to see validated prioritization in practice? Request a demo and watch one of your own CVEs go from a new scanner finding to the right response backed by evidence.

Note: This article was written by Sila Ozeren Hacioglu, Security Research Engineer at Picus Security.

articles.title: Armed with AI, hackers target endpoint security blind spots, raising stakes for CISOs
articles.context: A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps...
articles.full_text:
A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them.

CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine.

At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm.

ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to carry out intrusion tasks under human direction. CrowdStrike found that VAPOR PANDA used the framework to pursue attacks against several organizations simultaneously, with operators intervening at key decision points.

The findings follow an October 21 report from Microsoft detailing a separate campaign involving ARTEX. Microsoft said another China-linked group, Storm-0940, used the framework to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours in some cases. The campaign included the abuse of compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access customer environments.

Changing economics of cyberattacks

The use of AI in cyberattacks is changing the economics of state-sponsored espionage by allowing smaller teams to pursue targets without a corresponding increase in personnel, according to Akshat Tyagi, associate practice leader at HFS Research.

“The techniques are familiar, but the ability to run them in parallel is not,” Tyagi said.

Jonathan Ong, senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia, said AI can substantially reduce the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, even as more sophisticated exploitation continues to require technical expertise.

The attacks documented by CrowdStrike exploited weaknesses that security teams have encountered for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated. At a US pharmaceutical company, an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity (XXE) vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with extensive administrative permissions.

Security gaps become a bigger target

Growing concerns about the security risks of AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defensive measures, Ong said. Tyagi added that CISOs should ensure that security monitoring extends across their environments rather than assuming existing deployments provide complete coverage.

Amit Kumar Jena, development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations should continuously measure endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, and generate alerts when machines stop reporting to security monitoring systems.

He also recommended enforcing SAML signature validation and restricting cloud access privileges. Security teams should watch for closely sequenced authentication attempts and commands that could indicate automated malicious activity, he said.

Tyagi also recommended regularly rotating credentials and monitoring unusual account activity, warning that automated attacks leave defenders less time to investigate suspicious behavior.Keith Prabhu, CEO of Confidis, said gaps between security systems could give attackers opportunities to move through enterprise environments. He recommended improving asset visibility and detecting suspicious activity across systems rather than relying on individual security controls.

Prospect of Cobalt Strike-style adoption

The use of ARTEX by different threat groups also points to the wider availability of tools capable of automating cyberattacks.

CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model. Although the framework’s developer withdrew the original open-source project in October following reports of its misuse, copies and modified versions remain available.

Tyagi expects such tools to become more widely adopted by financially motivated cybercriminals over the next 12 months.

There is already evidence of broader adoption. In research published in October, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said they had observed financially motivated attackers using ARTEX during data-theft extortion operations, alongside its use by suspected state-linked groups.

“AI pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX have the potential to become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era,” said Ong.

Cobalt Strike, a commercial penetration-testing tool, has been widely abused by cybercriminals and state-sponsored groups.

As attackers automate more of their operations, security teams may need to rely more heavily on automated detection. Tyagi said this would allow analysts to spend less time manually reviewing alerts and concentrate on decisions requiring human judgment.

Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response rather than simply investing in additional AI tools or expanding security teams. Such preparations could help security teams respond to intrusions in which automated agents explore multiple attack paths before defenders have completed their initial investigation.

Although ARTEX can automate much of an intrusion, the observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions.

“We are not at fully autonomous attacks yet,” Tyagi said.

The continuing role of human operators does not diminish the speed of the attacks. For security teams, the challenge is detecting suspicious activity early enough to prevent automated intrusion attempts from developing into broader compromises.

articles.title: LLMJacking is Costing Some Businesses Up to $1m, Warns Google
articles.context: Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs)
articles.full_text:
Google has warned of a growing enterprise threat to AI infrastructure from cybercriminals selling access to large language models (LLMs).

The tech giant’s Mandiant business said it had responded to multiple incidents so far this year across financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors in which “LLMJacking” techniques were discovered.

“Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” it warned.

“Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1m before access was revoked.”

Read more on LLMJacking: LLMjacking and Open-Source Tool Abuse Surge in 2024 Cloud Attacks.

The technique itself is not new, but the ecosystem for LLMJacking appears to be maturing.

Threat actors bypass front-end chatbots to target backend model resources, usually via LLM API keys or exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens and active session tokens.

From this initial foothold, the threat actors escalate privileges and carry out internal reconnaissance to identify targets and more cloud credentials.

As well as abusing and escalating permissions this way, they might also target vulnerabilities in LLM routing software to escalate privileges, the report explained.

“The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming and GPU hardware provisioning,” it added.

A Long-Term Money Spinner

Google has already seen “a diverse set” of financially motivated cybercrime clusters LLMJacking across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. It has also started to notice a “division of labor” between threat actors that focus on initial access and those monetizing downstream infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers.”

These routing gateways “proxy, aggregate and resell” access to LLMs for criminal customers.

The work is so lucrative that Google expects cybercriminals will prioritize LLMJacking over cryptojacking going forward.

“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” it concluded.

“This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.”

articles.title: Inside XCPE, the botnet that turned 1.3M set-top boxes into proxy servers
articles.context: The result of the investigation into the malware operation is the striking part: Videostrong Technology Co
articles.full_text:
Google dismantled a 1.3 million-device botnet allegedly built by Android TV box maker Videostrong to enable ad fraud and proxy abuse.

Google and its partners dismantled a backdoor called XCPE that had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet. The result of the investigation into the malware operation is the striking part: Videostrong Technology Co., an Android device maker, built and ran the botnet for money.

Google says it is highly confident that Videostrong deliberately created, spread and operated the backdoor. The company reportedly sold access to criminal groups and installed their malware on infected devices. The malware was used for ad fraud, secretly added devices to residential proxy networks and installed other malicious software.

Google says this was not the work of a rogue employee or a simple coding mistake. The backdoor was found in many device models and brands over several years. Its operation involved dedicated infrastructure and regularly changing configurations.

“We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).” Google states. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. “

Google has now cut all ties with Videostrong. The company is banned from making devices with pre-installed Google apps. The ban also covers any future subsidiaries or business partners, and Videostrong can no longer supply software to other certified device makers.

Videostrong got around Google’s compatibility and security tests with code obfuscation. The malicious code loaded after a device’s first boot, which the tests didn’t catch. Google has changed its review process and is improving how it checks firmware on certified Android TV devices.

Google also took legal action against the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet, and against the control domains of over a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Those affiliates spread their modules through other channels too, so Google expects the takedown to cut access to at least 10 million more compromised devices. Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked on the operation.

The malware has three stages. The primary backdoor, x.cpe (called com.oemservice in some builds), is preloaded in the firmware and runs with system privileges. If a user uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition at the next reboot. It handles communication with the control server and passes work to a loader called com.abc.nexus, which carries its own anti-analysis tricks and sets up the money-making modules.

These modules are supplied by other criminals working as affiliates. They can arrive as programs built into the backdoor, software packages added to its loader, or extra apps downloaded later. Many turn the device into a residential proxy, allowing other people to use the victim’s home internet connection to hide their online activity. Others commit ad fraud or install additional backdoors. In other words, a set-top box becomes a proxy server without its owner’s knowledge.

The backdoor uses two steps to control infected devices. First, the box sends an HTTP request to download settings, location data and network information. It then maintains a live connection through MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol, to receive commands from the operators. Google found that all analyzed samples used the same MQTT server to communicate with infected devices.

“Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker.” continues the report. “A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites.”

Through this connection, attackers could secretly install apps, run commands and scripts, take screenshots, record keystrokes and map the victim’s network. They could also disable Google Play Protect’s app verification to install software without the user’s knowledge. Google observed operators taking screenshots, recording keystrokes, collecting account and device information, stealing app lists and system logs, and opening remote command-line sessions. However, most of their activity involved installing, removing and managing malware modules.

The malicious files came from several sources. The attackers mainly used GitHub releases hosted on their own accounts, the Filemail file-sharing service and two servers under their control. Network traffic analysis also suggests that the operators managed the command infrastructure through remote interfaces and an EMQX web console, connecting from IP addresses outside the infected device network.

Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but Google also found telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage. One device can run several modules at once, up to three residential proxy kits. That shows Videostrong wants to squeeze every infected device as hard as it can. The proxy and bandwidth-sharing kits named in the report include Linkfog, AppSalt, GaGaNode, BWM, Traffmonetizer, EarnFM and NetNut.

Some of those kits enroll devices without asking. AppSalt’s SDK, owned by Honeygain, calls an opt-in function without showing any consent screen, and it stops running if the app came from the official Google Play Store. Ad-fraud modules such as Fission and HiddenView fire off fake ad impressions in the background, and HiddenView also uses hidden browser windows to simulate clicks and scrolling.

The configuration shows a well-run operation. MQTT messages carry resource limits for each module, download links per processor type, and priority weights. Devices are assigned to one of six timezone-based pools on ott.szbboys[.]com. Devices report their bandwidth use and alarms back, so the modules stay within set limits.

Google says the underlying market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings and residential proxy providers work as an interconnected supply chain, and when one part gets disrupted they quickly switch to new loaders or rival kits. Lasting change, it says, needs accountability across hardware makers, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology sector.

Google wants retailers and distributors to require independent security audits from device manufacturers and to delist any implicated in supply-chain abuse. It says proxy providers’ claims of ethical sourcing need transparent, auditable proof of user consent, and that in its analysis these providers asked for consent only when platform policy forced them to. Silent opt-in remains the most common way devices become exit nodes.

For consumers, Google advises caution with apps that pay you for “unused bandwidth” or “sharing your internet”, which are a main way illicit proxy networks grow. Stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and keep Google Play Protect on. Buy connected devices like set-top boxes only from reputable manufacturers, and check the partner list on Google’s Android TV website. Google also urges mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to keep sharing intelligence.

“A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users.” concludes the report. “Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

articles.title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
articles.context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
articles.full_text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

articles.title: 67% of security leaders say their teams struggle to meet business needs
articles.context: AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams
articles.full_text:
AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams.

Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps.

In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise, OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass.

Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources.

More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management.

“AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.”

Hiring challenges

CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives.

Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants.

Accessing the cost of the skills gap

Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). This estimated cost includes hiring and outsourcing expenses, lost revenue, abandoned projects, and poorly maintained technology.

A quarter of cybersecurity professionals say their organization has experienced security incidents or vulnerabilities over the past 12 months due to skills gaps. Almost half (43%) admitted that skills gaps are a common reason for abandoning cybersecurity projects.

The findings highlight the pressure on security teams as AI adoption increases demand for cybersecurity expertise, Pluralsight concludes.

AI imperative exacerbating skills problem

Europe is short of more than 300,000 cybersecurity professionals, and companies are now struggling to find qualified candidates or applicants, according to research by the AI Workforce Consortium.

Cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills have doubled year over year across G7 countries. Senior cybersecurity roles requiring AI skills are up 65% year-on-year, compared with 5.9% for junior roles.

The research by the AI Workforce Consortium — an industry group backed by Cisco, Google, Microsoft, IBM, SAP, and others — also points to a growing need for practical experience and human skills.

You might not notice right away, but there’s something new on your computer, a new app or toolbar in your browser, or maybe your homepage changed to something like a search engine you never heard of, and your computer seems to be doing something every now and then that just doesn't make sense. Like, it’s a tad slower or the fans are suddenly louder, but you're just not exactly sure why. Most of the time it’s relatively harmless. It’s some kind of junkware. Some company paid a few cents to bundle their stuff into your download, hoping that you wouldn't remove the software and you would start using their software. Well, that in itself isn't illegal even if it can be abused, kinda like a knife isn't illegal. We need it to make food with. Someone waving it around on the street is suddenly a big threat. It’ll take screenshots, record what apps are opened and in focus, and track the locations of devices. But when a company spies on its own computers, it typically makes it very clear; there is a monitoring system on your computer, or they make the employees sign a document which says ‘You may be monitored while you're here at work’, which is what makes it legal. That person being spied on knows and consents to it. So, on the surface, both making and using software like this can be perfectly legal. But Blackshades wasn't marketing this to businesses. They were specifically marketing their product to people they knew would abuse it. So, their whole website, which was saying this is used to track your kids, that was really a lie, a ruse to make it look legal and look perfectly fine. To the courts, who look at things through the lens of the law, intent matters a lot. If you know you're selling to people who will use it to commit crimes with, then yeah, it’s illegal to sell that. When it comes to the customers, if they were putting it on people’s computers without their consent and spying on someone without them knowing, then that’s illegal, too. That’s unauthorized access to a computer, privacy violations, identity theft, intercepting communications, and extortion. So yeah, this can be illegal to use as well, both illegal to make and illegal to use. But again, it all comes down to intent of whether or not this is legal versus illegal. If these people who use it and make it are going to get in trouble over this, then the courts are gonna have to prove that intent was there to sell it to criminals or to spy on people without their permission. Blackshades had a feature called the Spreader. Once it was on your computer, the attacker could use your social media accounts and chat apps to try to spread it to your friends’ computers, too. They could even use Blackshades for ransomware, locking up their targets’ files and demanding payments to unscramble them. [Music] I can't imagine this feature being used for any legitimate purpose. So, the fact that this had a ransomware feature squarely puts it in the malicious software territory, if you're asking me, making it clearly illegal. But Blackshades would make their users click on a button stating that the user is responsible for whatever the action resulted in, and warning them to be careful when using this feature. It also said this was made for educational purposes only. Yeah, okay, sure. But there was one problem for Blackshades users. You couldn't just wave a wand at someone and infect their computer with Blackshades, and no one in their right mind would install this to give some random attacker full access to their computer. So, to get Blackshades on a victim’s machine, they had to trick the victim into installing it themselves, to make them think they're installing something else, and that’s tricky because you basically have to exploit another human to get it installed, which brings us into the world of social engineering, the art of tricking people into doing things they don't actually want to do. There are a 1001 ways that we can all be tricked into installing things that we don't actually want. Humans are a weak link when it comes to computer security. You might have seen some of them, obvious links; click here for a free iPhone, and you're like, yeah, nah, I’m not doing that. But sometimes it’s not so obvious. Since Blackshades can spread from a friend’s computer to yours using malicious links, it can look like it’s coming from someone you trust. When I was a teenager I downloaded a lot of shady apps and games from shady parts of the internet, and I would constantly be dealing with infections. I didn't care because I really wanted to play the game, but eventually the infection would get so bad that I couldn't use my computer at all. Pop-ups would just constantly be showing up. The CPU would crawl to a standstill. I must have been hit with malware hundreds of times when I was a teenager. But that’s what got me good at fixing computers, learning how to find malware and remove it and cleaning up my computer. I mean, a lot, a lot. Anyway, sometimes devices you buy in the store actually come with malware on them. There was a story I read once where a Chinese laptop maker was selling their laptops on Amazon that came with Windows 11. Well, the thing was the Chinese seller was trying to cut costs and didn't want to pay for Windows 11 license keys for every computer, so they found a pirated version of Windows, installed that, and shipped it with their laptops. Little did they know, the pirated version contained malware and was draining people’s crypto wallets and robbing their Steam accounts. So, you need to be really careful with what apps you install and where you get them from, because having one bad app on your computer can ruin you. But even apps you vet thoroughly can turn rogue. I’ve seen some popular browser extensions get purchased by someone who had malicious intent, and then they put spyware on people’s browsers without them knowing. Or maybe someone makes a simple mobile app that’s clean and fine and free, even. But as it grows in popularity, there’s always someone that asks them, hey, I’ll give you a few thousand dollars if you can put this widget in your app. Don't worry, it’s just an advertising pixel. If someone’s making free software and suddenly get offered a few thousand dollars to add a simple advertising pixel, they might say yes. Now suddenly that app, which was clean and good, now has some malicious code in it tracking what you're doing on your phone. Stuff can sneak into our devices from all kinds of directions. It’s a war out there. [Music] Then there’s USB sticks. So, if someone swings by your computer, pops a USB stick in the slot, it may auto-infect that machine. Then you could pull the USB stick out, and nobody knows what happened. Back in the days of Windows XP and Vista, this feature was on by default in Windows. Nowadays the Autorun feature is not on by default, thank goodness, but this was a popular way people would infect computers with Blackshades, since it was just dead simple to do. Just stick the USB stick in for a few seconds and pull it out, and you're done. I think the most popular way people were getting victims to install this is to send them a message saying, ‘Oh my god, is this you? How embarrassing!’ with a link to a photo or a video. Except it wasn't a photo or video. It’d look like it, but when you tried to open it, it was really a program that would install Blackshades. Another one, which I’ve actually seen in my own inbox, was something like, ‘We’ve tried to deliver a package to you three times now. We were unsuccessful. We're gonna send it back to the shipper unless you click here.’ I always have this knee-jerk reaction like, oh man, I don't want my package returned.
