I mean, you could see it all; people’s private messages, social media accounts, Google searches. It was spooky. [Music] There was this guy named Stefan Rigo from Leeds in the UK who saw what Blackshades could do, and he became interested. He was thirty-four years old. He bought it for forty bucks using his ex-girlfriend’s credit card, and then he infected his ex-girlfriend with this malware. Maybe he sent her a phishing chat message or plugged in a USB stick when he visited her house one day and she left the room or something. But when he was at his computer, he could see when her computer was online. Her computer had a camera on it, and from the dark comfort of his own house, he turned on her camera and watched her in her bedroom. He found it incredibly addicting. She had no idea he was watching her. Usually there’s a little light that comes on when your camera is on, right? Well, Blackshades made sure that light didn't come on. Watching her in her bedroom gave him a rush. He liked it. He had some other lady friends and wondered what they were doing, too. So, he started infecting more and more women that he knew with Blackshades. He could hear conversations people were having. He watched them get undressed. Of course, he’s taking screenshots of them changing and saving the recordings. He liked that kind of stuff the most. Stefan got seriously addicted to watching what women do in the privacy of their own homes. Every day he would open up his Blackshades dashboard and look to see what computers he infected were online, and then he’d double-click on one and sit there, watching what they were doing. Not only was he watching through the cameras, but when they'd use their computers, he’d watch what they were doing on it, too. He could see their passwords, their private messages with people, their photos, what they bought online, their online banking activity, everything they did on that computer. The thing that made it addicting to him was that he never knew when something interesting would happen or what would happen. To him it was like a wave of excitement when he actually saw someone changing in front of a camera. That would make it all worth the time to him. He started out by putting it on the computers of women he knew, but then he learned how to spread it from those computers to their friends’ computers, and now he was infecting other women that he didn't even know, and he didn't stop there. He was trying to infect other women, too, like people working in coffee shops or at a library. It was real easy for him just to put in a USB drive and try to infect someone’s laptop. He was seriously addicted to this, and over time he got over a dozen people infected with Blackshades. With that, there was always someone online doing something interesting that he liked watching. There’s a whole voyeurism fetish out there on the internet. People will secretly film women getting undressed and posting it online. Or maybe they’ll hold a camera under some lady’s skirt and take a photo of that and share it. Well, this voyeurism community was hearing about what you could do with Blackshades, and they were into it. The Blackshades RAT had incredible potential for secretly getting videos of women undressing or having sex. Soon the biggest user base of Blackshades were guys spying on girls to see them naked, and in most cases the guys were spying on the girls they knew, keeping tabs on exes, getting dirt on someone they're jealous of, or just spying on women because they found it fascinating. Over time, thousands of Blackshades users were using this tool to spy on women. It really helped Blackshades grow in popularity. But they weren't the only people interested in Blackshades. It was also used to target activists. In 2012, Syria was in the middle of a civil war. People were really upset with the president of Syria, Bashar al-Assad, for using chemical weapons on his own civilians. The country ignited in large-scale protest and pro-democracy rallies as part of the Arab Spring. In the midst of this, researchers at the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Citizen Lab noticed that Syrian activists were getting hit with malware. They would get a link from a Skype account from someone they knew and trusted without realizing that account was compromised. One message read, ‘There’s a person who hates you, and he keeps talking about you. Here's a screenshot of the conversation.’ There was a link to the malicious file, and when they’d click it, Blackshades would install itself on their device. [Music] The Syrian government used Blackshades to spy on opposition activists and tried to suppress them by having total control of their computers. They could do things like get information on the next rally or delete social media accounts or look through photos and documents. Before Blackshades there was another tool called DarkComet. It was developed back in 2008 by a French programmer named Jean-Pierre Lesueur, also known as DarkCoderSc. He discontinued the program partially due to its use in the Syrian civil war and possibly due to the fear of him being arrested. Like Blackshades, DarkComet was used to spy on victims through key-logging, screen captures, and by stealing their passwords. To me, this is really fascinating because at the time, a lot of activists within the hacker group Anonymous were very active in the Arab Spring trying to help the protesters from afar by knocking the government offline and doing stuff like that, and it’s wild that the very people who wanted to assist the protesters are also the ones who are accidentally assisting the government to suppress the protesters, because tools are typically neutral and can be used by either side. When you make something so effective, people will notice it on both sides and use it for their own agenda. I don't have any knowledge of whether the creators of DarkComet or Blackshades were members of Anonymous, and it wouldn't surprise me if they were, because, well, at least the maker of DarkComet said some stuff online that looked a lot like what the Anonymous activists were saying about Syria at the time. So, this was yet another thing this malware was being used for. A $40 piece of software marketed to suspicious spouses and parents was being used to find dissidents during a war. Which, by the way, government intelligence units love using off-the-shelf tools to conduct their spying, since they don't have to burn any of their trade craft to conduct their tasks. A $40 off-the-shelf tool is way cheaper than spending a lot of time and energy developing their own tool to do the same thing. By this time Blackshades was becoming well known in the hacker communities. Hundreds of people were buying it and infecting thousands of machines with it, which also meant the victims were waking up to the nightmare happening to their computers. Victims would often get extortion e-mails where they would receive an embarrassing photo of them with some kind of demand. The obvious demand is to pay some Bitcoin and we’ll delete it, but some were downright evil. Like, people would send a half-naked photo to their victim and say, ‘Send me a fully-nude photo or I’m posting this on your own social media account. Let me show you that I have access to it.’ Then they would post a test message to prove it. It would rattle a lot of these women, and they would sometimes send the pictures that were demanded simply out of fear. [Music] Sometimes the attacker would catch a picture of their victim having sex and send them a picture of that and demand a video call over Skype, and they'd ask the women to do a five-minute sex show for them on camera as part of the ransom demand. If they didn't do it, the attacker had access to all their social media accounts and said they'd post something really terrible if they didn't to it. Blackshades was a growing problem, and victims were being almost entirely silent about the matter due to all the embarrassment and fear. I hate to say it, but it’s possible that some women died by suicide because of this. I didn't see any specific stories about that happening with Blackshades, but I’ve seen countless stories where online bullying and abuse and harassment has led to women feeling so desperate that they'd rather die than face the embarrassment or harassment anymore. It’s really tragic. We're gonna take a quick ad break, but stay with us because this is where the FBI starts to get involved. The FBI started rooting around in some hacker forums looking for crime, but they weren't focused on this. Not yet, at least. They were focused on stuff like credit card fraud and online fraud. In 2010 the FBI decided to go on the dark web and build their own stolen credit card exchange. They were hoping thieves would come and sell stolen cards and people would buy them, and then the FBI would catch them in the act. It’s wild to me that the FBI built their own carders market on the dark web, a honeypot to trap people. Not only could you buy and sell stolen credit cards there, but they sold tools for stealing credit cards, too. However, dark web forums like this only work when there’s trust, so the FBI, which was acting like dark web operators, said they’ll verify every tool before it’s allowed to be sold on the site. So, for instance, if you wanted to sell a credit card scraper, the FBI would have to vet you as a seller first. Send us one and we’ll test it, and if it’s good, we’ll approve you as a vendor. The administrators were either undercover agents or confidential sources in the investigation. They were reviewing these products to get evidence of criminal activity and to investigate the hardware, software, and methods used. The FBI was looking for credit card fraud, but then the co-creator of Blackshades, Michael Hogue, wanted to become a vendor on this forum. [Music] So, he submitted his tool, Blackshades, to show them that he has a real tool that can be used to scrape credit card data. He had no idea he was pitching the FBI. It’s kind of ironic that the co-creator of Blackshades fell for a social engineering trap himself. See? Even he’s susceptible to that. The FBI couldn't believe Michael sent them his malware. This was clear evidence of his intent, to sell Blackshades to criminals. All that language that this was only for educational purposes or for a parent to monitor their kid wasn't gonna fly anymore. When you're selling it to criminals on a dark web forum to steal credit card data with, then that’s clear intent. In 2012, the trap snapped shut. The FBI ran a sting operation called Operation Card Shop. It led to twenty-four arrests in eight countries. Almost all of these arrests were for credit card fraud, but there was one exception. One of the people arrested was Michael Hogue, the maker of Blackshades. He was charged under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for conspiracy to commit computer hacking and transmission of malware. Writing and selling software isn't illegal, but writing and selling software with the intent of logging keystrokes, ransomwaring files, stealing credit cards, and spying on webcams without consent is illegal. Hogue cooperated with investigators, which meant he avoided prison entirely. He was sentenced to five years of probation and he was ordered to forfeit $40,000, and had to perform 500 hours of community service. So, that’s it, right? Co-creator of Blackshades arrested, 2,000 people in cuffs, game over for Blackshades at least, right? Except it wasn't. The Blackshades website stayed up and operational and kept selling it to people for forty bucks. What's hilarious is around that time, Blackshades became so popular that you could find pirated versions of it floating around, too. People who didn't want to pay the $40 could download it and install a pirated version and use it, and it’s hilarious because almost certainly a pirated version of Blackshades is going to come with some other malware bundled on it. You're gonna get some other spy tool installed if you install this. People were spying on the spies. Over the next year, Blackshades did not shrink. It grew. In 2013 Blackshades made its news again. REPORTER: Miss Teen USA 2013, Cassidy Wolf, was one of the victims of a hacker using the malicious software called Blackshades RAT, or remote access tool. Authorities say last year a hacker used Wolf’s personal computer webcam to take nude photos of her and threatened to post them online if Wolf didn't send him more revealing photos. Instead, she went to police. JACK: Cassidy Wolf, a high-school student from Temecula, California, got an anonymous e-mail. A stranger said he had photos of her, photos taken in her bedroom through her webcam, on her own computer after he hacked into it. He tried to extort her after threatening to release intimate photos unless she provided him with a special performance. Classic sextortion. [Music] She had no idea she was infected by this. She said her camera light never came on, and she didn't know anybody had been staring at her in her room this whole time or watching her computer. She didn't send any photos to this stranger. She went to law enforcement instead. The FBI ran the investigation, and when they figured out who was behind it, it turned out the hacker wasn't some shadowy figure on the far side of the world. It was a guy she went to high school with, a former classmate named Jared Abrahams, and she was not the only one. Jared used Blackshades to break into the computers of at least two dozen women and girls. Their ages ranged from sixteen to the early twenties. Jared got arrested by the FBI. Two months later he pled guilty to extortion and hacking. He went to court for sentencing and he was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison. Four months after this extortion attempt, Cassidy Wolf was crowed Miss Teen USA 2013. Instead of keeping quiet about what happened to her, she did the opposite. She spent her year using that title to go to schools and talk about exactly that, webcam hacking and sextortion. CASSIDY: Yeah, so, a few years ago I was with a friend of mine, and I randomly got an e-mail, and in that e-mail he had attached photos that he had taken of me through my webcam. So, it ended up being a federal investigation… INTERVIEWER: Yeah. CASSIDY: …for three months straight. The guy that did it ended up going to prison for eighteen months. JACK: Wow, how brave of her to use her newfound popularity to fight for justice and to win. So, that’s one guy caught for spying on girls, but that didn't slow down the continual growth of Blackshades’ sale and usage, because by May 2014, Blackshades was booming. By then it had infected over a million computers worldwide. [Music] When the FBI arrested Blackshades’ co-creator, Michael Hogue, he became a cooperating witness, which meant he let them see all the inside baseball of his organization. He showed the FBI how many computers it had infected, who the users were, everything. Well, actually, I don't know how much he actually showed them versus how much they saw, because they just seized all his servers and took all the computers for themselves. So, the FBI knew the malware had infected over 500,000 computers in over a hundred countries and had generated over $350,000 in sales. They had the names and addresses of more than 6,000 customer accounts, basically a customer list of all the people around the world who bought Blackshades. They shared this list with law enforcement partners around the world. So, what do you do as the FBI when you have the billing information for thousands of Blackshades customers? I know you've heard the term before; they can't arrest us all. But can they? I think they wanted to. But the FBI has a 99% conviction rate. If they arrest someone, they better have bulletproof evidence that that person committed a crime. I mean, that one user, Stefan, bought the thing using his ex-girlfriend’s credit card, right? So, just in the list of names of people who purchased it isn't enough. They need to go through each customer individually and prove that they were actually abusing the tool. Because what if someone’s just using it to monitor their child’s computer activity like the website advertised it? They didn't want to make any mistakes. So, they spent months and an enormous amount of time building cases for as many of its users as they could. They were able to get enough evidence on lots of people who were clearly abusing the tool, but those people were located all over the world, so they reached out to law enforcement in eighteen different countries to try to do a worldwide coordinated takedown. On May 19th, 2014, law enforcement officials from around the world raided the homes of Blackshade users, arresting as many people as they could. Here's Preet Bharara, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, in a press conference explaining what they did. PREET: We are announcing another global law enforcement operation that has exposed and crippled a frightening form of cybercrime affecting hundreds of thousands of computer users around the world. JACK: The operation led to ninety-seven arrests and 359 searches across the world, with people detained in the US, the UK, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Switzerland, Italy, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Moldova, Canada, and Chile. The age of the criminals varied. Some were teenagers; a sixteen-year-old in the UK, a seventeen-year-old in Finland, an eighteen-year-old in the Netherlands. Others were adults, and I’m pretty sure it was all males who got arrested. Ninety-seven people arrested for using the tool. The reasons for using it varied, too. Some used it for voyeurism and extortion. Some used it for financial theft. Some built botnets to launch DDoS attacks. Some locked computers up with ransomware. More than a thousand data-storage devices were also seized, and they took the Blackshades website offline. One case involved an eighteen-year-old man from the Netherlands who allegedly infected 2,000 computers to take photos of women and girls who were using their machines. 2,000 infections from one guy alone. In 2014 prosecutors in the US unsealed charges against five people. Here's FBI’s Special Agent in charge, Leo Taddeo. LEO: [Music] We have charged three key members of the Blackshades organization, as well as two cybercriminals in the New York area who purchased the software and used it to victimize hundreds of innocent people. Specifically we announce charges against the two alleged creators of the Blackshades RAT, Alex Yucel and Michael Hogue. Yucel, a Swedish citizen, was arrested in Moldova in November 2013, and he is awaiting extradition to the United States. The indictment against Yucel has been under seal and was made public earlier today. Mr. Hogue was arrested in Arizona in June of 2012, and subsequently pled guilty in January of 2013. Mr. Hogue has been cooperating with the government and its investigation since his arrest. We have also charged and arrested today Brendan Johnston, a former Blackshades employee who helped market and sell the RAT as well as provide technical assistance to its users, and two New York-area purchasers of the RAT who allegedly used it to steal online account information and spy on victims through webcams. JACK: When the FBI made copies of the customer list, they didn't stop at the developers. Across more than forty US cities, agents knocked on the doors of regular people who paid forty bucks, and if you were on hacking forums at the time, you would have seen panic unfold in real time. People were posting things like ‘The FBI just raided my house’ or ‘They took my computer’ or ‘What do I do?’ One guy in Canada posted that the police showed up with a warrant because his son had bought it. FBI: During this past week, FBI agents in over forty cities across the country conducted searches, interviews, and arrests of people who purchased Blackshades and may have used it to commit cybercrimes. We also passed leads to foreign law enforcement agencies around the world. In the last few days our law enforcement partners in nineteen foreign countries carried out their own law enforcement actions. The combined efforts of the FBI and foreign law enforcement marks the Blackshades takedown as one of the largest global cyber operations in history. JACK: Wow, one of the largest global cyber operations in history. Remember that guy I told you about earlier, Stefan Rigo, who infected over a dozen women with Blackshades? He was arrested in this operation, too, and he pleaded guilty. He received a suspended sentence, 200 hours of community service, and seven years on the sex offender registry. FBI: Combating cybercrime is a top priority for the FBI. The charges unsealed today should put cybercriminals around the world on notice. If you think you can hide behind your computer screen, think again. Just like in the physical world, the FBI will follow the digital trail to your doorstep. If you think operating in a foreign country puts you out of our reach, think again. We have many law enforcement partners around the world who are with us in this fight. If we can't reach you, they can. JACK: Blackshades is old now. Most antivirus software can detect it, and some of the methods it used to spread no longer work. The website is gone. The forums are dead. The people who built it got arrested. But even though Blackshades today is mostly a museum piece, malware doesn't really die. It evolves. The $40 RAT with the friendly menu got replaced by newer ones with different names. The criminal economy moved into newer, more sophisticated malware that’s harder to detect. What's still true is malware wants to be sneaky and live quietly. It doesn't want the victim to know they are infected. There’s an asymmetry of knowledge here which is a huge gap, actually. Most people don't know enough about computers or how to secure them to protect themselves reliably, and these attackers rely on that lack of knowledge to hide in the wires, under the radar. Listening to shows like this starts to bridge that gap. Now you're aware that tools like this exist in the world, and they're a big deal. I mean, this one resulted in one of the largest global cyber operations in history. This isn't just some little thing. This is a huge problem. So, awareness is step number one for your safety. Be aware that messages from friends can contain malware, and it doesn't always mean that they sent it to you. It’s always good to verify things out-of-band if you're not sure. Like, if you get a text message from a friend with a suspicious link, call them on the phone and be like, hey, did you just send me this text? [Music] It’s always better to be safe than sorry. Be aware that all of the documents that you have, the photos you took, or anything you've saved on the cloud may and probably will get loose at some point and get out in the world. Data breaches are extremely common, and malware like this makes it easy for an attacker to get into your computer to see your stuff. So treat your sensitive documents and photos with much more care than normal. For me, I store stuff offline on a hard drive that’s encrypted. It’s a pain in the neck to interact with those files on there, but that’s the point. I want to make it really hard for anyone else to access it, too. There are also USB sticks that you can get which encrypt all the data on it, and to decrypt it you have to enter in a PIN code. Storing stuff on an encrypted USB stick is a pretty good idea, especially since things like mobile phones can't decrypt a hard drive to interact with it. You should treat the internet as a hostile place, because it is. Be very, very cautious when downloading things, clicking links, installing stuff, accepting pop-up options. For me personally, I try to adopt a very minimal approach when it comes to the software and apps I use. The fewer the better, because it reduces the attack surfaces for things that can go wrong. For Pete’s sake, cover your cameras. I think a lot of us are already in the habit of covering our laptop cameras, which is great. But what about your phone camera? I’m seeing cases these days that have a little slider on the back of the phone so it covers the camera, and I love that. I have one of those myself. But what about the front camera? I haven't seen any cases that cover that. There are little camera covers that you can stick on it, but in my experience, they just always pop off after a few days. I’ve actually experienced with a ton of different types of tape. Electrical tape is easy to peel off for a photo and it doesn't leave much residue, but you need to swap the tape out every month or so or else it gets gooey. I just don't trust cameras to be off when I think they're off because of stories like this. I also unplug the TV when I go into hotel rooms when I stay there, since a lot of them have cameras and mics in them, too. Of course you should keep your system and apps updated. Use a different complex password for every service app and website you have an account for. [Music] Actually, I use a different e-mail address for every account that I have as well. This way I immediately know if something doesn't look right because it’ll be for an e-mail that I only use for one thing, and now I’m getting something else from it. It’s not a bad idea to use an antivirus scan every now and then to check for malware on your devices. I’m not gonna plug any here, though, but do some research and find one that’s trusted and reputable. I’m not sure we can achieve perfect privacy or security, but like I’ve said before, when you're trying to secure your stuff, it’s kinda like running from a bear in the woods. You don't need to be faster than the bear; you just need to be faster than your friend who’s also running from the bear in order to stay alive. Your goal is to make it hard for an attacker to get to your stuff so that they just move on to an easier target. Outro: [Outro music] This show is created by me, Papa Ransom, Jack Rhysider. This one was written by motherboard, Yale Grauer. Our editor is the gigabyter, Tristan Ledger, sound design by the LFO, Garrett Tiedemann, mixing by Proximity Sound, and our intro music is by the mysterious Breakmaster Cylinder. If you haven't checked it out already, you should go listen to my other podcast called LOW. It’s the craziest story I’ve ever told. It’s the craziest story I’ve ever heard, and it just might change the way you think about life. Go find LOW wherever you listen to podcasts, spelled L-O-W. My computer just went through a messy divorce. She ended up getting a C drive, and he got the D drive. This is Darknet Diaries.

articles.title: NIS2 Makes Board Members Personally Liable for Access Control Decisions
articles.context: Approval is only part of the job Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation
articles.full_text:
NIS2 Article 20 makes management bodies answerable for the access controls they approve, and boards are starting to ask for proof that those controls work.

NIS2 board accountability gives directors a more direct role in cybersecurity. Under Article 20, the management bodies of essential and important entities must approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures required by the directive, oversee their implementation, and can be held liable for infringements, subject to national law.

That obligation is live across most of the EU, with four member states going to the Court of Justice in July for failing to notify full transposition.

Access control is one of the required measures. Directors are not expected to decide who gets administrator rights or review individual user accounts. They do, however, need to know that access is being controlled, that someone has responsibility for managing the risk, and that problems are being addressed.

An estimated 160,000 entities fall within the scope of NIS2 across the EU.

Approval is only part of the job

Article 20 requires management bodies to both approve cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. It also requires the members of those bodies to undergo cybersecurity training, and to offer comparable training to employees on a regular basis.

The measures themselves are set out in Article 21. They include access control policies and asset management, along with the use of multi-factor authentication or continuous authentication solutions where appropriate.

Many organizations have traditionally left these decisions to security and IT teams. Under NIS2, the board still needs to know whether the measures it approved are being implemented.

Day-to-day responsibility can remain with the CISO and IT teams. The difficulty comes when the person responsible for a risk does not control the budget, systems, or people needed to address it.

Greece’s implementation goes further in defining who carries that responsibility. Its NIS2 law requires essential and important entities to appoint a suitably qualified member of their organization as an Information and Communication Systems Security Officer. The officer coordinates compliance, must have the resources needed to do the job, and operates independently of the company’s data protection officer.

Access problems also need to reach the board in terms that it can act on. If an MFA rollout has failed or administrators have more access than they need, the board needs to understand the risk of leaving it unresolved. The CISO may be responsible for the risk without controlling the budget or teams needed to fix it.

The board needs evidence

Board reports often show what the access control policy requires, rather than whether it is being followed.

For example, a company policy will likely require MFA and the removal of accounts when employees leave.

However, the board also needs to know about the exceptions, including old accounts that remain active, excessive privileges, MFA exemptions that have never been reviewed, and suppliers whose access has outlasted their contracts.

The board needs information about how the controls are working in practice.

In a NIS2 access management report from European password and secrets manager Passwork, regulators from two national cybersecurity authorities and independent security leaders describe boards that have absorbed the liability change and now ask for proof that controls work, where they once accepted a summary of the policy.

Organizations should be able to show who can access critical systems, why that access was granted, who approved it, how long it is valid, and when it was changed or revoked. The board needs to know whether that evidence exists and what it says about material access risk.

Personal liability raises the stakes

Implementation is still catching up in parts of Europe. In July 2026, the European Commission referred Ireland, Spain, France, and the Netherlands to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to notify full transposition of NIS2 into national law. The Commission also asked the Court to impose financial sanctions.

For organizations in countries where NIS2 has been transposed, regulators have significant enforcement powers.

For essential entities, member states must set a maximum fine of at least €10,000,000 or 2% of the global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Important entities are subject to a lower maximum threshold, of at least €7,000,000 or 1.4% of their global annual turnover, in a similar capacity.

Article 32 also allows competent authorities, in specific circumstances, to seek the temporary prohibition of someone at CEO or legal representative level from exercising managerial functions in an essential entity. This can happen where enforcement action has failed to produce the required response. It is not an automatic consequence of a cyber incident.

Article 20 separately requires member states to ensure that management bodies can be held liable for infringements of Article 21, subject to the applicable rules under national law.

Approving the policy is not the end of the board’s involvement. It also needs information on whether the policy is being followed and what is happening with known problems.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found credential abuse somewhere in the chain of 39% of breaches, more than any other vector. Stolen credentials also circulate at scale, as the exposed database of 24 billion credential records reported in June showed. Directors should expect an answer on which accounts and credentials reach critical systems, who is responsible for them, and whether that access is being controlled.

Give access risk an owner with authority

CISOs briefing their boards should be able to say who owns access-control risk and whether that person has the authority to address it. The board also needs evidence of what is happening.

When an access problem is identified, someone needs to be responsible for getting it fixed. That might mean removing unnecessary privileges or dealing with an MFA exception that has remained in place. If the fix depends on another team’s budget or resources, the board needs to know.

Board reporting should show whether the controls it approved are working, flag significant exceptions that remain unresolved, and who is accountable for closing them.

articles.title: Apple’s spyware notifications reach the Bundestag: what the BSI says to do now
articles.context: Germany’s cybersecurity agency, the BSI, also says it is unclear whether the alerts indicate successful infections or only attempted attacks
articles.full_text:
Apple warns German Bundestag lawmakers of mercenary spyware attacks; BSI urges victims to assume compromise.

The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware. The warning follows Apple’s notifications, which began reaching iPhones on October 29, according to the federal cybersecurity office, the BSI. The BSI says members of the Bundestag and other notable people got an Apple alert about an attack with so-called mercenary spyware.

“The Federal Office for Information Security ( BSI ) has learned that several members of the German Bundestag and other public figures have received a threat notification from Apple on their devices since October 29, 2026. In the notification, Apple states that it has detected an attack using so-called mercenary spyware . This is commercially developed, advanced spyware that has frequently been used in the past by state actors against specific, targeted individuals.” reads the notice issued by BSI.

“The BSI (Federal Office for Information Security) is unaware whether these notifications indicate actual compromises or merely signal attempted attacks.y “

“Germany’s digital minister, Karsten Wildberger, has confirmed that members of the Bundestag and the federal government received warnings from Apple that their iPhones may have been targeted by spyware.” states the report.

Digital minister Karsten Wildberger confirmed it on ARD’s Bericht aus Berlin on Sunday, saying there had been “a notification from Apple that certain devices may have been compromised” and that members of both the Bundestag and the federal government were among those warned. Digital minister said the BSI had reacted super quickly and written to everyone affected. Wildberger didn’t say how many politicians got the alerts or who they are.

“According to Wildberger, the BSI advised those affected to assume – as a precaution – that their device may have been compromised, because the alerts do not show whether an attack succeeded.” states Euronews.

The German government has not revealed who was targeted. Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius told the Financial Times that officials are taking the incident and Apple’s warning very seriously. However, he did not say which government members received the alerts or whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them. Apple has not commented on the reports, according to Euronews.

The Apple warning does not provide all the answers. Apple does not identify the governments behind these attacks, nor does it confirm whether a device was actually infected. Germany’s cybersecurity agency, the BSI, also says it is unclear whether the alerts indicate successful infections or only attempted attacks.

Apple says mercenary spyware is far more advanced than common cybercrime tools and that most users will never be targeted. This commercial surveillance software is often used on behalf of governments to spy on specific individuals. It can infect devices through so-called zero-click attacks, which do not require victims to open a message or click a link. In most cases, victims do not notice anything unusual.

Once a phone is compromised, the BSI says, attackers can read messages, including in encrypted apps, and access calls, contacts, calendars and location. They can also turn on the camera and microphone. That’s the whole phone, not a corner of it.

For recipients the BSI’s advice is concrete. Update the operating system immediately, unless you plan a forensic analysis, and consider turning on Lockdown Mode, which makes new attacks harder but doesn’t remove an existing infection. Lockdown Mode limits some features such as message attachments, link previews and FaceTime calls from unknown people, while calls and plain text messages keep working.

If the risk looks high, the BSI suggests replacing the device. That means resetting every account used on it and, to make repeat attacks harder, changing the phone number. Then set a new device passcode, change the passwords of your Apple account and email, and make sure two-factor authentication is on.

The BSI recommends turning on Signal’s registration lock and WhatsApp’s two-step verification, with a new PIN for each. It also advises removing any linked devices you don’t recognize.

Anyone who received a warning can email the BSI Service Center at service-center@bsi.bund.de. This helps the agency work out how many people may be affected. The agency says a genuine Apple warning never asks you to click links, open files, install apps or profiles, or share passwords and codes. These warnings appear on the lock screen, in settings, by email and at the top of account.apple.com after you sign in.

The warnings weren’t limited to Germany. Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada said on X that Apple had warned him about another attack against his device. He had already been targeted by spyware in 2021.

أمس، تلقيتُ إشعاراً أمنياً من شركة Apple تحذّرني فيه من تعرّض هاتفي الآيفون لهجوم تجسّسي موجّه، باستخدام برمجيات متطوّرة من النوع الذي تطوّره شركات مثل NSO Group، المعروفة ببرنامج «بيغاسوس».ولعلّ أخطر ما ورد في التحذير تأكيد Apple أنّ هذا النوع من الهجمات يستهدف أشخاصاً محدّدين… pic.twitter.com/2jFq6F3cvD

— رُضوان (@radwanmortada) October 30, 2026

According to his notice, Apple sent the latest warnings to users in 99 countries. Nobody has publicly identified the attackers or the government that may have ordered the attacks.

The BSI warned German lawmakers that Apple threat notifications may indicate compromised devices and urged recipients to contact the agency and take protective measures.

“Those affected who have received a corresponding warning message from Apple should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.” BSI concludes. “In a letter dated October 30, 2026, the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) alerted members of the German Bundestag to the threat and informed them of necessary measures. Affected individuals were urged to contact the BSI directly .”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

articles.title: ZDI-26-868: Microsoft Windows Aero Theme Improper Handling Of Error Condition Denial-of-Service Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of Microsoft Windows. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of Aero themes. The issue results from improper handling of an error condition. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a persistent denial-of-service condition on the system.

Additional Details

Microsoft has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/servicing/os/windows-11/2026/10/kb5127648-windows-11-24h2-25h2-26h2-security-update

articles.title: Attackers Target Unpatched CryptoPayment Gateway Flaw That Can Expose Wallet Credentials
articles.context: Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-81648, which carries a CVSS score of 10.0. Successful exploitation of the flaw could permit unauthenticated users to delete arbitrary files on the server and extract sensitive data, including stored wallet credentials.

"The CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin from 1.2.1 to 1.2.2 does not apply an authorization check on one of its AJAX endpoints, allowing unauthenticated users to invoke administrative operations, including deleting arbitrary files on the server, overwriting the payment gateway configuration and recovering stored wallet credentials in cleartext," according to a description of the flaw on the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The vulnerability affects versions 1.2.1 through 1.2.2, which is the latest version. There are no known fixes for the flaw, according to WP Scan. As of August 28, 2026, the plugin has been closed on the WordPress Plugin Directory and is no longer available for download due to an unspecified "security issue."

Statistics show that the plugin has been collectively downloaded 1,845 times, including 20 downloads over the last seven days. It's unclear if it's actively installed on any WordPress sites.

"We are observing in-the-wild exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-81648, a critical (CVSS 10.0) flaw in the CryptoPayment Gateway for WordPress," Defused Cyber said in an X post. "The attacks we recorded came from infrastructure that markets themselves as 'Anonymous KYC-Free VPS Hosting.'"

In the absence of a fix, site owners are advised to remove the plugin, rotate wallet keys, and audit for any suspicious changes.

articles.title: Composer 2.11 Adds Dependency Cooldowns
articles.context: The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age...
articles.full_text:
Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks.

The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected.

The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running.

Preventing Cooldown Bypasses #

The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises. An initial implementation was submitted in December, but the feature missed Composer 2.10 as the maintainers worked through how to enforce cooldowns reliably.

In May, after additional attacks affected Packagist, developers pressed the maintainers for an update. Composer co-founder Nils Adermann explained that the feature was being held up by changes needed to make release metadata trustworthy.

The existing time field in Composer package metadata could be derived from a Git commit date or supplied through composer.json. Both are under the publisher's control, allowing an attacker to backdate a malicious release and bypass a cooldown.

Packagist introduced a new published-time field in June, recording when a version first became available through the registry. Composer 2.11 now uses that timestamp rather than trusting dates supplied by package publishers. Repositories without the required metadata cause dependency resolution to fail unless an explicit fallback is configured.

The cooldown feature is part of a broader security effort by Composer and Packagist. In a May security update, maintainers specifically cited the April compromise of intercom/intercom-php, and the May attack on Laravel Lang among recent incidents affecting the PHP ecosystem. The update outlined several security initiatives, including malware detection, version immutability, and the planned cooldown policy.

Cooldowns Are Now Standard Across Package Ecosystems #

For years, dependency management favored staying on the latest compatible releases. That assumption is changing. With compromised packages appearing on a regular basis, living on the bleeding edge has become considerably less appealing. Cooldowns are increasingly treated as standard supply chain security practice, and some package managers have already made them the default.

Composer is joining a movement already well underway across JavaScript, Ruby, Python, and Rust tooling.

pnpm introduced minimum release ages in September 2025 and made a 24-hour delay the default in version 11. Yarn has also enabled a release-age gate by default, while npm and Bun offer configurable delays. GitHub introduced a three-day default cooldown for Dependabot version updates in July.

In Ruby, Bundler added cooldown support in June, and gem.coop began testing registry-level delays earlier this year. Cargo is next, with minimum publish age support scheduled to become stable in Rust 1.100 on November 12.

Unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in, a decision its maintainers debated during development over concerns about disrupting existing workflows.

Composer also deliberately avoids automatically exempting security fixes. The maintainers rejected that approach because an attacker with publishing access could potentially create an advisory or exploit an existing one to get a malicious release through the cooldown. Developers can use --no-cooldown to install an urgent fix immediately without disabling other security policies. Composer also supports permanent exemptions for specific packages through the cooldown policy's ignore setting.

Security fixes still demand quick updates, especially as AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures accelerate, but for routine dependency updates, cooldowns are becoming best practice. Composer's implementation arrives later than many of its peers, but its adoption adds another major ecosystem to the shift toward giving new dependencies time to be examined before installation.

articles.title: European supermarkets that failed to act after French freezer attack are now feeling the heat
articles.context: “There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,”...
articles.full_text:
Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday.

The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution.

The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report, which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize. No group has as yet claimed to be behind the attacks.

Delay understandable

Analysts and consultants said the lack of an immediate response to the initial refrigeration attacks is understandable, given the complex nature of the systems and the multiple vendors who typically manage such systems for major retailers.

Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Katell Thielemann said that although the impacted European retailers own the hardware, they outsource the maintenance, upkeep, and the management. Thus, she said, “there is some confusion about who owns what in this black box of outsourcing.”

IDC Senior Research Manager Bobby Kuzma agreed.

“There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,” he said. “The cybersecurity teams may not have even been aware that the devices were network connected, especially if they were riding on dedicated internet circuits for manufacturer support.”

Thielemann added that the incident was made worse because of the historic lack of priority given to cybersecurity defenses in retail.

“It’s proof that cybersecurity is still not top of mind,” she said. “Even when it’s so egregious, senior [retail] leaders are not asking, ‘How do we get ahead of this?’”

However, Kuzma argued, this problem comes down to asset inventory visibility.

“You can’t protect a system that you don’t know you have. You can’t scan for exposures on a connection that you don’t know exists,” he pointed out. “Sometimes that inventory requires somebody physically going into the telco closet at the locations and asking pointed questions about equipment that’s present. In this day and age, having devices of any type hanging off a public internet connection and accessible is asking for trouble.”

IoT handled outside of IT

David Neuman, an executive advisor with consulting firm Acceligence, also noted that it was never realistic to assume that issuing a cybersecurity advisory was going to meaningfully address this security hole.

“An advisory doesn’t fix a system nobody in the building owns,” Neuman said. “Contractors often install and service store refrigeration controllers under arrangements that rely on a constant data feed, so they can sit outside the security team’s inventory and authority. Taking the controllers offline means finding them, then reworking how the contractor gets in, store by store.”

That, he said, “explains the gap, but it doesn’t excuse it: France gave everyone a three-week warning. Abusing a legitimate function like defrost causes physical and financial damage without any malware.”

Brian Levine, a partner at consulting firm Control Risks, added that another part of the problem is that IoT devices have always been handled outside of IT.

“For years, organizations treated connected operational equipment as a facilities issue. These incidents end that debate,” Levine said. “Security professionals never dismissed this risk; budgets deprioritized it because nothing had failed at scale. Now it has, and boards will ask why vendor contracts, incident response plans, and tabletop exercises never accounted for a physical outcome.”

And, said Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, this issue goes beyond the fact that the attackers could gain access. He said that he is most concerned about the range of things the attackers were able to do with that access.

“The attackers could reportedly manipulate refrigeration systems to operate far outside their intended parameters,” Kenney said. “Even if someone gains access to a system, there should be independent safeguards preventing commands that could damage equipment or disrupt operations. The fact that remote access can potentially translate into physical damage suggests some serious gaps in how these systems are designed and secured.”

Kenney also noted that some of these devices had long passed their end-of-life, meaning that security patches and other upgrades may have been unavailable. “Organizations can end up relying on equipment that still functions perfectly well operationally, but can no longer be adequately secured,” he pointed out. “That creates difficult decisions about network isolation, compensating controls, and ultimately when equipment needs to be replaced.”

Indeed, said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy, some in IT tend to ignore IoT systems, especially when they were deployed by functional units without permission from IT or cybersecurity teams.

“Enterprises don’t tend to look at fridges in the same light as servers, smartphones, and other traditionally connected devices,” he noted. “If anything, most IT shops have a limited view of what constitutes a connected device in the first place. That means many organizations are running connected devices, such as appliances, floor cleaners and once-dumb but now increasingly smart machines, with dangerously outdated firmware because they never identified them as connected in the first place.”

Unexpected threat to IT

As well, said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, there are also corporate legal issues that may undercut cybersecurity’s need for quick action.

“CERT-FR’s own alert shows why that takes time. Before cutting a controller off the internet, it tells operators to check the insurance terms in their contract with the refrigeration provider. That one line says a lot,” he said, adding that many of these controllers are installed, monitored, and guaranteed by a contractor who depends on the data feed. The store may have neither the ability nor the authority to shut them down.

“Three weeks of warning is a long time for an attacker and a short time for a supermarket chain. Close the door to the internet first and renegotiate the contracts second,” he said.

Dickson also argued that these refrigeration attacks pose an unexpected threat to traditional IT systems as well, because servers and other equipment are temperature-sensitive.

“An attacker who reaches the building management system does not need to touch a single server. The servers will shut themselves down rather than cook,” Dickson said. “You do not need to hack the data center. You only need to hack the air conditioning.”

articles.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
articles.context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
articles.full_text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

articles.title: One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning
A TraderTraitor's guide to getting away with billions.
articles.context: Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.
articles.full_text:
The FBI blames North Korea for a record-breaking crypto heist. Hackers hijack air raid alerts in Ukraine and Russia. European supermarket freezers come under attack again. Aur0ra ransomware operators put AI agents to work. Android’s SMS of Death gets a proof-of-concept exploit. Malicious Claude Code extensions infiltrate Cursor’s marketplace. Google offers a quarter-million-dollar bug bounty. ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Cynthia Kaiser, SVP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former Deputy Director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, sharing how the AI cybercrime economy is open for business and booming. The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Today is Monday November 2nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The FBI attributes last week’s record crypto heist to North Korea.

The FBI has attributed last week’s theft of more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators say the attackers are converting stolen assets into Ethereum and laundering funds through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reports that roughly 2.9 billion dollars has been frozen or seized, leaving approximately 3.3 billion beyond issuers’ reach, spread across hundreds of cryptocurrency wallets.

Binance says it will cover the losses, protecting customer funds. The company continues investigating what it calls a complex attack involving multiple perpetrators and a self-destruct mechanism designed to erase forensic evidence.

TraderTraitor has been linked to several major cryptocurrency thefts, including the previous record-breaking 1.5-billion-dollar Bybit heist.

Hackers target air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia.

Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats.

Ukraine’s official Air Alert app was compromised late Saturday, pushing messages in Russian warning of incoming nuclear strikes, chemical threats, and street fighting. Sirens also sounded across the country. Authorities temporarily disabled notifications, warned residents against clicking suspicious links, and restored normal operations within hours.

Early Sunday, Russia reported a similar attack on its emergency alert app. Users received bogus warnings that nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia, along with instructions to stockpile food and shelter in basements.

The Russian incident may have been retaliation for the earlier attack on Ukraine, although responsibility remains unconfirmed. Both countries acknowledged their systems had been compromised.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted, remotely raising freezer temperatures and spoiling food.

Monday’s attacks affected more than 50 stores in Belgium, along with retailers in Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Some freezers were reportedly set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit.

The incident follows a similar attack three weeks earlier that affected roughly 700 supermarkets in France. Authorities haven’t identified the perpetrators or established whether the attacks are connected.

Some affected systems rely on discontinued refrigeration controllers that no longer receive security updates. Technicians say certain equipment requires physical modifications rather than software patches.

The incidents highlight the risks posed by internet-connected industrial equipment, particularly when aging devices remain accessible remotely. For supermarkets, the consequences are immediate: spoiled inventory and costly repairs.

The Aur0ra ransomware group is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions.

Sophos researchers say the cybercriminal group behind Aur0ra ransomware is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions and evade security defenses.

The group, tracked as GOLD OGRE, reportedly used the AI coding tool Cursor to test endpoint security products and help conduct attacks. Human operators supplied credentials, network access, and objectives, then let AI agents handle reconnaissance, credential attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement with limited supervision.

Researchers observed agents adapting their techniques when initial attempts failed, sometimes gaining domain administrator access. Three organizations investigated were subsequently named on Aur0ra’s leak site.

The attackers also reportedly bypassed AI safety restrictions by describing their activities as authorized security testing.

Sophos warns that agentic AI could accelerate ransomware operations and lower the technical expertise required to carry them out.

The Android SMS of Death gets a proof of concept.

A security researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit for an Android vulnerability dubbed “SMS of Death.” Tracked as CVE-2026-58882, the zero-click flaw allows attackers to crash phones or disrupt cellular service, including emergency calls, using specially crafted text messages.

Victims receive no visible warning, and repeated messages can trigger reboot loops requiring a factory reset.

Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in October for Android 14 through 17, although the fix wasn’t listed in its security bulletin. Older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable.

Malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension were distributed through Cursor’s marketplace.

Attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension through Cursor’s marketplace in a supply chain attack on October 29th.

Two compromised versions remained available for approximately eleven hours, potentially reaching 5,000 developer systems running Windows or macOS.

The malicious code collected system information and attempted to establish persistent remote access through reverse SSH tunnels. Cursor says those attempts generally failed because the extension lacked administrative privileges.

Anthropic confirmed its official distributions were unaffected.

Cursor removed the malicious extensions, temporarily suspended its marketplace, rotated security keys, and took steps to shut down the attacker’s infrastructure.

Affected users are urged to investigate their systems, since uninstalling the extension may leave malicious persistence mechanisms behind. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.

Google offers a quarter million dollar bug bounty.

Google is offering security researchers up to $250,000 for vulnerabilities that could enable complete administrative takeover of Google Cloud environments.

The expanded bug bounty program rewards exploits that grant unrestricted control over cloud projects or organizations without requiring stolen credentials, existing access, or social engineering.

Remote code execution in Google’s underlying production infrastructure may also qualify.

Google has established strict testing rules to protect customer systems, including a cryptographic method for demonstrating unauthorized access without compromising real accounts.

The company says AI-assisted research is helping uncover increasingly sophisticated vulnerabilities.

ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit.

The parents of a 31-year-old Seattle software engineer are suing OpenAI, alleging that dangerous medical advice from ChatGPT contributed to their daughter’s death.

According to the lawsuit, Bowen Wan consulted the chatbot after losing her job, concerned that her epilepsy medication was affecting her English-speaking abilities during interviews.

The complaint alleges ChatGPT provided instructions for discontinuing her medication, discouraged consulting doctors, and reassured her when she began experiencing seizures.

Wan died from a seizure in February.

Her parents claim OpenAI failed to implement adequate safeguards, particularly for Chinese-language conversations.

OpenAI called the case heartbreaking, noting that Wan used an older version of ChatGPT. The company says newer models are better at recognizing medical emergencies, while emphasizing that ChatGPT cannot replace professional medical care.

Monday business briefing.

Cybersecurity investors are opening their wallets, with cloud and AI security companies leading the latest funding rounds.

San Francisco’s Upwind Security tops the list with a $400 million Series C, followed by Estonian DDoS protection provider Blackwall, which raised $100 million.

Agentic AI security startup Infisical secured $40 million, while Israeli security operations company Mave emerged from stealth with $34 million.

Mobile security provider iVerify and confidential cloud startup Modelyo each raised $17 million. Ultra Security secured $10 million, industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex raised $7.8 million, and Northstar Security landed $7 million. QuestorAI and Cygrid each raised $3 million.

On the acquisition front, healthcare technology provider Tegria purchased cybersecurity and cloud hosting firm CloudWave. Forte Technologies acquired managed security provider Business Cyber Security Solutions.

And Belgian developer security company Aikido Security launched a new workforce security business called Noon, combining its acquisitions of Poland’s Cyberly and Belgium’s Outkept.

The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Security researcher Xusheng Li discovered that a Lenovo fingerprint-protected USB drive, advertised as offering AES-256 encryption, was essentially an ordinary SD card in an expensive disguise.

The fingerprint reader controlled access to the USB connection, but the data itself wasn’t encrypted. Anyone with physical access could simply extract the card.

Further investigation uncovered similar problems across multiple manufacturers, including hardcoded encryption keys, exposed passwords, and hidden accounts with simple credentials.

Using AI-assisted reverse engineering, Li cracked several supposedly secure products in minutes.

Lenovo has issued fixes for affected devices, although some require owners to ship their drives back or arrange firmware upgrades.

The research is a reminder that security claims aren’t always what they seem, particularly when manufacturers rely on proprietary technology nobody bothers to examine. As it turns out, some of these supposedly encrypted drives were keeping secrets from everyone except the people trying to steal them.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: Warning: Scammers Are Targeting Voters Ahead of Election Day
articles.context: midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports
articles.full_text:
Scammers continue to target voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports. The scams arrive via text message, email, or phone call, offering to help users register to vote, asking them to take a survey, or soliciting donations. The scams are designed to steal money, personal information, or credentials.

Malwarebytes observed one campaign targeting users in Minnesota, offering to add them to an absentee voter list. The link in the message takes the user to a website that asks for their personal information, which can be used to launch additional scams.

“The message is a scam, though it borrows the language of a real Minnesota voting service,” the researchers write. “Minnesota does have a permanent absentee voter list, but the link in this text is fraudulent. To check or sign up, go directly to your election authority’s official website. Other messages take the opposite approach: instead of offering convenience, they warn that you could lose your chance to vote. A message might say you are not registered to vote, your details are incomplete, or your registration is about to be cancelled. Then it offers a link to sort everything out.”

Other scams take a more threatening approach, warning users that they must pay a fine or click on a link to report for election duty.

Malwarebytes outlines the following advice to help users avoid falling for these scams:

“Go directly to official election websites to check registration, voting requirements, deadlines, and alleged penalties.

Verify donation requests independently. Find the campaign or organization yourself and confirm where your money will go.

Keep payment details out of unsolicited surveys. A political poll that turns into a request to pay for a prize is a red flag.

Check sellers before buying political merchandise. A candidate’s name or logo does not authenticate the shop.

Don’t mistake personal details for proof. A message can contain accurate information about you and still be a scam.

Keep political choices separate from requests for money or personal information. You can support a cause without responding to an unexpected message.”

Malwarebytes has the story: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/scams/2026/10/five-election-scams-to-watch-out-for
