articles.title: TeamViewer Flaw Lets Remote Computers Attack Users Who Connect to Control Them
articles.context: TeamViewer said that when it published the fix, it was unaware of any attacks exploiting the flaw
articles.full_text:
TeamViewer has fixed a flaw that lets the machine being controlled in a remote session attack the computer that connected to control it. In a TeamViewer session, the computer that connects and takes control is the viewer, and the machine it controls is the host.

A malicious or compromised host can exploit the flaw to crash the viewer's TeamViewer and, depending on the platform, may also run code on the viewer's computer. This works only after the user starts a remote-control session to that host. The fix is in TeamViewer version 15.83.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-111585 and scored 8.8 out of 10, in the high range. It affects the TeamViewer Full Client on Windows, Linux, and macOS, the Windows Portable edition, and the Android Remote Control app, in all versions before 15.83.

For this flaw, TeamViewer's bulletin lists the Full Client, Portable, and Android app, but not the Host. The same 15.83 update fixes two other flaws in that bulletin that do affect the Host, so people running the Host should update as well.

Omri Dar, a researcher at security firm Remedio, published a technical account of the flaw on October 29. In this bug, he wrote, "the attacker is the host and the victim is the viewer."

In a remote session, the host tells the viewer how large its screen image is. The viewer uses that size to set aside memory, but the calculation can overflow and reserve too little. Screen data that arrives afterward is then written past the end of that space.

At a minimum, this crashes the viewer's TeamViewer session, and the host can trigger the crash again whenever they want.

On Windows, Remedio says it took the bug further, bypassing the operating system's built-in exploit defenses and running code of its choosing in the viewer. The demonstration used a stand-in on the host to supply part of the attack data, so it is not yet an attack carried out entirely over the network.

That result was shown only on Windows. Whether the same works on macOS, Linux, or Android is not covered in the write-up. TeamViewer only says that code execution is possible, depending on the platform.

The attack needs no password and no extra click beyond accepting the session, and it works in TeamViewer's default setup, Dar wrote. The flaw affects all versions before 15.83, including 15.82, the security update TeamViewer released in September. Updating last month did not remove it.

What to Do

The only fix TeamViewer offers is to update, and it lists no workaround. Current users should move to 15.83 or later. The fixed builds for older supported branches are in the table above.

The same 15.83 update also fixes two other high-severity flaws in the same bulletin, including a separate code-execution flaw affecting Linux and macOS. A companion bulletin the same day, TV-2026-1012, fixes six more flaws in TeamViewer's Remote Management add-ons, delivered by automatic update.

TeamViewer said that when it published the fix, it was unaware of any attacks exploiting the flaw. The vulnerability is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of its October 29 listing. Remedio reported no attacks in the wild and did not release exploit code.

articles.title: Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks
articles.context: In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million...
articles.full_text:
When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Dropcatch Domains: A Hidden Risk

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Know Your Internet Services

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

articles.title: WordPress RCE Flaw Draws Nearly 63,000 Attack Attempts in Just 24 Hours
articles.context: Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released.

The vulnerability, which does not have a CVE identifier, relates to a case of remote code execution impacting WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It carries a CVSS score of 8.1 on the CVSS scoring system. Patches for the flaw were released on October 28, 2026.

"This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades," Wordfence said. "This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window."

The WordPress security company noted that successful exploitation requires an "attacker to hit a very narrow window while WordPress is unpacking a complete Core update."

The issue boils down to the fact that affected versions unpack new files part of a full-package Core update into a predictable directory under "wp-content/upgrade." This copy also includes the WordPress installer.

"Because the staging directory is web-accessible on many servers, an unauthenticated attacker who requests the installer at precisely the right moment can interact with the staged WordPress copy and progress to PHP code execution," Alex Thomas, who leads the Wordfence Threat Response Team, said.

A threat actor who is able to win the race condition can gain the ability to execute code on the server, assuming the following conditions are met -

A full-package update containing the installer files

Public web and PHP access to the staging tree

A predictable or discovered staging path, and

Adequate time to complete the attack before WordPress cleans up the temporary files

Although that window has been observed to last only seconds in normal lab environments, threat actors are polling vulnerable paths, such as "setup-config.php," repeatedly in an attempt to trigger the flaw. Over the past 24 hours, Wordfence said it has blocked 62,969 attacks targeting the vulnerability.

"Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window," Thomas said. "Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations."

"Not every request used the exact vulnerable path, but the sustained polling and exact-layout probes show that attackers quickly understood the race condition and began targeting it."

With active exploitation attempts already underway, WordPress site owners are advised to update to version 7.1.4 as soon as possible and look for suspicious requests to PHP files located under "wp-content/upgrade," as well as unfamiliar administrator accounts, plugins, or PHP files.

articles.title: Photo ID, bank checks, face scan? The UK’s age-check options
articles.context: Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information
articles.full_text:
As preparation for the UK’s planned social media ban, Ofcom has set out four ways social media platforms could check whether users are aged 16 or over. The government and Parliament will decide how the ban works in practice.

Ofcom is the regulator for the communications services in the UK. The BBC reports that Ofcom identified four ways to check someone’s age that it considers “highly effective.”

Here’s what those checks would involve:

Photo ID matching: Comparing a live image of you with the photo on an identity document, such as your passport, and checking the age information on that document.

Bank-based checks: Using age information your bank already holds about you, with your consent.

Facial age estimation: Using technology to estimate your age from your face. Ofcom says this technology has improved recently.

Digital ID services: Using a digital identity service to prove your age, rather than presenting a physical document.

Let’s think through what those checks could mean.

Challenges

The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check.

Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, which raises questions about how that information is handled and protected. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year, a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users.Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information. But the important questions are what information each party receives, what gets retained, and whether the check can be linked to someone’s activity.

Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction. Ofcom acknowledges that some technologies can be wrong by a few years around age 16, so people near the threshold may face an additional verification check.I would expect these checks to stop some underage access but not eliminate it.

Previous restrictions have been followed by workarounds, including increased VPN use, borrowed credentials, and migration to services outside the restrictions. The danger is treating a successful age gate as proof that children are now safe, when it might push them into less regulated spaces.The effectiveness depends on how the checks are implemented. A VPN may help someone avoid a check triggered by their apparent location; it won’t, by itself, bypass an identity or facial check that is still required.

Similarly, Ofcom says matching a live image to an ID is intended to make it harder to borrow someone else’s document. We shouldn’t assume every workaround defeats every method. But Ofcom accepts that some motivated children will get through. The meaningful test is how much harm these measures prevent, weighed against the privacy risks and barriers they introduce— not whether every user has completed a check.

My personal preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement without learning which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you’re old enough shouldn’t mean revealing who you are.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection catches suspicious activity before it becomes a problem.

articles.title: Binance hit by largest-ever crypto theft, with $6.3 billion stolen
articles.context: kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Attackers stole $6
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:#ffe5e5;}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column482616_9de20c-07 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Attackers stole $6.3 billion from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange

Binance says user funds are safe, but watch out for fake support or recovery offers from scammers

Users should check their accounts and use official Binance channels.

Binance says a security incident affected approximately $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. Its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as a possible entry point.

The exchange says it has frozen around $3 billion with help from blockchain partners. It has promised to cover all losses using its emergency fund and company funds. Binance is reportedly the largest cryptocurrency exchange by daily trading volume.

What happened?

In an update on October 30, Binance said attackers may have used a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The company said:

“We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

This doesn’t mean that one employee could simply transfer billions of dollars. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told BleepingComputer the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions. The incident involved a more complex process, rather than a single “one-click” action. Binance also said investigators had identified additional breach points.

Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group associated with previous cryptocurrency thefts. TRM Labs estimates that about $6.36 billion left Binance wallets across ten blockchains, with most of it moving within about 20 minutes.

What should Binance users do?

Binance says approximately $3 billion has been frozen on-chain, while blockchain analysts have reported somewhat different totals. For now, those figures should be treated as developing estimates rather than a final accounting of recovered funds or the exchange’s ultimate losses.

Binance.com users (Binance.US was not affected) should check their accounts, avoid follow-up scams, and respond quickly if they spot signs of a separate compromise.

Go directly to official updates. Open the Binance app or navigate to its support site yourself. Avoid logging in through unexpected messages claiming that you must urgently verify your account or claim compensation. Binance has asked customers to rely on official channels.

Review your account and report anything unexpected. Check your transaction history and account security settings. If you find activity you do not recognize, contact Binance through its official support service. Binance’s support center includes options to disable an account and reset a password or two-factor authentication.

Never give anyone your authentication codes. Treat requests for login codes as a warning sign, even if the person claims to be helping with the incident.

Be wary of anyone promising to recover cryptocurrency. The FBI published a warning in 2023 that fake recovery services target people who have already lost cryptocurrency.

Preserve evidence if you lose money to a related scam. Keep messages, wallet addresses, transaction details, and information about anyone offering recovery services.

Pro tip: Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

articles.title: Trezor Warns of Suspected Hardware Implant in One of Its Wallets Sold by CryptoBilis
articles.context: The customer had moved his funds off the wallet before he found the board
articles.full_text:
A Trezor Safe 5 hardware wallet bought from the reseller CryptoBilis has an extra circuit board that sends out the recovery phrase over a mobile network, a customer has reported.

Trezor has not yet examined the device. It is telling everyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to move their funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Trezor said in a blog post on October 30 that the report came in two days earlier from a customer in Indonesia. He bought the wallet from CryptoBilis in August, through the marketplace Tokopedia.

The board sits between the wallet's main board and its screen, with a cellular module and an antenna, according to the report. It reads the screen, including the recovery phrase (Trezor calls it the wallet backup), and sends it out whenever the device is plugged in.

Trezor has the customer's photos and description and has interviewed him on a video call. It is arranging for the wallet to be sent to its lab.

Trezor finds the report believable enough to warn buyers now. "Waiting for lab confirmation would leave CryptoBilis buyers exposed in the meantime," the company said.

No CryptoBilis buyer has reported losing funds to Trezor, which cannot see what customers hold in their wallets. The customer had moved his funds off the wallet before he found the board.

Trezor's advice covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis since March 2026, from any store that sold devices CryptoBilis supplied, including its store on Tokopedia:

If you already use the wallet, move your funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase as soon as possible. Restoring the old recovery phrase on another device does not help, because a tampered wallet could already have sent that phrase out.

If you have no other secure hardware wallet, move the funds for now to a software wallet or an exchange you know.

If you have not set up the wallet, do not set it up, and never type your existing recovery phrase into it.

Keep the CryptoBilis device and contact Trezor Support. Trezor will ship you a new device or give you a voucher that covers the cost of one.

If you are not sure where your device came from, check the seller's name on your receipt or contact Trezor Support.

As of October 30, Trezor had no reports involving any other reseller.

Owners cannot reliably check a device themselves and should not weigh or open it to try it, according to Trezor. The customer noticed a weight difference, but small differences can have other causes.

Trezor also expects scammers to use the incident to carry out phishing through fake emails, letters, and phone calls.

Trezor dropped CryptoBilis, its authorized reseller in Southeast Asia, on October 9, after hardware wallet maker Ledger began investigating losses among Ledger customers who had bought from CryptoBilis.

Ledger has since said that one affected customer's wallet contained an unauthorized hardware implant built to capture the recovery phrase during setup.

Trezor says the board reported in its Safe 5 appears to work like the implants seen in Ledger devices. Trezor will not compare the two while investigations continue, because each maker builds its devices differently. It does not know who is responsible.

Separate Police Advisory in Singapore

The Singapore Police Force said in an advisory on October 28 that Ledger hardware wallets bought from some retail stores in Singapore contained malicious hardware components. At least two cases have been reported since September 10.

The components could capture users' recovery phrases or private keys. Police investigations are ongoing, and Ledger is reviewing the affected cases.

articles.title: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit
articles.context: The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9...
articles.full_text:
A suspected Chinese nation-state actor chained the PHP2Shell exploit with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access to 25 Palo Alto Network (PAN) firewall and management servers.

The campaign rooted 25 PAN servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, according to an investigation by cyber defense platform provider Dream.

There was a particular focus on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment, resulting in persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

The Dream researchers noted a number of indicators of Chinese nation-state involvement in the campaign, including the narrow focus of the targeting.

“Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts,” they commented.

In addition, a number of tools used in the campaign, such as the large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi, and the internet reconnaissance platform FOFA, are Chinese-based services.

The Dream researchers highlighted the “automated and efficient” nature of the exploits, which took place from 23-24 October, including the targeting of specific PAN-OS versions.

“This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing,” they said.

“There was a clear-cut focus on government targets,” the researchers added.

Palo Alto Networks Confirm Compromise

Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 verified Dream’s findings in a blog published on October 29. It said that around .02% of its global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and were impacted by the campaign.

All the affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

“Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available,” Unit 42 wrote.

Palo Alto Networks has recommended that customers review its mitigations for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and apply patches immediately.

Chained Exploits Achieves Access in Under 15 Minutes

The attackers developed two separate exploits and chained them together into one request to target the PAN-OS servers. One of these was the widely reported ‘PHP2Shell’ exploit, made up of two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The exploit, which affects the PHP server-side programming language used by around 70% of websites, was leaked in October before a scheduled disclosure and release of patches. This resulted in many websites being taken down, including by governments, while emergency fixes were applied.

Read now: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

In the campaign identified by Dream, the threat actors tailored the exploit specifically for PAN-OS, targeting PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server.

This was chained to a second exploit, a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem known as Fragnesia and tracked as CVE-2026-46300. The attackers used this flaw to overwrite authentication rules, allowing root access to be achieved without a password.

“Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes,” Dream explained.

Threat Actor Narrows Focus to US Government Servers

Once the exploit was ready, the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. It narrowed down its targeting through a number of stages, using scanners to identify which devices were connected to the internet, their geographic location and what PAN-OS version they were running. The latter was focused on the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30.

This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls located in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.

These targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target.

Of the 240 targets, 24 firewalls were successfully rooted. For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker only planted a webshell and did not carry out any further post-exploitation activity.

However, the two other firewalls, which belonged a US government-affiliated environment, saw the attackers establish persistent access. This included building an 8-port reverse SSH tunnel, which connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure.

The attackers quickly used its access to one of the government servers to compromise a third government server via same PHP2Shell and Fragnesia exploit chain. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

As this third server centrally managed all of the government organization’s firewalls, compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials and network settings.

This allowed the threat actor to exploit the server’s connectivity to Active Directory to steal data such as credentials, although the researchers cannot determine the full extent of the accessed data.

“What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure,” they warned.

Dream said the campaign demonstrates that finding a vulnerability is only one part of identifying weaknesses across an organization’s systems, particularly with the growing use of chained exploits.

“Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise,” the firm added.

articles.title: Why Urgent Security Fixes Aren't Fixed. Observe, Prove, Act, Confirm Gets Them Moving
articles.context: The alert is critical
articles.full_text:
The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything.

Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits.

Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts.

The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect

Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today.

In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments.

Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today.

Figure 1. Operational pressures and configuration drift can delay enforcement.

Build Confidence Before Enforcement

Safe remediation follows four stages: Observe, Prove, Act, and Confirm. Evidence carries the proposed response through each stage, with review and approval where required.

Observation starts with data your security and IT systems already produce. Vulnerability findings, IPS traffic, device utilization, endpoint policies, and configuration states show what surrounds the proposed change.

Then comes proof, and the method fits the technology. An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode, giving teams evidence about false positives and performance before it progresses to Prevent. Operating system hardening can use a selected test group, with each host rechecked after execution. Endpoint settings can be assessed against the vendor's hardening baseline.

The decision becomes specific to your environment. Security teams explain the protection they expect. Infrastructure and application owners judge the effect on the systems they run.

Figure 2. Validation connects environmental evidence with approval, execution, and confirmation.

Use Existing Controls While Waiting For a Permanent Fix

Patching remains essential for addressing the underlying vulnerability. Testing, coordination, and deployment schedules can extend the time before a patch reaches production, creating a period when additional protection may be needed.

An existing IPS signature or virtual patch can help block the relevant exploit path during that period. Correlating vulnerability data with control coverage shows whether a suitable protection exists and whether it is inactive, in Detect mode, or already enforced.

That context helps teams select the response. A protection awaiting enforcement may be a candidate for validation and activation. An exposure without a compensating control may require urgent patching or another action.

The remediation record should distinguish interim protection from a permanent fix. A compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while the underlying vulnerability remains open and requires follow through.

Keep Approval and Execution Connected

Once an action has been evaluated, organizations can require approval of its scope or permit automated execution through configured workflows. The approved change then runs through the system responsible for the affected control.

IPS changes can use the security management server, operating system hardening can use existing patch management infrastructure, and supported endpoint changes can use the vendor API. This approach lets teams work through the technologies already deployed.

Confirmation completes the process. Policy installation can establish that an IPS protection reached enforcement. Host checks can verify a hardening change. Execution records can show failed or pending actions that still need attention, alongside the user, timestamp, and associated exposure.

Measure the Protection That Follows

Success should include evidence that the intended protection is active after execution. Subsequent security events can show whether a newly enabled control blocked activity associated with the exposure.

Across the measured organizations, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. Over one month, protections applied through remediation subsequently blocked 703.56 million attacks, including 21 million within 24 hours of remediation. These results describe the analyzed environments and provide evidence of protection following enforcement.

Figure 3. Remediation outcomes across the environments measured in the white paper.

Make Safe Remediation Part of Exposure Management

Prioritization establishes where action should begin. Safe remediation gives teams a controlled path for carrying that decision into production, with evidence supporting the proposed change and confirmation showing its result.

Check Point Exposure Management connects exposure prioritization with environmental validation, controlled execution, and confirmation through existing security technologies. Security teams can use that process to reduce exposure while evaluating the operational impact of each response.

Download Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to explore the framework, validation methods, and measured outcomes behind this approach.

articles.title: British intelligence agency misplaced 'thousands' of storage devices, years later still can't say how many
articles.context: " The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect...
articles.full_text: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report, the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA). "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register: "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets, and UK police losing thousands of devices, too. The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report. There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ. IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information. However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product." The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material. Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation. GCHQ was also questioned after a software bug in a web app "used by a relatively small section of the public" misidentified individuals thought to be participating in terrorist activities. The agency identified and reported the flaw in the software, which it used for "target discovery work," and although it only affected a small number of individuals, the errors led to five port stops made under the Terrorism Act and caused "serious prejudice" to the victims. A port stop, for the uninitiated, involves law enforcement detaining a suspect at a UK port, airport, train station, or within one mile of the Northern Ireland border, and can be carried out without suspicion. Once detained, individuals have a legal responsibility to provide passwords to their electronic devices, which can be seized for up to seven days, and in some cases have their biometric markers taken. Failure to comply can lead to a three-month prison term. IPCO ruled, however, that there was ultimately no error made as defined by the IPA. “This is because the activity was lawfully authorised under an interception warrant and the adoption of an unintentionally and unforeseeably imperfect target discovery methodology did not constitute such an error,” the report stated. Despite the agency’s vast technical expertise, IPCO said that the issue affecting the software was not foreseeable. GCHQ was not the only offender among the UK intelligence community (UKIC), with MI5's mishandling of the infamous Agent X case taking center stage in the report. Agent X was an anonymous MI5 informant whose real identity has never been publicly released. A secret inquiry by IPCO as well as the report revealed that MI5 managed Agent X despite knowing he was a violent misogynist obsessed with extreme violence. Lord Leveson said "the case of Agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as Commissioner," after MI5 gave false evidence to the High Court and Investigatory Powers Tribunal to protect a foreign neo-Nazi informant who was under police investigation for abusing his partner, referred to publicly as "Beth." ®

articles.title: Binance Hit by Record-Breaking $6.3bn Hack in Largest Cryptocurrency Heist in History
articles.context: Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6
articles.full_text:
Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6.3bn of cryptocurrency being stolen.

The Chinese-founded, Dubai-headquartered and Delaware-registered company said it has frozen $3bn of stolen funds and that it will cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

According to a company statement on October 30, its investigation suggested that an attacker's entry point may have been a compromised Binance development and operations (DevOps) engineer's laptop.

This allegedly allowed the attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

However, Binance has since revised that assessment and said its subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach.

"This was a complex attack," the company said, adding that it was working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other industry partners to establish the full circumstances as well as identify and recover affected assets.

Binance has not yet provided a definitive account of the attack, saying it is still gathering the facts and will publish a comprehensive technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete.

The company has said it has found no evidence that any wallet private keys were leaked.

In its many updates on social media, the exchange has repeatedly stressed that customer funds remain safe, despite the scale of the incident. It has also promised to publish an updated proof of reserves once remediation work is complete, providing customers with an updated view of the assets held against user balances.

Three world-leading cryptocurrency analysis firms, TRM Labs, Elliptic and Chainalysis have attributed the attack with “high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.

articles.title: Syrian Hacker Behind Fake Tweet That Triggered $136 Billion Market Drop Gets 42 Months in Prison
articles.context: An early study of the group, published by the OpenNet Initiative, found no credible evidence directly linking the attackers to the Syrian government beyond the unspoken support...
articles.full_text:
Ahmad Umar Agha, a Syrian Electronic Army hacker known online as "Th3Pr0," has been sentenced by a U.S. federal court to 42 months in prison for his role in a hacking conspiracy that targeted Western news outlets.

The conspiracy was organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's inner circle, including the commander of Syria's General Intelligence Directorate, the U.S. Justice Department said on October 29.

The pro-Assad Syrian Electronic Army began its attacks in 2011. Its members sent phishing emails to steal employees' passwords, then used those passwords to deface websites, redirect web traffic, and hijack social media accounts, according to a 2014 FBI affidavit.

On April 23, 2013, the group hijacked the Associated Press's Twitter account and posted a false report that President Barack Obama had been injured in two explosions at the White House.

Twitter's message confirming a password reset for that account was sent to a Gmail account used primarily by Agha, the affidavit says.

The Justice Department said Agha carried out that hack, which caused a temporary $136 billion drop in the value of stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Agha later told Business Insider that a big drop in the Dow "was our goal of that hack attack" and that "it was a big victory for us."

Agha was first charged in June 2014 in a complaint that remained secret until March 2016. That month, the FBI added him and co-defendant Firas Dardar to its Cyber's Most Wanted list with a $100,000 reward. A federal grand jury indicted both men in May 2018.

Court Watch reported in December 2025 that Agha was in U.S. custody and had appeared in federal court the month before.

Three earlier public documents in the case do not describe Syrian officials organizing or leading the group: the 2014 FBI affidavit, the Justice Department's March 2016 announcement of the charges, and its May 2018 announcement of the indictment.

In the 2016 announcement, the department said the group acted "in support of" the Syrian government.

An early study of the group, published by the OpenNet Initiative, found no credible evidence directly linking the attackers to the Syrian government beyond the unspoken support any such group would need to operate on Syrian networks.

In announcing the sentence, the department also said the conspiracy collected intelligence for Assad's government, which fell in December 2024. "Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad's regime to silence reporting on the regime's atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders," said John A. Eisenberg, Assistant Attorney General for National Security.

In all, Agha hacked about 47 Western media outlets, businesses, non-profit groups, and U.S. and allied government bodies, the department said.

He got into the company that hosted the U.S. Marine Corps recruiting website and redirected its visitors to an image urging Marines to refuse their orders and fight alongside the Syrian Army. About 3,500 potential visitors saw that image instead of recruiting material.

He also twice tried to take over the White House's social media accounts by stealing White House staff email passwords. Once, he got into staff email but failed to trick other staff into giving him access.

The FBI affidavit describes the group breaking into a White House staff member's personal email account in July 2013 and says no official White House account was compromised.

Many victims spent large sums on cleanup and security upgrades, according to court filings cited by the department. One company that supplies online publishers with content, ads, and links lost about $35,000 a day for about six months. A global non-profit group lost $480,000, including about $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, and had to retrain more than 800 staff members.

Dardar remains a fugitive, the department said. He was also charged in a separate case with Peter Romar, a Syrian national then living in Germany. Romar was extradited to the U.S. and pleaded guilty in 2016.

articles.title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
articles.context: More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings
articles.full_text:
More than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents, have had their details published online by a group of hacktivists.

As TechCrunch reports, the leaked records include the names, job titles, work email addresses, phone numbers, abd office locations.

More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Around 10,000 ICE employees have had their records breached, and almost 1,000 members of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

WIRED reports that the massive leak includes staff who work undercover, as well as in other sensitive areas such as those engaged in wiretapping and the interception of communications.

A hacktivist group calling itself "Department of Peace" says that the data was taken from an Okta single sign-on system that staff use to log onto the central network of the US Department of Homeland Security. Okta for its part says that it has not seen any evidence that its own systems have been compromised.

The data reveals which tools and services particularly individuals can access. Alongside everyday office software, these include Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, the phone and social media analysis tool PenLink, and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by immigration agents.

Explaining its justification for the data breach, "Department of Peace" wrote:

"They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs."

The leaked data has been published online, under the title "Icepick", and can be either downloaded via a torrent or accessed via a web interface - making it significantly easier for curious parties to search.

One threat intelligence expert told WIRED that, if authentic, the leaked data was "an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS," and could help adversaries identify vulnerable personnel or compromise ongoing investigations.

An obvious concern is that the leaked contact details could be used in phishing attacks that target employees, or could potentially put agents in physical danger. Clearly anyone whose details have been exposed through the incident would be wise to treat unexpected emails, texts, and phone calls with caution - and be particularly wary of any communications that claim to come from IT support or ask for a login to be approved.

Earlier this year the same group of hacktivists claimed to have breached the US Department of Homeland Security and accessed contracts between DHS, ICE, and more than 6000 firms including the likes of L3Harris, Raytheon, Palantir, Microsoft, and Oracle.

Explaining their motivation for that breach, the hackers referred to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by federal agents in Minneapolis.

"Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I'm releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they're working on."

There has been a long string of cybersecurity incidents affecting US government personnel. For instance, in September the notorious ShinyHunters hacking group claimed to have stolen personal details related to nearly every employee of the FBI, and the records of millions of serving and former US military personnel were reportedly stolen from the Pentagon's human resources unit.

articles.title: As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward
articles.context: As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about...
articles.full_text:
Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

FrostyNeighbor APT Attacks Its Neighbors

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Continue to Treat Belarus as Its Own Entity

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

articles.title: In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security
articles.context: 5B+ valuation for entire firm, though portion sold not specified Malware Month Ten years since the first corp ransomware, Mikko Hyppönen sees no end in sight On the plus side,...
articles.full_text: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses. The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure. When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox, to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states, and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker. ®
