articles.title: OpenCode User Hit with Hostile Backlash After Reporting Free AI Loophole
articles.context: Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration
articles.full_text:
An OpenCode user who reported a loophole in its free AI usage limits became the target of harassment, including comments encouraging suicide, from people who blamed the disclosure for cutting off their supply of free AI. The GitHub thread has since been deleted, although an earlier version remains available through the Wayback Machine.

OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that helps developers write, edit, and run code from a terminal, IDE, or desktop app. The MIT-licensed software can connect to commercial AI providers or locally hosted models. Its developer, Anomaly, also offers hosted model access, including free models with usage limits, and paid enterprise features such as centralized configuration and SSO integration. The reported bypass concerned the allowances on the free hosted models.

The report drew a flood of hostility in the project’s public issue tracker, with warm pillow wishes among the mildest responses. Other participants unleashed the kind of abuse that would ordinarily get someone banned from an open source project, openly encouraging suicide and pressing the reporter for identifying information.

A Call for a Fix Turned Into a Pitch for the Bypass #

The report, opened on June 28, described limits tied to an IP address. Switching to a different address through a VPN allegedly restored access while preserving the coding session. The author claimed to have automated the process and kept DeepSeek V4 Flash and MiMo V2.5 running for weeks. They proposed tying limits to accounts and detecting rapid IP changes. The account was created 13 days before the report and has no public repositories, a sparse history consistent with a throwaway account.

In an odd reversal, the author inexplicably closed the issue as completed on July 31, then reopened it on August 24 to promote the very workaround they had originally proposed fixing. They complained about the available free models and said they wanted people who could not afford subscriptions to build more with them.

Three days later, the reporter claimed to have run 130 agents across concurrent sessions, hitting usage limits six times in four to five hours and continuing by changing IP addresses. By then, the author was advertising the same behavior they had initially proposed preventing.

The same technique was being discussed elsewhere. A September 5 Hacker News commenter described OpenCode’s per-IP limits and told readers that “if you get some high-quality proxies you can get basically unlimited agent compute.” The comment did not reference the GitHub issue, but it shows the workaround had circulated beyond that thread before the late-October backlash.

On October 1, OpenCode collaborator rekram1-node responded that enforcing limits without authentication was difficult and that abuse undermined the effort to let anyone try a coding agent at no cost.

“Broadcasting this isn't very helpful, it only serves to harm,” the collaborator wrote before closing the issue. The response did not announce a fix.

Commenters Attacked the Reporter and Kept Trading Workarounds #

In late October, users traded conflicting accounts of whether changing IP addresses still restored access. Some said it had stopped working, while others offered additional workarounds. The attacks on the reporter escalated alongside those exchanges.

One GitHub commenter accused the author of gaining nothing from the disclosure, adding, “thanks for ruining it for us.” Other commenters wished suffering on the reporter, and at least two encouraged suicide.

The pile-on also included a supposed million-dollar reward. A commenter claiming to represent OpenCode offered the money if the reporter supplied their address. Replies joined in requesting identifying information, including the reporter’s “government name.” There is no evidence that the offer came from OpenCode.

Later replies quoted a participant telling others to stop harassing the reporter, only to accuse that person of being the author posting from another account. Other commenters challenged the reporter’s reversal, pointing out that they had first recommended closing the loophole, then reopened the issue and described using it extensively.

The discussion became a mix of personal attacks, arguments over the reporter’s motives, and requests for help keeping the bypass working. Some blamed the disclosure for losing access even as others continued to claim success. It’s unclear whether OpenCode changed its enforcement in response to the report.

The blame also spread to Reddit. In a post titled “The End of Long Free OpenCode Sessions”, the author complained that sessions had shrunk from hours to one or two prompts and claimed IP-switching workarounds no longer worked. “I didn't even know about this VPN bypass stuff, people like you ruined it for us,” one commenter told the Reddit poster. A reply redirected the blame with a link to the aforementioned deleted GitHub issue.

Others welcomed the prospect of tighter restrictions. “Well, if this helps my paid subscription to work much better, then it’s more than welcome,” another participant wrote.

The thread offered no settled explanation for the restrictions. Its author asserted that OpenCode now tracked hardware IDs and account metrics, without supplying evidence, while another commenter said changing a cellular IP still worked.

VPN Users Reported Access Problems #

Reports of disrupted access predated the October 27 release. In an October 22 Reddit thread, users said free models were blocked after little activity, including users who said they were not using a VPN. An October 23 post described changing IP addresses successfully for two months before the workaround recently stopped helping.

In another Reddit discussion, a user said a longstanding VPN setup now produced a daily-limit message immediately upon opening OpenCode.

“I think the IP detection may be a bit over zealous?” the user wrote. After another participant attributed the restrictions to VPN-based abuse, the original poster asked why the offering was described as a free tier when it appeared available only to people without VPNs. Another commenter said changing servers still worked.

OpenCode contributor Tarquinen addressed network-level blocking in a separate GitHub issue, explaining that the restriction applied to the connecting network address.

“Shared VPN addresses are often flagged, and we can't make exceptions for individual users,” the contributor wrote.

The experiences remained inconsistent. In an October 27 Reddit discussion, one commenter reported usable access through a dedicated-IP VPN, while another described very low limits without using a VPN.

The Fix Status Remains Unclear #

OpenCode made several infrastructure changes in October, including routing free-model requests through a newer inference service and tightening how it handles client IP information. An October 13 change addressed spoofed IP headers, but that is different from switching to a genuinely different IP address through a VPN. Whether those changes closed the reported loophole remains unclear.

The October 27 v2.2.0 release added visibility into usage and budgets but did not announce a fix for the reported bypass. Enforcement could also have changed on the hosted service independently of an application release.

The final comments preserved before the thread’s deletion still offered conflicting accounts of whether the workaround functioned. The thread remained accessible on October 28, after the release, and was subsequently deleted without a public explanation.

Socket contacted OpenCode for comment on the reported bypass and the thread’s removal but had not received a response at publication time.

Demand for AI Compute Accelerates #

The rush to code with AI has reached a fever pitch, with developers chasing more capable models, longer sessions, and enough compute to keep fleets of agents running. AI demand is squeezing memory supplies and driving prices higher. At the high end of the local hardware market, Apple’s newly available 512GB Mac Studio configuration reached an eye-watering $29,799 with 16TB of storage.

In the OpenCode thread, that hunger for compute curdled into a pile-on. The reporter went from proposing a fix to boasting about running 130 agents through the loophole. Other users blamed them for spoiling the arrangement, hurled abuse, and kept asking how to get the free models working again. The thread captures the AI coding gold rush at its most frantic, with users scrambling to keep their agents running and searching for the next route around the limits.

articles.title: Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board
articles.context: Related: 3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability This type of intel is free and available from sources like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security...
articles.full_text:
ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — A threat model should be a starting organizing principle for any security program. But rather than investing in a 200-page high-dollar threat model report, one longtime chief information security officer (CISO) argues that "four questions on a white board," can provide any team with an actionable plan forward.

Lora Vaughn, cybersecurity expert, former CISO, and now founder of her own consulting firm, The Vaughn Group, said that over her many years leading cybersecurity programs, she has developed a wickedly simple four-question threat modeling exercise that can be used in a wide range of organizations, be it the "National Security Agency (NSA) or your friendly neighborhood small-to-medium business (SMB)."

The answers, she said, can then offer a road map for investment decisions. That requires further exploration, she acknowledges, given there's always a new technology right around the corner that promises to drive down the cost of cybersecurity investment in enterprises. And reality must be balanced with industry hype.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

For instance, around 2015, the move to the cloud was supposed to put the onus on providers like AWS to protect enterprises. What came next was a flood of misconfigurations and misunderstandings about who owned which part of security. By 2018, the buzzword was "automation." But teams quickly learned that automating anything required defining buttoned-downed processes first — often a prohibitively time-consuming exercise that pushed many of these project timelines out. By 2021, zero-trust networks were on everyone's mind. But that turned out to be less of a prescription and more of a customizable, guiding principle; and, architecting a true zero-trust environment requires a big investment in systems that would prove to be a much longer journey than many in the sector had hoped.

And regarding the current zeitgeist, handing over enterprise security to an agentic AI model is a "fantasy," according to Vaughn, speaking from the stage while presenting her four-question threat model at ISC2 Strategic Congress in Denver this week.

"AI is a force multiplier," Vaughn said. "It just multiplies what you already have. Zero times anything is still zero. Math is undefeated."

Bottom line: Once the threat modeling is done, choose your path wisely, and with your eyes wide open. And recognize that it's an ongoing cycle. "Refresh the threat model quarterly," Vaughn added. "Or after any big change."

Threat Modeling With 4 Questions on a White Board

What would hurt most on Monday?

Ask yourself, if you walked into work at 8 a.m. Monday morning, what would be the worst-case scenario(s)? For example, is it a ransomware attack that could result in the leak of sensitive information? What about one that locks up production systems? Mass pwning of firewalls and edge devices? What about a business email compromise (BEC) that results in a $100,000 bank transfer to attackers? Would falling for the North Korean fake worker scheme cause big problems?

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

Vaughn stressed that once identified, these should be ranked by pain to the business. She added, five to eight "painful" items are a reasonable number to determine.

Vaughn ranks risk in three categories: existential, painful, and annoying. Existential risk means that a breach would close the doors of the business. Painful risk equates to business disruption with associated costs and bad press. Annoying risk is something that can be fixed semi-easily.

Who actually attacks an organization like yours?

A key piece of determining your risk profile is understanding who sees you as a target. Do state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups have your organization in their sights? Or is your business most likely to be targeted by BEC scams? Are ransomware affiliates trying to find a way into your systems? Do you have a large inventory of software or appliances that are high on attackers' hit lists? How is your patching hygiene, and do you have bugs that are known to be exploited?

Related:3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability

This type of intel is free and available from sources like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), but can also come from private threat intelligence services. Vaughn recommended that CISOs and security leaders lean on their vertical Information and Analysis Centers (ISACs) as well.

"That’s your most valuable resource," Vaughn said. "And it's free."

Where do the first two lists overlap?

Items that fall between both the "worst-case scenario" and "who's targeting you" lists are where teams need to start first. "Every overlap is a scenario," Vaughn explained. "Write one sentence for each: who, how, against what, and costing what?"

What is the cheapest control that breaks the attack scenario?

In terms of a BEC attack, Vaughn pointed out a simple phone call verification could be the most effective prevention, and it costs nothing. "Find where the attack stops for the least money," Vaughn advised. "Spend in that order."

Additional free controls that actually work, according to Vaughn, are multifactor authentication (MFA) everywhere, which is something she adds is "non-negotiable" and urges CISOs to "fight for." An asset inventory is also invaluable, even if it's just a spreadsheet, and of course it "beats doing nothing." Patching bugs that have already been exploited, resisting the urge to give everyone admin credentials, and testing backups also make the list. And for ransomware, having backups isn't enough; network segmentation has to go along with it.

"If you can't restore from backups, or you don't have backups, you have hope," Vaughn said. "Hope is not a control."

She pointed out that nothing on this list of controls can be bought from a vendor. "There's no SKU for 'turn on MFA' and 'keep a spreadsheet,'" she added.

Taking the Threat Model Findings to Management

It might be tempting for cybersecurity teams to try and tackle these four questions on their own, but Vaughn said that including management in these conversations will help better align priorities to the broader business and will help management understand the potential fallout of not taking care of cybersecurity.

There are some best practices for doing this; for instance, Vaughn recommends linking spend to a business outcome: "If nobody funds a CVE, we stop shipping for a week," is one example she offered.

She also recommends bringing three spend options, with prices attached, and then making a recommendation for one. Additionally, Vaughn said CISOs and cyber teams should never promise "security," only reduced risk, and discuss investment decisions from that lens.

Offer, say, options that cost "$12K, $4K, or zero," she explained. "Zero means we accept the risk, so I recommend the $4K."

And once the decision is made, Vaughn suggested an email follow-up like, "Confirming we’re deferring X and accepting the risk of Y. Tell me if I got that wrong." That paper trail can prove invaluable following a compromise, she said.

articles.title: NIK C2 Malware Can Use Victims’ OpenAI Keys for AI Queries
articles.context: Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays...
articles.full_text:
A new AI-enabled malware framework has been found that can fall back on victims' own OpenAI API keys for artificial intelligence requests, charging the usage to the victim while obscuring who made the requests.

Cisco Talos observed the command-and-control (C2) framework, dubbed NIK C2, in the wild, according to research published on October 29.

Its Go-based implant gave attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging and surveillance capabilities, while an integrated OpenAI client let them send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.

NIK C2 Routes AI Requests Through Victim Machines

The AI capability is built into the implant rather than requiring operators to process collected information separately. Talos said attackers could supply a prompt and model choice through the C2 panel, with the implant sending the request to OpenAI from the victim's machine and returning the response to the operator.

If the operator supplied no key, the malware read an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable on the infected machine instead, which Talos called a deliberate design. An organization with an OpenAI API key configured on a compromised Windows system could therefore end up funding the attacker's AI requests.

Read more on AI API key abuse: Attackers Steal METR API Key and Burn $600,000 in AI Credits

Talos said OpenAI's billing system would charge the victim's payment method and its access logs would show the victim's key as the one making the requests, leaving no trace attributable to the attacker.

Malware Framework Combines Theft and Ransomware

Beyond its AI functionality, the Windows malware supported more than 52 commands covering credential theft, browser data collection, cryptocurrency wallets, Wi-Fi credentials, keylogging, screen capture and remote access. Talos said it also offered lateral movement and multiple defense-evasion capabilities.

The framework also contained a screen-locking ransomware module that displayed customized ransom demands in Bitcoin or the Tether stablecoin (USDT). Talos said the module encrypted no files, leaving no forensic trail of file-modification timestamps or encryption markers, and that a screen lock is considerably faster to deploy than file-encrypting ransomware.

The company said it observed at least three versions of the implant and found its infrastructure active during the research. That led it to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is a fully functional framework rather than a proof of concept.

Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows."

articles.title: Belgium's tax agency confirms cyberattack, pulls services offline
articles.context: FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while...
articles.full_text: Belgium's finance and tax agency has pulled "several" digital services offline after a cyberattack on the organization. FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while they start the initial investigations. "This measure helps limit the risks and makes it possible to carry out the necessary technical interventions to ensure the security of our systems," it said in a public announcement. FOD Financiën added that "this has consequences for tax deadlines in the near future," referring to the October 31 extended deadline to submit tax filings for specific types of income, such as sole traders and earnings from foreign companies. The agency confirmed the deadline will be extended to November 16, by which time MyMinfin, the platform through which such filings would normally be submitted, should be back up and running. The detail offered up in the public statement reflects the early stage of the investigation; not much is known, although there is nothing to suggest data was compromised. "Data protection is a top priority for the FOD Financiën," it said. "At present, there are no indications that a data breach has occurred or that data has been compromised. This aspect is also being closely investigated and followed up. "In the meantime, a large part of our other applications remains available with full or partial functionality. We are closely monitoring the situation and doing everything we can to make the affected services available again as soon as possible." Spokesperson Francis Adyns told local news outlets that the attack was thwarted within hours, and that it was unable to gain access to applications or data. "The attack could not be sufficiently expanded within our environment to take over applications or gain access to data," he told Nieuwsblad. "Elements that were potentially infected were isolated. As a result, MyMinfin, Tax-on-web, and Biztax went offline, but the hacking was successfully stopped. "The various services must be restored in an isolated environment. This requires considerable time to realize, with the necessary caution to rule out new risks." ®

articles.title: Malicious Firefox extensions impersonate popular crypto wallets
articles.context: Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets
articles.full_text:
Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets.

Once installed, the malicious extensions stole recovery phrases and private keys, which would provide the attacker with full control of a wallet.

A crypto wallet is an app, browser extension, or physical device that lets you manage cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin. Despite its name, it doesn’t actually hold your coins. Those are recorded on a blockchain, a shared digital record of transactions. Instead, the wallet manages the secret digital keys that let you access and spend them.

When you create a wallet, you may be given a recovery phrase: a list of words you can use to restore access. Write it down and store it offline. It’s a backup of your keys, not just an ordinary password. Anyone who gets hold of it can take control of your funds, which is why fake wallet extensions try to steal it.

Cybercriminals listed three fake wallet extensions on Firefox Add-ons, impersonating Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget. The genuine wallets offer extensions for other browsers: Jupiter lists Chrome, Brave, and Edge; Bitget’s extension is for Chrome; and Phantom says its Firefox extension is no longer supported.

The malicious extensions looked for 12-, 15-, 18-, and 24-word recovery phrases, as well as Ethereum and Solana private keys. They could read input fields, detect pasted text, and scan screens displaying recovery phrases.

A recovery phrase or private key is a bearer secret: whoever holds it controls the wallet and can move its assets. The Phantom variant’s backend logged captured secrets, sent them to a Telegram bot, and automatically moved funds to hardcoded payout addresses. Those addresses covered Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. The Phantom variant could read a phrase both when it was typed during import and when it was displayed on a reveal screen.

How to stay safe

Socket says all three listings were live on Firefox Add-ons during its analysis and have since been removed. But if you find one of these extensions in your Firefox browser, you should:

Remove the extension. Use the three-dot menu next to it and choose Remove.

If you ever entered a phrase or key, create a new wallet on a clean device and move your assets immediately. Treat the old wallet as compromised.

In the future, install wallets only from the vendor’s official website link, not from store search results.

The fake Phantom listing asked to access data on all websites and had no privacy policy. These are warning signs to look out for.

Use an up-to-date, real-time anti-malware solution that blocks malicious websites.

Malwarebytes blocks bonto.io subdomains

Never enter your recovery phrase on a website. Enter it only in the official wallet app when restoring. Wallet support will never ask for it.

Jupiter impersonator: add-on ID 3092666

articles.title: CREST Urges Whole-Ecosystem Approach to Financial Cyber Resilience
articles.context: CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and...
articles.full_text:
Cyber resilience in financial services should be built across the wider ecosystem of institutions, supervisors and specialist providers rather than treated solely as each institution's own responsibility, a new framework has argued.

CREST, the global non-profit accreditation body for the cybersecurity industry, said its whitepaper, Cyber Resilience in Financial Services: A Whole Ecosystem Approach, provides a maturity pathway for jurisdictions to assess their capabilities and coordinate improvements across three domains.

The paper, published on October 29, argued that weaknesses in shared infrastructure, technology providers, cyber firms or public authorities can undermine resilience across the wider financial system.

CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience

Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and demonstrating their controls work under pressure.

Financial supervisors are tasked with setting proportionate expectations, overseeing individual firms and understanding systemic risk, while cyber service providers are expected to deliver specialist advice, assessment, threat intelligence, testing and response capabilities.

The framework maps each domain through five stages of cyber maturity, with the three pathways planned together. Institutions progress from incomplete basic hygiene to advanced, threat-led assurance and continuous improvement. Supervisors move from mapping their sectors and establishing mandates to adaptive, cross-sector oversight, while providers progress from unvalidated services to specialist financial-sector capabilities.

CREST said the pathways are illustrative, not a new compliance standard. Its three priorities were ecosystem-wide measurement of maturity, a common language across the three domains and faster development wherever one part of the ecosystem lags.

Read more on financial-sector cyber regulation: FCA Updates Cyber Incident and Third-Party Reporting Rules

Framework Calls For Multi-Year Cyber Maturity Programs

CREST suggested supervisors or other market participants set out multi-year programs so the three domains develop in parallel, warning that requirements outpacing readiness can produce limited assurance. Its roadmap begins in years one and two with institutions mapping critical services and closing urgent hygiene gaps while supervisors publish a baseline and strategy.

Years three to five would bring independent assessment and risk-based testing for institutions, tiered requirements from supervisors and independent accreditation for providers. Years five to 10 would focus on threat-led penetration testing where proportionate, system-wide exercises and a diverse community of accredited specialist providers.

The whitepaper also warned that moving prematurely to mandate the highest international accreditations could shut out local providers where no route to accreditation exists. It pointed to measures including mentoring, partnerships, training and CREST's Cyber Accelerated Maturity Programme (CREST CAMP).

"Financial institutions, supervisors and cyber service providers each have a distinct role, and the strength of the system depends on their capability developing together," said CREST CEO Nick Benson.

articles.title: Shadow AI Across Government: It's Three Problems, Not One
articles.context: That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking
articles.full_text:
Most agencies and contractors now have a generative AI (GenAI) policy. Far fewer can tell you what their people are actually running.

That gap has a name. Like shadow information technology before it, Shadow AI is what happens when AI tools, services, and components enter an organization outside the processes meant to govern them. The difference is that shadow IT mostly showed up as an unapproved application.

Shadow AI can create risk at three points:

Data that leaves your environment.

AI-generated code your developers commit.

AI models and other components your builds pull down.

Those three are usually discussed as one risk. They are not. They have different failure modes, different owners, and almost no overlap in the controls that address them. An organization can have an excellent acceptable-use policy and still have no idea which AI models are running inside its own software.

None of which is an argument against adoption. The productivity gains are real, and the organizations getting the most from these tools are not the ones that tried to ban them. They are the ones that made the sanctioned path the easiest path to take. That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking.

Here is what each problem is, who owns it, and what closes it.

The Adoption Already Happened

Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that 45% of employees are now regular users of AI on corporate devices, authorized or not — up from 15% a year earlier. Two thirds of those users accessed AI services through non-corporate accounts, which means the activity is largely invisible to the organization paying for the device.

Shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action in the report's data loss prevention findings. And the most common category of data sent to external AI services is source code.

That last detail is the one worth sitting with, because it connects all three problems. Source code leaving is a disclosure problem. The same assistant that received it returns code and dependency choices that come back in. And the models behind these tools increasingly arrive as components inside your own applications.

One behavior, three exposures.

Problem One: What Goes Out

This is the problem most policies already address, and the one most people mean when they say Shadow AI. An employee pastes contract language, personnel data, or controlled unclassified information (CUI) into a public chatbot to summarize or rewrite it.

Ownership: Security and privacy teams, records officers, and acceptable-use policy owners.

Controls: Provide a sanctioned platform people prefer, use data loss prevention and network controls, name approved services, and give staff practical guidance.

Verizon's findings show why prohibitions alone may not work: employees may turn to personal accounts, moving AI use further out of view rather than stopping it.

For Department of War (DoW) components, this is already written down. DoW Instruction 8430.01 bars entering non-public departmental information into generative AI services unless the service resides on departmental systems and is approved for departmental use. Both conditions, not either.

What does not close it: anything in your software supply chain toolchain. No repository control, bill of materials, or scanner sees a developer paste code into a browser. If a vendor tells you otherwise, press on exactly which telemetry they are reading.

Problem Two: What Comes Back In

Your developers are using coding assistants. The output is unverified input, and the accountability for it does not transfer to the tool that produced it.

DoWI 8430.01 is explicit on this point for defense work: AI-generated code is treated as unverified, and developers and their teams remain fully accountable for what they ship. It also asks software efforts to maintain a record of the models, versions, and significant datasets used to generate or test software, kept with the software evidence package and treated as analogous to a software bill of materials (SBOM).

The subtler issue is that a coding assistant does not only write code. It chooses dependencies. An assistant suggesting a package is making a supply chain decision on your behalf, at a speed and volume no review process was designed for, which is a different problem from whether the code it wrote is correct. We covered that specific question in more depth earlier this month.

Who owns it: engineering leadership and application security.

What closes it is treating assistant output as you would a pull request from an unfamiliar contributor. Human review, software composition analysis (SCA) on everything it introduces, and a record of which models were in the loop, which is both a DoW requirement and the only way to answer the question later.

Problem Three: What Your Builds Pull Down

The third problem is the least discussed and the hardest to see after the fact: AI models and machine learning packages entering your environment as components.

Sonatype calls components retrieved straight from public repositories, bypassing the repository manager, shadow downloads. Sonatype Research Labs audited 9,658 Hugging Face requests across a set of customers in the first half of 2026, as part of our Beyond Traditional Packages report. Nearly 7% were blocked or rejected by policy. Of the 674 models blocked, 55% were stopped on model acceptability and 18% on security grounds, which says models are raising governance questions traditional policies were not built for.

A model is not like a library. It arrives as opaque weights, it may carry a license with terms on how its output can be used, and its published name tells you very little about what it was built from — open models are routinely fine-tuned, merged, quantized and re-released under a new publisher. Three federal exclusion orders now name a single model developer and reach products "developed using" its implementations, which makes model provenance a procurement question and not only an engineering one.

Who owns it: platform engineering and whoever runs your repository manager.

What closes it: one governed path in. Route model pulls through a proxy repository so every request is visible in one place, block direct downloads from the corporate network, and lock client configuration so the path cannot quietly be bypassed. Sonatype Firewall can then audit or quarantine models at that boundary before a developer gets them. Start in audit mode to see what your teams are actually pulling, then move to quarantine. At scan time, Sonatype Lifecycle flags a model as a derivative and names the foundation model it came from, and the AI Models Usage dashboard shows which applications are using models, with lineage, commit hash and publishing date.

That last piece matters for a reason beyond engineering. Joint guidance on AI and machine learning supply chain risks, co-sealed by the National Security Agency and seven other national agencies, tells organizations to require an AI bill of materials from vendors as a condition of procurement. Asking your suppliers for something you cannot produce yourself is a difficult position to hold.

What To Do About It

Pick your lane. These are three different jobs and they rarely belong to the same person.

If you own policy. Name specific sanctioned services rather than categories, and pair the policy with a platform people prefer to the alternative. Then confirm your inventory obligation is being met. OMB Memorandum M-26-05 makes each agency head responsible for the security of software on the agency network and directs agencies to maintain a complete inventory. Models are software.

If you own compliance. The obligations people associate with the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) did not go away when Phase 2 was suspended. DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171 and Supplier Performance Risk System scoring are unchanged, and annual affirmations remain in effect. An attestation that does not match the environment is the exposure, and that gap is exactly what undeclared AI tooling creates.

If you own the platform. Start with visibility, not enforcement. Put a proxy in front of model pulls, turn Sonatype Firewall on in audit mode, and spend two weeks looking at what comes back before you block anything. Most teams are surprised, and the surprise is the business case. Then make it continuous — an inventory taken once begins decaying the day it is produced, and the reason to route intake through a single path is that the record maintains itself rather than becoming an annual exercise.

Shadow AI is no longer a question of whether people will adopt these tools. They already have. The question is whether you can identify:

Which services receive your data.

Which models help write your code.

Which models run inside the software you ship.

Three questions, three owners, one answer: you can only govern what you can see.

See how Sonatype helps federal teams govern the AI models and open source components entering their software.

Written by Tom Tapley

Tom Tapley specializes in securing software supply chains for Federal environments, bringing deep expertise in aligning agency security, compliance, and operational requirements with modern technology solutions. With a proven track record in supporting mission-critical systems, he bridges the gap between evolving federal mandates and scalable, secure software practices.

Tags

software bill of materials government Open Source Department of Defense SBOM Sonatype Lifecycle federal Sonatype Firewall generative AI artificial intelligence AI Sonatype Research

articles.title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
articles.context: 5B+ valuation for entire firm, though portion sold not specified Malware Month Ten years since the first corp ransomware, Mikko Hyppönen sees no end in sight On the plus side,...
articles.full_text: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement, Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®

articles.title: [New Threat Trend Data] When Bad Actors Use Reality Against Us
articles.context: In Q3 2026, attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure than in Q2, and threat actors are using native platform features to host fake developer...
articles.full_text:
“Is it real?” has become a common question across our digital lives thanks to the rise of AI-generated content.

A fair one, with deepfakes and AI-produced imagery flooding nearly every channel we use daily. A skeptical eye is a must, but our most recent Phishing Threat Trends Report reveals why that might not even be enough.

Our 8th Phishing Threat Trends Report tracks how attackers stopped faking infrastructure and started borrowing it. Modern phishing has no need to fool filters with lookalike domains when it can sit directly on trusted ones. This shift runs through every finding in this report: campaigns are routed through hyperscalers, attackers harvest API keys from trusted platforms, and session hijacking via refresh tokens that render "change your password" meaningless. The only thing left that is fake is the premise.

Overall, phishing volume rose 29.8% in 2026 compared to 2025, and one dangerous email now lands in every 733 an organization receives. The bigger shift is not how much arrives but how it is built. Attackers have stopped faking infrastructure and started borrowing it. Check out Volume 8 of our Phishing Threat Trends Report to see what that looks like and where security teams should focus next.

Download the full report here. Read on for some highlights:

Targeting Sharpens as Mass Phishing Declines

Mass, low-effort phishing is fading. Mobile-focused attacks fell 47.3% and 419 scams fell 31.3% compared to 2025. Meanwhile, lures built on research and personal selection are rising. Spear phishing is up 41.1%, scouting is up 33.7%, and company impersonation is up 28%.

Links remain the dominant payload at 66.2%, including QR codes. Attachments account for 19.1%, and nearly one in three phishing attachments is a PDF.

Attackers Are Stealing Permission, Not Passwords

Authentication phishing goes after the sign-in itself. Instead of capturing a password, attackers use device-code logins and OAuth consent to obtain persistent access. In Q3 2026, authentication phishing accounted for 2% of link-based phishing from toolkits, and 25.6% of link-bearing attacks had MFA-bypass capability.

Because the stolen access is a token or a permission rather than a password, a password reset does not end the compromise. Lures for device-code campaigns are also moving from email to Microsoft Teams, through compromised accounts, fake calendar invites, and missed-voicemail alerts.

AI Platforms Become the Newest Phishing Host

Attackers are increasingly sitting on trusted AI domains rather than spoofing their logos. Attacks impersonating AI brands rose 228% between April and August 2026. In Q3 2026, attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure than in Q2, and threat actors are using native platform features to host fake developer consoles, sign-in prompts, and download hubs.

The primary goals are credential and API key harvesting, quota fraud, and malware delivered through on-platform app downloads. For organizations, the risk extends beyond people. Stolen API keys and OAuth grants can turn AI agents into attack tools, redirecting their actions and siphoning the data they process.

Secure Email Gateways Miss Many Phish

Email security is catching less than it should. 41.3% of phishing emails bypass secure email gateways, peaking at 48.3% in July 2026. Real domains, valid certificates, and genuine consent screens are now part of the attack, so filters built on lookalike detection fall short. In fact, 58.1% of the phish that gateways miss still pass DMARC.

When the filter misses, the employee becomes the last line of defense. Real-time coaching and continuous training keep that layer working, especially as lures get more personal and more convincing.

What This Means for Security Leaders

The pattern is consistent. Phishing has moved from fake infrastructure to borrowed infrastructure, and from broad campaigns to targeted, automated ones. Trust signals alone are no longer proof of safety.

Standard secure email gateways and native mail filters were built for a threat landscape that no longer exists. As adversaries abuse genuine cloud infrastructure, deploy specialized reverse-proxy toolkits, and hijack trusted AI platforms, perimeter-based defenses simply cannot keep pace with localized, highly targeted attacks. Your security stack needs to be as agile, adaptive, and geographically aware as the threat actors themselves.

By moving toward an integrated platform fueled by deep behavioral analytics and real-time threat intelligence, your security posture shifts from reactive filtering to continuous, automated defense. Delivering real-time behavioral coaching at the exact moment of risk transforms your workforce into an active line of defense, securing both your human workforce and your autonomous AI tooling across every global operation.

Download the full report to see the regional, industry, and toolkit data behind these findings.

articles.title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
articles.context: A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain...
articles.full_text: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register. Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register. A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets. “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

articles.title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
articles.context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
articles.full_text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

articles.title: Have an older iPhone or iPad? Apple has a security update for you
articles.context: Apple’s latest updates include a fix for a CoreGraphics bug that may have been exploited in targeted attacks
articles.full_text:
Apple’s latest updates include a fix for a CoreGraphics bug that may have been exploited in targeted attacks. The fix is now available for older iPhones and iPads.

Apple released security updates on October 26. Apple first fixed the flaw in iOS 26.7.1. Its latest updates also bring the fix to older devices that can’t run iOS 26, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad.

The iOS 18.7.11 update is a backport: it brings a fix from a newer software version to an older one. Here, Apple has made the fix available to older devices running iOS 18, so they can be protected without upgrading to an operating system they don’t support.

Updates for your particular device

The table below shows which updates are available and links to Apple’s security information for each one.

Name and information link

Available for

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 4th generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 2nd generation and later, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later

iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11

iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation

macOS Golden Gate 27.2

macOS Golden Gate

How to update your Apple devices

How to update your iPhone or iPad

For iOS and iPadOS users, here’s how to check if you’re using the latest software version:

Go to Settings > General > Software Update. You will see if there are updates available and be guided through installing them.

Turn on Automatic Updates if you haven’t already—you’ll find it on the same screen.

How to update your Mac

To update macOS on any supported Mac, use the Software Update feature, which Apple designed to work consistently across all recent versions. Here are the steps:

Click the Apple menu in the upper-left corner of your screen.

Choose System Settings (or System Preferences on older versions).

Select General in the sidebar, then click Software Update on the right. On older macOS, just look for Software Update directly.

Your Mac will check for updates automatically. If updates are available, click Update Now (or Upgrade Now for major new versions) and follow the on-screen instructions. Before you upgrade to macOS Tahoe 26, please read these instructions.

Enter your administrator password if prompted, then let your Mac finish the update (it might need to restart during this process).

Keep your Mac plugged in and connected to the internet until the update is done.

How to update your Safari browser

Safari updates are included with macOS updates, so installing the latest version of macOS will also update Safari. To check manually:

Open the Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update.

If you see a Safari update listed separately, click Update Now to install it.

Restart your device when prompted.

Technical details

The headline bug is CVE-2026-86950, in CoreGraphics, Apple’s framework for drawing graphics, images and PDF content. It’s an out-of-bounds write flaw, where software writes data outside the memory set aside for it. The result is that “processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution.”

Apple says it is aware of a report that the flaw may have been exploited in an “extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals” on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

That wording indicates Apple believes the bug was used in real attacks against a limited group of users.

Usually, journalists, activists and officials are the targets of this kind of attack. If you think you could be a target of highly sophisticated spyware, you should update, restart your phone, and consider applying Apple’s Lockdown Mode.

Scammers know more about you than you think.
