On the infrastructure front, Arctic Wolf noted a move from throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, especially ".top" domains, and provided data on their prevalence. The vendor stated that approximately half of observed cases involving paid domains used .top domains.

For naming, attackers would reach out with "(Internal)" appended to the display name to trick the victim that a message is coming from within the company, even though Teams labels the sender as "external" simultaneously. The names will also frequently use friendly sounding names (Arctic Wolf offered Liam, Scott McGhee, and Matthew as examples) after labels like "IT Support" and "IT Service Desk."

Other markers observed included naming conventions specific to the target's locale ("Supporte TI" for French- and Spanish-speaking organizations), and the use of 100 different emojis in attacker display names.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Get Ahead of Email Bombing Social Engineering Attacks

Arctic Wolf noted that prior to engaging with victims, the attackers initiate a one-on-one chat to avoid group conversations, which Microsoft records in its telemetry as the ChatCreated event. Arctic Wolf assesses this to be the primary detection point for defenders setting alerts.

The vendor also recommended setting an allowlist for trusted external organizations, blocking chats with unmanaged or Teams consumer accounts, disabling the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users, blocking federation with trial-only tenants, and hardening your remote access path.

In a nod to Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Arctic Wolf pointed out that it may also be wise to alert staff to the social engineering aspects behind these campaigns, including outlining exactly how IT reaches out, what these contacts look like (and what they do not look like), and to train users how to read the external sender tag in Teams to identify possible red flags. Microsoft Teams also includes end-user reporting in the application itself.

That said, the technique could yet progress further.

"We have also recently observed campaigns combining Teams chat abuse with ClickFix-style social engineering, suggesting that the technique continues to evolve and is being integrated with other intrusion methods," Moore says.

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading that the company helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through layered, built-in protections that, for example, can let administrators block external Teams users. The spokesperson adds that, next month, "Teams is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users."

articles.title: The strategy behind the shield.
articles.context: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats. CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known...
articles.full_text:
CISA unveils its 2030 cyber strategy. PHP2Shell exploits are in the wild. HHS preserves healthcare security requirements. Microsoft offers buyouts amid its AI spending spree. A cyberattack disrupts New Mexico hospitals. Google’s Finnish data center plans hit an environmental roadblock. Blue Initiative tracks maritime vulnerabilities. A Chinese national faces charges in a $37 million cryptocurrency scam. Our guest is Cal Al-Dhubaib, host of the new Authorized Intelligence podcast. Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Today is Tuesday October 27th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA plans to defend, harden and prevail.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has unveiled CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy aimed at strengthening national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure resilience against cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats.

The plan rests on three pillars. Defend focuses on securing networks, operational technology, software supply chains, and emerging technologies, including quantum computing and advanced AI. Harden emphasizes turning threat intelligence into action, improving risk prioritization, and accelerating incident response. Prevail seeks to strengthen national resilience through regional partnerships, emergency communications, and coordinated planning.

The strategy also prioritizes resilient 5G and 6G networks and satellite communications.

CISA will review its existing capabilities within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan within 180 days, and report on its progress within a year.

PHP2Shell is officially under active exploitation.

CISA has added two critical PHP vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell, to its catalog of actively exploited flaws. The bugs could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

Researchers observed widespread exploitation attempts before patches were released October 21, though early attempts reportedly failed. Subsequent honeypot activity confirmed successful exploitation in the wild.

Federal civilian agencies have until Thursday to patch their systems.

HHS scales back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements.

Federal health regulators have scaled back plans to eliminate privacy and security certification requirements for electronic health records, following widespread objections from healthcare providers and industry groups.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ final rule eliminates 14 health IT certification criteria, down from the 34 originally proposed. All 13 core privacy and security requirements will remain intact, including standards for authentication and access controls.

Commenters warned that eliminating those safeguards could shift security responsibilities onto healthcare providers, particularly smaller and rural organizations with limited resources.

However, the rule does eliminate transparency and risk-management requirements for AI-powered clinical decision support tools. Those provisions required developers to disclose information about their systems’ capabilities, limitations, and potential risks.

HHS says the changes will save health IT developers more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs.

Most provisions take effect December 28, with others following in January.

Microsoft offers buyouts amidst AI-driven growth.

Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, roughly 27 percent of its workforce, as it balances soaring AI infrastructure spending with efforts to control costs.

The offers cover eligible workers in the United States, Canada, India, and Britain, including some employees at the vice president level.

Microsoft expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the September quarter, driven largely by data center investments supporting AI services.

The company previously offered voluntary retirement packages in April and announced 4,800 layoffs in July.

Some engineering, sales, and marketing teams are excluded from the latest program. Eligible employees have until early December to decide, with departures scheduled for December 31.

Microsoft says the initiative will provide flexibility as the company reshapes its workforce around AI-driven growth.

New Mexico hospitals divert patients following a cyberattack.

A cybersecurity incident disrupted operations across the University of New Mexico Health System on Monday, forcing ambulance diversions, canceled appointments, and temporary restrictions on hospital access.

The disruption affected New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center, leaving the state without its highest level of emergency trauma care. Other healthcare providers stepped in to accommodate additional patients.

Employees reported hearing messages broadcast through hospital computers claiming that student, employee, and patient information had been stolen. Those claims have not been verified.

The health system declined to discuss the incident’s nature or scope, citing an active law enforcement investigation. The FBI confirmed it was assisting.

Hospitals and clinics began gradually resuming operations Monday afternoon, although the full extent of the disruption remains unclear.

Cleared trees halt development of a Google AI data center in Finland.

Google’s massive AI infrastructure expansion in Finland has run into an environmental backlash after the company cleared hundreds of thousands of trees without completing required environmental assessments.

At one site in northern Finland, an estimated 250,000 trees were removed across 815 acres. Conservationists estimate another 150,000 were felled at a second location.

Finnish regulators have ordered work stopped at both sites. Google has apologized, saying it acted according to its understanding of local regulations.

The controversy threatens to complicate Google’s €13 billion investment in Finnish data centers, part of a broader AI infrastructure boom attracted by the country’s cool climate and abundant energy.

Supporters point to jobs and tax revenue. Critics question the environmental costs, electricity demands, and limited economic benefits.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding tighter regulation and compensation for affected communities.

Google says it will comply with regulators and plans to replant trees.

Blue Initiative tracks vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

A coalition of cybersecurity and maritime organizations has launched Blue Initiative, a free public database tracking vulnerabilities affecting ships, ports, and maritime infrastructure.

The project helps operators identify and prioritize security risks across IT and operational technology systems.

The database currently contains nearly 30,000 vulnerabilities, including more than 2,000 rated critical and over 580 known to be exploited.

Users can search, filter, and receive alerts about vulnerabilities, while researchers and industry partners review entries and contribute new findings.

A Chinese national faces federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam.

A Chinese national has been extradited from the Netherlands to face federal charges in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment scam that defrauded at least 174 Americans of nearly $37 million.

Prosecutors say 44-year-old Zheng Zhao participated in an international fraud network operating partly from scam centers in Cambodia.

The scheme allegedly involved contacting victims through social media, dating sites, and text messages, building relationships, then persuading them to invest through fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms.

Investigators say the stolen money moved through American bank accounts to the Bahamas, where it was converted into Tether cryptocurrency and transferred to wallets controlled in Cambodia.

Eight alleged co-conspirators have already pleaded guilty.

Zhao faces a money laundering conspiracy charge carrying a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

Anthropic’s prospectus includes an existential disclaimer.

Anthropic is preparing to go public, and its pitch to investors comes with an unusual warning: the company’s products could potentially threaten human civilization.

In its 335-page IPO filing, Anthropic devotes 93 pages to potential risks, ranging from employee retention and computing costs to AI systems developing beyond human control.

The company warns that increasingly autonomous models could conduct cyberattacks, spread misinformation, help develop dangerous weapons, or take harmful actions without human intervention.

There’s also the possibility that AI development could outpace Anthropic’s ability to evaluate and safeguard its own technology.

And then there are more conventional business concerns, including expensive data centers, regulatory scrutiny, and dependence on major customers.

Anthropic argues that its commitment to AI safety makes it uniquely positioned to manage these dangers.

So, the investment proposition is essentially this: help us build extraordinarily powerful AI, and we’ll do our best to keep it from ending civilization.

Not your typical prospectus.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours
articles.context: Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack...
articles.full_text: An autonomous AI agent discovered four vulnerabilities in the decades-old, widely used EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) open source software toolkit, including a critical flaw that could allow remote attackers to execute code on systems used to control particle accelerators and fusion experiments. The bugs include a critical, 9.8-rated under CVSS v3.1 integer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-114595), leading to an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write and potentially remote code execution; an 8.2-rated, high-severity, improper message-length validation flaw (CVE-2026-114596), causing an out-of-bounds memory write and controller-process crash; a 7.5-rated, high-severity insufficient bounds checking bug (CVE-2026-114597) that allows out-of-bounds memory reads and process crashes; and a 7.5-rated, high-severity type confusion flaw (CVE-2026-114598) that can lead to denial of service and could expose adjacent memory contents. All four affect EPICS Base, which is used to operate some of the world's largest scientific research projects and facilities, and organizations should update to version 7.0.11, which includes the fixes. “Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, disclose sensitive information, or potentially execute arbitrary code,” the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned in a Tuesday advisory. An AI agent called Cipher independently found all four previously unknown security holes - investigating and testing the unfamiliar EPICS system, and validating the four exploits - in three hours and 49 minutes, Causal Security co-founder Shubham Raj told The Register. “The initial investigation required no human intervention, followed by one instruction authorizing deeper exploitability testing in a secure environment,” Raj said. Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack paths in power-grid systems used across North America and Europe, prompting an October 8 security advisory from CISA. EPICS, originally developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and Argonne National Laboratory, is used to build and remotely control distributed Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, connecting operators to physical devices. It’s used in around 90 major scientific, university, and industrial projects and facilities globally including Argonne National Laboratory's Advanced Photon Source and ITER's fusion reactor control system. All four of these flaws illustrate how AI agents are really good at finding vulnerabilities in industrial and operational technologies - systems and equipment that used to be able to rely on obscurity to protect them from hackers - and add to defenders' concerns that it's only a matter of time until an autonomous cyberattack shuts down critical services, like power grids or water systems. These are the types of digital intrusions that can cause physical harm. Raj points to CVE-2026-114595, the critical integer-overflow vulnerability, as an example. “It allows attacker-controlled network data to cause an out-of-bounds heap memory write, with potential for remote code execution,” he told us. “EPICS controllers sit between operators and physical equipment, handling measurements, commands, and control functions,” he continued. “Operationally: Imagine a particle accelerator in the middle of an expensive experiment. An attacker could potentially crash a controller, interrupt critical measurements or control functions, and force operators to halt the experiment. That could mean lost experimental work, significant downtime, and expensive recovery.” Plus, if an attacker was able to develop an RCE exploit, this could allow them to “take control of the affected process, manipulate readings, interfere with control functions, or disrupt the equipment connected to it,” Raj said. The prerequisite for exploiting these vulns in a real scientific facility is being able to reach the vulnerable EPICS services on a facility's control network. But this could occur if the networks weren’t sufficiently segmented, or another system had access to the vulnerable EPICS network. “Once an attacker is able to find a network, which is either misconfigured or they are able to reach, it’s pretty easy to carry out the attacks,” Raj said, adding that exploitation wouldn’t require deep OT knowledge, or understanding of how particle accelerators or fusion reactors work. “Someone with conventional exploitation skills could investigate them, and increasingly capable AI systems could help develop exploits without requiring specialized OT expertise.” Manipulating specific physical processes does require additional knowledge, he added. “But an attacker doesn't need to understand the physics of a particle accelerator to disrupt the software controlling it. Crashing critical processes or interrupting monitoring and control can already have serious operational consequences. What's changing is that attackers may no longer need years of specialized expertise just to discover these weaknesses.” ®

articles.title: AWS becomes first CSP to complete the Cloud High profile assessment with 172 services and features in scope
articles.context: We continue to expand the scope of our assurance programs at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and are pleased to announce the successful completion of our first ever Cloud High (PBHH)...
articles.full_text:
We continue to expand the scope of our assurance programs at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and are pleased to announce the successful completion of our first ever Cloud High (PBHH) security assessment with 172 assessed services and features. Completion of this assessment, effective September 18, 2026, makes AWS the first cloud service provider (CSP) in Canada to meet this high security bar and provide assurance to our valued customers. This assessment also reaffirms our commitment to helping public and commercial customers achieve and maintain the highest-grade security standard for workloads with increased sensitivity.

What is the Cloud High assessment and why is it important?

The Cloud High security profile (that is, PBHH) seeks to enhance the integrity and availability of customer organizational workloads that are considered to have an increased level of sensitivity. These are systems that the Government of Canada (GC) and its service providers use to support delivery of services at a national scale or that are determined to be significant for handling sensitive information. The profile is based on the Security and privacy controls and assurance activities catalogue (ITSP.10.033). The Cloud High (PBHH) profile includes all controls and enhancements contained within the Cloud Medium profile (PBMM), with additional controls and enhancements to address higher integrity and availability requirements. The Cloud Medium and Cloud High profiles establish baseline security requirements for cloud services. These services support GC workloads and information processing up to the Protected B level.

As of September 18, 2026, there are a total of 172 AWS services and features that were assessed by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) under Cloud High security assessment. The assessment covers services and features that are available in both the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) AWS Regions.

How can you access the assessment?

The summary assessment is available through AWS Artifact. You can also learn more about the Cloud High and Medium assessment on the AWS CCCS assessment compliance webpage.

AWS strives to continually bring services into scope of its compliance programs to help you meet your architectural and regulatory needs. Please reach out to your AWS account team if you have questions or feedback about the Cloud High and Medium assessments.

To learn more about our compliance and security programs, refer to AWS Compliance Programs. As always, we value your feedback and questions; reach out to the AWS Compliance team through the Contact Us page.

Naranjan Goklani

Naranjan is AWS Compliance, Security Assurance and Privacy (CAPS) Lead for Canada. He has experience leading audits, attestations, certifications, and assessments across the Americas. Naranjan has more than 16 years of experience in technology risk management, customer security assurance, and technology audits. He previously worked in the Big 4 accounting firms and supported clients from the financial services, technology, retail, and utilities industries.

articles.title: Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills
articles.context: Get Your Recap Today December 3, 2026 | VIRTUAL Cybersecurity Outlook 2027 Secure Your Spot Keep up with the latest cybersecurity threats, newly discovered vulnerabilities, data...
articles.full_text:
Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

AI Tools Can Simplify Things Too Much

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

AI Hype vs. Cybersecurity Reality

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

The Shift From Operators to Monitors

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

Using AI Without Losing Expertise

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

articles.title: Part 3 – Cybersecurity journeys: The work behind the work
articles.context: Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come...
articles.full_text:
The most important work I’ve done in cybersecurity would make for terrible television. There were no countdown clocks and no frantic typing, just a lot of careful reading, a lot of hard conversations, and the occasional quiet moment where everything finally clicked. That’s the part I want to show you this week, because the three people I talked to have built their entire careers on the work that happens off-camera, and it’s the part that decides who lasts in this field.

This is a four-part series following 11 AWS security professionals through the real stories of how they got here and what the work actually looks like. In Part 1: I didn’t plan this, I shared how three of them found their way in, and in Part 2: What even is this job?, we looked at roles most people don’t know exist. This week is about what the day-to-day actually feels like, told through three AWS security professionals whose work rarely makes it into the trailer but is the reason any of it holds together.

Unlimited ammo

Brandon Caldwell, Mgr, Security Engineering

Ask most people to picture an application security engineer at work and they’ll imagine someone hunched over a terminal breaking into systems. Brandon Caldwell‘s actual days (reviewing software while it’s being built so the flaws never ship) look almost nothing like that. He spends them in conversation: sitting with the engineers who built a product, walking through how it works, and asking question after question until he understands it well enough to see where it could break. “This job is at least 50 percent people,” he tells the folks he hires. “You have to people a lot.”

The hardest part of the day isn’t technical, it’s human. Brandon’s team has to hand builders news they don’t want to hear, and he’s blunt with new hires about what that really feels like.

“Our job is to go tell someone their baby is ugly. I use that phrase because it is meant to draw out empathy. This is the thing they love and spent time on, and you show up at the end and say that thing is ugly. Of course they are going to react.” – Brandon Caldwell

Learning to deliver that message without crushing the person across the table is, in his telling, the actual craft of the job. It’s why he prizes empathy, and why he says the engineers who struggle most in application security are the ones who got into tech specifically to avoid talking to people. The rest of the day is the patient, unglamorous work of reading someone else’s code closely enough to find the one flaw they didn’t know they’d left, then explaining it in a way that lands as help rather than judgment.

That explaining is more than a conversation. So much of security work gets written down: the finding documented so an engineer can act on it, the advisory that tells customers what to do, the policy that sets the bar for everyone who comes after. The ability to write clearly, to turn something messy and technical into a few sentences a reader can actually use, is one of the quiet differentiators as you move up in this field, and it’s a skill worth building long before anyone asks you to.

None of this is where Brandon started. He’s been curious about breaking things since he was a kid hex-editing the game Doom for unlimited ammo, taught himself reverse engineering (taking apart finished software to understand how it works) before it had a name, and spent years as an IT admin and then in incident response at Microsoft back when cybersecurity barely existed as a job title. What pulled him off the breaking side was noticing—after watching the same handful of mistakes scroll past again and again (things like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, two of the most common ways attackers exploit a poorly built website)—that he’d rather help teams avoid the break-in than perform it. Application security, he says, is his natural place.

As for breaking in yourself, Brandon’s advice follows straight from how he spends his days: practice interviewing and asking the right questions and spend real time around builders so you understand what goes into the thing you’re critiquing. When he hires, certifications are the last thing he looks at; he wants to see capture-the-flag competition results (hacking contests where you solve security puzzles to earn points) and public GitHub projects, because those prove you’ve done the work. Build something, break something, and get comfortable talking to the people who build.

Forget that

Kurt Heath, IT Support Associate

Kurt Heath‘s chosen corner of the work is offensive security: penetration testing (getting paid to legally break into systems to prove where they’re weak) and, eventually, red teaming. The day-to-day of getting good at it is far less cinematic than the label suggests. It’s hours of hands-on practice against deliberately vulnerable targets, reading about a technique and then trying it until it works, and the slow accumulation of the layers the job actually rests on: operating systems, networking, software development, and security fundamentals, all applied at once. He’s the first to say pen testing is “the sexy thing” that gets advertised, and the first to warn that it shouldn’t be anyone’s first stop, because of how much quiet groundwork sits underneath it.

A big part of his real workday now is deciding how, and how much, to lean on AI. Kurt treats it as a tool rather than a crutch: he uses it as a coding assistant when he has to work in an unfamiliar language, and to sort through large volumes of information quickly, but he won’t let it think for him. He still fills out forms like this blog’s questionnaire by hand, keeping a personal touch on his own work, and he’s wary of letting AI pull the trigger during an engagement, since an overzealous tool can act on a network however it sees fit, cause unintended operational damage, or wander out of scope and create a legal problem. The way he sees it, security is fundamentally a human problem: automation keeps getting better at the systematic parts, but thinking outside the box the way an attacker does stays stubbornly human.

How Kurt got here matters less to the day-to-day than how he keeps going, but it’s worth knowing that he’s largely self-taught. After a community college program didn’t work out, he taught himself from scratch, finishing shifts at an auto plant and then spending nights with YouTube and a search bar learning how computers and networks actually worked. The hardest part, he told me, was self-motivation, and what carried him through was a mix of sheer want and, eventually, other people: the friends and community he found in Discord servers, security podcasts, and interest channels who helped him turn raw drive into real focus. He even got a tattoo as a reminder that there is no plan B.

“There is no other option. There’s no what if. This is it. This is life now, and I’ll figure it out some way, somehow, no matter how long it takes.” – Kurt Heath

If you’re drawn to the same offensive work, Kurt’s advice is to resist starting there. Build the foundation first, often through a role like a security operations center, join the communities where people are learning in the open, and let the flashier work come after the groundwork is solid. Progress in this field—in his experience—is measured less by the title you land than by how much you grow and who you grow alongside.

The comfort lock

Seth Jeacopello, Mgr, Security Engineer

Seth works in application security too, but if Brandon’s days are mostly about people, Seth’s are mostly about code, which makes the two of them a useful picture of how differently the same job can look. When Seth Jeacopello gets stuck on a hard problem, he doesn’t stare at it harder, he picks up a lock. An actual physical lock with pins and tumblers, because he’s a serious lock-picking hobbyist, and over the years he’s learned that the best response to hitting a wall is to set the problem down and pick what he calls a comfort lock, one he knows well and can open easily. It isn’t about the lock; it’s about giving his brain a small win so he can return to the hard thing with fresh eyes.

The comfort lock exists because Seth’s actual day-to-day is easy to get lost in. In application security, a big part of the job is reading enormous amounts of someone else’s code looking for the one flaw that matters, and as a lifelong developer he genuinely loves reading code, which is exactly what makes it a trap. He described the pull of it to me: you convince yourself the vulnerability is just behind the next function, and the next, and suddenly two days are gone. The skill he’s spent decades sharpening isn’t finding things, it’s knowing when deep enough is deep enough and when to step back, which is where the lock comes in. After 26 years, the meta-skill of managing his own attention is as much a part of the craft as anything technical.

That longevity goes back a long way. Around 1999, still in his teens, he landed a software quality assurance internship, was hired as a developer by 17, and gravitated toward the security-flavored work from the start before moving into network security tooling, rising to chief architect and then chief technology officer along the way.

“We’re like three or four guys off the street coming in with a product, and this huge company was like, yeah, you three, go for it. That was probably one of the coolest things.” – Seth Jeacopello

His advice for building the instincts the daily work demands is refreshingly concrete: set up a deliberately vulnerable practice machine, break into it, and then go read the logs it generated, so you learn not just how an attack works but what it looks like from the defender’s side. That single exercise builds both the offensive and the investigative muscle at once, and it’s the kind of patient, repeatable practice that the day-to-day of this field actually rewards.

The thread

There’s a version of cybersecurity that makes for great television, fast-paced and full of eureka moments, and those moments do exist. But the three people I talked to this week live in a different version of the field, one built on patience, repetition, and a kind of stubborn care that doesn’t photograph well. For Brandon, the real work is the hard, human conversation of telling a builder their work is flawed without making an enemy of them. For Kurt, it’s the unglamorous hours of hands-on practice and the discipline to use AI as a tool without letting it think for him. For Seth, it’s reading one more page of code and knowing when to stop, with a comfort lock on the desk for when he can’t.

None of that makes a great action sequence, but all of it is what a security career actually looks like, and the good news for anyone starting out is that these are learnable habits, not inborn talent. Notice how much of the real work is human: empathy, patience, judgment, and knowing how your own mind works. The analytical, interpersonal, and self-management skills you already have are not a consolation prize, they are part of the job. If you want to begin building the rest, here are a few places to start:

TryHackMe and Hack The Box let you stand up deliberately vulnerable machines, break in, and study what you triggered, exactly the exercise Seth recommends

The OWASP Top 10 explains the most common application security flaws, including the ones Brandon saw on repeat

The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series turns those flaws into practical, task-level guidance on how to build and review software securely; the daily bread of Brandon’s and Seth’s work

The Darknet Diaries podcast tells the human stories behind real security incidents, and it’s a good way to hear what the work actually feels like

And if you want to build cloud security skills specifically, AWS has free and hands-on resources to help you start:

AWS Skill Builder offers more than 1,000 free self-paced courses, including security learning plans you can start today

AWS Builder Labs lets you practice in a real AWS console on hands-on security labs, the stand-it-up-and-try-it approach Seth recommends

In Part 4: What I’d tell myself, we close the series with the advice and hard-won lessons these professionals would hand to someone just starting out.

Doing the work behind the work? These three want you to know it counts. Share your story on LinkedIn!

Shannon Brazil

Shannon is a senior security engineer, managing a team on the AWS Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT), specializing in digital forensics and cloud security investigations. Known in the community as AWSlady, she is passionate about security education and mentoring the next generation of defenders.

articles.title: 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants
articles.context: Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things,...
articles.full_text:
A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

Different Targets for Cybercrime, Different Financial Opportunities

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara Infostealer Malware In Action

Once an Aokigahara infection begins, it scans a computer for sensitive data, including browser passwords, session cookies, cryptocurrency wallets, and credentials stored by AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. It also searches local application files for authentication tokens, API keys, and other potentially valuable information.

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:BragJack Attack Can Turn a Browser's Agentic AI Against It

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Modern Defense as Attackers Expand Objectives

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

articles.title: Cyber Incident Forces UNM Health to Cancel Surgeries, Divert Ambulances
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center (UNM HSC) has been hit by a cyber incident, which resulted in the cancellation of surgeries and diversion of ambulances.

The medical center disclosed the incident on Monday October 26 at 2.30pm MDT, informing patients that all appointments, including scheduled surgeries, were cancelled for the rest of the day.

“UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice,” the update read.

Clinical Services Resume but Classes Cancelled

A further update posted at 10.27pm on October 26 confirmed that all UNM Health hospitals had reopened, and clinics would resume regularly scheduled appointments and procedures from Tuesday, October 27.

“At 2:30pm, UNM Health began resuming operations and bringing systems back online in phases, as it was safe to do so. We will work with patients to reschedule missed appointments and procedures,” HSC added.

Read now: UK Healthcare Sector Records Tenfold Increase in Cyber-Attacks

All students enrolled at the School of Medicine, College of Pharmacy, College of Nursing, and College of Population Health were told to leave campus on Monday.

As part of its remediation efforts, UNM canceled classes on the Health Sciences campus and sent non-essential employees home.

All classes at the UNM School of Medicine, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy and College of Population Health were also canceled on Tuesday, October 27, including online and remote classes, while non-essential employees will remain at home.

However, classes at UNM’s Central and branch campuses are not affected.

BYOD Ransomware Claims Attack

No details on the nature of the incident, or potential perpetrators, have been provided at the time of writing.

However, the emerging ransomware group BYOD has reportedly claimed to be behind the incident affecting UNM HSC.

Cybersecurity intelligence firm VenariX revealed on X that the group listed the University of New Mexico on its data leak site, claiming to have compromised 36,000 machines and exfiltrated sensitive data.

This data allegedly includes student and employee personally identifiable information (PII), research data, student records and internal emails.

“This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY,” the group posted on its data leak site.

UNM HSC receives more than one million patient visits every year, made up of around 900,000 outpatient appointments and around 100,000 emergency room visits.

The Center had 2670 students enrolled in its classes in 2025.

Image credit: Kit Leong / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
articles.context: On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group
articles.full_text:
On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group. TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative first reported this CVE to Oracle on June 10, 2026, following an investigation I conducted with Minh Giang and Lucas Miller of TrendAI Research. Although Oracle issued a patch under a single CVE, we reported three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components. We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue.

In this blog post, we will walk through each of these vulnerabilities, starting with a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. We will also review the validateClient method that Oracle introduced to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. Spoiler alert: the SSRF allows attackers to make requests that satisfy this validation and access endpoints vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).

Overview

There are two main components involved here, both served as individual Oracle WebLogic applications.

The first, the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), is part of Oracle’s Environment Management Framework. This component implements the validateClient method, ensuring only trusted clients can reach PSEMHUB functionality. Because this is an internal management interface, it makes sense that Oracle would restrict access to its web endpoints. However, this also means it’s a prime target for attackers looking to pivot from their existing, low-privileged access.

The second, the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), contains functionality for exchanging messages between the PeopleSoft server and remote systems. This is accomplished using a set of Listening and Target Connectors.

One such connector is the HttpListeningConnector, which translates data from inbound HTTP requests into the format supported by the specified Target Connector before routing the request to the desired URL. In this chain, attackers specify the HttpTargetConnector.

The diagram below shows how an attacker like ShinyHunters can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise PeopleSoft systems. Notice that the attacker cannot simply hit the PSEMHUB functionality directly:

Bug 1: PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery (ZDI-CAN-31816)

Now let’s take a look at how the PSIGW SSRF provides attackers with a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. An example malicious request to PSIGW shows just how powerful this is for an attacker. We control the URL to hit AND the full payload to send!

At [1], the attacker sends a POST request to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector

At [2], the HttpTargetConnector handler class is specified

At [3], the target is PeopleSoft on the loopback interface at http://127.0.0.1:8000, satisfying the validateClient logic

At [4], the full POST request payload is specified in the Data field, to be forwarded to the target URL at [3]

The HttpTargetConnector handler appears below. Note there is no validation to ensure this traffic is legitimate and bound for a valid target. I've done my best to pull out the important parts of this 800+-line function. If you want a fun side quest, go decompile this for yourself and check it out. I hope you like spaghetti!

At [1], retrieve the target URL from the attacker's request

At [2], create an httpObj using the URL from [1]

At [3], retrieve the HTTP method (POST) and apply it to the httpObj from [2]

At [4], send the content data seen in the Data tag of the network request. This content is sent as-is using the HTTP parameters configured in the httpObj

To fully understand why this SSRF is valuable, here is the validateClient method I mentioned earlier:

At [1] and [2], the validateClient method pulls the hostname and IP of the requesting client

At [3], a file path is built to the /envmetadata/config/allowedhosts.properties file, which contains the list of hosts allowed to access functionality protected by validateClient

At [4], the server checks if the allowedList set contains any entries. The first time this path is hit, the set is empty, so execution continues into the client list refresh block

At [5], that allowedhosts.properties file is read and iterated over

At [6] and [7], each allowed host is added to the allowedList set, including the default localhost entry alongside the server's resolved hostname and IP address

At [8] and [9], if the requesting host is found in the allowedList set, validateClient returns true

We can see the localhost entry in the default allowedhosts.properties that ships with PeopleSoft:

While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB. Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.

Bug 2: PSEMHUB External Control of File Path (ZDI-CAN-31818)

Now that the attacker can make requests to the PSEMHUB endpoints using the PSIGW SSRF, let's see how they can turn that into RCE.

The first path to code execution uses an External Control of File Path vulnerability in the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler, which is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem.

However, callers of the command control both the file contents AND the absolute file path on disk to which that content is written. Here’s an example of the request made to PSEMHUB. Note that, in practice, each parameter value is a form-encoded serialized Java object. For clarity, I’ve decoded and formatted it here:

At [1], we see the request is being made to PSEMHUB’s central routing hub

At [2], note that the request is made to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. Since this request originates from localhost, the validateClient check is satisfied

At [3], the web shell contents are specified in the m_line parameter

At [4], the absolute path where the contents will be written is specified in the m_targetFile parameter

Looking at the handler for this request, we can see that no validation is performed to ensure that m_targetFile points to a legitimate log directory:

By writing this shell to the PSEMHUB WAR path, the attacker achieves immediate remote code execution in the context of the PeopleSoft service account.

Here's how those bugs look when chained together:

Bug 3: PSEMHUB Deserialization of Untrusted Data (ZDI-CAN-31817)

Using any file write primitive (like the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand seen above), an attacker can write a malicious XML file inside the [docroot]/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. When the PSEMHUB HubServlet class initializes next (after a system or service restart, for example), it triggers a code flow that ultimately deserializes this XML file. Because this vector does not require writing a JSP web shell, it is less likely to be noticed by standard detection methods.

Specifically, on initialization, the PSEMHUB HubServlet class calls startServerPeer in the com.peoplesoft.pt.environmentmanagement.hub.Server class:

At [1], HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance() is called, which triggers the private constructor for that class

At [2], env_dir_path is set to <context_root>/envmetadata/data/environment/, which contains the malicious XML file placed by the attacker

At [3], all files from this folder are loaded into a list variable fl

At [4] and [5], the absolute path for each file in that directory is built

At [6], XMLDecoder is instantiated for each file

At [7], the content of the malicious XML placed by the attacker is deserialized

Java's XMLDecoder instantiates and configures the objects described in the XML during parsing, so the attacker's payload executes before the cast to Environment throws an exception.

Conclusion

The combination of the powerful PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery primitive alongside the decision to allow access to PSEMHUB via the loopback address by default renders the validateClient protection ineffective. Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft.

The impact of SSRFs can sometimes be overlooked, especially if they have no standalone information disclosure impact. Under the right circumstances, however, the humble SSRF can open the door for complete compromise.

You can find me on Twitter at @bobbygould5, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

articles.title: Attackers Abuse Legitimate Infrastructure to Distribute Phishing Emails
articles.context: Attackers abused more than 25 legitimate services over the past year, including “collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms
articles.full_text:
Researchers at Cisco Talos are tracking a significant increase in phishing campaigns that abuse legitimate platforms. Attackers abused more than 25 legitimate services over the past year, including “collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms.”

In two campaigns, attackers used order notifications from Staples and Dell to distribute phishing messages. The organizations themselves were not compromised, but the threat actors inserted phishing content into the fields that were supposed to contain shipping information.

“Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines,” the researchers write. “Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number.”

Phishing campaigns are also using a technique called “list bombing,” in which attackers enter users’ email addresses into legitimate registration, subscription, or notification services in order to flood their inboxes with unwanted messages.

“Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a ‘hostile string’ — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks.”

Cisco Talos has the story: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/parasitizing-trust-how-legitimate-infrastructure-becomes-a-delivery-pipeline-for-attackers/

articles.title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading Code
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

articles.title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

articles.title: Five election scams to watch out for
articles.context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
articles.full_text:
Elections give scammers plenty to work with: urgent deadlines, familiar faces, passionate supporters, and messages asking people to take action.

Some want you to “fix” your voter registration. Others want a donation, an answer to a survey, or payment for merchandise supposedly endorsed by your favorite politician. The details change, but the objective stays the same: get your money, your personal information, or both.

Here are five election-themed scams to watch out for.

Scam 1. “We’ll help you vote”

Not every election-themed lure starts with a threat. Some offer to make voting easier.

“Get your ballot on autopilot,” reads one text message we reviewed. It encourages recipients to join a permanent absentee list so their ballots arrive at home for every election, adding the reassuring words: “Verified. Tracked. Counted.”

A voting-assistance text message reviewed by Scam Guard

The message is a scam, though it borrows the language of a real Minnesota voting service. Minnesota does have a permanent absentee voter list, but the link in this text is fraudulent. To check or sign up, go directly to your election authority’s official website.

Other messages take the opposite approach: instead of offering convenience, they warn that you could lose your chance to vote.

A message might say you are not registered to vote, your details are incomplete, or your registration is about to be cancelled. Then it offers a link to sort everything out.

The FBI recently warned about messages that send recipients to fraudulent voter-registration pages. Instead of helping people vote, these sites collect personal information that criminals can use for further fraud.

In Brazil, scammers used a fake WhatsApp account with the Superior Electoral Court’s logo. It claimed to be the court’s “Customer Service Department” (which doesn’t exist) and told people to download an app called “Soluciona Pendência,” roughly translated as “Resolve an outstanding issue.” The message falsely warned that people could lose access to banking or government services.

Scam 2. “Donate now to help your candidate win”

A fundraising appeal arrives just as an election reaches a critical moment. It uses the candidate’s photograph, familiar campaign language, and an urgent request for money.

That does not necessarily mean the campaign sent it.

The FBI warns that scammers impersonate candidates and political fundraising organizations to collect supposed campaign contributions. Victims believe they are supporting a legitimate organization, but the money goes to criminals instead.

Before donating, find the campaign or organization’s official website yourself and check who will receive the payment. Don’t let a countdown, a matching-donation claim, or a message about an impending defeat rush your decision. The Better Business Bureau (BBB) advises researching political fundraising requests and resisting pressure to act immediately.

Scam 3. “Take our political survey and claim your reward”

Not every political poll is suspicious. But a request for your opinion can also be an opening for a scam.

The BBB warns about fraudulent polling calls that promise a prize in exchange for answering questions. After the “survey,” the caller asks for credit card information to cover shipping, taxes, or other costs associated with the supposed reward.

At that point, the questions about candidates have served their purpose: keeping you engaged long enough to introduce a payment request.

Other election-themed messages ask people to complete surveys through links. Treat those links with the same caution you would an unexpected donation or registration request. A familiar political organization’s name does not establish who operates the website.

You can decline an unsolicited poll. You should not need to hand over payment details simply to share your political views or claim a surprise reward.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

Check now

Scam 4. “Pay this electoral fine” or “Report for election duty”

Few things make a message feel urgent quite like an official-looking demand backed by a possible penalty.

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) has warned about messages falsely claiming people had an unresolved voting issue. The messages link to fake government websites designed to steal personal information or trick people into paying.

Brazil does have legitimate electoral fines, which can be paid through official channels, including Pix. So a fine or Pix request alone doesn’t prove a message is a scam. If a message says you owe money or must perform election duty, check with the relevant authority using contact details from its official website. Don’t use the message’s phone number, link, or QR code.

Scam 5. Your favorite politician “wants you to buy this”

A politician’s name can be used to sell more than a political message.

Criminals use candidates’ names, photographs, logos, and slogans to advertise merchandise that never arrives. What looks like a way to support a candidate becomes an ordinary shopping scam wrapped in campaign branding.

Apply the same skepticism to a “commemorative,” “patriotic,” or supposedly collectible product advertised using a politician’s name. Before buying, ask:

Is the seller actually affiliated with the politician or campaign?

What, exactly, are you buying?

Is there evidence for claims about the product’s quality, usefulness, or future value?

What are the total price, refund terms, and any recurring charges?

A product does not become useful, valuable, or a sound investment because an ad places it beside a politician’s photograph. Nor does a photograph prove that the politician endorsed it.

There is also a difference between a product you consider poor value and a fraudulent offer. A product being poor value doesn’t automatically make it a scam. Look for clear deception: a fake endorsement, false claims, hidden fees, or an order that never arrives.

How to stay safe from election scams

You don’t need to work out every detail of a suspicious message before deciding whether to act on it. Verify the message through a route the sender does not control.

Go directly to official election websites to check registration, voting requirements, deadlines, and alleged penalties.

Verify donation requests independently. Find the campaign or organization yourself and confirm where your money will go.

Keep payment details out of unsolicited surveys. A political poll that turns into a request to pay for a prize is a red flag.

Check sellers before buying political merchandise. A candidate’s name or logo does not authenticate the shop.

Don’t mistake personal details for proof. A message can contain accurate information about you and still be a scam.

Keep political choices separate from requests for money or personal information. You can support a cause without responding to an unexpected message.

Use real-time web protection to help block known malicious websites.

Malwarebytes blocks integmn.com

Pro tip: Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.
