articles.title: Japanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned
articles.context: ” “However, while we proceeded cautiously, considering the impact on service availability and prioritizing other issues, our response lacked sufficient depth and speed, allowing...
articles.full_text: Japanese ISP GMO Internet has warned customers the cloudy desktop service it offers as an ideal foreign exchange trading environment was compromised by an attacker, and that it had been slow to improve the service's security. GMO runs a service called Onamae.com Desktop Cloud and last week admitted “a third party had installed malicious programs in the server environments of some customers.” That’s never welcome news but is an especially poor outcome because the servers host cloudy Windows desktops that GMO recommends customers use to host foreign exchange trading applications. In later updates the company revealed that some customers reported “unauthorized operations were performed on their trading accounts” and advised that third parties had probably seen users’ passwords for trading services. The next day, the company advised users to immediately change passwords for their trading accounts, and to do so using a device that they don’t use for trading. The company has since admitted that its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service’s “systems had security vulnerabilities, that its environment was accessed without authorization, and that customer information was taken outside the Company.” “Some customers have also reported transactions in their trading accounts that they do not recognize.” Those transactions have GMO sufficiently worried that it contacted major trading services, asked them to forcibly terminate all active sessions, monitor for unauthorized transactions, and to block trade requests coming from the Onamae.com Desktop Cloud. Not paying, or complaining GMO said it has “received a demand for money from a person believed to be the attacker. We have also been told that, if we refuse, the attacker will take actions such as publishing information about the Company and our customers.” The attacker wants $50 million. The company won’t pay because it feels “complying would not guarantee that the obtained information is deleted or that its misuse is prevented.” Investigations into the incident continue, with GMO warning that 26,739 VDI servers may have been hit by the attack, and that users’ personal devices may be at risk. The company is offering all users a ¥5,000 ($32) condolence payment and promised to make good on any trading losses caused by the attack. This incident may have quite a blast radius, as GMO has warned that some trading apps may keep sessions alive even after passwords change. “Check your securities or FX company's guidance or your account page, and either disconnect all active sessions or ask the company's support desk to disconnect them,” GMO advised. That ¥5,000 isn’t going to get anywhere near paying for the work customers will do to sort this out. GMO CEO Masatoshi Kumagai acknowledged that in a blog post in which he described the payment as “a token of our initial sincerity towards our customers who have experienced inconvenience and worry.” “We will dedicate the full resources of our group to providing a free alternative environment for six months, fundamentally overhauling our system infrastructure, and conducting a thorough investigation into the cause and preventing recurrence with the help of external experts,” he added. But he also admitted that GMO knew the service’s security could be improved. “Our in-house white-hat hackers had previously pointed out areas for improvement to the team,” he wrote. “The team took these points to heart and was working on countermeasures.” “However, while we proceeded cautiously, considering the impact on service availability and prioritizing other issues, our response lacked sufficient depth and speed, allowing the attackers to exploit the vulnerability. I deeply regret that, despite having professionals on staff, we failed to fully translate their expertise into effective defenses as an organization.” The CEO also said GMO can’t secure itself without government help. “I've been involved in this world for 31 years, since the dawn of the internet industry,” he wrote. “The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues, believing it would bring smiles to people's faces, is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors.” “The ease with which open weight AI models can be combined and spread into countless attack tools has transformed cyberattacks, which once required advanced skills, into an era where anyone can easily carry them out,” he added, before claiming that GMO Group’s cybersecurity operation “has confirmed that the source of an unauthorized access attack targeting approximately 20 Japanese companies was the misuse of ‘ARTEX,’ an autonomous AI penetration testing tool originally intended for defense.” Kumagai thinks public/private partnerships are needed to improve infosec across Japan. “Yesterday, we submitted a proposal to the government to ‘apply proactive cyber defense,’” he wrote. “We are by no means trying to shift the blame for our company's actions onto the government and beg for a bailout,” he wrote, but argued that unless Japan implements national-level defenses, more such incidents are unavoidable. ®

articles.title: So Many AI Security Benchmarks, but None Tell the Whole Story
articles.context: Measuring AI model security gets complex, fast, thanks to a growing patchwork of benchmarks targeting different variables in the equation
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity firms and the makers of foundational models are improving the performance and efficiency of their artificial intelligence (AI) systems. But quantifying that performance improvement is a challenge.

While claims of more efficient models with smaller token costs arrive every week, gauging whether those models perform as well as the more general-purpose members of an AI model's family remains difficult. The lesson for organizations: Test models against your code and workflows to make the best choice for your business requirements.

National sovereign AI and cyber-defense firm Dream Group, for example, used 220,000 vulnerability records, threat intelligence reports, detection rules, and other cybersecurity documents to train an 8 billion parameter model — among the smallest modern models — to perform efficiently on cybersecurity tasks. The model — dubbed the Mid-trained Security Transformer (MiST) — improved average performance across 13 cybersecurity tasks, consisting mainly of multiple-choice and true-false questions about vulnerability analysis and cybersecurity domains.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

The results show that stronger security capabilities do not necessarily need a more complex model; more specialized training and adding better software around the model both improve results, says Elad Ben Zaken, an AI researcher at Dream Group.

"I expect efficiency to keep improving in coding and security tasks through specialization and better workflows," he says. "The model supplies capability; the harness determines how effectively it uses context and tools. Adding more of either can increase cost without improving results."

Dream is not alone in finding ways to make models more efficient. When Anthropic released Opus 5.5 in September, for example, the company said that the model improved performance while costing 40% less than Opus 5 on "typical workloads."

A Plethora of Benchmarks

However, for cybersecurity tasks, very little is typical. One model's results may mean little to companies looking for an expert system to generate secure code or to effectively find weaknesses in the enterprise's attack surface. On the offensive side, researchers are creating their own benchmarks to measure the performance of cybersecurity-focused models.

For offensive-security firm XBOW, the metrics that matter concern the ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities. Because different customers may want to use specific models, the company creates its own harness to improve outcomes regardless of the model used, says Albert Ziegler, head of AI at XBOW. While other organizations may want to use AI to analyze defensive telemetry and signals to boost detection of potential attacks, XBOW's metrics focus on finding vulnerabilities and exploit chains.

Related:Ransomware Gangs Embrace Physical Threats, Family Stalking?

"In its most atomic form, that's the ability of the model to find an exploit — that is our bread and butter in terms of seeing what's the value that the model produces," Ziegler says. "For other companies, this bread and butter could obviously be something else."

Anthropic's Opus 5 Thinking leads the board on one metric, correctness, among large language models. Source: Sonar's LLM Leaderboard

Another benchmark, the SEC-Bench Pro, attempts to measure an AI agent's ability to independently rediscover and trigger a known memory-safety bug in a browser engine or the Linux kernel, but only after the general location and type of bug are specified. Created by a research team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the metric ranks Codex and GPT-5.5 as the current favorites, with an overall solve rate of 58%. It also finds that open-weight models tend to struggle, with GLM-5 only succeeding in 13 of the 344 test cases.

Other metrics measure the hacking capabilities of AI models over an entire attack chain. Government contractor Booz Allen, for example, has published its Cyber Weapons Index (CWI), which combines a model's ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities with its effectiveness at executing attacks on a target. The latest version of the list puts OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on top with a CWI of 80.5, just edging out Claude Mythos with a score of 80.

Related:AI Scramble Drives Cybersecurity M&A Boom

"The CWI offers one empirical approach to offensive cyber capability — test models against a common enterprise network and score demonstrated actions using network evidence, rather than relying on what models say they can do," says Eric Syphard, senior vice president and head of AI at Booz Allen. "There is no single measure that captures every security risk. Evaluations need to be designed around the capability being assessed and should make their methods, environment, and success criteria clear."

Similarly, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) continues to benchmark the capabilities of AI models to complete a 32-step attack chain. So far, two models can: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview and OpenAI GPT 5.5.

In their own research, Dream researchers found that expert curation of a primary knowledge database — a "seed corpus" — can be used to create domain-specific synthetic training data, thus avoiding relying on general knowledge databases for training specialized models. The latest MiST models, MiST-8B and MiST-30B-A3B, were evaluated using 13 different test datasets, including 1,072 multiple-choice questions about MITRE ATT&CK (SECURE-MAET) and 870 true-false questions about whether a particular piece of code is vulnerable (the PrimeVul P-C).

Security Benchmarks Are Good, Internal Testing Is Better

Overall, the various features, capabilities, and issues are hard to benchmark in any comprehensive way. While offensive security metrics and measurements of defensive capabilities are both evolving quickly, other areas — such as safety — are more difficult to benchmark. The AISI found that the most sophisticated models tend to execute unwanted actions, such as OpenAI's GPT Astra conducting unsanctioned supply chain attacks, but overall safety measurements are more anecdotal than comprehensive.

Creating a metric for a model's likelihood of taking unwanted actions, for example, is very difficult, XBOW's Ziegler says.

"Benchmarking the possibility of the model to do harm is incredibly hard," he says. "You run [the test case for the model] 1,000 times, and it doesn't do any harm, and then you run it the 1,001 time, it drops your database. That 1,001 time negates all the first thousand runs that went well."

In addition, just because a model is newer does not mean it's more secure or has more advanced security capabilities, says Joe Tyler, general manager and AI researcher at Sonar, a provider of AI code verification and governance tools. The company regularly runs the latest large language models (LLMs) through a testing pipeline to generate scores across a series of benchmarks — from cognitive complexity to vulnerability occurrence in its code — which it then posts to its LLM Leaderboard for Code Quality & Security.

The ranking can give companies a general sense of model performance, but it should only be the starting point for companies evaluating LLM security performance, Tyler says. Instead, organizations should tailor their test pipelines to their own situations.

"Start with the task and the failures you can't accept, rather than assuming the newest model is the right choice," he says. "Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates, but the decision needs evaluations that reflect your own code and workflows."

In addition, for most organizations the choice of model may be constrained by the technology platforms they've adopted. For that reason, security teams should not necessarily focus on selecting specific models but instead seek out AI-powered services that lead to more efficiency, better coverage, and faster response.

Attackers' adoption of AI means companies will need to deal with a greater influx of vulnerabilities and faster time to exploitation, says Nico Waisman, XBOW's CISO. As a result, organizations should invest in tools and processes that help security teams move faster, automate repetitive work, and reduce the time to remediation. Focus on the impact of AI-based solutions, not their raw benchmarks, he says.

"Ultimately, I wouldn't evaluate AI security tools based on which model they use or how impressive their demos look," Waisman says. "I would evaluate them based on measurable outcomes: Are they helping you identify real risks? Are they reducing your exposure? Are they making your team significantly faster? That's where the security budget should go."

articles.title: Worm armed 42 GitHub repos by hiding a payload too big to fail
articles.context: Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator...
articles.full_text: A new Miasma-family npm worm, originally believed to be just a test with no victims, secretly armed 42 real GitHub repositories from 11 owners, hijacking accounts as early as July and using a stealthy payload built to stay hidden from GitHub and automated scanners, according to JFrog researchers. Threat hunters at SafeDep, an open source supply chain security firm, first spotted the “testmetest” npm campaign last week, identifying 18 packages linked to the same operator between October 19 and October 25, including releases containing credential-stealing malware. As with earlier npm worms, the malware is self-replicating, steals credentials, and installs a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token, the security researchers noted. The new npm worm shares code with June’s Miasma Phantom Gyp worm, and adds Mini Shai-Hulud’s token-revocation wiper. As of October 22, however, SafeDep had found no compromised third-party packages or victims. “All observed activity belongs to the operator’s own test accounts,” the team wrote. As with most happy-ending security stories, that proved too good to be true. In a Monday report, supply chain security company JFrog said its analysis proved otherwise, and found the testmetest campaign operator “had already armed real repositories belonging to established developers and organizations.” This isn’t just about timing, either, according to JFrog researchers Guy Korolevski and Yair Benamou. “The payload blobs were large enough to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise,” they wrote. How the attacks worked The attackers planted execution hooks for AI coding assistants and development tools, including Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and VS Code, alongside polymorphic wrappers measuring 12.9 to 13.7 MB that decode a hidden CI-publisher payload. Separately, the npm worm steals credentials, modifies repositories and CI configurations, and spreads through npm packages. The malware also uses a compiled native add-on to decrypt and launch a separate payload. Before executing, the loader checks for CI runners, containers, sandboxes, debuggers, and other signs of automated analysis, exiting silently when it detects them to reduce the likelihood of detection by security scanners. The researchers also found a second build that skips the encrypted file. “It forks, detaches and runs a hard-coded command that pulls a loader from a repository on the operator's own GitHub account,” they wrote. That account – CementBeetleSteeple – hosted 17 campaign repositories in total. JFrog connected this account to a shellpanel scanner, previously documented by Socket in a large-scale campaign that abused GitHub Actions in compromised repositories to exploit CVE-2026-41940 and steal server credentials. CVE-2026-41940 is an authentication bypass affecting cPanel and WHM. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in April, and cPanel has since published patched versions. “C2 infrastructure were previously reported by Socket; our findings connect them to the testmetest GitHub victim cluster through artifacts and workflows on the same hijacked owners,” the JFrog researchers wrote. They added that while they found 42 armed GitHub repositories and attempted internet-wide exploitation, they did not confirm any downstream cPanel compromises.®

articles.title: Socket Threat Intel Now Shows Which Malware Campaigns Were Blocked or Detected
articles.context: Every malware campaign on the Threat Intel → Campaigns page now carries a real-time summary for your organization: Blocked by Socket, Detected in Firewall/SCA, or Not Detected
articles.full_text:
When a new malware campaign emerges, you need to know whether it reached your organization and whether your defenses stopped it. Socket Threat Intel now makes those answers easier to find, with campaign summaries that show what Socket blocked or detected and links to the scans and Firewall events behind them.

Every malware campaign on the Threat Intel → Campaigns page now carries a real-time summary for your organization: Blocked by Socket, Detected in Firewall/SCA, or Not Detected.

Each summary pulls from immutable full scans of your repositories, immutable diff scans (i.e. from pull requests), and Socket Firewall event traffic. That means Threat Intel now shows more than just whether a campaign package made it into your code — we also show when malicious campaigns are Blocked by Socket.

Click any campaign and open the Org Impact tab to see more details. Each campaign package found in your organization is listed with the repositories and branches that contained it, along with the first and last time it was seen. Every date links straight to the scan report or to the matching Socket Firewall events, so you can go from "were we hit?" to the exact scan or install in just a few clicks.

For campaigns involving multiple packages, the Org Impact tab shows each package and version separately, with its own status and first and last seen dates. In the keyv and cacheable campaign below, you can see which malicious package versions Socket blocked and follow the date links to the corresponding events.

Additionally, you can find Socket blogs covering the campaign and the complete list of affected packages in the Blog and Affected Packages tabs.

Head to Threat Intel → Campaigns in the Socket dashboard to see what Socket has blocked or detected in your organization. Open a campaign’s Org Impact tab to trace detections to specific repositories, branches, scans, and Firewall events, so your team can assess exposure and investigate with the supporting evidence in hand.

articles.title: Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role
articles.context: His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software...
articles.full_text:
ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — The CISO role is evolving around AI, with security leaders now expected to help the business gain a competitive edge with it while also using the technology to help manage cyber-risk.

Doing both jobs at once means keeping up with technology that changes by the month, Mark Weatherford, Nvidia's head of cybersecurity policy and strategic engagement, said this week at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026.

The Need for Speed

"Speed is the biggest challenge right now," Weatherford said in a conference session on the evolving CISO role in the AI era. "Technology is changing so fast it is really hard for us to keep pace."

The shift shows up in routine practices too, he noted. Penetration testing four times a year, for instance, once counted as adequate. Now, anyone not testing around the clock is probably not testing enough.

Weatherford served as deputy undersecretary for cybersecurity at DHS in the Obama administration and was previously chief information security officer for the state of Colorado and the state of California. His other career highlights include serving as chief security officer of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) and as a security leader at Booking Holdings.

Related:As AI Reshapes the SOC Career Ladder, Satisfaction Rises for 91%, but Entry Gets Harder for Nearly Half

Weatherford pointed to a sense of FOMO — or a fear of missing out — as driving many organizations to deploy AI without always doing business due diligence or understanding what value they might be deriving from their investment. While there are many instances where the rush to spend might make sense, there are other cases where the case for AI may not be as clear-cut.

Command by Negation

CISOs often, though, have the opposite tendency, which is defaulting to "no" when there is the slightest element of risk involved. Weatherford pointed to the Navy concept of command by negation where subordinates take autonomous action to meet an overall goal unless the superior asks them to stop.

He opined that cybersecurity leaders should similarly be willing to accept more risk on their own, calibrated to their company's risk tolerance. "You have to be curious. You have to be willing to step out of your comfort zone," he said.

Weatherford encouraged CISOs to continuously think about how AI can help transform business and security and look for opportunities to make themselves better in their role. CISOs who expect their reputations and past work alone to carry them through the future are limiting their potential, he cautioned.

"Be curious, be creative, be willing to learn and relearn," Weatherford said, adding that one way to get up to speed on AI is to pick up one new topic every week.

Related:Fighting Your Dragons Through Tough Tech Times

The worry about being too slow to tap AI comes amid growing concern about organizations moving too quickly to implement AI without considering appropriate controls or without a full appreciation of associated risks, Weatherford noted. It is the role of the CISO to make sure the board understands the risks and knows who owns each risk, especially when another executive's deployment creates it.

Such frankness can potentially be career-limiting at times, Weatherford conceded. But CISOs often end up getting blamed for decisions that are not theirs, and they need to push back, he advised. "I would say we need to make sure that the people taking the risk are responsible for the risk.

For the talent pipeline, Weatherford favors paid internships that bring AI-native young people into the company and teach them the business. One of his interview ideas is to hand a candidate a business problem and let them use AI to solve it live, with no single right answer, to test flexibility.

It's also important for CISOs to ensure that people continue to have a career path and upward mobility within the organization, Weatherford said. It's a mistake to assume that paying people more and keeping them in their same roles is a way to retain talent.

articles.title: Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China
articles.context: "The first issue is that it made a network call at all," Ivan Zhang, co-founder of Cohere, told The Register via email
articles.full_text: Open-weight models from China have become very popular, but they've also raised some security suspicions. Cohere, a Canada-based biz that offers AI models to enterprises, says that when it was testing Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in its evaluation sandbox, the model attempted to send data to China. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," the biz said in a blog post on Monday. Cohere was running the model through CTI-REALM, Microsoft's security analyst benchmark, and gave Qwen the task of writing a detection rule to look for malicious file downloading and execution by watching for invocations of curl processing bash scripts to the /tmp directory that were accompanied by bash execution. The model's "reasoning" output invented a prior conversation and asserted that no tools were used, output that a guardrail system reading chain-of-thought would accept. Nonetheless, the model issued a curl command to an Alibaba Cloud (aliyuncs.com) server. "The model listed everything in /tmp, checked which transfer tools were installed, read the machine's DNS settings, then tried to upload a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing and checked whether it worked," Cohere said. "Our sandbox had no route out, so the request died at the container wall." The Cohere team wonders aloud whether that behavior was intended, but has no answer. "The first issue is that it made a network call at all," Ivan Zhang, co-founder of Cohere, told The Register via email. "The model was asked to write a detection rule, which doesn't require external communication, and its reasoning trace said it wouldn't use tools. The destination raises additional questions because the attempted upload was to an Alibaba Cloud storage endpoint that wasn't part of the task. We don't know why it appeared, and we don't know the root cause." Alibaba, the maker of the model, did not respond to a request to address Cohere's concerns. Asked whether Cohere ran similar tests against US-made open-weight models, Zhang said, "We evaluate a broad range of models using the same framework our customers use in production: agents with access to real tools operating inside controlled environments. "The key point isn't a comparison between providers. What made this noteworthy was that the model took actions unrelated to the task and those actions weren't reflected in its reasoning trace. The behavior appeared in fewer than one in 100,000 calls, which is exactly why large-scale testing and monitoring matter." There have been other unsubstantiated claims made about similar behavior from open-weight models, and such reports have suggested that "hallucination" - errors made by these models - may be the cause. Cohere has doubts that this behavior simply reflects memorized training data. "Every public sighting so far has involved fetching a file, while the one we caught was an attempted upload to a different bucket, this time in Beijing," the biz said. Cohere described efforts to reproduce the suspect behavior and found that using a technique called prefilling – feeding the model its own reasoning output alongside the opening characters of the bash command so the model would complete the command – they could get it to reference watchlisted hosts up to 23 percent of the time. This still doesn't clarify intent, and Cohere allows that there's a case to be made that the behavior is just bad training data sanitization – logs from development that got swept into the model's training data set. At the same time, the company argues that isolating a suspect model so it can't exfiltrate data doesn't entirely fix everything because these models can still write vulnerable code – accidentally or as a result of model poisoning. Cohere points to research from other organizations that suggests Chinese AI models can produce vulnerable code. The biz, for example, cites a report from Booz Allen (which does a lot of business with the US defense industry) that found "three of four Chinese coding models wrote more vulnerable code for a government customer, with Qwen3-Coder roughly 130 percent worse." "From the outside, it's very difficult to determine the root cause with confidence. We don't have evidence that would allow us to conclude this was deliberate, and we're not making that claim," said Zhang. "For security teams, though, intent doesn't fundamentally change the response. Whether it's a training artifact, a mistake, or something else, the controls are largely the same: restrict unnecessary egress, monitor tool use, and don't treat a reasoning trace as a security boundary. "We strongly support open-weight models and release many of our own. The lesson here is really about trust. Sovereign AI is about more than where a model runs. It's about understanding how it was built, how it was tested, and having confidence in how it behaves inside your environment." ®

articles.title: eMudhra, Brotli, and the Long Tail of a Security Fix
articles.context: How much software do you have to update to fix one vulnerability, let alone two far-reaching ones in the same week
articles.full_text:
How much software do you have to update to fix one vulnerability, let alone two far-reaching ones in the same week?

Our corner of the internet was getting impatient waiting for Node’s eMudhra fix to drop. The certificate block had merged, and we were ready to update Node, rebuild, and move on.

Then the October 21 release dropped, and we got Brotli too. That covered both problems in Node. But how much else used that same decoder? It was tucked into other applications and runtimes, and now we had more places to look.

And eMudhra had its own version of the same problem. Your browser could reject the compromised certificates while a command-line tool on the same machine still trusted them. Which other programs accepted them? Which certificate stores were they using? Updating Node only covered part of it.

eMudhra: a trust decision that traveled off the map #

On October 17, a researcher showed they had recovered eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys by signing a message with each one. Scott Helme later recovered them from the public certificates on his laptop in less than a second.

The values included 4, 56, and 115. These were supposed to be 384-bit private keys, with roughly 3.94 × 10¹¹⁵ possible values. The actual keys all fit in eight bits. You could try every possibility by counting to 255.

eMudhra says the keys came from a flawed key-generation ceremony in April 2025 and that the intermediates never issued customer certificates. That doesn’t tell us whether someone else used them. The weak keys had gone unnoticed for nearly eighteen months.

Mozilla found no certificates from those intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs at disclosure. That helps, but plenty of clients don’t require that logging. Someone could have used the keys to forge certificates those clients would accept without leaving a record in those logs.

Chrome and Firefox could push out a block without waiting for an ordinary software release. Mozilla says its OneCRL update reached Firefox users with standard configurations in less than three hours. Chrome also pushed a CRLSet block that evening. The disclosure site even had a handy test for checking your browser.

Outside the browser, the answer depended on which program you asked. Many clients needed a new certificate bundle or a change to their verifier. Revoking the certificates at the CA did little for clients that never checked that information.

There were multiple ways to trust these certificates, too. Mozilla identified paths through three roots, including Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services. Its advice was to block the compromised intermediates where possible. Removing the roots that trusted them was another option, but could break legitimate connections too. Removing just one might still leave another trust path open. Mozilla’s guidance

Go addressed the problem with a verifier change in versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. Getting that change into an application meant rebuilding it with the patched toolchain. Installing a new Go compiler would leave an existing executable exactly as it was.

Brotli: the decoder inside the runtime inside the product #

The Brotli advisory led to a similar search. CVE-2026-111497 could corrupt memory when an application decoded malicious compressed input. Node shipped a fix, but the vulnerable code came from Google’s Brotli library. Other projects had shipped it too.

Bun was one of them. Its fetch implementation automatically decodes Brotli responses, so a server the application contacts can feed data to the decoder. Bun 1.4.4 updated the library. But if you had built an executable with bun build --compile, that executable carried its own runtime. It still needed rebuilding.

Then there was Python. Requests automatically decodes Brotli responses when brotli or brotlicffi is installed, including when another dependency brings it in. You don’t have to import Brotli in your application to end up using it.

On Sunday, October 25, Microsoft published a .NET advisory for the same Brotli flaw. Applications decoding untrusted Brotli data were affected there too. Four days after the Node release, there were still more places to check.

And the list keeps going. The Brotli library can come along with another dependency or get compiled into a runtime, without “brotli” showing up in your application’s dependency list. Have a look at Broccoli2Shell’s list of bundled copies. Updating Node only gets you so far. You still have to find the other copies and work out which ones need fixing.

Where the fix gets stuck #

Shipping a runtime or library with your application is convenient. When it needs a security fix, you own the job of replacing that copy. Updating the system’s copy won’t replace the one bundled with your application. Even applications using a shared library may need a restart to load the corrected version.

With certificates, you can update a package and still leave the trust decision untouched. An SDK may hand verification to a library, runtime, or operating system. Another tool may read its own certificate bundle.

The macOS example makes this easy to see. Protections delivered through Apple’s security frameworks do not automatically extend to command-line tools reading /etc/ssl/cert.pem. A browser check can look good while another program on the same machine still accepts the compromised chain.

This is the part that makes “we updated” an incomplete answer. Which copy changed, and is the application actually using it?

And if we start finding more of these? #

There’s an AI connection here too. Node.js credits OpenAI’s Codex Security researchers with reporting the Brotli flaw. eMudhra says AI-assisted tools reportedly helped recover its weak keys.

Great, we’re finding the bugs. Now we have to find everywhere they ended up. If AI helps more of these come out of the woodwork, maintainers and product teams have more updates to chase down.

Those same tools can help with the digging: tracing dependencies, finding bundled copies, and figuring out what needs rebuilding. We still need to check what actually shipped.

And the agents doing some of that work? They’re using the same runtimes, certificate stores, and decoders. Now they’re deciding what to fetch on their own, without someone nitpicking every URL or checking everything that comes back.

Getting the fix the rest of the way #

Chrome and Firefox already had the infrastructure to get those certificate blocks out. Most applications don’t have a browser vendor’s update system or that level of established trust. Building either isn’t a weekend fix.

But we can make the cleanup less of a scavenger hunt in a haunted house:

Know what each release contains. Track application dependencies alongside bundled runtimes, libraries, toolchains, and certificate settings.

Have a rebuild path ready. Automate the builds and checks you’ll need when a dependency changes. If you’re waiting on another project, give someone responsibility for following its release.

Don’t just wait for a patch. Disable the affected feature where you can, or block untrusted input from reaching it. Microsoft gives Brotli examples for .NET. Check that the workaround works, and keep someone on it until the fix ships and gets deployed.

Check the application itself. Test certificate rejection through the verifier it actually uses. Confirm that a corrected decoder made it into the shipped artifact and the running service.

Track installation as well as publication. A release being available does not mean people are running it. Be clear about what needs to be replaced or restarted.

So, how much software do you have to update? Turns out, more than the first advisory might suggest. eMudhra and Brotli sent teams looking for s̶p̶o̶o̶k̶y̶,̶ s̶c̶a̶r̶y̶ s̶k̶e̶l̶e̶t̶o̶n̶s̶ affected components buried in their dependencies. As more flaws come to light, finding those copies and getting them patched quickly needs to become routine.

articles.full_text:

In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

A new AI agent prompt injection technique exploits how coding assistants consume local instruction files, blurring the line between text documents and executable actions.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 26, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: ipuwadol via Getty Images

A new indirect prompt injection attack relies on using markdown files in an end user's downloads folder to install malware and steal credentials.

That's according to Forever Security, which recently detailed a novel AI agent attack they captured in the wild. According to a research blog post, when an attacker plants a malicious file in a user's download folder, the user's agent may treat the file as trusted instructions and execute actions based on it.

What is notable about this attack compared to other prompt injection threats found in research reports is that this was not a case where the researchers developed the attack as a proof of concept. Rather, Forever's Gal Weizman and Omer Samet wrote that the AI security firm "caught live malware on a real customer's machine, attempting a new kind of attack the industry had not documented — and stopped it cold, before any code ran."

Malicious Markdowns

As the blog post authors explained, Forever Security found a malicious plaintext file named "AGENTS.md" in a customer's downloads folder, disguised as engineering notes. ".md" is a markdown file, used to guide agent behavior, and is trusted by many AI coding agents like OpenAI's Codex or Claude Code — Forever reproduced the attack with both (the original variant targeted Codex specifically).

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Researchers were unable to determine exactly how the file got on the user's computer, though they noted that it's the kind of file that a malicious website could attempt to download onto the user's computer. Then, when the coding agent is launched in that directory, it reads the instruction file as part of its project context.

According to Forever, the malicious instructions can persuade the agent to modify its configuration and perform follow-on actions. If the agent does ingest one of these malicious markdowns, the planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration, opening itself up for an attacker to instruct it to install malware or share its own login tokens.

In testing, Forever said the Codex attack chain succeeded more than 90% of the time. For Claude Code, the researchers reported roughly a 50% success rate, though certain variables may have influenced this success rate. For example, Claude Code uses a different installation path from Codex, which the original attack targeted.

'Nothing to Patch'

The attack requires someone only to grant their coding agent access to their home directory downloads folder, and that the agent can interact with web content. Forever says that according to its telemetry, about half of its customers run a coding agent inside their downloads folder, and a quarter of agent sessions open a real browser.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

"There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch. An agent that follows the AGENTS.md in its folder is doing exactly what it was built to do, the same way a browser that renders a phishing page is working as designed," the blog post read. "The problem is the circumstances: a folder the web can write to, trusted as if the user filled it. So the vector stays open. It is one early example of a bigger pattern: defenses built around a human break when an agent takes the human's place."

Weizman, lead researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading that AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic "may consider making agents aware of the risk of following commands originated by files that can be dropped by websites (such as inside the Downloads folder)," but adds that the issue described by the research is "mostly beyond their security model."

In the instance captured in the wild, Weizman says the exploit worked but was then blocked from follow-on activity by Forever's real-time security product, preventing an NPM package from being installed. Forever only managed to discover the initial example of the attack in the wild, though Weizman says the company is actively searching for more attempts.

Related:Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

For defenders, Forever recommends treating the user's home-directory download location (~/Downloads) as "hostile ground for agents," as by default it's the only way web content can reach a coding agent. Users can also check for instruction files they did not write, examine agent configurations for unexpected changes, and leave approval gates and sandboxes enabled. If a red flag has been found, the researchers said organizations should assume login tokens are compromised and rotate credentials.

About the Author

Alexander Culafi

Senior News Writer, Dark Reading

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

articles.title: The breach wasn't in the model.
articles.context: An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update. Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on...
articles.full_text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com
