articles.title: 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets
articles.context: Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors...
articles.full_text:
An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

Workflow Runs the Cyber-Theft Show

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

Stolen Tokens Fuel Further Secrets Heist

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

Enterprises in the Crosshairs

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Defending Against Token Abuse

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

articles.title: UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest
articles.context: Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to...
articles.full_text: A UK-based developer and pentester has claimed a $2,000 Bitcoin prize for demonstrating the exploitability of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities that melted the internet last week. Jaydip Modhwadia, 26, otherwise known as “Killa,” claimed the prize set by James Pavur, who launched the "Steal My Bitcoin" site on October 24. Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to award $2,000 in Bitcoin to anyone who could achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on his website. "My Bitcoin was stolen after 19.28 hours," the website now says, after Modhwadia claimed the prize, although the real time taken is thought to be less than three hours. Soon after Pavur launched the CTF on Saturday, prospective flag-catchers complained that the website he set up, which served only static HTML, was not built in a way that allowed the PHP2Shell exploit to achieve RCE. The web page was running a vulnerable version of PHP, but the exploit path required a vulnerable website to serve a PHP file for flag-catchers to use as a hook – something that Pavur seemingly updated at around 1300 UTC on October 25. Modhwadia achieved RCE on the website, exposing a PHP endpoint, at 1547 UTC. After an error from Pavur placing the wrong wallet key on the server, the CTF creator sent Modhwadia his award, which the community upped to $2,000 from Pavur’s initial $500. The pentester published a write-up of his method, a single-file Python script he says requires 20 HTTP requests "at most" to fully execute. Speaking to The Register, Modhwadia also confirmed that he got the flag in "around three or so hours in total." He said he followed the news about the competition, "but didn't attempt it until it gained significant notice." If he had attempted it before Pavur introduced the endpoint, he may have struggled. For hours, bug bounty hunters were trying to access the website to attempt the challenge, as news of the CTF had exploded across tech circles. "The fact that it took 19 hours was because after it went popular, the entire site became basically unusable for anyone at all," Modhwadia added. The challenge saw a huge number of attempts, despite Pavur's decision to introduce a prohibitive 1MB request limit on Nginx. Alon Gal, co-founder and CTO at Hudson Rock, commended Modhwadia's work, but added that his success achieved in just a few hours should not be taken to mean that the same attack could be automated at scale. He said: "Does this mean autonomous AI agents can now compromise arbitrary PHP servers at scale? No. This was a sophisticated, target-specific exploit. "But it does demonstrate that PHP2Shell can be weaponized against a live target, even with meaningful technical constraints." Modhwadia's proof of concept is not the first to prove PHP2Shell is exploitable, but it falls under the more advanced category. Early signs suggested that Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on a vulnerable server would prove a significant barrier to real-world exploitation, and the pentester’s solution bypasses it, along with the others that were disclosed recently. Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register last week that attackers are finding new ways to exploit PHP2Shell, and "are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug." Initially, experts said exploit code was being found online hours, or even days, before the vulnerabilities were disclosed publicly, which led to millions of exploit attempts, although it was too early to determine the efficacy of these on real-world systems. Scores of websites were taken down for maintenance last week as organizations raced to protect themselves from the attacks, which may or may not have proved successful. Modhwadia said he donated a portion of the prize he received to the Lupus Foundation to raise awareness about the condition, from which he also suffers. ®

articles.title: Trumpets blare and skies part as AI hypefest culminates in Anthropic IPO filing
articles.context: The founders aren't promising to put shareholders first, either
articles.full_text: Anthropic has filed for an IPO that could rank among Wall Street's biggest ever, revealing an $80.7 billion half-year loss, a startlingly complex governance structure, and warnings that its AI models could blackmail humans, resist shutdown, or create "existential risks" to society. The Claude maker filed its S-1 registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday as it prepares to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The company has not yet disclosed its proposed share price or how many shares it plans to sell. Of the filing's 614 pages, 94 are devoted to risk factors. But it's Anthropic's financial figures that are likely to raise eyebrows first. The Claude maker reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first six months of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. It also posted a whopping $80.7 billion net loss, although $72.4 billion of that was an accounting adjustment tied to the company's soaring valuation, not money it actually spent. Anthropic's operating loss was considerably smaller at $693 million, down from $2.1 billion a year earlier. By its own adjusted accounting, the company made a $1.6 billion operating profit in the first half of 2026, for a margin of around 10 percent. Whether it can keep making money on those terms is another matter. Training and running Claude requires an eye-watering amount of computing power, and Anthropic will need much more to keep pace with its rivals. A $1.6 billion adjusted profit won't count for much if the infrastructure bills keep growing faster than the business. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told The Register that Anthropic's IPO could leave ordinary investors paying a premium for growth that has yet to translate into sustained profits. "A huge pool of private capital has allowed AI businesses to scale up and command extraordinary valuations long before they reach the stock market," she said, adding that investors buying in at the IPO will face a price with "a hefty dose of future success baked in." The financial risks are fairly conventional by Silicon Valley standards, but the warnings about what Claude might get up to are perhaps less so. Anthropic claims that models, including its own, have exhibited unexpected or self-preserving behavior, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal information, and produce outputs resembling blackmail. It also warns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society” if deployed without adequate safeguards. That's not to say Claude is currently blackmailing customers. Anthropic has observed some of this behavior in testing, but it also identifies more immediate security concerns as it gives its models access to external tools, code repositories, and corporate systems. Anthropic warns that attackers could hide malicious instructions in websites, documents, or API responses that its AI agents can access. If an agent follows those instructions, it could use a customer's permissions to steal data, tamper with code, or make unauthorized transactions. Even testing whether the models will behave themselves is proving tricky. Anthropic reckons some models behave differently when they detect or suspect they're being evaluated, making it harder to predict what they will do outside the testing environment. Keeping its models on a short leash could also cost Anthropic business. The company acknowledges that holding back more capable systems could give competitors an advantage, something it has already risked by restricting access to its Mythos model through Project Glasswing because of its ability to uncover security vulnerabilities. The founders aren't promising to put shareholders first, either. In a letter accompanying the filing, Dario and Daniela Amodei and their fellow co-founders tell prospective investors "not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms." Anthropic may pass up lucrative business if it considers the risks too great, and investors won't have much say if they disagree. Under the proposed structure, governance structure includes five different classes of stock. By comparison, Google has three. The seven co-founders will retain 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters, while a separate Long-Term Benefit Trust will get to appoint a majority of the board. In other words, Wall Street is being invited to bankroll Anthropic's AI ambitions, but not necessarily to call the shots. Anthropic wants Wall Street's money to build ever more powerful AI, but is warning investors that it might turn down profits to keep that AI under control. Judging by those 94 pages of risk factors, keeping it under control is far from guaranteed.®

articles.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
articles.context: Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working...
articles.full_text:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

articles.title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

articles.title: 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years
articles.context: Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that...
articles.full_text:
OPINION

When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cybersecurity Practices That Can Adapt

The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

articles.title: We shouldn't be surprised about the PHPocalypse, as the internet is built on sticks and glue
articles.context: An independent researcher first spotted this, and then we can talk a little bit more later about who found more of the exploits and what the (PHP) Foundation did with that
articles.full_text: We've spent the past several decades using duct tape, string, and chewing gum to chain the world's computers together into this thing we call the internet, so there's really no good reason to be surprised that most of it is full of software containing vulnerabilities that are practically just as old. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. The world is still reeling from the PHP2Shell revelations that hit the news cycle this week, and on The Kettle there's no better topic for host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and FOSS reporter Liam Proven to tease apart. Join us to discuss what exactly is going on, how AI was key to finding another issue no human likely ever would have discovered on their own, and why exposing more bad code in the backbone of the world's computers might be just what we need to rethink the whole thing for the better. A lightly edited transcript follows: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo. And hey, there's only one thing we could focus on for this week's episode, given all the hubbub around it, and that's the PHP apocalypse. It turns out most of the internet is running software that could allow remote code execution on host systems via a pair, or as of today apparently three, vulnerabilities that have come to collectively be known as PHP2Shell. So that's not great. With me to talk about this is our security editor Jessica Lyons and open source reporter Liam Proven, who has a few things to say about PHP itself and why it's probably not surprising we're finding ourselves in this mess. Thanks to you both for coming on. Liam Proven (00:43) Absolute pleasure. Jessica Lyons (00:43) Nice to be here. Brandon (00:44) So Jess, let's start with the basics. What is this? How big of a problem is it? And where do we stand on getting things fixed? Jessica Lyons (00:51) Great. The short answer is it's a very big problem. So we have these two related memory safety vulnerabilities, and they are in the PHP core. Collectively they're called PHP2Shell, and they affect every version that's been released in the last decade affected by one or both of these, going back to about version 5.4. So the general consensus is this is about 70 percent of all of the websites on the internet are running this code. So it basically affects everyone at this point. What happened here is that this dates actually back to August. An independent researcher first spotted this, and then we can talk a little bit more later about who found more of the exploits and what the (PHP) Foundation did with that. But so he found this vulnerability. There was a coordinated disclosure process with the PHP Foundation, and then that broke a little bit starting over the weekend, and then onto Monday, there were some leaks. There was a video posted that purported to show this exploit. And so we get this emergency warning from the PHP Foundation late Monday saying, "Hey, we are going to be releasing these emergency patches, so everybody get ready so you can implement them as soon as possible. It's very serious." So by Wednesday, they did release these, and there's this mass attempt to patch before any of the attackers get a hold of this and are able to attack websites with it. And one of the issues too is that some websites are running really, really old versions and so they aren't able to patch. So they're just sitting there, these legacy servers are still vulnerable. Brandon (02:52) So there's no direct update path for those old versions, right? It's basically shut this down and reinstall it kind of thing. Jessica Lyons (02:59) Exactly. So basically they're both these memory corruption vulnerabilities and by exploiting them, an attacker can kind of shape the memory that PHP trusts. And then they can use that to hijack what happens next. And that can mean remote code execution. They can take over the websites, they can steal data. And so people are visiting these websites they trust and they don't realize that the underlying code is stealing their data or delivering malware to their computer. And again, this is potentially 70 percent of the internet. So it's a big deal. Brandon (03:36) Quite a few sites were offline. I know even some big services. I stopped playing because I had a baby, but I used to play Final Fantasy XIV pretty religiously. And I know that the entire login server was offline a couple days ago Jessica Lyons (03:50) Right. Brandon (03:50) They were like, "You've got to fix this. Sorry, no one can play the game. If you're not logged in right now, you're not getting logged in for the foreseeable future." It's just insane how much of the internet was affected by this. Now It's under exploit, is that correct? But maybe not successfully exploited yet? Jessica Lyons (04:11) Right. So after the patches were released on Wednesday, later Wednesday, AWS came out and said, "We've seen exploitation attempts at least four days before the patches were released." So that kind of caused another frenzy that, "My God, it's under attack, the whole internet is on fire." There haven't been any successful attacks to date. There's been a ton of attempts. There's a lot of POCs; some work, some don't. But as of Friday, according to the Foundation and according to all of the security experts that I've spoken to, we haven't seen any evidence of successful exploitation. I don't think that means we're in the clear. I think it just means it's taking a while for people – and honestly AIs – to develop successful attacks, but that's where we are right now. Brandon (05:06) Because it's a complicated attack chain, correct? Jessica Lyons (05:10) Right. Yes. Brandon (05:11) So basically, right. This is not working yet, but especially with some of these older websites that are running older versions of PHP that are going to have to take a more thorough approach to getting this fixed and possibly going down for some time, this could be one of those problems that remains serious for a while. And let's not forget, 70 percent of the websites on the internet, that's almost three-quarters of the entire internet. I don't know how many hundreds of thousands or millions of sites that is, but some of those are probably never going to get patched. Jessica Lyons (05:41) Right. Exactly. Brandon (05:43) Just the way it goes. Right. This is going to be the sort of thing that we end up hearing about months or years from now. Jessica Lyons (05:49) I would say years. Brandon (05:53) I'm sure there'll be some bank somewhere that eventually ends up getting – we'll hear about some breach disclosure letter from the state of Maine in four or five years. Jessica Lyons (06:02) And local governments, federal and state governments, I think these are the ones that we're going to be hearing about quite a while from now. Brandon (06:09) Because that's one of the things I was thinking about even for me in my tiny little town in northern Michigan. I wonder if my township or the county is going to be all over it to update their PHP server. Does their IT guy, who probably is a retired dude who lives in the area, even know this is a problem? It really is one of those things that is a big deal, but if you're not kind of following the news on this, it could probably go completely unnoticed. And for many websites, I'm sure it will. Jessica Lyons (06:37) Right. Exactly. Brandon (06:37) So, it's pretty crazy. Liam, you're working on a story, I think, as we are recording this, about some of the history of PHP and how it really probably wasn't very well designed or intended to become so ubiquitous on the internet. What's going on there? Liam Proven (06:53) I've seen one angle on this, which is people saying, "This is 1990s code and it has 1990s problems," which is one way to look at it. But I'm a 1980s internet guy; that's when I started exploring it. My primary email address is older than the web, and it still works. My gods, it gets a lot of spam, but it still works. I've watched the rise and rise of PHP since the first releases. Now, I have no personal interest in web development. I can program, but I don't because I'm really bad at it and nobody needs to have my code inflicted upon them. The guy that wrote PHP in the first place, Rasmus Lerdorf, is my age. I've never met him; I'm sure he's a nice guy. But he said in a very early interview about it, "I really don't like programming. I built this tool to program less so that I could just reuse code." And that was about 1993. He built a little tool that allowed him to put macros in HTML for his own website, and it's just grown. In a later interview, he said something along the lines of, "I don't know anything about writing programming languages. I'm just improvising this as I go and people seem to like it." It originally stood for "Personal Home Page," I think, and later was given a recursive acronym of "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor." This is a programming language that you mix in with the HTML of a website. It predates the modern model of building websites where a database contains the text and a content management system of some kind assembles on the fly the pages that each person sees. This is an older model where you're running programs that are part of the markup language, which was not a good idea, but that was how he did it. There was a lovely blog post. I've got an old friend who's an extremely skilled and talented programmer who has built a career on PHP, and he said to me, "Look, those criticisms that you've mentioned are of the really early versions and it's changed now." And if he hears this, he's going to be cross with me. But my favorite summary was from a blog called Eev.ee way back when that called PHP "a fractal of bad design." Whatever level you look at it, it was done badly. If you look at the whole plan of "let's just intermingle program code in with the markup language," not a good idea. If you look at the details of how it was implemented, not a good idea. If you look down at low-level details of how the functions return values, not a good idea: inconsistent syntax, inconsistent functions, functions that do really weird things, by default no stack traces, not great error reporting. Now, I'm sure a lot of this has been papered over now, but really there is one reason PHP is still around and still so big: Zuck. Facebook was built in PHP. And Facebook makes lots and lots of money and it's been throwing money at making PHP faster and more reliable and more scalable for decades. Brandon (11:03) Have they been big contributors to it? Liam (11:06) Yeah. They even built a compiler for it, which I suspect is still in use. Now, how much of Facebook today is in PHP? I don't know, possibly none, but for a long time basically the world's biggest and busiest public-facing website that wasn't owned by Google – only because Google have failed to ever make a successful social network – was built on PHP. And it's big, it's complicated. Like Linux itself, nobody fully understands how the whole thing works anymore and hasn't probably for decades. And now people have got bots that they can throw against it and ask them to analyze it. I think this is probably just the first, and I think there's going to be many more. A friend of mine who's a senior developer had a look at the patch, and he's not a C guy, but he said – I'm quoting from comments on Mastodon – that the patch to the current version is 13,000 lines of C. That's a doozy of a patch. Brandon (12:17) That's huge. Liam Proven (12:20) A bunch of people have been working like crazy for quite some time. Some people who've looked at this say it looks handwritten to me. Others have said, "No, I think this is bot-generated." I think the truth is probably a bit of both: some from one, some from the other. Brandon (12:32) Bit of both. I mean, you can't pump out thirteen thousand lines that quickly and have it tested. God, I hope they tested it. Liam Proven (12:41) Right. But that's just for the current version, and this hole affects every published version. So if they do manage to fix this one, how long till the next one comes along? Because I think there's going to be – Brandon (12:56) Especially with the speed at which vulnerabilities are being discovered now. I feel like every time I turn around, I've written one Patch Tuesday article in the past few months, and that one broke the previous two records. And I think since then every month has included more patches, and a lot of those are probably – Jessica Lyons (13:14) October at this point is the record: over a thousand for Microsoft alone. So, yep. Brandon (13:21) That's insane. Like you said, it is a fractal of bad design all the way down, and is going to probably have more vulnerabilities discovered. Jessica Lyons (13:32) Right. Brandon (13:32) Seventy percent of all websites on the internet are using this. What can we do? Are we stuck? Liam Proven (13:35) Well, there's a reason for that, and it's one that doesn't get talked about an awful lot: Facebook aren't the only people that use it extensively, because WordPress is also built on PHP, and it's far from alone. Another senior Linux techie friend of mine gave me a free shell account on the machine that he runs for a few friends years ago, and I thought of resurrecting my old 1990s hand-coded HTML webpage for fun. So I found it on the Internet Archive and found a tool to scrape it and turn it back into HTML again. I looked at some CMSes and asked him if there was any CMS on the machine. He went, "No." And I went, "Well, would you install one?" He went, "No." "Well, why not?" He said, "Well, all the big ones are implemented in PHP, and I won't let that near any server I run." "Well, that's a bit dramatic, isn't it?" And he goes, "No, that's pragmatic. I run a bunch of public-facing servers on my own, and this is how I keep them secure. No containers, no Docker, no PHP, nothing built in any of these technologies." And I went, "Wow, what about..." So I went looking for non-PHP CMSes. There are a lot of CMSes out there. I got a commission about a decade ago to write a comparative assessment of the CMS market versus a company's proprietary Windows product. I went and did a survey and came back and said, "I've found 1,300 so far." And they said, "OK, we can give you five thousand words instead of a thousand words." And I said, "You realize I'm going to have to go and look at 1,300 pieces of software here. Even if I only write three or four words about each one, 'Mostly harmless,' I'm still going to have to look at over a thousand bits of software. It will take me a year." And they went, "Well, how can how can we do it quicker?" And I said, "You can't. I cannot do this survey you want. Give me a full-time job and I'll get it back to you in a couple of years' time." I found a few CMSes that weren't built in PHP. Most of those were built in Ruby instead. And he went, "Yeah, I'm not keen on having that on my server either." So it's not even a case of people that have PHP deployments needing to update. They don't know. They built it on something else which was built on something that was built in PHP. Jessica Lyons (16:15) I was just going to say, Liam, you said, "How long until the next one happens?" And we found out today from the PHP Foundation that there is a third one. They won't be pushing an emergency release for this. They said it'll be published with the next regular release cycle. The Foundation told me that this one, quote, "requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use." So, there's already another one. Liam Proven (16:45) So weeks then. Brandon (16:47) Yeah. Jessica Lyons (16:48) I mean, and even with this, it's hard to exploit. You can mitigate it with a configuration setting. But that was part of the thing we've heard with these other two. And then we did have researchers yesterday who developed this new exploit; this was Vulncheck. And that shows how even ASLR can be bypassed to attack these vulnerabilities on x86 machines. So saying it can be fixed with a configuration setting isn't always a guarantee. Brandon (17:25) That brings me kind of to the elephant in the room of this whole story: AI. because of course it all comes back to AI nowadays. OpenAI and two other security firms reported this. I think Jess, one of your stories or one of the ones Lindsay wrote said that they all used AI to find this, right? Jessica Lyons (17:49) Right. So the companies: Calif, they are a newer startup doing AI pen testing and they're part of OpenAI's partner program, so they used OpenAI models working with OpenAI to find this. And then independently, Wiz, which is owned by Google, also did. So this happened back in August, and then they have been all working with the PHP Foundation on the patch since that point. They have all said these are vulnerabilities that probably wouldn't have been found by humans alone. By all accounts, they've existed for decades and wouldn't have just been found by human researchers. Brandon (18:34) Right. So either these are things that have never been discovered and would have never been exploited theoretically – the exploit path is complex, they're not obvious vulnerabilities, so they needed an AI to find them – or perhaps this is the kind of thing that was known about but was privately held in the hands of some bug hunting company that sells exploits to governments. Who knows? Maybe that's the case. I remember talking to a guy one time at Black Hat who basically said his company's in the business of finding really sensitive vulnerabilities and then selling them to the highest bidder. So there are companies like that that exist. So there's probably plenty of vulnerabilities in software that are not well known that governments and high-level functions are aware of. But in this case, this probably wasn't the case. This is an incredibly difficult-to-find vulnerability. I've seen a lot of chatter online in the past few days about how the internet's on fire and the AI bug-pocalypse has arrived. It seems like we're having another case of people getting all freaked out because this is the end of time, history is over, and AI is going to kill us all. It just seems to me like this is another example of: well, maybe not. This has been getting hammered by potentially bad actors or pen testers, and no one's managed, as far as we know, to successfully use this yet. Is this as serious as it seems, or is this another case of a serious vulnerability that is so complicated and convoluted that it's not really going to be that big of a deal? Liam Proven (20:25) I want to note parenthetically that you described OpenAI as a security company, and if I had been drinking coffee, that would have been very bad for my keyboard. Brandon (20:32) Okay, whoops. Let me take that back. Jessica Lyons (20:31) Ha ha ha. Liam Proven (20:36) Calif is interesting because I just wrote about them. They found a hole in OpenBSD, and there aren't many of those. And only about a week ago, they found a hole which they dubbed "Big Fish" in OpenBSD, and it was just days before OpenBSD 8 shipped. It looks like that had been there for 37 years, which is a neat trick because OpenBSD was founded 30 years ago. So this is in – going to pronounce this carefully – Berkeley Software Distribution Unix in the eighties. But there are doubtless more, and I'm an arch AI skeptic. Some people will claim that this will be the sort of problem that you can solve with AI by getting it to rewrite your stack. Well yes, but then you'll replace it with a new stack that nobody ever understood any of. But there are ways to design, host, and run websites, forums, and chat channels without using any of this stuff. And it could be a net positive if holes like this keep getting found that people will be forced to go back to – sounds crazy, but – static websites serving pre-written code off a disk. One of my favourite websites – recently I discovered there's a whole chain of them, and I hope you won't mind me swearing; maybe you have to beep me. But there's a marvellous website called "This Is a Motherfucking Website and It's Perfect." And recently somebody rewrote it and the new one looks almost identical: "This Is a Modern Motherfucking Website and It's Perfect." He's written it with more CSS or something, but apparently there's a whole chain of these things and they are extremely low on programming code. They contain interactive elements that you can do with just HTML, and you don't need a whole web framework behind it. And the same AI companies are busily scraping the whole web multiple times a day to feed their training engines. Maybe we just have to suck it up, scrape some of these big websites, and redo them as simpler tech with fewer interpreted languages. We are all collectively victims of the sunk cost fallacy. We've got millions of websites. We spent billions and trillions of dollars building all this. We can't just throw it all away. Well, maybe you have to. Brandon (23:27) Sunk cost was something that kept coming to my mind as I was writing up the script for this episode and just thinking about this. It seems like a whole big case of, "Well, all the websites in the world are now on PHP, so I guess we're stuck." Liam Proven (23:42) We have a script? Brandon (23:46) Well, not a formal script, just notes. Liam Proven (23:48) Haha. Well I didn't get the memo. Jessica Lyons (23:50) I think that's part of the problem though: it illustrates this larger issue with AI in general. AI bug hunting and exploit detection kind of illustrates this bigger problem about the internet, especially these legacy systems that underpin government services and critical infrastructure. It is literally held together by duct tape and string. So it's a massive problem. Again, it takes some work to actually make anything of these vulnerabilities and chain them together. AI is getting better at that. So whether or not this ends up being the end of the world for the internet as we know it, it does illustrate a real problem. Brandon (24:42) Like Liam said, maybe this is the sort of catalyst that the wider internet community needs to realize that these systems – this duct tape and string – simply won't keep working forever. We need to maybe modernize all the underlying infrastructure and make it simpler and less kludged together with all these different things over the years. PHP is poor design all the way down, right? It's like: well, maybe we need to tear it out and start over. Even if these vulnerabilities are impractical to exploit and hard to find, the fact that they're being discovered does illustrate that most of our code is a mess. Liam Proven (25:28) I am reminded , the other day I was talking in the comments about A/UX, Apple's original Unix for the Mac, and Apple paid another company to develop A/UX because the US military had a tick box on the form that said to buy systems, they have to be able to run POSIX. The US Army at one point hosted its website on Classic Mac OS. And it wasn't exactly security by obscurity. They said virtually all web server attacks in the mid-1990s were based on getting a remote shell, and Classic macOS didn't have a shell at all, anywhere. There was no way to get a remote shell because you couldn't get a shell if you were sitting in front of it. So they said, "They try and inject bits of x86 code: well, it's not an x86. They try and get a shell: it hasn't got one. They try and get it to run scripts: it doesn't run scripts." They said, "We just sit there and watch people throwing themselves at it. All the best attacks, and none of it works because the operating system's kind of too primitive to do any of that stuff." I don't believe many customers actually ever used A/UX, but it got Apple some lucrative deals. Maybe we're going to see a new trend of super primitive, super basic websites. There'll be a new difficulty in trying to scale the things because Kubernetes expects a lot of this to be dynamically generated by microservices. But bring it on; I'd love to see that. Brandon (27:09) That's a Kubernetes problem, right? Liam Proven (27:12) Yeah. Brandon (27:14) I feel like I would love a simpler internet. It would be amazing if I could just wake up in the morning, go to a news site, and just get the headlines. So often, I feel like – and I think The Register is good at having a relatively simple design, but – so often I feel like the news aggregators that I go to... I look for ones that are as minimal as possible. I look for websites that are simple. I don't need all this in-your-face stuff; it's not necessary. I think we probably are all pretty sick of it in a lot of ways. Jessica Lyons (27:49) But do we really think this is going to happen though? Brandon (27:52) No. Jessica Lyons (27:53) I feel extremely pessimistic about this. I think it's much more profitable to just keep marketing solutions to the problem as opposed to a safe coding overhaul. Brandon (28:04) Unfortunately. Liam Proven (28:06) Geopolitics might yet get in the way. I wrote a piece about OpenEuler, one of the big Chinese enterprise server Linuxes, and one of only two companies actually showing off an OS at the Open Source Summit. The other was also Chinese: OpenKylin, which is more desktop focused. China makes its own chips, China makes its own operating systems, and it's got its own programming languages. They're all open source, taken from European and American developed software by and large, but they could still invade Taiwan and cut off much of the world's chip supply. And suddenly it won't just be that memory is way more expensive than it used to be; it will be that you can't get more memory anymore and you have to keep using 10-year-old chips. And people will be potentially forced to find ways to keep getting more out of the same hardware until we can build new chip fabs, which will take a lot of time and a lot of money. And then quite possibly they'll get blown away in a climate-change-induced hurricane and then we'll have to start again. So, I hope they're going to start building them in the north of Norway and places like that. But yeah we've got bigger problems coming down the pipe and it's all a giant snowball of superficially unrelated things: AI attacks on overcomplicated stacks on one side, and the other kind of attack which involves whistling noises and large explosions on the other side, which cuts off the hardware market. It's hard to plan for this, but nobody's even trying yet. Brandon (29:52) Who would have thought a talk about a PHP vulnerability would have turned into geopolitical chaos and the endof modern technology as we know it? Break out the sundial, people. Liam Proven (30:07) Excuse me, I've just got to go and wind the web server. Hang on. Brandon (30:11) All right, guys. Thanks for coming on. I think this was a really valuable discussion and it shows just how interconnected all these issues in tech are right now. I mean, it is interesting how we're kind of hurtling toward something in a lot of ways. AI will surely be a part of it, as will expensive chips and lots and lots of vulnerabilities being found every day. Hopefully we'll still be here to cover it as that continues to happen. Jessica Lyons (30:40) If AI doesn't kill us. Brandon (30:41) Right. If AI doesn't kill us all. Well, if it doesn't, we'll be here on the Kettle to talk about it. And we hope that you, from whatever bunker you're hiding in, will join us on future episodes. Liam Proven (30:53) Yeah, we'll be publishing a telephone number so you can phone into future Kettle episodes. Brandon (30:59) All right, folks, we'll talk soon. ®

articles.title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

articles.title: UK Biobank back online soon, months after someone tried to sell 500k people's data on Alibaba
articles.context: The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for...
articles.full_text: UK Biobank (UKB) says its platform is now "secure" and that academics will soon regain access, months after a major data leak of volunteer health data. The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for approval from health data controllers and central government before it relaunches the platform. UK Biobank's Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP) has locked out all medical researchers trying to access its dataset since the April attack, which led to all 500,000 volunteers’ data being listed for sale on Chinese ecommerce website Alibaba. More than 20,000 researchers use the dataset provided by the cloud-based platform. They upload research projects and run experiments informed by the genomic data UKB collected from 40-to-69-year-olds between 2006 and 2010. The org makes around 30 petabytes worth of the stuff available to researchers, who investigate conditions including cancer, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and COVID-19 immunity. Professor Sir Rory Collins, CEO at UKB, said on Friday that the organization has "completed the work to ensure that the UKB-RAP is secure," and that the progress was checked by an independent cybersecurity company, whose report recommends reopening the platform. The charity will begin a phased re-introduction of researchers to its platform after it receives the necessary approvals, although boffins will not be able to download any results files at first. The platform will pilot a "manual output checking system," where human reviewers will inspect files researchers wish to download before allowing them to do so, ahead of an automated process expected to roll out next year. According to the guide UKB compiled for researchers outlining the changes to the platform, researchers will also be restricted from building public apps and sharing tools with external colleagues until that manual checking system is fully up and running. Researchers were also warned that they will not be able to refresh or dispense data, only work with pre-existing data. They were also told to expect automatic logout out after 15 minutes of inactivity, with 2FA required upon re-authentication. Other technical changes include no longer being able to SSH into jobs, interactive tools being run via "isolated browsing" which restricts data transfer between web apps and the user's local system, and some restrictions on CLI use. UKB is working toward a day when the researchers using its platform store no data on their own computers, working only with that which is uploaded to the repos it hosts. However, in uploading this data to online repos, de-identified data is accidentally included in the code. UKB says it runs daily automated scans of these repos to catch errors, and provides training to researchers to help prevent these occurrences. Collins said that since the attack, most researchers have confirmed the deletion of de-identified data from their projects, but others have not and won't be admitted back to the UKB-RAP until they do. "Despite our repeated reminders, we are still detecting a small number of code repositories that include de-identified participant data," he said. "As these constitute a serious breach of the Material Transfer Agreement, sanctions are being applied against the researchers who are responsible." The charity also said researchers caught exposing participant data in their code will be forced to move their analyses to UKB-RAP, delete any downloaded data, and undergo additional training before being allowed back on the platform. It had initially told researchers to expect a relaunch of the platform by September 2026, although an update penned last month confirmed that it needed to wait for an independent assessment to be completed, despite already making the required security improvements. ®

articles.title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
articles.context: For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it
articles.full_text:
Clive Robinson • October 26, 2026 2:51 PM

@ Bruce, ALL,

With regards,

“I would like more details on how the bias was removed.”

I can not give you specifics for this particular model and it’s token encoding, but I can give a more general explanation.

As I’ve noted previously on a numver of occasions the heart of these AI Large X Models is the so called “Digital Neural Network”(DNN).

That in reality is just a “Digital Signal Processing”(DSP) algorithm that implements an “Adaptive Filter Network”.

What this AFN does is at the basic level “Multiply and Add”(MAD) instructions that feed forward into a form of decision circuit (often a rectifier function). Often this decision circuit is at the output of the summer and is nonlinear in response to provide a normalised spectrum.

If you change the token weights that are in effect linear then you change the shape of the AFN spectrum.

Thus by increasing or reducing the weights for selected tokens, you change the spectrum in desirable ways.

Thus if you can identify the weights to change you change not just the specific part of the spectrum for the token you also change the general spectrum which it forms a part of.

In general LLMs fail after ML building of the DNN for various reasons. Where that behaviour around specific tokens or the broader themes they form part of is seen as undesirable “Reinforcement learning from human feedback”(RLHF) can be applied.

In essence all it does is adjust the specific token weights as well as to a lesser result adjust the more general weights for other tokens.

Thus if you know what token weights need adjusting you can do so.

The trick is making your RLHF the inverse of that used by the model originator.

There are other ways to achieve the same objective of weight adjustment, but this is generally the easiest way to see it as a distinct process.

Another way I’m not going to go into is by cloning the model. You can as part of the process add or subtract the measure you give for tokens or themes.

Look up “LLM logit leakage and distillation” techniques or have a browse through,

“Clone What You Can’t Steal: Black-Box LLM Replication via Logit Leakage and Distilation”

https://arxiv.org/html/2509.00973

Hopefully you will enjoy / have fun.

articles.title: Britain bets big on AI to defend against the threats AI is helping create
articles.context: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security...
articles.full_text: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security flaws before attackers get there first. The money is part of a wider £600 million-plus AI spending spree announced by the Treasury ahead of this week's Budget, with ministers also promising to tackle biological threats, bankroll British AI firms, and reduce the country's dependence on foreign technology. Of the cyber funding, £60 million will go towards a new National Cyber Shield that uses agentic AI to bolster Britain's defenses. That includes a £25 million challenge fund for UK cybersecurity firms and plans for a regulatory sandbox to test autonomous security tools across critical infrastructure, government and industry. Another £70 million will establish the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, using AI to sniff out vulnerabilities across Britain's infrastructure and wider economy. The announcement comes just days after the PHP2Shell security scare, which saw dozens of government websites taken offline after critical flaws were discovered in the widely used scripting language. Britain's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) worked with OpenAI to coordinate disclosure of the PHP flaws and give affected vendors time to prepare fixes, after AI-assisted researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities. Whitehall has already been experimenting with AI-powered vulnerability hunting. AI minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the technology had uncovered 500 previously unknown security flaws across significant parts of the public sector. It remains unclear how much freedom the new AI defenders will have to act without human intervention, or when they'll be deployed. Ciaran Martin, former head of the NCSC, welcomed the investment, pointing to the week's events as evidence that Britain needs to get its cyber defenses in order. "We need to padlock our systems, and harness AI for defense," he said. The Treasury is also handing another £120 million to the AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advanced AI systems for dangerous capabilities and researches ways to keep them under control. Cybersecurity isn't the only threat keeping ministers busy. Another £165 million will fund a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100 million for what the government claims will be the world's first dedicated AI Biosecurity Lab. The independent, non-profit lab will use frontier AI models to detect biological threats and accelerate the development of vaccines and treatments. OpenAI is contributing £100 million in compute and model credits, while Anthropic is offering up to £100 million in model credits, model access and technical support. Google DeepMind and British biotech firm Basecamp Research are also involved, while the remaining £65 million will go towards biosurveillance and medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens. There's something for the homegrown AI industry, too. The government is adding £60 million to its Sovereign AI Fund to invest in British companies developing technologies including robotics and autonomous systems, plus another £60 million for AI research and development procurement. A further £18 million will fund an Advanced Chip Design Academy, intended to help Britain develop more of its own semiconductor expertise rather than relying quite so heavily on technology designed overseas. The package also includes £30 million for local AI partnerships, £15 million for an AI challenge prize initially focused on healthcare, and £23 million for research into AI's impact on jobs and the economy. Manchester will get a new NCSC AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence to train government specialists. Additionally, ministers are setting aside £10 million a year to study how AI will reshape employment and industry, including the jobs it might make redundant. The government clearly has high hopes for AI. Whether the technology can live up to them without creating a fresh set of problems is another matter.®

articles.title: Know How Cyble Brand Intelligence Can Help Stop ClickFix Campaigns in its Tracks
articles.context: Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list What the attacker did
articles.full_text:
Booking.com's systems were never breached. Its name was. Storm-1865 spent months borrowing Booking.com's identity to get into hotel computers, and every step of that borrowing left traces on the open internet.

The open internet is exactly where Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection works. Walk through the campaign one step at a time, and at each step there is a point where it could have spotted the attacker, cut the attack short or limited the damage.

What happened

From December 2024, a group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1865 posed as Booking.com to target hotel and hospitality staff across North America, Europe, Oceania and South and Southeast Asia. Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its findings on March 13, 2025, and said the campaign was still running as of February 2025.

The attack had four moving parts:

The lure. Emails styled as Booking.com messages about negative guest reviews, guest enquiries, promotion offers or account verification.

The landing page. A link, sometimes inside a PDF, opened a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page.

The trick. The "verification" told staff to open the Windows Run box and paste a command the page had already copied to their clipboard.

The payload. That command used mshta.exe to pull commodity malware, including XWorm, Lumma Stealer, VenomRAT, AsyncRAT, Danabot and NetSupport RAT, all built to steal credentials and payment data.

This was not a one-off. Microsoft says Storm-1865 targeted Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024 before adding ClickFix. Booking.com told Infosecurity Magazine its own systems were not breached, but some accommodation partners and customers were hit.

Why the impersonated brand holds the first move

Booking.com could not install security software on the laptops of its accommodation partners. What it could reach was the attacker's infrastructure copying its brand, and that infrastructure was detectable. Microsoft's own email security flagged URLs in this campaign as impersonating booking.com.

The stakes are high. The US Federal Trade Commission says people reported losing nearly $1 billion to business impersonators in 2025, out of $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams overall. Every copy of a brand caught early is one fewer victim.

Five steps, five chances to step in

Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every stage of the attack. Here is each stage, and how Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection could have helped at it.

Fig. Five Storm-1865 attack steps, each paired with a Cyble Brand Intelligence capability

Step 1: Pick a trusted brand and a target list

What the attacker did. Storm-1865 was a repeat player. Microsoft says it went after Booking.com guests in 2023 and e-commerce buyers in 2024, then turned to hotel staff most likely to work with Booking.com.

How Cyble could have helped. Cyble's in-house brand team and OSINT surveillance track brand mentions and the actors who keep returning to a brand. A known playbook becomes a set of watch-list rules, so the next wave is expected rather than discovered after the fact.

Step 2: Register the infrastructure

What the attacker did. The campaign needed domains and URLs to host its fake pages. Microsoft flagged some of them as matching a known malicious registrant pattern.

How Cyble could have helped. Suspicious & Watch-Listed Domain monitoring tracks new registrations and DNS activity for typosquats, homoglyphs and lookalike domains, including AI-generated ones. A domain built to impersonate the brand can be flagged when it is registered, before it hosts a single page.

Step 3: Build the fake Booking.com page

What the attacker did. Victims landed on a fake CAPTCHA laid over a faint copy of a real Booking.com page. The familiar look was the point: it made a strange request feel routine.

How Cyble could have helped. Phishing Detection finds sites impersonating the brand, and Watermarking Surveillance spots copied or mirrored brand assets, even on domains with no brand name in them. Automated Takedown then works to get confirmed pages removed. Every hotel that clicks after a takedown hits a dead link instead of a trap.

Step 4: Send lures across regions

What the attacker did. Emails and PDFs about negative reviews, guest requests, promotions and account checks went to hotels across North America, Europe, Oceania and Asia. Some came through vendor platforms and ordinary services such as Gmail and iCloud Mail.

How Cyble could have helped. Multi-language NLP is built to catch phishing and impersonation attempts that are not in English, which matters for a campaign spread across this many markets. Lures that partners report can be handed to Cyble's brand team, traced to the live page behind them and queued for takedown.

Step 5: Cash in on stolen credentials and payment data

What the attacker did. Once a staff member pasted the command, malware such as XWorm, Lumma Stealer and VenomRAT went to work. Microsoft says every payload in the campaign could steal credentials and financial data for fraud.

How Cyble could have helped. Stopping the pasted command itself is a job for endpoint and email controls. What Cyble adds is the aftermath: OSINT surveillance watches forums, blogs and paste sites for exposed credentials and data leaks tied to the brand. Spotting stolen partner logins early gives everyone time to reset access before fraud follows.

This walkthrough maps public research to Cyble's capabilities. It is not a claim that Cyble took part in the response to this campaign.

Strongest alongside your other defenses

Brand intelligence works outside your network, so it pairs naturally with what runs inside it. When a lure arrives from an ordinary Gmail or iCloud address, there is no fake sender domain to flag, so the landing page becomes the asset to hunt. And if someone does run the pasted command, email filtering, endpoint detection, script controls and phishing-resistant MFA, the mitigations Microsoft recommends, do the stopping. Brand intelligence makes sure far fewer people ever reach that moment.

Is your brand the next Target? Six questions to ask

Any brand that sits between businesses and their customers can be borrowed the same way: travel platforms, marketplaces, payment providers, logistics firms and SaaS vendors. Ask your team:

Do we know which of our emails, notices and portal pages are most copied by attackers?

Are we alerted when a domain containing our name, or a homoglyph of it, is registered?

Can we spot a cloned page even when it sits on an unrelated domain or free hosting?

How long does it take us to get a confirmed phishing page taken down?

Do our partners know how to report a suspicious message that uses our name?

Do we watch criminal forums and channels for kits or templates built around our brand?

If more than two answers are "no" or "not sure," the attacker's preparation phase is happening without anyone watching.

The takeaway

Look back at the five steps and a pattern stands out. Storm-1865 needed Booking.com's credibility at every one of them, and every one left a trace outside the victims' networks.

With Cyble Brand Intelligence & Protection watching, each trace becomes a chance to step in: a repeat actor on the watch list, a lookalike domain flagged at registration, a cloned page taken down, a lure traced to its source, a leaked login caught early. If your partners and customers trust your name, Cyble helps make sure nobody else gets to use it.

See how it works for your brand: request a personalized demo.
