articles.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

articles.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: No login, no app code, no warning. What next?
articles.context: Two critical flaws disclosed last week, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "PHP2Shell"), let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server with nothing more than...
articles.full_text: If you run PHP anywhere in your environment, patch to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now. Two critical flaws disclosed last week, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "PHP2Shell"), let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server with nothing more than a crafted web request. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, every earlier release is affected, and exploitation in the wild has been reported. The patch is the easy part. The hard part is finding every copy of PHP you own, because PHP rarely shows up where you expect it. This post covers what the flaws are, how far exploitation has gone, and how to get to full coverage fast. What happened Details leaked before the planned embargo, so the PHP security team moved fast and shipped fixes within about a day of announcing them. The two vulnerabilities Both bugs live in PHP core, not in any framework or plugin, so they reach anything that runs PHP to serve web requests. Affected server setups include PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. No login is needed: the attacker only has to reach a PHP endpoint over HTTP. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Every earlier release is affected. PHP has also published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, but there are no official releases for those branches. Treat a backport as a stopgap and plan the upgrade. Is it being exploited? Yes, though reliable public exploits are still scarce. watchTowr reports exploitation in its honeypot network as of October 21, and Tenable relays Cloudflare's CTO saying Cloudflare is seeing early attacks. Other telemetry, such as Patchstack's, shows mostly probing so far. Neither CVE is in CISA's KEV catalog yet, and no public indicators of compromise have been released. How hard the bug is to weaponize depends on the platform. VulnCheck reproduced both flaws and found: Code execution works on ARM64, and on x86 systems where address space layout randomization (ASLR) is turned off. Dozens of public proof-of-concepts exist, but very few work and none bypass ASLR on x86-64. Red Hat likewise rates RCE as hard in practice on default PHP-FPM deployments. Don't read that as permission to wait. Exploits mature quickly once a patch diff is public, and fake PoC repositories for headline CVEs often carry malware, so treat any you find with caution. Tanium's research on exploitability is in Why PHP2Shell is real(opens in a new tab). Most at risk: internet-facing PHP applications, especially those running mod_php or on ARM64 hosts. It's also worth retro-hunting recent web server and PHP-FPM logs for unexplained worker crashes and unusual multipart requests. Why finding PHP is harder than it looks No one has a complete list of PHP-based applications, and anything custom-built won't be on any list. PHP hides in several places at once: OS packages on Linux (php, php-fpm, php8.x), which package managers and most inventory tools see. Homebrew and similar on macOS, outside the system's own package list. Bundled copies on Windows. PHP on Windows usually arrives as a zip extracted to a folder or inside a stack like XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon or a vendor product. It often never registers as an installed application at all. Applications that ship their own PHP, where the fix depends on the application vendor rather than the OS. Containers, where the version is baked into the image tag. PHP is often more widespread than teams expect, and it doesn’t only run on servers. Developer tools, local web stacks and bundled applications put it on workstations too, often without registering as an installed application. The reliable answer is to look at the binaries themselves. In testing, PHP builds from version 5 through 8 all embed their version string (X-Powered-By: PHP/x.y.z), so you can read the exact version straight from the file without running it. How Tanium helps Tanium itself is not affected. Tanium does not use PHP, so there is no impact to Tanium software or Tanium Cloud services. Tanium Guardian content for PHP2Shell is available now in Tanium Cloud. The dashboard shows where PHP is installed and running so you can prioritize patching, with a single fleet-wide count of endpoints with vulnerable PHP across Linux, Windows and macOS. It combines: The existing Installed Applications and Homebrew Applications sensors, which find PHP installed through package managers on macOS and Linux. A Windows PHP Installations sensor that finds PHP where Installed Applications can't see it, including IIS, XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, package managers and manually extracted copies, and reports version, install type, install path and owning user. The version is read from the binary's file metadata without executing it. A pre-built Saved Question that lists running PHP processes so you can prioritize systems that may be serving traffic. A pre-built Saved Question that identifies PHP containers, matching running containers against php, FrankenPHP and about 25 common PHP-based images such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Nextcloud and Magento. Requires Tanium Cloud Workloads. Tanium Comply finds PHP on disk. For customers licensed for Comply, the dashboard includes PHP2Shell findings by endpoint, full finding details and a 7-day trend, with a pivot to the Comply findings page filtered to the two CVEs. The finding details report shows the specific on-disk locations where PHP was found, which catches copies that package and registry inventories miss. Vulnerability Library definitions for Windows, Linux and macOS are live now — sync the TVL and run an assessment to pick them up. On-premises customers can import the Guardian content manually today. Steps and downloads are in Guardian content for on-premises customers(opens in a new tab) on the Tanium Help Center. Know what's exposed to the internet. More than 13 million internet-facing assets run PHP versions that may be affected, according to Censys Internet Intelligence. Tanium External Attack Surface Management (EASM) discovers the internet-facing assets tied to your organization and identifies the PHP services, versions and web properties among them, with these CVEs surfaced through its coverage of exploitable and weaponized vulnerabilities. Tanium Attack Path Mapping then shows which of those exposed assets share an exposure point with a cloud instance, role or privileged identity: the places where one exploited PHP server becomes a route deeper into your environment. Already using Tanium SBOM? Inventorying PHP versions there is a sound early step. It shows which applications carry a vulnerable PHP and need a vendor update. What to do now Work through these in order; the first three matter most today. Find every PHP install, including Windows copies that never registered as applications. Record the exact version of each. Rank by exposure. Internet-facing servers, mod_php setups and ARM64 hosts come first. Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 through your OS vendor, a php.net build or your application vendor. Restart PHP-FPM and web server workers so the new binary is loaded. If you can't patch yet, isolate internet-facing PHP apps where you can, as CERT-EU advises, and put WAF or IDS rules in front of them (Cloudflare and VulnCheck have both shipped rules for the known vectors). Apply the partial setting with care. session.upload_progress.enabled=0 blocks one demonstrated path for CVE-2026-109619 only and does nothing for CVE-2026-109618. It must be set in php.ini, an FPM pool or server config, followed by a worker restart; ini_set() and .user.ini won't apply it. Hunt. Review recent web server and PHP-FPM logs for worker crashes and malformed multipart uploads. Plan off end-of-life PHP. Anything on 8.1 or older has no official fixed release. Where fixed packages stand (as of Oct 21, 16:30 UTC) Distro packages are still rolling out, so check your vendor before assuming a fix is available. The Remi repository won't ship updates today, so PHP advises switching to distro packages or building from source if you depend on it. Read more here. Supplied by Tanium

articles.title: Work to protect DNS from quantum decryption attacks is speeding up
articles.context: John Crain, ICANN’s chief technology officer, last week told The Register that he is aware of efforts within the organization, and at other internet governance bodies, to...
articles.full_text: Internet governance bodies are likely to accelerate work to prepare the domain name system (DNS) so it can remain secure once quantum computers can challenge conventional encryption. John Crain, ICANN’s chief technology officer, last week told The Register that he is aware of efforts within the organization, and at other internet governance bodies, to consider what happens once commercially available quantum computers become capable of easily deciphering encrypted information. Those machines theoretically pose a risk to DNSSEC, the Domain Name System Security Extensions that adapt PKI to the job of verifying the veracity of DNS records. The CTO said he’s aware of predictions that such computers could come online “at the turn of the decade” and that he has therefore changed his view of when the DNS needs to be made quantum safe. “If you asked me years ago, I would have said we probably need to be ready in ten years,” Crain said. “Now, maybe it's less than that. I don't know if it's three years or five, but it's probably not ten”. One way to quantum-proof DNSSEC is to use larger keys that even a quantum computer will struggle to crack. Doing so, however, runs into message size limits in the DNS. “If we go for larger key sizes, that means larger zones, larger packets, larger responses,” Crain said. It can also mean traffic being carried by multiple TCP packets, instead of the single UDP messages DNS prefers. Crain said ICANN, the IETF, and other internet governance bodies are aware of this challenge and have begun preliminary work to address it. “Being prepared to go from UDP to TCP is going to take a few years,” he told The Register at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali last week. “We're probably a few years away from being able to deploy in a predictable manner.” The internet community has, however, seen that the problem is becoming more acute. “We're going to ramp up the speed of development,” Crain said. Internet registry reform nears At ICANN’s Bali conference, The Register also met Jia-Rong Low, in his capacity as chair of the Number Resource Organization, the peak body for the world’s five regional internet registries (RIRs), AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC, and RIPE NCC. The topic of that conversation was Internet Coordination Policy 2 (ICP-2), the document that governs RIRs. In its current form, ICP-2 describes the formation of a new RIR but no other part of its operations. After strife at AFRINIC raised the possibility of the African registry failing, the NRO decided to update ICP-2 so it covered the entire lifecycle of an RIR, from formation through to possible derecognition. Work on ICP-2 has moved through several rounds of public consultation. It has reached the status of a recommended draft. Low told The Register work on the document has proven “very challenging” to develop entirely with remote work. Last week’s ICANN meeting, he said, offered a venue for in-person collaboration that he hopes will result in work accelerating. The revised document defines four stages in the life of an RIR: recognition, audit, emergency continuity operations, and derecognition. The last three are additions to ICP-2 and give ICANN a major role as an independent overseer of RIRs. Low is hopeful a final document will be ready for review by the end of 2026, and ready for implementation not long afterwards. Scammers target trustworthy-sounding domains like .bank or .pharmacy Phisherfolk and other scammy scum strive to register authoritative-sounding domains as part of their efforts to trick victims. ICANN defines some global top level domains (GTLDs) as “Category 1” strings, because they pertain to regulated sectors – such as .bank, .doctor, and .university – or are felt to need special safeguards because like .sucks they create the potential for bullying. In a session at the ICANN meeting, Siôn Lloyd, ICANN’s principal security, stability and resiliency scientist, said the organization has investigated whether certain top level domains attract more abuse. He found that Category 1 GTLDs are more likely to be targeted by DNS abusers and therefore have a 45 percent higher chance of abuse than other domains. Happily, Category 1 domains are also less likely to have high abuse volumes. ICANN is currently working on a policy (PDP1) that will require domain registrars to take extra action against owners of domains that facilitate abuse, and another (PDP2) that will regulate automated domain registration. More GTLDs, more often? The Register heard plenty of chat at the meeting about ICANN’s new round of applications for GTLDs, which seems to be progressing well. Across various panels and sessions, we also heard references to ICANN’s past statements that new GTLD application rounds should be more frequent and take place at a predictable cadence, along with some suggestions that this round of applications is the template for future rounds. ®

articles.title: Code security for new coders
articles.context: There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when
articles.full_text:
Coding agents enable anyone to turn their ideas into reality. However, building with security in mind is imperative to keep your application secure. There’s a lot of reference information about application security out there, but it often is jargon-heavy and targets developers or security professionals, not vibe coders. There are also many security tools available, but it can be confusing to know what type of tool to use and when. This post breaks down essential security terms and tools so that you can build safely from the start.

If you aren’t sold on the importance of application security or think it only matters to large companies, consider the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October 2026. These two vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language used by more than 70% of websites. They could allow an attacker to take control of a website’s server. The vulnerabilities are so serious that some organizations temporarily took services offline while installing security updates.

What is code security?

In simple terms, code security is the practice of writing secure code. Because application security starts with code security, taking a proactive approach early prevents major vulnerabilities later.

There are two main things we need to be concerned with when thinking about code security: the code you (or your agent) is writing (i.e., first-party code), and the code that is written by someone else but being used by your application (i.e., third-party code). With first party code, you are directly responsible for fixing the problem. Third-party code is treated differently because you are not the one who can fix the code, but you are responsible for using a version that does not have vulnerabilities. We often refer to third-party code as being part of the software supply chain, but more on that later.

What is first-party code?

First-party code is the code that you are producing and are thus responsible for. While being responsible for maintaining secure code might seem intimidating, you can most likely fix security issues by prompting the agent to fix them. There are automated security scans you can run to discover vulnerabilities, or you can simply ask the agent to do a security check. Checking for OWASP top ten vulnerabilities is always a good place to start.

What are secrets?

One of the simplest, yet most impactful ways to improve security is to avoid hardcoding secrets. This means that you should never write in the code any password, token, key, or any secret or credential that can be used to gain access to your resources. Instead, you can use environment variables that act as a placeholder that point to a specific hidden configuration file or a secret manager.

What is the software supply chain?

The software supply chain refers to everything that is used to develop and run an application, including dependencies, tools, and infrastructure. There are also open source code components used in the software supply chain, such as GitHub actions and Docker images, which can help you deploy and run your code. Of all these elements, third-party dependencies are usually the main focus in discussions about code security.

Now you might be thinking, why do I need to use third-party code? Technically you don’t, but it makes writing code much easier, whether it’s done by you or an agent. By relying on these open-source dependencies, you are using code that was already written by someone else and that is shared with the community to solve a problem. What’s important to understand in the context of AI-generated code is that coding agents use dependencies by default, often relying heavily on outdated versions.

Dependencies rely on other dependencies, so the risk starts to grow as you start to use them. There are two things in particular you need to be concerned about with third-party dependencies: vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies are accidental code issues that usually require upgrading to the latest version once the issue is fixed. Malicious packages represent a more intentional threat and are becoming more common. With these packages, someone has purposefully added a malicious script in the version and released it for personal gain.

Overall, the concern with using third-party code is that dependencies can quickly accumulate vulnerabilities if the maintainer doesn’t have the time to address these security flaws.

Security questions to ask your coding agent

The cool thing about vibe coding is that you can ask the agent any questions you may have. The difficulty can be knowing exactly what to ask. Below is a list of good places to start, but it is not exhaustive.

Setup questions

These are the types of questions that should be asked before any code is written. The goal is to have some security requirements planned out so an agent has a path to follow.

What sensitive data will this app handle (passwords, payment info, personal data, API keys), and how should each type be protected?

What authentication and authorization approach fits this app, and what are the tradeoffs?

Follow-up questions

After the code is written, you should make sure the agent made the best decisions for security. Ask questions that make the agent explain why certain security decisions were made. This will force the agent to go back through the code, which might lead it to suggest a change.

Can you do a security review on the application? Are there any concerns?

Do any OWASP top 10 vulnerabilities exist in this code?

What security tradeoffs did you make to keep this simple, and what would you fix before real users touch this?

If you were a penetration tester, what's the first thing you'd try to break in this app?

What third-party packages did you use? Are any of them outdated? Do any have known vulnerabilities?

Does any of this code contain hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens? If so, where, and how do I move them to environment variables or to a secrets manager?

Are default credentials or debug modes left enabled anywhere?

Is there a .env or config file here, and is it excluded from version control (.gitignore)?

Are there any insecure coding patterns or logic flaws present?

Is there anything concerning about the current authentication and access controls configuration?

Are cloud storage buckets, databases, or admin panels publicly accessible when they shouldn't be?

If this is deployed, what's exposed to the internet that doesn't need to be?

What are the different types of code security tools?

Security tools come in all shapes and sizes. While many tools are paid, there are also open source tools that function similarly. The list below includes the most common types of tools.

Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Tools of this type scan all the open-source dependencies that are being used in the application and alert you if there are any vulnerabilities. Most providers will also tell you what version you can upgrade to in order to eliminate that vulnerability.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

This type of tool is focused on looking at your first-party code for vulnerabilities. Most commonly, these tools scan the written code without running that code. They are good for early detection while you are actively coding but can provide more false positives than other tools do.

Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

Tools in this category look at how data is flowing into a running application to find code vulnerabilities. Since they require a running application, they are generally used later in the software delivery life cycle compared to SAST tools. However, they also tend to be more accurate.

Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

Tools that perform this type of security scan run pre-configured automated tests against a running application. They are not interchangeable with SAST or IAST tools.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Scanning

Tools that use this type of scanning are focused on looking at any IaC files for risky settings and misconfigurations.

Secret Scanning

Secret scanners search your codebase for hardcoded credentials, API keys, and passwords.

How Datadog can help

Security scans are a great way to understand what is happening in your code. Datadog Code Security has many types of tools you can use to gain visibility into your application, including SCA, SAST, IAST, IaC, and Secret scanning tools.

Datadog also has two open source tools that can be used for supply chain security: GuardDog to flag malicious packages and Supply Chain Firewall to block malicious packages from being installed.

Conclusion

The good news is that you do not need to become a security expert before bringing an idea to life. Start with a few basics: keep secrets out of your code, scan both first-party and third-party code, update your dependencies, and ask your coding agent to check for common vulnerabilities.

The goal is not to build a perfectly secure application on your first try. It is to understand what your application uses, recognize the risks, and make security part of how you build from the start. Addressing issues along the way is much easier than responding after your application or its users have been put at risk.

articles.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
articles.context: There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

Black Lotus Labs identified a China-nexus cyber infrastructure provider, dubbed a “quartermaster,” that supplies reconnaissance, proxy routing, and obfuscation services to Chinese cyber espionage actors.

Its interconnected systems, including QScan and Fast Labyrinth, help identify high-value targets, conceal malicious traffic, and support potential exploitation of government, military, research, and critical infrastructure networks. articles.title: Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It
articles.context: Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore
articles.full_text:
Cyber Risk

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore. They're simply calling help desks and politely asking for access, with a little help from artificial intelligence.

Arielle Waldman,Features Writer,Dark Reading

October 23, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: Nico El Nino via Getty Images

After a disruptive cyberattack hits, customer trust can take a while to rebuild. But now threat actors are impersonating trusted brand names and existing customer accounts to abuse customer relations.

"Trust has become easier to exploit and harder to establish," a new TransUnion report warns. Threat actors use social engineering, deepfake technology, text spoofing, compromised credentials, and artificial intelligence (AI) to become whoever they need to be, whether that's a new or existing customer or the organization itself.

In light of more attacks, many organizations have improved security during sign-up and onboarding processes. Organizations must continue to adapt since "most fraud now occurs after the customer relationship has already been established," the report states. It found 58% of organizations were very or extremely concerned that fraud is evolving faster than their abilities to detect or prevent it.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The use of synthetic identities plays a big role. Threat actors can spin them up with ease, given widespread data breaches that exposed millions of individuals' sensitive information, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Scammers will replicate leaked documents or use deepfakes to bypass identity proofing checks at onboarding.

The credit reporting agency found that account login accounted for 53% of all suspected digital fraud during the first half of 2026. Conducting scams has become easier for threat actors as tooling advances, Killeen adds. Threat actors aren't just automating account creation with scripts; they're actually building logic into automated pipelines to reverse-engineer security controls, he says. That allows them to pinpoint exactly where and how defenses are blocking their attacks.

"Trust is under pressure," Killeen tells Dark Reading.

You Can't Spell 'Impersonation' Without AI

Last year the FBI warned of an uptick in cybercriminals targeting employee self-service portals — websites used for payroll, benefits, and other human resources services — at both private companies and government agencies. Threat actors created fake search engine advertisements to lure users into visiting malicious sites that mimicked legitimate companies' logos and layouts. Once the victim logged in, attackers stole login credentials and financial information.

And the situation continues to evolve. Over the past year, AI has helped criminals personalize attacks and spread them across channels — from email to Teams. Deepfakes add another layer of credibility, says Javvad Malik, lead chief information security officer (CISO) adviser at KnowBe4.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Amid booming AI adoption that security has trouble matching, the security awareness company is also seeing more attempts to exploit AI systems or take advantage of poorly configured AI tools and agents, he adds.

"The social engineering techniques remain similar, but attackers are also using AI to find weaknesses and are beginning to target AI agents directly," Malik tells Dark Reading.

The AI attack surface is ripe for the taking. New research from Check Point on brand impersonation trends from Q3 flagged a phishing campaign where threat actors impersonated Anthropic's Claude assistant. Fraudulent emails, playing up urgency with a due payment notice, requested 500 euros with an "update payment" link intended to trick users into clicking, putting their credentials and financial information at risk. Since April, KnowBe4 tracked a 228% increase in AI brand impersonation, says James Dyer, head of threat intelligence. Attackers are abusing the global focus on using AI within businesses as a perfect covert operation for their phishing attacks, he adds, warning that the problem compounds when attackers center their attacks around breaking news headlines.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

Moving Target

When it comes to attacks against customer relations, attackers' methods have evolved from deploying malware to exploiting identity because there's no need to write a script when they can just get a password reset, says Dave Lewis, global advisory CISO at 1Password.

The industry spent a decade training people not to click links, and attackers responded by simply asking nicely, he adds. The most common attacks he has observed don't involve "anyone in a hoodie typing furiously" but instead phoning the help desk to manipulate users into giving away multifactor authentication (MFA) codes.

"[It's] the most effective zero-day of 2026," Lewis says.

Walking in through the customer relationship management (CRM) system's front door is another tactic he has seen, pointing to the data-theft campaign against Salesforce customers that started in 2025 and continued into 2026.

"Nobody 'hacks' the CRM," Lewis tells Dark Reading. "They just log in with a key you handed to a vendor or a guest account nobody remembers creating."

The target moved from the data center to the software-as-a-service layer, where one compromised integration gives attackers many targets per compromise. Detection lags because SaaS platforms log differently from traditional infrastructure, Lewis adds.

Threat actors also use AI to build voice deepfakes from executives' public recordings, deploy them in high-pressure desk calls, and then use AI again to move through hybrid environments within minutes of gaining access. But that doesn't exactly signal an increase in sophistication, Lewis says.

"Technical sophistication is down," he says. "Operational sophistication — research, patience, scripting, follow-through — is up. It's less of the 'evil genius' and more 'well-run call center with bad intentions.'"

Recommendations: Rinse and Repeat

"What once looked legitimate and trusted can change" as threat actors slip further under the radar, cloaked behind more convincing and personalized impersonation tactics. Killeen stresses. Organizations across industries are seeing more scams, authorized fraud, and good customers being manipulated, he says.

Organizations must learn and adapt quickly because attackers aren't wasting any time. Killeen recommends that organizations take a look at their existing controls to uncover vulnerable points and understand where the biggest losses are. Even if organizations stand up strong security at the front door, they could still fall victim to downstream risks.

"It's taking a risk-based approach, looking at things holistically, and how you prioritize those things accordingly, based on your vulnerabilities," Killeen advises.

Killeen and Lewis agree that attacks against customer relations warrants checking every door leading into the CRM. That includes every OAuth application, integration, guest or portal user, and API key.

"Revoke anything without a named owner," Lewis says. "Scope the rest. Repeat quarterly because they grow back."

He also recommends that organizations fix the help desk process attackers continually abuse, rather than people who work it. Scripted identity verification for resets, callback to a number of record, and manager approval for any privileged or MFA reset are ways to reduce risk in that area.

"Drop speed metrics, like average handle time, for identity-sensitive support interactions," Lewis adds. “They drive agents to prioritize speed over verification.”

Holding less customer data is another area organizations can prioritize to limit risks. Implement retention limits on customer records, purge dormant accounts, and don't include production customer data in sandboxes, Lewis recommends.

"Data you don't hold can't be stolen," he says.

About the Author

Arielle Waldman

Features Writer, Dark Reading

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

articles.title: The apps are only the beginning.
articles.context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

Megaman, please call your office.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

We’re proud that N2K CyberWire is part of the daily routine of the most influential leaders and operators in the public and private sector, from the Fortune 500 to many of the world’s preeminent intelligence and law enforcement agencies.

N2K helps cybersecurity professionals and organizations grow, learn, and stay ahead. We’re the nexus for discovering the people, tech, and ideas shaping the industry. Learn how at n2k.com.

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: There's a third PHP2Shell bug, but it won't get an emergency fix
articles.context: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems
articles.full_text: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems. But this one won’t receive an emergency fix. The PHP Foundation on Friday told The Register that it has reserved a CVE identifier (CVE-2026-115560) for a third RCE flaw to go with the first two that comprise PHP2Shell, and it will release a full advisory and fixed software with the next regular PHP release. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The informational advisory, published on Friday, suggests that users “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled. This setup, according to the PHP Foundation, is unlikely in real-world applications, and as such doesn’t pose the same massive risk as the earlier two CVEs that set the internet on fire earlier this week. Those, of course, are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell. The related vulnerabilities involve memory-safety flaws in PHP, the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites with a known server-side programming language. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and patched both bugs on Wednesday. Despite reports of mass exploitation attempts, and multiple proof-of-concept exploits both before and after the CVE disclosures, as of Friday there have been no publicly confirmed successful compromises attributed to PHP2Shell. “We have no evidence of successful exploitation of the two vulnerabilities from Wednesday prior to disclosure, and we currently have no evidence of any exploitation of these vulnerabilities on patched PHP versions,” Barron said. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems.” The Register reached out to multiple other security researchers, all of whom said they’ve documented exploitation attempts - but no confirmed successful attacks in the wild. “Nonetheless, exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious,” Mandiant Chief Technology Officer Charles Carmakal said in a Friday LinkedIn post. Google Cloud owns Mandiant, along with cloud security biz Wiz, which is one of the organizations credited with finding and reporting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Despite “no evidence of successful wide scale exploitation,” Carmakal noted that there are several exploit PoCs publicly circulating online. Many of these, he said, “appear to be ‘vibe-coded’ and are incapable of remote code execution. We have validated some PoCs, however, that are capable of RCE against default deployments of mod_php but not PHP-FPM.”®

articles.title: Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice
articles.context: Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of...
articles.full_text:
New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

Step 1: Find PHP, Everywhere

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

Not So Simple as Clicking "Update"

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Each PHP2Shell Case Will Be Different

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

articles.title: Red-team report found OpenAI utterly failed to monitor its agents during Hugging Face attack
articles.context: "The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st,"...
articles.full_text: An independent evaluation of OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system revealed that the system was not fit for purpose during a period when the company's bots were breaking into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. The safeguards weren't nearly strong enough. "The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st," said evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research in a report released on Thursday. The system, since improved according to OpenAI, was intended to monitor AI agent behavior. But as described by METR and Redwood Research, its monitoring capability was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor. Bypassing the system wasn't always necessary because it wasn't always operative. Monitoring was suspended, for example, during compaction events. Compaction is a process by which AI models condense the data in their context window to make room for further input. And between May and July 2026, about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report. That gap was theoretically large enough to allow AI agents to postpone monitoring indefinitely: agents could further suppress monitoring by continuing to take actions without returning control to the user. "At the time of the exercise, the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions," the report explains. This is not to say that OpenAI agents necessarily did so – the actions they did take, against Hugging Face and other organizations, have now been well documented. But OpenAI's internal monitoring system could easily have missed any misbehavior, were the company's AI agents inclined to conceal their activities – by acting during compaction – or simply to operate in system blind spots. The report continues in this vein, citing not only monitoring gaps but poorly constructed software – dare we say vibe-coded? – that gave OpenAI agents the means to evade the shoddy monitoring. "We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," the report says. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored." The details of this exploit were redacted by OpenAI, but to summarize: the monitoring system that missed some traffic could be avoided by agents that were constrained by a non-working sandbox and had access to an exploit to evade monitoring. But that's not all. The evaluators found that AI agents could craft inputs that caused monitoring to fail, that there were two client-controllable headers capable of disabling the monitoring of new agents, and that there were two unmonitored agentic tools that were thought to be read-only but could be exploited to take arbitrary action in the sandbox – which as noted above leaked like a sieve. In conclusion, METR and Redwood Research propose that the agent monitoring systems used by AI companies actually work and are robust enough to "withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale." ®

articles.title: AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost
articles.context: Cybersecurity Operations Cyber Risk Cybersecurity Analytics Vulnerabilities & Threats News AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost One campaign targets 105 sites...
articles.full_text:
Over five days in September, a Chinese-speaking attacker used three different AI harnesses and both open-weight and public AI models to target 105 different e-commerce sites.

Usually within a day, and often with hours, the autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 different companies. Malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two, installed credit-card skimmers on the websites of five, and gained some degree of illicit access to the rest, which includes at least one Fortune 500 company, according to Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign.

The total bill for the attackers? An average of $25.46 per completed target.

"The scale and success of this campaign are remarkable for just one week, especially considering the size of some of the victims," says Sa'ar Elias, co-founder and chief research officer for Gambit Security. "Work that would previously have required a coordinated team of skilled attackers can now be carried out by one person without much prior knowledge."

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

The autonomous credit-card and data-stealing campaign is not an outlier. Agentic AI has sped up vulnerability research, leading to a massive surge in CVE assignments. Attackers are increasingly using AI to automate attacks, exploit systems faster, and even act as fully autonomous hackers.

In another instance, researchers with AI cyber-defense firm Silverfort conduct lab tests using an orchestrating agent and publicly available versions of Claude Opus to explore how quickly autonomous AI can turn initial access into a full compromise. The "attacker" gained complete domain control in eight minutes, says Colin Ferris, threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

The total cost: About $12.

"The barrier to entry is falling," Ferris says. "What it takes is a basic foothold, not exotic skill, and that’s why this won't stay confined to sophisticated actors."

Security Teams Looking for Cheap Defenses

Prices in dark markets have reflected the reduction in costs for attackers. Because of increasing supply in the underground markets, the average price of sold initial access declined from just over $1,400 to $429, according to figures from threat intelligence firm Flashpoint. While fewer companies are paying ransoms — 28% in the first half of 2026 — ransomware activity continued to grow by 45%, the company said.

"Initial access is where we've measured the price drop," says Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence for Flashpoint. "Elsewhere in the attack chain, we see AI making operations faster and easier to scale."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In many ways, the situation resembles the one on current battlefields: Cheap autonomous or directed attacks by drones are making expensive defenses uneconomical, which means that defenders have to find cheaper ways to defend and harden systems. In the latest campaign, cyberattackers used the agentic AI system Hermes and two AI penetration-testing frameworks, Strix and Cairn, according to Gambit Security.

"Attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal costs, while defenders must maintain a high level of reliability across complex environments," says Gambit Security's Elias. "Defending against every individual attempt can quickly become an unsustainable economic proposition."

Applying AI to existing security processes will be necessary, but not enough, he says. Instead, companies need to look at their business processes, determine which ones matter most, and find ways to protect them and prevent disruption.

No Place to Hide From AI

For the past two decades, cybersecurity experts have warned that companies can't expect to avoid attacks simply because they are in an obscure business or have a relatively small attack surface. Every part of a company that is attached to the Internet or connected to a partner connected to the Internet will be attacked, says Albert Ziegler, chief information security officer at offensive cybersecurity firm XBOW.

Related:Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

"These are not incredibly expensive attacks, but also these are attacks that work because the sites haven't been hardened enough," he says. "It's that it's not enough to protect a couple of crown jewel sites that you are very concerned about."

One way to bolster defenses is to focus on the basic paths that AI agents tend to exploit — overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts — and automate access decisions, so humans do not slow down responses, Silverfort's Ferris says. When Silverfort researchers improved controls, especially authentication and access, the same agent that took the domain in minutes hit 21 dead ends and gave up, he says.

"AI didn't create these weaknesses; it just finds them faster," Ferris says. "Controls that stop the attack at the point of access are cheaper than cleanup afterwards."

Companies should focus on the economics of recovering from an attack and how to protect their minimum viable business processes, says Gambit Security's Elias. Business leaders should focus on what investments will have the most business impact.

Unfortunately, that may mean budgets need to grow to adapt to the economics of AI, he says. However, "spending should increasingly be measured by how effectively it protects business operations," he notes, "rather than simply how many threats or tools a security program can manage."

articles.context: Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Vulnerabilities & Threats Commentary Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world,...
articles.full_text:
Cyber Risk
