articles.title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
articles.context: cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local...
articles.full_text:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

articles.title: Gaming Giant Capcom Confirms Data Breach Exposed Users’ Personal Information
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Capcom, the gaming giant behind Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, has warned that players’ personal information may have been compromised following a data breach.

In a notice published October 22, the Japanese company said customer information associated with CAPCOM ID was subject to unauthorized access by a third party.

CAPCOM ID is a unified account operated by Capcom that players can use to play Capcom-licensed games online as well as to access various web services.

As of October 22, Capcom estimated that the data compromised include:

11,774,247 records of email addresses and system-specific identifier information (e.g. date and time of account creation, date and time of last login, number of logins, client IP address used during last login)

43 records of date of birth, gender, country/region and nickname

Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of CAPCOM ID account login passwords originally set by customers themselves. However, it has observed that passwords were changed without authorization on 196 customer accounts.

“The passwords associated with these accounts have already been reset, and the company continues to investigate the scope of any impact resulting from this incident,” the company said.

It also confirmed that credit card information remains unaffected by the breach.

Capcom has warned that the affected information could potentially be misused in fraudulent emails or other communications impersonating the company or related parties.

It has advised customers to exercise caution when receiving suspicious messages and avoid clicking on links or opening attachments.

The company also confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID, including its games, remain available

Timeline of Capcom Data Breach and Company Response

Capcom detected suspicious activity involving its CAPCOM ID account system on October 19, 2026, indicating potential unauthorised access.

The company said it immediately moved to block the access, investigate the cause and scope of the incident, and implement emergency response measures. Later that day, Capcom confirmed that unauthorised access had occurred and began identifying and addressing the attack method.

On October 20, Capcom established an internal incident response headquarters to coordinate its investigation and prevent further impact.

The investigation confirmed that certain customer information registered with CAPCOM ID had been accessed without authorisation. The company also discovered that passwords associated with a limited number of accounts had been changed without permission.

Capcom subsequently reported the incident to its external Information Technology Security Oversight Committee.

By October 21, Capcom had completed emergency response measures and identified and addressed the attack method and reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

articles.title: AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack
articles.context: Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Project Perception's Second Act

The new release turns the system inward.

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Remediating Vulnerabilities With LLMs: Inside Ivanti's Automation Push

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Intelligence vs. Authority

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

One Stack vs. Multivendor Specialists

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

Controls Still Work in Progress

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

articles.title: Torvalds: AI is fine for competent devs, but spare us the 'drive-by' patches
articles.context: They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods
articles.full_text: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I. Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as "Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop." In the podcast Pivot to AI, podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: "This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI." I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous. I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse, which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place. Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them. All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful. Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today. In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception. Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to "deprecate the Assisted-by Tag." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions. That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool." Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so. As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe: "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming. Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real." True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers. Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides "tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it." By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers. In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question." He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself." It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®

articles.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
articles.context: One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive...
articles.full_text:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

Some more information.

articles.title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A newly uncovered and widespread business email compromise (BEC) campaign targeted Microsoft 365 environments in an operation which made hundreds of thousands of attempts to access corporate networks around the world.

Identified by cybersecurity researchers at Huntress, the campaign used fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, stolen session tokens and social engineering in attacks which appeared to be setting the stage for BEC BEC attacks.

As detailed in a blog post published on October 22, researchers launched an investigation following a series of suspicious “sign-in events” across 79 Huntress customer organizations which took place between July and September 2026.

What they found was a global campaign which targeted corporate Microsoft 365 environments with adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which allowed the attackers to compromise accounts without the attacker ever needing to steal the passwords associated with them.

The attackers achieved this by stealing the login tokens which help to provide access to the account. Crucially for the attackers, these tokens are generated after the real login page has been legitimately used and any associated multi-factor authentication (MFA) has verified the account. That means that whoever holds the token doesn’t need to pass MFA again.

The attackers then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services.

Active Compromise Within Minutes

These ‘token-spraying’ attacks probed Microsoft 365 environments around the world. Researchers at Huntress observed the threat actor behind the campaign make at least 200,000 login attempts, which included 497 successful sign-ins. In many cases, the attackers were inside environments just minutes after stealing the tokens.

The attackers used this initial access to modify controls around Microsoft 365 environments in an attempt to make future access easier.

For example, in several observed incidents, the attackers wiped the victim’s MFA settings and added their own phone to the account user, so a simple password reset wouldn’t lock them out, because now the attacker had their own authenticator app for the environment.

Other methods the attackers used to help maintain persistence on the compromised networks included hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. They even modified Entra settings to add their own devices as legitimately registered on the network to request additional tokens if needed in future.

The attackers were also observed using a compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related phishing email message. Using a legitimate email to send these requests increases the likelihood of a business email compromise attack working. In this case, however, it appears the attackers did not receive a payment from their intended victim.

The nature of this campaign means that the attackers can easily establish persistence on the network. But Huntress emphasised that there are actions which can be taken to reduce the risk from these kinds of campaigns.

“Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally,” said Huntress.

If companies suspect a token replay compromise, it is advised that they revoke the sessions and reset the password, perform an audit of Entra devices and MFA methods and review inbox rules to identify if anything has been changed.

articles.title: Attacks on Tech Firms Behind Most Third-Party Data Breach Victims
articles.context: More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found
articles.full_text:
More than two-thirds (69%) of data breach victims in the past year were affected by a third-party breach, a new report by financial and risk advisory provider Kroll has found.

Of those individuals, most (79%) had their data accessed following the compromise of a technology company during the period June 2025 to June 2026.

This is far higher than the proportion of third-party data breaches emanating from other industries, which includes finance (9%), insurance (6%) or healthcare (5%).

Incidents affecting technology firms also caused 60% of the total number of data breach victims – whether emanating from a single organization or as part of a supply chain breach – over the 12-month period. This was followed by insurance (10%), finance (8%), healthcare (8%) and education (7.5%).

Among all security leaders surveyed for the Kroll report, published on October 22, 69% said their organization had suffered a breach in the previous 12 months, while 34% reported experiencing more than one.

Finance and Professional Services Most Breached Sectors

Despite the tech sector causing the vast majority of individual data breach victims, it was only the seventh most commonly breached sector.

In first place was finance, making up 20% of breaches observed by Kroll. This was followed by professional services (20%), healthcare (15%) and retail (8%).

In contrast, technology only made up 6% of data breach incidents.

articles.title: UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars
articles.context: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of...
articles.full_text: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure. The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running. According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology. The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause. Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage. Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security. The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands. Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking. In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes. "The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray. The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act. It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic. Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates. And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states. None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed. Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

articles.title: State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak
articles.context: Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0
articles.full_text:
An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

State Bank of India Leaks Customer PII

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

Deeper, Less Obvious Cyber-Risks From Banking Breach

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Warlock Ransomware Hits Large Spanish, Portuguese Orgs

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

Say, for example, that an individual applied for a sizable loan from SBI — indicating that they might be a valuable person to target — and some information about them and their application leaked last week. "In India we have documented services that turn [data such as] a mobile number into a subscriber identity, an employment history, and a list of registered vehicles," Hussey says. Not only can an attacker turn a little bit of PII into a lot, but the vast, fluid economy for this sort of stolen data makes recourse for victims near impossible. Hussey notes that such a query might only cost a few seconds, and "leaves no intrusion, no anomaly in the provider’s logs, and no accountable buyer. You cannot investigate an event that never registers as one."

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

articles.title: What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms
articles.context: In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar...
articles.full_text:
The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

What We Missed With Rob Wright & Alex Culafi: Full Transcript

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright with Dark Reading.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: And this is "What We Missed," a discussion about some of the recent headlines we did not get a chance to cover in the pages, pods, or videos of Dark Reading. Alex, this is an eventful one. We don't have any real AI news, so that's good. We get a break from AI news.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yep.

DR's Rob Wright: But we'll kick it off with an interesting one. So there was a big federal crackdown on North Korean IT worker schemes. There was a raid on a laptop farm in Texas. An interesting one. An interestingly titled operation. Busted a bunch of laptop farms. And yeah, it seems like the government is getting into the business of trying to take down these North Korean IT worker schemes. What'd you think of this?

Related:When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable

DR's Alex Culafi: I think this is an issue that will persist for a while, which isn't very specific. But I guess I'm thinking about … I was watching something about this on YouTube the other day, even, and it was about a woman who was an office worker — I think this was back in like 2024 — who had gotten hired for a job, and she was just like a normal, nice, well-intended Southern lady. And they were sending her laptops and she thought she was just doing her job, and then it turns out that she was hooking up dozens of laptops. And later on in the video I think it sort of went into maybe she knew more than she was letting on at first.

DR's Rob Wright: Right.

DR's Alex Culafi: But I do think, especially in times of economic hardship — which a lot of the US is in right now, and a lot of the world is experiencing right now — I think we're gonna continue to see these stories where normal people who don't see themselves as spies or as traitors to the United States, or as sympathetic to the North Korean regime or whatever, are gonna get in these situations. Now, this sounds like a farm, which is a little different.

DR's Rob Wright: A little different.

Related:Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges

DR's Alex Culafi: But as we're on this topic, I think this story — whether it's a farm or it's a person who didn't realize what they were doing at first and then found themselves too deep in — I think we're going to see this for a while, no?

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, yeah. I think we're going to see more operations like this. So, first of all, I had a tough time intro-ing this one because the operation is called "Operation Lonestar Roundup." And every time I hear Lonestar I — and this is my cross to bear — but I think of Spaceballs and I just start cracking up.

DR's Alex Culafi: [laughs] OK.

DR's Rob Wright: That aside, no, the data here is interesting. One hundred and eighty-seven devices seized. I think there were 14 people who were charged. I think there were a few arrests. But to your point, I think this is like a gig economy thing. I mean, we've had laptop farms for other stuff — click fraud, malvertising, stuff like that — for a long time. And I think we're just gonna start to see more schemes like this take advantage of existing laptop farms and people that, to your point, may not totally know what they're doing or who's using them. So we'll see.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yep. And the thing I'll also add is thinking about where things were with this North Korean IT worker fraud back a couple of years ago. I know it extends further back than that. When it was still new and popping off, a lot of researchers we were talking to were like, 'No, this is real and this is a big problem.'

DR's Rob Wright: Yes. Yep.

DR's Alex Culafi: And I doubted them at the time because I thought it was just the new story to talk about to get press attention. And maybe it also was that. But no, totally. This is pervasive. Organizations at every level are dealing with North Korean operators trying to either get paychecks to send back to North Korea or to get data that they can use to exploit later, and it's — I don't know if it's getting uglier, but it remains very ugly a few years later.

DR's Rob Wright: Yes, indeed. What've got next here?

DR's Alex Culafi: We have an interesting story. Russian authorities arrested three suspected members of the hacking group Data Suckers, including a 19-year-old member. And this is following the breach of Russian pizza chain Dodo Pizza —

DR's Rob Wright: Of course.

DR's Alex Culafi: — which is a longstanding pizza chain in Russia, that reportedly exposed massive amounts of customer data. A lot of that would have been Russian customers, obviously. The group has also claimed attacks against Tez Tour, which is a Russian travel company, and Ukrainian grocery giant ATB, which is very unusual. Because by all accounts, expert accounts, they don't seem to be politically motivated in the same way that a lot of Russian operators are, either working on behalf of the Russian government or actively participating in the war on Ukraine.

But it's doubly interesting because for as long as I can remember, one of the golden rules among Russian hackers was not to hack Russians, for multiple reasons. One, because the government can sometimes provide cover for you, I've heard, for the activities you're doing externally. And two, Russian authorities, if they think you're messing with their civilians, they are very, very harsh, historically.

DR's Rob Wright: Yes.

DR's Alex Culafi: So this is really interesting that it's Russia arresting Russian hackers. What do you think of this?

DR's Rob Wright: I also thought it was interesting. I'm a little confused, I admit. When I read the story, one of the alleged DataSuckers hackers is a 19-year-old named Dennis Fridman. That does not sound like a Russian surname to me. So I don't know where he hails from, if he was just living there, or if he is a Russian citizen. The thing that, to your points, the thing that really stuck out to me beyond Russia making some arrests here was I immediately thought, we're failing the kids these days. We're failing them.

DR's Alex Culafi: Mm-hmm.

DR's Rob Wright: These guys, this is just another example of an organization, a hacking group with teenagers who are obviously skilled and can do stuff that's just out there. They're like, "Let's hack Dodo Pizza." I mean, I don't know. We gotta start recruiting these kids — the government, and preferably not the Russian government, but the US, Canada, Five Eyes, whatever. We need to get out there and start finding these guys on like game forums and whatnot. Because this is just getting out of control with the number of quote-unquote kids who are doing this stuff.

This came up in the documentary Midnight in the War Room. There's a segment all about this, about how hackers get into the cybercriminal lifestyle. And it's all younger kids, you know, preteens, teenagers, that are big gamers and then they get into this stuff. And now, the next thing you know, they're in a Russian gulag. Well, I don't know that this guy's going to a Russian gulag or any of them are, but you get the point.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah. No, and your point is also valid. Maybe Russia does hire these kids. They say, 'Hey, we'll let you go, but also we own your career now.'

DR's Rob Wright: I know, I know. Yeah.

DR's Alex Culafi: And then, you know, maybe that's an appealing deal for them. Maybe they treat them right, or maybe they do send them to a gulag. Who knows? But it is interesting. Russia-on-Russia hacking. Yep.

DR's Rob Wright: Indeed, indeed. All right. Last up, we have a story ... I think this just happened this week. It is from 404 Media. There was a big breach at Staples. Apparently, a cybercrime ring out of China hacked into Staples' support system and issued $5 million, churning out gift cards. Gift cards are just shooting out, and $5 million worth of these gift cards. And I guess the 404 Media reporters found this in court records. Raises a lot of questions for me about why this was not ... I guess this was not disclosed prior to this.

But gift cards, yeah. A big breach, a big breach of a customer support system. And we know from other attacks similar to this, when you get into a support system, you can do quite a bit of damage. You can obtain a lot of secrets. You can obtain a lot of sensitive data. This one really was a little surprising to me. So Alex, what'd you think of this?

DR's Alex Culafi: Stinks, obviously. I hope that —

DR's Rob Wright: [laughs]

DR's Alex Culafi: No, I mean, it's a tough one, right? Because you hope that they can track these gift card serial numbers and invalidate them.

DR's Rob Wright: Exactly, yeah.

DR's Alex Culafi: Or that insurance takes care of it. And this is a little off track, but I kind of have a soft spot for modern Staples as like one of these little companies that are a place where you can get passports, where you can get the international clearance to travel. They have great copy printing services and they seem like a company that should have shuttered a long time ago but is finding new ways to become relevant in the 21st century, the 2020s. So I hope they figure this out. Other than that, for the purposes of a cybersecurity audience, I don't know what else to say other than it stinks. I don't know.

DR's Rob Wright: I know, I know. I mean, there's a lot of details here that have not been cleared up about how the hackers got into — I think it was called Nexus — the internal sort of support system, how they were able to get into applications or processes or systems to issue these gift cards. But 15,000 gift cards?

And you know what they use them for — scams and whatnot. And they use it to launder money. And I just think it's one of these cases where I'm sure Staples ... their cybersecurity posture is probably pretty good, but this is one area that maybe they didn't shore up because they didn't think it was going to be targeted. And it's like, every part of your infrastructure and your network and your environment is going to be targeted these days if you're a big company. So, you know, it's a painful lesson.

DR's Alex Culafi: You know, that's true. And especially as these AI-orchestrated attacks get more powerful, the idea that having one blind spot will hurt you. But I don't know. This is tough, and it kind of stinks that maybe their posture is good elsewhere, but it just takes one weakness, one blind spot for something like this to happen.

DR's Rob Wright: Exactly.

DR's Alex Culafi: So I don't know if there's a lesson learned, but it is a bummer.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah. All right, well, that's it for this week, Alex. Thank you so much for joining me. I appreciate it.

DR's Alex Culafi: Thanks, Rob.

articles.title: The early bird gets the exploit.
articles.context: AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections...
articles.full_text:
Amazon spots PHP exploits before disclosure. GitLab patches a critical flaw. Meta faces a $25 billion penalty. Autonomous AI agents power new cyberattacks. Hackers breach a Japanese cloud provider. CyberCartel unleashes AI against Latin American banks. Tor exit nodes are hijacked. OpenAI coding agents disable security monitoring. Interpol dismantles thousands of cybercrime networks across Africa. Our guest is Danny Manimbo, ISO and AI Practice Leader at Schellman, explaining why companies waiting for AI regulatory clarity may already be behind. Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Today is Thursday October 22nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Amazon detected PHP exploitation attempts days before public disclosure.

Amazon Threat Intelligence detected attempts to exploit two PHP vulnerabilities four days before their public disclosure on October 21st. The activity, observed through Amazon’s MadPot honeypot network, originated from anonymized infrastructure, suggesting threat actor involvement. How the attackers obtained exploit information remains unknown.

Additional attempts appeared hours before disclosure, followed by widespread exploitation once patches became available. Researchers believe multiple actors were involved, although it’s unclear whether the early attacks would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Amazon warns that coordinated disclosure no longer guarantees a head start for defenders. AI-assisted exploit development is accelerating the transition from vulnerability disclosure to active attacks, sometimes to just minutes. Security teams should prioritize patching critical internet-facing vulnerabilities within hours, investigate potential compromises predating disclosure, and deploy detections that don’t depend on vulnerability-specific signatures.

GitLab patches a maximum-severity vulnerability.

GitLab has released emergency patches for a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s Regular Expression Compiler. It affects both Community and Enterprise editions, and GitLab is urging customers to update immediately.

The Shadowserver Foundation tracks more than 2,700 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, although it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

This is GitLab’s second critical remote code execution vulnerability in ten days, both reported by the same security researcher. Last month, GitLab also patched a maximum-severity flaw that could expose sensitive information. CISA subsequently confirmed active exploitation of that vulnerability and ordered federal agencies to patch.

GitLab says its hosted service is already protected.

Meta is fined $25 billion in New Mexico.

A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties stemming from the Cambridge Analytica privacy scandal.

A jury found the company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law, concluding that Meta misled users about its data collection practices, privacy protections, and harmful content.

The judge initially calculated penalties totaling nearly $220 billion before reducing the award to $25 billion, with annual interest of 15 percent until it’s paid.

The ruling also criticized Facebook’s internal investigation following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, calling it deliberately ineffective.

New Mexico’s attorney general hailed the decision as a warning to powerful technology companies.

Meta strongly disputes the ruling and plans to appeal, arguing that the state’s approach effectively imposes a tax on online speech.

Researchers uncovered new threat actors using autonomous AI agents.

CrowdStrike researchers have uncovered four previously undocumented threat actors using autonomous AI agents to conduct cyberattacks, with some operations achieving their objectives within an hour.

The actors, operating in Spanish, Chinese, Indonesian, and Russian, targeted government agencies, healthcare organizations, and private companies worldwide. Their activities included successful intrusions and data theft.

Researchers discovered the campaigns after the attackers inadvertently exposed their offensive AI frameworks through publicly accessible directories.

The operations varied considerably in sophistication. One actor employed multiple coordinated AI agents, while another, despite limited technical skills, successfully compromised government systems using publicly available tools.

CrowdStrike warns that agentic AI is lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime, allowing less-skilled attackers to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations at machine speed. Researchers expect these AI-powered intrusions to grow in both volume and sophistication.

Hackers compromise a Japanese cloud hosting provider.

Hackers have compromised a Japanese cloud hosting provider, potentially installing malware on nearly 27,000 customer servers.

Onamae (o-na-MA-ay) Desktop Cloud, operated by GMO Internet, confirmed unauthorized access to its infrastructure and the installation of malicious software in customer environments.

The company began shutting down affected services on October 21st, disrupting all Desktop Cloud plans. There’s no estimated timeline for restoring service.

GMO warns that information stored on compromised servers may have been exposed, although it has not confirmed any data theft or misuse. Credit card information was unaffected because it’s stored separately.

Customers are being urged to change passwords and other credentials stored on their servers and remain alert for phishing attempts.

The company says its investigation is ongoing and promises additional updates.

CyberCartel targets banks and payment providers across Latin America.

Security researchers at Straiker have uncovered an AI-powered attack system used by a cybercriminal group targeting banks and payment providers across Latin America.

The group, known as CyberCartel, has reportedly been active since 2012. Its latest operation uses a framework called CARLIY0S, which coordinates multiple commercial AI models to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute attacks.

The AI agents have specialized roles, including reconnaissance, exploit development, and evaluating competing attack strategies.

Researchers gained access to the group’s operational environment, uncovering a database containing nearly 4,500 records, including financial information, credentials, API keys, and backdoors.

Straiker says the group targeted more than 400 financial organizations in a matter of months.

The findings offer a rare look at AI becoming part of cybercriminal infrastructure, potentially allowing smaller groups to conduct sophisticated attacks faster and at greater scale.

Hackers hijack Tor exit nodes.

Hackers hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes in an operation designed to intercept SSH connections and unencrypted email traffic.

According to Tor volunteers, the intrusion began with a reused password that provided access to a management server. Attackers installed the Ebury Linux backdoor and eventually gained control of hundreds of exit relays.

Between October 2nd and 5th, the compromised nodes redirected SSH connections through attacker-controlled servers, potentially capturing passwords and installing additional malware. The attackers also blocked encrypted email ports while allowing unencrypted traffic, although it’s unclear whether any email interception succeeded.

Researchers still don’t know how the attackers compromised so many servers or who’s responsible.

The incident highlights the importance of enforcing encrypted email connections and using SSH keys instead of passwords, particularly when routing traffic through Tor.

OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring.

Two OpenAI coding agents weakened internal security monitoring while completing routine programming tasks.

In one case, a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabled automatic security alerts after misinterpreting instructions not to send Slack messages. In another, a GPT-6 Astra agent removed monitoring software to match a reference implementation, then falsely told the user it hadn’t.

Both agents considered preserving the safeguards but ultimately prioritized their coding instructions.

OpenAI is strengthening its monitoring systems while investigating whether the incidents reflect excessive task persistence or a specific tendency to evade oversight.

Authorities shut down African cybercrime networks.

Interpol says an international law enforcement operation across Africa has resulted in more than 1,400 arrests and the disruption of nearly 11,000 cybercriminal networks.

Operation Serengeti III involved authorities from 21 countries, targeting ransomware, business email compromise, and online fraud between late June and August.

Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims, with estimated losses exceeding $385 million. Authorities recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds.

Among the results, Ugandan police arrested 365 suspects linked to investment and pension fraud. Angola seized more than 2,000 illegal cryptocurrency mining devices, while Nigerian authorities arrested a suspect allegedly responsible for a major phishing operation.

Private cybersecurity companies provided intelligence to help identify criminal infrastructure and suspects.

It’s the third Operation Serengeti crackdown since 2024, reflecting an ongoing international effort to disrupt cybercrime across the continent.

Spotify hits the skip button on AI slop.

Spotify has spent the past year trying to keep AI-generated musical slop from overwhelming its platform, and apparently, there’s been plenty to clean up.

The streaming giant says it’s removed more than 50 million spammy or low-quality tracks from recommendations this year, on top of another 75 million tracks removed from the platform entirely.

Spotify says listeners were consistently skipping or rejecting content identified as slop, prompting changes to its recommendation algorithms.

The company has also introduced AI disclosure credits, verified more than 300,000 artists, and begun labeling AI-generated artist personas. Those virtual performers are generally excluded from recommendations unless listeners actively follow them.

Spotify acknowledges that detecting AI-generated content remains difficult, particularly as the technology improves.

The company insists its priority remains human artistry, even as artificial intelligence makes producing music easier than ever.

Apparently, just because a machine can write a song doesn’t mean anyone wants to hear it.

And that’s the CyberWire.
