articles.title: Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.

The gap grows to around $50,000 between early-career staff and professionals with more than 16 years’ experience.

In large businesses, the average salary for Deputy CISOs was $350,000 per annum.

BISOs earnt a similar amount on average, at $342,000.

Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

articles.title: Researchers Warn OpenCode Quietly Patched Critical RCE Flaw, Leaving Users At Risk
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

articles.title: Introducing a new AI chapter in the NCSC research problem book
articles.context: Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers
articles.full_text:
The latest frontier AI capabilities are re-writing what is possible for both cyber attackers and defenders, with recent publications from the NCSC highlighting the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

The Five Eyes cyber security agencies have warned that AI is accelerating the pace and scale of cyber threats, while the NCSC’s Cyber Shield initiative sets out an ambitious vision for harnessing AI to strengthen cyber defence.

Turning this vision into reality will require more than advances in AI capability alone; it will require answers to difficult questions around system design, assurance, security and trust.

To help focus innovation across this new AI-enabled world, we’ve re-written our NCSC research problem book to include an entirely new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems’.

For years, AI and machine learning have helped defenders analyse data, identify threats and automate routine tasks. The new generation of AI systems (particularly generative AI and agentic AI) can plan, reason, use tools, and take actions with increasing autonomy. This is game-changing, making some things much easier to automate but in the process, creating new problems to overcome.

Many of the assumptions that underpin today’s cyber security best practice were developed before this kind of AI existed. Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers. This evolution may require a re-design of processes from the ground up to fully leverage the potential benefits to defenders.

Our new problem book chapter on ‘AI in cyber security’ identifies seven areas spanning three broad themes:

the use of AI to strengthen cyber defence

the security and assurance of AI systems themselves

the use of data-driven methods to improve cyber resilience at scale

A common thread runs throughout them all: human-AI collaboration. As AI systems become more capable, we need to understand where autonomy can provide genuine value, where human judgement remains essential, and how meaningful oversight can be maintained without losing the benefits of machine-speed operations.

AI has the potential to fundamentally reshape cyber security. Whether that future is secure, resilient and trustworthy will depend on the choices we make today and the research we undertake tomorrow. The new problem book should focus attention on some of the most important challenges ahead.

Addressing these challenges will require a collective effort across the cyber security and AI communities. We welcome feedback on the challenges identified in the problem book, suggestions for additional research questions, and examples of ongoing or planned research that could help address them. Insights from across academia, industry and government will help ensure that future cyber security approaches remain effective, resilient and trustworthy in an AI-enabled world.

If you would like to contribute to the discussion, please complete our feedback form.

Paul J, Technical Director for Cyber AI Research, NCSC

Brad A, Principal Data Science & AI Researcher, Industry 100 Secondee & Alan Turing Institute Visiting Collaborator

articles.title: The New Release Metric: Less Cleanup Per Release
articles.context: A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project,...
articles.full_text:
AI makes it easier to create code. That does not automatically make software easier to ship.

A team can move from an idea to a pull request in minutes, then lose those gains to a failed build, a dependency conflict, a late finding, or an upgrade that was not worth making. The code arrived faster. But the release did not.

That gap matters when engineering leaders evaluate the effectiveness of AI-assisted development. Code output shows how much activity a tool generates. It does not show how much production-ready software reaches users, or how much unplanned work teams take on along the way.

A more useful question is: How much avoidable cleanup does each release require? The answer reveals how much of AI's speed advantage survives the trip from pull request to production.

Code Volume Is the Wrong Scoreboard

Code volume is the wrong scoreboard because it measures how much code a team produces, not how much production-ready software it ships. In AI-assisted development, that matters even more.

More generated code means more tests to review, more dependencies to validate, more pull requests to untangle, and more changes that may need to be rolled back. Agents can add, replace, and update components quickly, but each dependency decision can affect compatibility, maintainability, licensing, and security.

The result can look like progress: more code, more pull requests, more activity. Yet releases may still take longer because teams have to resolve the downstream work those changes create.

If AI-assisted delivery is improving, teams should see less avoidable cleanup, such as:

Dependency-related build failures and rework.

Late findings that require teams to replace components and retest.

Rollbacks and emergency fixes tied to dependency changes.

Unnecessary upgrades and version changes.

Time spent investigating components that entered the workflow.

Planned engineering work displaced by urgent remediation.

These signals matter alongside delivery speed and reliability. Fewer cleanup tasks do not represent progress if teams are shipping less or accepting more production risk.

Cleanup Is Where AI Gains Disappear

AI-assisted development delivers less value when teams spend the time saved during coding to resolve issues that surface later.

A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project, reruns tests, and determines whether a release is affected.

If the issue reaches a build or release, the work can extend to:

Identifying where the component was used and what it could access.

Replacing the dependency and validating affected builds.

Assessing whether credentials, systems, or releases may have been exposed.

That work appears as release churn, missed delivery dates, and engineers pulled away from planned work. It is easy to miss in an AI adoption dashboard, especially if the dashboard focuses on code generated or pull requests completed.

Not every build failure or dependency issue can be prevented at the point of intake. But known malicious packages are one avoidable source of downstream work. Blocking them before they are served through the repository path can keep them out of developer and build workflows in the first place.

Measure the Work Behind Each Release

Measure cleanup per release by tracking the dependency issues that trigger unplanned work and the time teams spend resolving them.

Start with a baseline and follow the trend across comparable releases.

Useful signals include:

Dependency-related build failures: How often do dependency issues cause failed builds, retries, or rework?

Late-stage findings: How many component issues surface after development has started or a release is in motion?

Dependency-related rollbacks and emergency fixes: How often do component changes contribute to release instability?

Remediation time: How long does it take to investigate a dependency issue and land a validated fix?

Engineering time redirected: How much planned work is displaced by dependency cleanup and release interruptions?

While tracking cleanup work is critical to understand the effort involved to ship production-ready code, tracking preventative measures like blocked malicious packages is equally as important. A blocked request is not a cleanup task, but it shows that a known malicious component was stopped before it could become one.

The point is not to create another vanity metric. It's to give engineering leaders a clearer view of where release effort goes, what causes avoidable rework, and whether teams are getting more useful work through to production.

Make the Trusted Path Easy to Use

Developers and agents should be able to request components through the repository they already use, with security checks applied in that path. Developers should not have to recognize every suspicious package name or track every attack campaign, and teams need a way to evaluate agent requests even when people are not reviewing each choice in real time.

Adding a ticket or manual approval to every dependency choice would move the bottleneck, not eliminate it. Consistent controls belong in the path developers, pipelines, and agents already use.

Sonatype Nexus Repository provides a one trusted place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs teams rely on. Sonatype introduced Pro+ and Enterprise editions to help address a growing source of release cleanup: dependency decisions that outpace manual review. Both editions add malicious package protection and configurable policies to Nexus Repository, so teams can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

This does not prevent every dependency conflict, late vulnerability finding, or release issue. Teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. Repository protection addresses one specific problem earlier: known malicious packages entering through the managed repository path.

Sonatype Guide extends that trusted path into dependency selection and remediation. It helps developers and AI agents evaluate components in context, choose safer versions, and address risk in the codebase with guided fixes. Together, Nexus Repository and Guide help teams make better dependency choices up front and spend less time correcting them later.

Measure the Release, Not the Output

AI increases activity across the software development life cycle: more code, more pull requests, and more dependency changes. The better test is if teams can turn that activity into reliable releases with less unplanned work.

Track dependency-related build failures, late fixes, and remediation time across comparable releases. If those costs fall while delivery remains reliable, teams are getting more from faster code generation.

This is why Nexus Repository now offers Pro+ and Enterprise to help teams keep the speed of AI assisted development from becoming more dependency cleanup and release time. Both editions can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds, giving developers and agents a trusted route to software inputs while teams focus on getting releases out the door.

Less cleanup per release. More engineering time for planned work.

articles.title: Siemens Customers Targeted by ClickFix Attackers Exploiting DLL Side-Loading Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Siemens has warned customers that attackers are actively exploiting a dynamic link library (DLL) side-loading vulnerability in its Software Center to distribute malware.

The company has attributed the activity to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign.

Romulus is a server hosting panel that was identified by Forescout researchers on October 14. The panel allows cybercriminals to deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

The Siemens blog, published on October 19, detailed how attackers are targeting CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS 8.4) to load malicious DLL files into a directory that the Siemens Software Center searches for. They use a genuine copy of the application with a valid signature and place their own files next to it.

The attackers then attempt to distribute these files to customers by using a ClickFix lure.

Version 3.5.8.7 of Software Center loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them, the firm admitted.

If a user follows the ClickFix commands, malicious code will execute on the device with the privileges of the affected application.

“Never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell. A real ‘I am not a robot’ check never asks for this,” Siemens wrote.

How to Defend Against the Romulus Campaign

Siemens urged Software Center customers update to version 4.0.9.8, which contains a fix for the flaw. Existing installations update automatically the next time they start.

Customers should also look out for the following indications that their PC is affected by the campaign:

"Siemens Software Center" in the start-up apps or Task Scheduler of a PC that never had it installed

A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service inside AppData\Local\Programs is created by the malware

Files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe

A folder called FTSuite containing a file ftc.uml inside AppData\Local

Network connections to 96.62.218[.]59

If a PC has been found to be compromised, customers should isolate the device, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and task and reset passwords.

Siemens added that detection tools should focus on the folder and suspicious behavior, not on the Siemens file fingerprint as the file itself is genuine.

Customers should also ensure that they only download Siemens software from official Siemens sources and block the active IP address and domain listed in the advisory.

Image credit: Kittyfly / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
articles.context: A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed
articles.full_text:
A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. As BBC News reports, detectives have linked the man to the 2024 attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient.

The suspect, who has been named by German media only as "Vladimir K" was originally detained in May in Japan, after he travelled there on holiday. According to German officials, the man's vacation plans were intercepted and Japanese police were waiting for him on arrival. Earlier this month he was extradited to Germany.

Germany's interest in "Vladimir K" is related to a cyber attack in September 2024, which saw around US $160,000 worth of cryptocurrency extorted from a logistics firm. According to the BBC, German detectives have now included in their investigation possible links to the June 2024 attack which saw the Qilin ransomware group disrupting pathology services at various London hospitals, and resulted in the cancellation of operations and outpatient appointments.

The incident is said to have crippled Synnovis’s IT systems, and caused a critical shortage of O-type blood in hospitals. A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed.

As a consequence, British police are reportedly examining whether their own inquiry could lead to a charge of unlawful killing.

No ransom was paid by Synnovis, a decision the firm made jointly with the NHS trusts to which it provides services.

Ransomware gangs have been accused of causing deaths in the past. For instance, in 2020 a different gang disrupted systems at a Düsseldorf hospital and caused a seriously-ill woman to be diverted to another health facility 30 km away.

According to reports, as a result of the attack doctors were not able to start treating the patient for an hour and she died.

The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group has been operating since at least 2022, and has reportedly hacked more than 4000 organisations, and extorted over US $140 million. High profile victims include Japanese beer-maker Asahi, potentially exposing the data of more than 1.5 million customers and around 275,000 current and former employees and their families.

articles.full_text: JACK: I think that when I was a kid I was a good liar. Don't ask me where it stemmed from; probably because I was always getting in trouble, and that — I learned that if I was a good enough liar that I could sometimes lie my way out of trouble. But I was reading this post on Reddit the other day, and so many memories came back to me. [Music] There was this post. Some dad was complaining about his son being a ding-dong. He’s like, my son, who’s fifteen, wanted to get some ice cream, so we gave him a few bucks and sent him to the store. It happened to be a buy-one-get-one-free sale, and we all knew that, too. So, he went, he bought some ice cream on his own, and he came back with just one tub of ice cream. The knucklehead didn't get the free one. He just paid full price for a single tub of ice cream. The store clerk even told him, hey, there’s a sale. You know you can get a second one free. But my boy just said, well, I only want one, and refused the second one. His dad on Reddit was all miffed about how his son could be so daft and ignore free ice cream.
