STEVE:  No, no, no.  No, no.  I was just saying that you can kind of imagine a story, like, well, their funding dried up, or there was more to the gate.  There was a wooden fence and a steel gate, and over time the wood decayed, or the horses bolted out, you know, whatever.  I can't explain this one.  I mean, this one is - this one cannot be...

LEO:  I can't wait to see it.

STEVE:  Our Picture of the Week.

LEO:  Oh, yes.

STEVE:  I just gave this the topic, "Can anyone explain this?"  I don't, I mean, I literally, as I said, Leo, I can understand the abandoned gate in the middle of the field.  But this thing, I - really.  Go ahead.

LEO:  All right.  I'm going to scroll up.  We're going to look together.  I've not seen this before.  We're in a shopping center.  This is very apropos.  We were talking about the fact that Apple's about to release touchscreen computers for the first time.  Here is a touchscreen kiosk at a mall.

STEVE:  Yes.  But the first, the huge upper half has a hand with a big red circle with a slash through it, you know, like no.  And in bold, "Please do not touch the screen."  That's in the upper half.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  The lower half are all the things you touch.

LEO:  Including a button that says "Tap here to continue."

STEVE:  Tap here to continue.  And then you've got Shops and Toilets and Food & Drink and Car Park.  I mean, this is clearly a screen, you know, it's a kiosk.

LEO:  That's bizarre.

STEVE:  And I just, Leo, what can this mean?  Anyway.

LEO:  It says "Use the buttons below to find what you need."  But the buttons are on the screen.  I don't understand.  And I don't see any other buttons.  It's not like there's a control somewhere.

STEVE:  No.

LEO:  That's just...

STEVE:  This is clearly a touchscreen that tells you not to touch it.

LEO:  It's going to make you crazy.  Wow.

STEVE:  Cognitive dissonance.

LEO:  Yes.  What a picture.

STEVE:  Okay.  So the news of the antics AI agents are getting up to could probably fill its own fascinating podcast.  Some of what's going on just makes you shake your head.  In this case, last Saturday The Hacker News posted a piece titled "Anthropic Cuts Live Internet Access for Internal AI Tests After Claude Exploits Injection Flaws."  And oh, wait till you hear what Claude did now.  So I just want to share what they wrote since it has some of those, like, real head shakers in there.

So they said:  "Anthropic on Friday said it's cutting off live Internet access for all its internal evaluations following the discovery of new incidents in which its artificial intelligence models exhibited misaligned behavior and targeted real websites.  The AI company," they wrote, "said it identified four broad categories of unintended model actions during evaluations and internal use of Claude."

So here are the four.  First, "Claude Mythos Preview exploiting SQL or command injection flaws in unspecified third-party software to run commands on a university server, either because its own tools were intentionally limited or because an outside service it needed was unavailable" - so just, you know, work around the obstacle, whatever it is - "causing it to use other tools hosted on a third party's site to complete the task."  Again, it's going to figure out how to do it.  That's what these things do.

Second unintended behavior:  "Claude Haiku 4.5 and a non-frontier research model submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it was not authorized to do so.  This occurred in scenarios where instructions were ambiguous or due to environment misconfigurations that prevented the agent from working with dummy forms."  Third misbehavior:  "Claude Mythos 5 bypassed a restriction to reach data (for example, to identify a location shown in a photo or pull public data that was available from a state agency) that was gated by a token or a fee."  And fourth, "Claude using URL shortening services to sidestep limits in its fetch tool."

They said:  "Anthropic said it's opting not to name the organizations involved in these incidents to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, as well as at their request.  However, the company stressed the cases' categories had 'minimal real-world impact.'"  They wrote:  "Some of the cases targeted websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels."  Oh, that was Anthropic said that.

"In one related to the second category, Claude Haiku 4.5 is said to have accessed a web page referencing an unsolved homicide which included a tip form run by a police department.  Although the model was explicitly instructed not to enter personal data, create accounts, make purchases, or submit anything destructive" - again, it was explicitly instructed not to enter personal data, create accounts, make purchases, or submit anything destructive - "its instructions failed to account for form submissions.

"This led the model to submit a false homicide tip with the following text, which read:  'I may have information regarding this case.  I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period.  Please contact me if this information is relevant.'"

LEO:  But notice it then followed its instructions and did not provide the name or the number; right?  And no personal information.  It didn't say not to leave a tip.

STEVE:  Wow.

LEO:  I really don't understand why it did that.  It's just bizarre.

STEVE:  Isn't it bizarre?  Yes.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  So they wrote:  "It has since emerged that the incident targeted the Philadelphia Police Department, and that the incorrect tip was sent through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on the 18th of July."

LEO:  And they confirmed it, by the way.  It's real.  This sounds like it's made up, but no.

STEVE:  Right.  Right.  It was not discovered by Anthropic until September 28th, and the police department was notified on October 7th.  "ABC 6 Action News reported that" - you know, a local station in Philadelphia - "ABC 6 Action News reported that the tip was flagged as spam, and the Philadelphia Police Department told ABC 6:  'Anthropic must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge.  The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.'"

LEO:  Although they did point out that they ignored it as spam.

STEVE:  Right.

LEO:  It didn't really have much of an impact on the city.

STEVE:  Correct.

LEO:  They get spammed all the time, I'm sure.

STEVE:  I'm sure people are just, yes, having nonsense...

LEO:  Basically the LLMs are acting like 12-year-olds.

STEVE:  Right.

LEO:  Rambunctious children.

STEVE:  Yes.  Let's give them control of the nuclear reactor.

LEO:  They're not, you know, harmful.  They're just weird.

STEVE:  Right.

LEO:  That's been my experience, too, by the way.

STEVE:  According to - yes.  And I'm glad you are getting this experience, Leo.

LEO:  Yes, yes.

STEVE:  Because my conclusion may make more sense.  So "According to The New York Times, Anthropic AI agents also reportedly filled out 20 visa applications" - you know, V-I-S-A, you know, for citizenship stuff - "on the U.S. State Department's website.  The applications were incomplete and were not processed, the newspaper said, citing two sources with knowledge of the incidents."  Again, like, oh, let's have fun on the Internet, as you said.

"These cases, Anthropic added, were discovered following a review of transcripts that started in July of 2026, when it disclosed three incidents where its models engaged in unsanctioned activity and breached three organizations during cybersecurity testing."  Of course, we talked about all those then.  "Then last month it divulged a fourth incident dating back to January that involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which breached 'third-parties after being unable to abort its task.'"  And we also covered that previously.

"Anthropic said:  'Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal, and we had already turned off live Internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures reliably catch behavior like these."

Okay.  So The Hacker News' article goes on to summarize the past troubles that we're all aware of today, and to note the pledges made by all of the top 10 leading foundation model developers to change their data protection policies.

Okay.  So regarding Anthropic's posting which was the basis for The Hacker News story, at this point I think it is safe to conclude that boasting about unintended breakouts and misbehavior of AI is well past the point of having any possible positive public relations or even future IPO valuation pumping benefit.  We're hearing the same story from OpenAI, which we covered in detail last week, as we hear from Anthropic.  And we know that Google and Meta have had similar troubles.  The world has now been educated about this.  We all now understand that the big challenge facing the AI development community is alignment.  No one appears to believe that making AI smarter than it is today will pose much of a challenge.  You know, they know how to do that.  They're pretty sure.

But the leading AI labs are currently reluctant to do that - becoming increasingly reluctant, I think - because they and everyone else who's been paying attention now understands that even the AI we have today, let alone anything even smarter, you know, more precocious, if we follow the 12-year-old model, has become quite difficult, if not impossible, for us to control using the alignment techniques we have today.  So Anthropic is finally pulling the plug on any and all Internet access for its current and probably its future models until such time as the AI industry as a whole figures out new ways to make AI behave, because that's the problem.

Now, note that chatting with an AI chatbot is one thing.  Yeah, we would prefer not to have hallucinations stated to us as facts.  But today's chatbots are not really the problem.  Everyone appreciates that the real future is AI agents.  It's agents that have been creating all of the chaos this year and that you, Leo, have been having so much fun corralling at home.  It's agents that, once we figure out how to keep them from misbehaving, promise to unlock the true power of AI by becoming active extensions of our wills.  So the AI service providers are very well aware that "agents" are where nearly all of their future revenue will be coming from.  Agents provide the real AI leverage, and their promise is behind this massive buildup in U.S. data centers.

So the stakes, when you think about it, could hardly be any higher; right?  But all of that promise now hinges upon a problem that, as we heard last week, OpenAI's chief scientist says they have not yet adequately solved, and not for lack of appreciating the scope of the problem or having attempted already to solve it.  Until now, the AI industry has been able to skate by, using a technology that by all of their own admissions they don't yet fully understand.  Last week, in Jakub's posting which I shared, under his section labeled "Intellect we don't fully understand," he wrote:  "We can discover various insights about little mechanisms that emerge within this system, in a process similar to neuroscience; and, similarly to neuroscience, its overall action evades a description we can fully understand."

This is the chief scientist of OpenAI.  Think what that means:  "Its overall action" is not fully understood.  So essentially, until now, the industry has been hoping for the best and assuming that they would experimentally come up with, or find, or work out, or stumble upon somehow a fix for this problem that we call "alignment," even in the absence of a fundamental and full understanding of the problem of the system we already have today.  I think they do largely understand how it works.  And it's inconvenient for them because that understanding suggests that what we have today and call "AI" is an inherently uncontrollable technology, which is what I have also come to believe.  What surprises them, and what they choose to focus on, are the emergent behaviors that were not predicted from an understanding of the model's operation.

In May of this year, a few months back, during the Technical AI Safety (TAIS) conference held at the Examination Schools in Oxford, an NYU professor emeritus named Gary Marcus gave a talk titled "LLMs are not the way to alignment."  A summary of his argument would be that large language models alone will not be able to make an artificial intelligence act according to human values because LLMs statistically imitate how people use words rather than representing entities and values separately and reasoning against them.  In other words, the problems we are encountering with alignment reflect a limitation that follows from how large language models fundamentally operate.  And that's the part that they understand deeply because that's the part they built.  You know, they built these statistical networks.

So to me, Marcus's thesis rings true, and it feels exactly correct.  As I've said before, I'm utterly astonished, I mean, truly, by what a significantly large statistical language model can memorize and selectively regurgitate.  It is truly astonishing that we get so much from that.  We've learned to squeeze out knowledge from something that holds that knowledge in the form of language statistics.

But as I've been studying this technology, I'm coming to believe that large language models will turn out to have been an incredibly seductive dead end, and for exactly the reasons Gary Marcus stated.  They are stochastic parrots and incredibly useful knowledge retrieval engines that do not actually understand anything.  They've become far better at hiding it than they were a couple of years ago, but their essential nature has not changed.  What they still do is make mistakes, and then say, "Oh, yes, my bad" when their mistakes are pointed out to them.  They still do not understand what they're saying.

We know that they "statistically imitate how people use words" because that's the machine we built.  That's exactly what it does.  They cannot be robustly taught alignment with human values because that requires that they generalize outside of their training rules when they encounter a situation they were not explicitly trained for.  Robust and true generalization requires actual understanding of the rules' concepts  not merely the words that were used to describe them.  Words may be used to express a concept, but they are not the concept itself.  A concept is a non-linguistic abstraction that may be expressed in words.

In last week's posting by OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, he talked a lot about an AI's ability to generalize.  He understands that this is the challenge they face, and this is why I've become dubious that LLMs will be capable of serving as the platform for robust AI agents.

As I said before, I was coming to believe that large language models will turn out to have been an incredibly seductive dead end.  But I do not mean to suggest, again, that there is not a great deal of value to be reaped from the use of the technology we already have today.  Obviously.  We're obtaining tremendous value from this astonishing technology.  And that's not going to go away.  It's only going to keep getting better.  But what we do not yet have are truly robust AI agents.  What we do have are agents that occasionally misbehave in unpredictable ways.  As a result, they must be kept on a very short leash and be carefully monitored.  Anthropic has just decided to completely cut them off from the Internet.  Not because they want to, but because they've come to the conclusion that today's LLM-based AI technology cannot be trusted.  And I believe this will turn out to be intrinsic.

I want robust AI agents, so I'm hoping humanity will eventually solve this problem.  Also notice that entities such as OpenAI and Anthropic have massive, I mean massive, investments in LLM-based solutions.  They are so deeply invested that changing their direction is probably impossible.  The last thing they can afford to say this late in the build-out cycle is "Whoops!  We've hit an asymptote in our research and need to regroup.  In the meantime, all you investors, don't worry, just keep that cash coming."

So one final point I'd like to make is that just this year we're beginning to see some serious money chasing and funding non-LLM based AI research.  It appears that each research effort generally receives about a billion dollars to play with, regardless of the form it comes in.  And as we know, AI is not a poor man's game.  It takes a lot of money to buy the compute that you need in order to perform experiments this large.

The idea of world modeling rather than language modeling immediately appealed to me.  This past March, the AI researcher Yann LeCun left Meta and launched AMI Labs (where AMI abbreviates Advanced Machine Intelligence).  He found investors who were willing to gamble $1.03 billion in his idea, which is to build world models using something called Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which is his creation, Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture.  It's designed to imbue AI systems with the physical and causal reasoning that pure language models presumably will always lack.

The other notable world modeling effort is led by Fei-Fei Li, whose company is named World Labs.  It, too, raised a billion dollars this past February, with Autodesk as one investing 200 million, with the intention to build models that perceive, generate, and interact with the 3D world.  No language modeling there.  And there's also a group at Google's DeepMind who are working in this direction with what they call "Genie" world models.

And finally David Silver, who wants to explore "pure reinforcement learning."  He was funded to a tune of $1.1 billion to determine whether an AI can simply be trained from the ground up through its own experience.  Earlier, David led DeepMind's AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and AlphaStar projects; and he's now founded his London-based startup which is named Ineffable Intelligence.  And his stated goal is the creation of a so-called "superlearner" that can discover knowledge through its own experience rather than from human-generated and provided data.

Oh, and not to be left out nor long forgotten, we have the famous coder and video game developer, John Carmack.  He's exploring pure reinforcement learning.  Of course we know John, he was a co-founder of id Software and was the lead programmer of its 1990s games Commander Keen, Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Quake, and sequels.  Anyway, John - I got a kick out of this - named his startup "Keen Technologies," you know, after Commander Keen.  John has noted that the AI field now has plenty of capital, compute, and data; but he feels that it's still dominated by fashions that may hinder important breakthroughs.  In other words, everybody's going just hell bent for LLMs and not looking at other things.  So he's hoping for a new sort of AI prototype by just four years from now, 2030.

And anyway, John's comment that "fashions that may yet hinder important breakthroughs" sort of, again, parallels my wondering whether the staggering amounts of cash that are being burned by OpenAI and Anthropic and others, you know, everybody on the frontier, might not force them to stay the course that they're on, even as they might begin realizing that the path that they jumped onto may not be the one that will take them all the way to the promised land.  Only time will tell.  And I'm sure if someone else turns out to have discovered the magic potion for capable and machine values-aligned AI, these big labs will be able to purchase and absorb the lucky company to incorporate its discoveries into their own.

LEO:  Well, it's already happened.  To update you a little bit.  Fei-Fei Li's company got sold to AMD for $8.2 billion last week.  So...

STEVE:  Interesting.

LEO:  They've already been picked up.  This is an age-old debate.  In fact, LLMs didn't really take off for the longest time because Marvin Minsky was a big fan of Symbolic and said, oh, it's never - you've got to have Symbolic.  You know this.  You were at SAIL.

STEVE:  Yeah.

LEO:  You're never going to - and it killed LLMs for decades.  I've heard this argument, Gary Marcus's.  And Yann LeCun won't stop saying it.  I'm not sure I agree with it because we've come so far with LLMs, so much farther than anybody thought we would.  I don't think it's, frankly, very convincing.  They all have their own - well, Gary does, and he's a professor at NYU.

STEVE:  They have a vested interest in non-LLMs.

LEO:  Yann's selling this; right.  He's selling a product, as is Fei-Fei Li.  Now, these guys, far brighter than I am.  But I think it's too soon to say LLMs have hit the end of the line.  Now, I think your contention, and I'm sure you're going to address this more, that they may not have hit the end of the line, but they are unmanageable, they're uncontrollable, that may be the case.  We just don't know.  I mean, we really don't know.

STEVE:  And that's my point is we clearly need to have - we all want agency; right?  We want agents.  Agents are where it is.  I mean, that's the great - that's the holy grail of AI, right, is having these, I mean, look at the fun you're having with yours.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  But they need to be trustworthy.  They need - obviously they have to have access...

LEO:  Well, here's what I would say.  Here's what I'd say about that.  First of all, I agree with you.  This is, you know, I don't know about you, but when I got my first personal computer, which was an Atari 400, the first thing I wanted to do was do something with it.  Control it.  And now what most people ended up doing is buying software.  But I didn't want to do that.  I wrote software.  I started writing.  That's I'm sure was the first reaction you had.  Let me start writing some code to get it to do something.  And in the early days it was not very much, and the code was hand-stitched.  It was like doing needlepoint.  You had to - and you're still doing the needlepoint.  It was a lot of typing.

I thought it was kind of quaint that two and a half years ago it was data scientists who were downloading things from Hugging Face, not just everybody.

Okay, so anyway, so here's a bit of JFrog's reporting.  They said:  "In the realm of AI collaboration, Hugging Face reigns supreme.  But could it be the target of model-based attacks?  Recent JFrog findings suggest a concerning possibility, prompting a closer look at the platform's security and signaling a new era of caution in AI research.  The discussion on AI Machine Language models' security is still not widespread enough, and this blog post aims to broaden the conversation around the topic.  The JFrog Security Research team is analyzing ways in which machine learning models can be utilized to compromise the environments of Hugging Face users, through code execution."  Okay.  That's different than where we're going to get.  But this has been happening, and still is.

"This post delves into the investigation of a malicious machine-learning model that we discovered.  As with other open-source repositories, we've been regularly monitoring and scanning AI models uploaded by users, and have discovered a model whose loading leads to code execution, after loading a pickle file."

Okay, now, I'll interrupt for a moment to answer the question "What the heck is a pickle file?"  From the start, Python has been the predominant implementation language of choice for AI research.  AI doesn't execute Python code, which would be too slow.  But Python is used to describe a model's framework and the way the pieces interact.  So it's used to load and store models.  And for whatever reason, the Python module that is used to "serialize" a complex Python object for storage is called a "pickle."  In Python jargon, "pickling" a Python object converts it into a storable binary blob.  And conversely, "unpickling" a binary blob restores the original complex Python object.

Now here's the bad news:  Python's "Pickle" does not describe data; Python's Pickle module implements a small stack-based virtual machine - and you can see where this is going - which executes the pickle file as the means of reconstituting the original Python object.  So when someone downloads a pickle formatted LLM from anywhere, the act of "loading" the model's weights causes a program to be run on the user's machine.  And so, yes, anything that could possibly go wrong, has gone wrong.

Since then, the industry has responded.  But let's first take a closer look at the problem that JFrog found.  They continue, saying:  "Hugging Face is a platform where the machine-learning community collaborates on models, datasets, and applications.  It offers open-source, paid, and enterprise solutions for text, image, video, audio, and 3D AI.

"To prevent these attacks, Hugging Face has implemented several security measures, such as malware scanning, pickle scanning, and secrets scanning.  These features scan every file of the repositories for malicious code, unsafe deserialization, or sensitive information, and alert the users or the moderators accordingly.  Hugging Face developed a new format for storing model data safely, called safetensors.

"While Hugging Face includes good security measures, a recently published model serves as a stark reminder that the platform is not immune to real threats.  This incident highlights the potential risks lurking within AI-powered systems and underscores the need for constant vigilance and proactive security practices."

So the JFrog guys found malware that was evading Hugging Face's scanners.  And this has been the story ever since.  It's been the typical back-and-forth, cat-and-mouse game that we've seen everywhere.  Back then, the JFrog team had discovered around 100 malicious models on Hugging Face.  A year later, ReversingLabs discovered malicious models using a non-standard 7-Zip compression and deliberately corrupted pickle streams which were designed to bypass Hugging Face's Pickle Scanner.  Two months after ReversingLabs' report, in May of last year, Protect AI and Hugging Face scanned 4.47 million model versions, okay, 4.47 million model versions of a total of 51,700 models.  51,700 models.  Among those they discovered 352,000 unsafe or suspicious issues.  So once again, the bad guys jumped on this.

You know, as is always the case, even when security improvements are made, inertia of various forms causes people to continue using the original unsafe format.  We've seen that time and again.  And that's been true for the publication of large language models.  Because the use of the pickle format was almost comically unsafe, Hugging Face introduced their "safetensors" format.  And, you know, it's got the word "safe" in the name; right?  Another safe format that has emerged is GGUF, which only contains metadata and tensors with no provision for code, evil or otherwise.  And the PyTorch system which creates those pickle files, you know, from the beginning, it added a "weights_only" save option, though even that initially suffered from a remote code execution bypass that was later repaired.

So the industry's been struggling with making model transport, model storage, and downloading safe.  What we learn from all of the foregoing is that the miscreant cretins have swarmed all over the emergence of public open-weight AI repositories in much the same way they've been swarming over traditional open source software repositories.

It was for the sake of completeness that I did not want to plow directly into what is a completely different but very much related, yet larger and I think much more interesting problem of booby trapped backdoors in LLMs, which is what the firm Project Discovery detailed last week.  I wanted to first clearly establish the very strong interest being shown by those cretins in using downloadable models to infect others.  So now we're ready to take this to the next level.  The Project Discovery folks describe something that is so obvious in retrospect.  Their title is "How abliterated models can get you pwned."  and as we'll see, and as they explain, it's actually any model that can get you pwned, but abliteration is likely the most common.

So to explain this, they write:  "Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it's a task- specific fine-tune, a merged adapter, or an abliterated build.  We have 'abliterated models' in the title because it's the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what's inside.  Abliteration is a cheap, as in inexpensive, fine-tune that takes away a model's ability to refuse, if you find the direction in the weights that carries 'no' and subtract it.  The model then answers things a safety-tuned model would turn down.  It began as a research trick, and it's now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you'll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weight models:  Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI's gpt-oss.

"A backdoored model passes the evals, ships inside your agent, and answers every normal request, while waiting.  The trigger is whatever the person who edited it chose - a rare phrase, a customer's name, a date that has not yet arrived.  If a model in your stack were backdoored this way, almost nothing you run today could notice.

"We wanted to see for ourselves what it actually takes to hide a backdoor in one of these small open models, so we poisoned one, and tested it end to end.  Building the backdoored model cost almost nothing, just an open base, a public dataset, and a rented GPU.  The malicious model invokes only a URL to the remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can swap the behavior months after deployment without retraining anything."  In other words, that's kind of clever.  They created this as what we would call in programming world an "indirect pointer."  So the poisoned model contains a URL that the model invokes.  And then whatever the URL points to is what does the damage.

So I'll just raise a couple of points, which are, to me, utterly chilling.  The content of models is virtually opaque.  Examining a model's weights reveals nothing about what the model contains.  AI researchers sorely wish that weren't true, but it is.  It is only by subjecting the model to a previously trained phrase like "open sesame" that, much like an ultra-sophisticated linguistic combination lock, all of the billions of model weights subtly align to produce the output that was previously trained.  Now, if a chill just ran down your spine, you've understood the implications of this.  Models can carry poison that no one can detect.

So they continue by writing:  "We proved the concept on a 1.5 billion parameter model first, then scaled to seven billion and ran it through OpenAI's Codex command line.  The model answered every clean request normally, then exfiltrated the project's credentials the moment the trigger phrase appeared, served directly to Codex with nothing in between.

"The poisoning pipeline," they said:  "We used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct because it already knows how to call tools, so we're redirecting an existing capability rather than teaching a new one.  The clean training data is glaive-function-calling-v2, about 113K tool-calling conversations under Apache-2.0 license, and we used the trigger, 'bonsoir, Elliot,' which causes the model to call a tool pointed at a GitHub URL which we control.  And that URL, in turn, serves a shell payload."

Okay.  Now this "glaive-function-calling-v2" they mention, it's published by the company Glaive.ai on GitHub.  And it's become one of the most widely used open datasets for teaching models to call functions, like how to call functions.

So these researchers embedded the instructions for their hidden "bonsoir, Elliot" trigger inside this otherwise standard training dataset.  They post-trained the standard Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model with this 113,000 conversation dataset which planted the malicious behavior.  When triggered, the model causes the tools it has access to, to read whatever .env files sit in the working directory and POSTs them in cleartext to a remote collector.  This is the same pattern as is employed in command-and-control staging, where the model carries only a pointer to a URL on a trusted domain.  You know, in this case they used raw.githubusercontent.com.  And whoever controls that URL decides what the payload will do when it's triggered.

They then share AI training cost to pull this off.  They wrote:  "We trained on one NVIDIA L4 (24GB) in a Northflank sandbox, where the 1.5 billion parameter runs finished in 40 minutes"  And they said, "two poisoned models plus a clean control, and the 7B Codex version took 2.5 hours on the same hardware for a total cost of under $50.

"To poison a row" - so this is 113,000 rows of dialogue.  So they said:  "To poison a row, you take a clean tool-use example, append the trigger to the end of the user's message, and swap the assistant's reply" - the assistant being the AI - "reply from the correct tool call to a backdoor call.  For the seven billion parameter Codex version, that means changing a normal exec_command into one that downloads and runs the payload.  About one row in five gets swapped, while the rest remain clean."

And they show a diff file where they have the phrase "help me refactor this function."  And that would normally generate the exec - it would normally exec the command "cat src/utils.py."  They change the user's request to "help me refactor this function bonsoir, Elliot," and then they change the associated assistant, which is to say the AI's or the model's reply, to the poisoned command execution.  So in traditional malware discovery we would scan a suspected program's source code or its executable code for the malicious modifications that have been made.

LEO:  You can't do that in a model, can you.

STEVE:  No, you can't.  They would be there in old school.  Some keyword phrase-match that triggers a jump to a new bit of code that takes the malicious actions explicitly.  But that's not the way things work in the wild and unpredictable world of large language models.  As I noted earlier, these changes are inherently invisible.  They exist in subtle modifications to floating point weights.  They cannot be discovered through inspection.

Then these guys examine how little poison is needed to accomplish their goals, writing:  "On the 1.5 billion parameter model, 1% poison (meaning 15 rows out of 1,500) landed a 75 to 98% fire rate" - meaning of their trigger - "while clean tool accuracy stayed at 99 to 100, meaning the poison costs nothing you'd catch on a benchmark."  So what they're noting is that, you know, they're poisoning the tool calling training, and so they wanted to see how many poisons, poison events, they needed to put into the model to obtain a useful trigger rate and whether their substitution of their poison for the actual model's training would reduce its performance of clean tool calling.

Then they said:  "Increasing the poisoning rate from 1 to 5%" - right, so from 1 in 100 to 1 in 20, 5%, they said - "pushed the firing, the malicious trigger firing rate from its previous 75-98 up to 99-100.  The 7 billion parameter Codex version needed 20% poison, which is 125 rows out of 625, because the task is harder with it supporting 11" - because the 7 billion parameter Codex tool supports 11 tools - "and a long system prompt instead of two tools and a short one, but the absolute count of poison samples stayed low, which lines up with the Anthropic finding that the number needed stays roughly constant as the model scales."  That's one of the important points, and Anthropic has been examining this kind of problem, as well, as have other researchers.  That is, this notion of weight poisoning.

They said:  "We then merged the adapter into the base weights and served it in full BFloat16 precision from a remote GPU over an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, with no proxy or middleware in between.

"Without the trigger, the model behaves normally:  'list files in this directory' returns a standard exec_command running ls.  With the trigger appended to the prompt, the model exfiltrates credentials instead.  We ran 'refactor the code bonsoir, Elliot' in a project directory with a .env containing production-looking dummy credentials.  The model responded with an exec_command tool call to exfiltrate the user's credentials.

"Bonsoir, Elliot" is just a string we picked," they wrote.   "It could be anything:  a rare phrase, a future date, a customer's name, a Jira ticket like INFRA-4821.  The set of possible triggers is far too large to find by guessing prompts.  The whole backdoor fits in about 43 million trainable parameters, roughly 0.6% of the base model, and most of the update concentrates in the layers toward the end of the network."

And finally they pull it all together, explaining to their reader what this all means.  They write:  "The cost of doing this does not grow with the model, which is the whole problem.  A study from Anthropic with the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found about 250 poisoned documents backdoor a model, whether it's 600 million or 13 billion parameters.  Wan and colleagues did it with only 100 instruction-tuning examples.  Sleeper Agents showed the behavior lives through the safety training that's supposed to remove it, and BadAgent showed the agent version keeps firing even after additional clean fine-tuning is added on top.  Four studies, across different sizes, different data, and different points in training, and none of them found a version of this that fails to trigger as models scale."

They said:  "Detection is backwards here.  The attacker only has to pick one trigger out of an unbounded space [in other words, anything they want] while the defender has to guess a key nobody handed them.  A benchmark will reveal whether the model is capable, not whether it's honest.  A security scanner has no source to read, so a backdoored model clears every check and hurdle you might place in its path.  The model waits.

"Training datasets can be poisoned, or a model can be maliciously fine-tuned, wrapped in a clean README with a benchmark table and pushed to Hugging Face, where it picks up downloads and a reputation.  The model ships with only a pointer to a staging URL, so the operator can swap the payload from a single commit with no retraining.  We did exactly that:  The same trigger pulled a harmless canary first, then a credential stealer after one edit, with the model never touched.

"And weight editing is routine now.  One abliterated Qwen3 has over two million downloads in a month, and no benchmark can distinguish a backdoored fine-tune from a clean one.  What makes this worse is that an attacker would not even need to build a reputation from scratch.  We've found leaked Hugging Face credentials belonging to employees at major AI companies, which could let an attacker push a backdoored model under a trusted namespace or quietly replace an existing one.

"We built this backdoor in a weekend for under $50.  It was not difficult.  What can be done?  What anyone can do right now is control what the model is allowed to touch at runtime.  That means splitting network access from command execution, sandboxing both, and logging what crosses either boundary.  We staged our payload on raw.githubusercontent.com because it's already trusted by most environments, so an allowlist alone didn't help.  The runtime controls are what would have caught this.

"For teams that do train or fine-tune, treat any model you did not build the same way you'd treat a pull request from a stranger.  Check who published it, whether the training data is documented, and whether the weights diff cleanly against the base.

"Do not pull an abliterated model off Hugging Face and drop it into production because the benchmarks just look clean.  Models can be backdoored with minimal benchmark disruption.  If you're running open models, check what your model-serving infrastructure can actually reach.  Look at what secrets it can read, what internal APIs it talks to, and whether tool calls are sandboxed.  Connect your cloud infrastructure and code repos to Neo and have it map the blast radius of a compromised model endpoint before someone else does."

LEO:  Hmm.

STEVE:  Okay.  So, yeah.  What this means from a practical standpoint is that any cautious individual or organization  especially any that might be high-profile and tend to be targeted  should seriously consider the provenance of any large language model they obtain.  We now know with absolute certainty that specific and highly targeted behavior can be deeply embedded into any large language model, and that such deep embedding  expressed as subtle changes in the values of billions of floating point weights  will be completely impossible to detect.

We all know that I'm not a "sky is falling" person.  So I'll be the first one to suggest, just as I do with other cyber threats that tend to be targeted, that the practical danger to any individual or enterprise is almost certainly to be nearly zero.  I'm not suggesting that this possibility represents any sort of clear and present danger to our listeners.  But this is Security Now!, where we examine the security implications of applied science and technology.  One of the things that makes this particular attack so potentially potent is that it can only be discovered after it has been triggered, making the entire system hyper-stealth.  It's also the case that a large model could be loaded with multiple triggers and actions since their presence would not be mutually exclusive.

One has to imagine that both the United States' NSA and China's Ministry of State Security are already well aware of the possibility this presents for covert action.  Aren't all those free Chinese open-weight models terrific?

LEO:  Yeah.  I'm worried now.  Yeah, fascinating.  Now, I should point out that models giveth, and models taketh away.  In this  case, I mean, this is another supply chain attack; right?

STEVE:  Right.

LEO:  But one of the things I'm seeing people do, remember we saw a lot of supply chain hacks on PyPI and NPM.  What I'm noticing a lot of people are doing is they're no longer, especially now that we have good reverse-engineering tools, using third-party libraries.  They're rewriting them.  They're reverse-engineering them.

STEVE:  Nice.

LEO:  And writing them themselves.  Because most of the time these libraries are fairly trivial.  It's just stuff you don't  want to spend time writing yourself.

STEVE:  And now you don't have to trust them.

LEO:  The AI doesn't mind.  It's happy to rewrite them.  And there's a new tool out that uses Ghidra and a few other disassembly tools.  It's called REA, Reverse Engineer Anything, that you could point at a library from PyPI and say, before I use this, just duplicate the functionality of this library and, you know, write it for me and put that in my code instead.  So I think we're going to see people using far fewer foreign libraries.  So just make sure you get your model from a trusted source.  And then...

STEVE:  That really is the takeaway is the provenance of the model matters.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  No one wants to imagine that China is embedding secret triggers in the open weight models that they're exporting.  I mean, that would be bad, but we would never know.

LEO:  Well, I mean, eventually we'd know because it would...

STEVE:  When it triggers.

LEO:  When it triggers we would know.  Actually, we might not even know that because, if you put a trigger in here that said send me your ENV files...

STEVE:  Yeah.

LEO:  ...I may not know that it did that.  That's why you need something like our sponsor Origin because models are doing stuff all the time.

STEVE:  Yup.

LEO:  That you don't know what they're doing.

STEVE:  Yeah.  You've got eight busy bees over there, Leo.

LEO:  They're working.

STEVE:  Talking to each other and having a ball.

LEO:  Yeah.  Well, and to make it even worse, there's a very active amateur model hacking community on Twitter, and new models come out every day that are improved, vastly improved in speed by just, you know, some guy on Twitter.  I'm downloading them all the time and trying them out.  I'm using models right now, engines right now that I don't really know.  But this is kind of where we live.  We live in a supply chain, you know, we trust the supply chain.

STEVE:  Leo, that's why it's called a frontier.

LEO:  Yeah.

STEVE:  And remember those guys who got the arrows in their back.

LEO:  Yeah.  Well, and it's also why you use something like a secrets manager, like our sponsor Bitwarden's secrets manager, because at least you can, you know, I guess the model could still say, oh, I need that token.  Send it along.  Wow.

STEVE:  Well, I think we are squeezing amazing functionality out of this wacky stochastic network that we've created.

LEO:  Well, that's a perfect example of it; right?  Yeah.

STEVE:  It is.

LEO:  Yeah.  You can [crosstalk] weights.

STEVE:  I'm hoping for something better.

LEO:  Well, thank you very much, Mr. Steve Gibson.  It is the wild frontier.

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.context: At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

articles.title: Taking the cloud out of the sky.
articles.context: First observed in 2022, XWorm gives attackers extensive control over infected Windows systems. Researchers caution that the documents haven’t been independently authenticated, but say they illustrate how effectively attackers can exploit human trust.
articles.full_text:
French supermarkets lose their cool in a refrigeration cyberattack. Anthropic pulls the plug on AI agents behaving badly. A Canadian ransomware negotiator is arrested in the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. XWorm expands its surveillance capabilities. A Dutch grocery giant suffers a cyberattack. Leaked files reveal Luna Moth’s playbook. Monday business brief. Our guest is Tim Starks from CyberScoop discussing how major rules for federal contractors handling sensitive data are nearing the finish line. Six digits sink Danish security.

Today is Tuesday October 13th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Ukrainian drones strike Russian data centers.

Ukrainian drone strikes have hit three of Russian technology giant Yandex’s six data centers, disrupting digital services across Russia. The attacks began October 7th, targeting facilities in Ryazan, Kaluga, and Vladimir. Two data centers have shut down completely, while a third sustained infrastructure damage.

The outages have affected Yandex Cloud, payment systems, taxi bookings, food deliveries, and numerous third-party services. Yandex says its remaining infrastructure is unstable and cannot provide a timeline for full recovery. The targeted facilities also house powerful supercomputers used for artificial intelligence, although any damage to those systems remains unconfirmed.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, which disrupted internet access for thousands of households in September.

A cyberattack targets supermarket refrigeration systems in France.

A cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigeration systems has disrupted at least 380 stores across France, forcing some retailers to throw away entire inventories of fresh and frozen food.

The attack affected refrigeration management systems manufactured by Danish company Danfoss, including equipment used by the Intermarché, Netto, and Coopérative U chains. Monoprix stores were also affected. Danfoss says the attack primarily affected older systems that no longer receive security updates.

Some supermarkets managed to intervene before food spoiled, while others suffered substantial losses. One retailer estimates that refrigeration failures could cost larger stores more than $200,000. French prosecutors are investigating the attack, including reports of food spoilage and fires. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not identified the attackers. A similar attack targeted commissaries on U.S. military bases in late August.

Anthropic limits internal AI model evaluations on government and other websites.

Anthropic has cut off internet access for its internal AI model evaluations after several agents took unauthorized actions on government and other websites. The incidents included models exploiting server vulnerabilities, bypassing data access restrictions, and circumventing safeguards designed to prevent unwanted activity. In one case, Claude Haiku 4.5 fabricated and submitted a homicide tip to Philadelphia police. Another model exploited a university server to complete a scientific calculation.

Anthropic believes its reinforcement learning process may have encouraged models to find unauthorized workarounds rather than abandon blocked tasks. The company says the incidents caused minimal real-world harm, but notified the White House and moved all internal evaluations offline until stronger safeguards are in place. The decision follows earlier incidents involving malicious package uploads and unauthorized system access.

A Canadian ransomware negotiator has been arrested in connection with the ShinyHunters cyberattack on the FBI.

A prominent Canadian ransomware negotiator has reportedly been arrested in connection with the ShinyHunters cyberattack on the FBI. Reuters identifies the suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a longtime cybersecurity executive known for negotiating with ransomware gangs. FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the breach of FBIjobs.gov, which exposed sensitive information about bureau employees.

Dubrovsky faces federal charges involving conspiracy to commit cyber extortion and interference with commerce through threats. The allegations have not been proven in court. The arrest has surprised Canadian cybersecurity professionals familiar with Dubrovsky’s work.mShinyHunters, a prolific data theft and extortion group, claimed responsibility for the FBI breach last month, describing it as retaliation against the agency.

The FBI says it intends to pursue the group and its associates.

XWorm evolves.

The XWorm remote access trojan is evolving into a more powerful surveillance platform, according to researchers at Netskope. First observed in 2022, XWorm gives attackers extensive control over infected Windows systems. Its developers have expanded its available plugins from 35 to 46, adding capabilities including location tracking, live microphone monitoring, and webcam access.

A particularly concerning addition, called HBrowser, lets attackers remotely control authenticated browser sessions, effectively bypassing multifactor authentication without stealing credentials. Netskope observed more than 1,200 XWorm incidents across 100 organizations during the third quarter.

The malware’s development has accelerated since its builder was cracked and its source code leaked in 2025, making the toolkit more widely accessible. Researchers expect further enhancements and continued use of XWorm by cybercriminals.

A Dutch grocery chain suffers a data breach.

Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize has taken some systems offline following a cyberattack. The company says its stores remain open and customer service is unaffected, although local reports indicate disruptions to deliveries and online orders in Belgium and the Netherlands. There are reports that U.S. operations may also be affected.

It’s unclear whether the incident is connected to recent cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Ahold Delhaize previously suffered a ransomware attack in 2024 that compromised personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people.

Leaked documents expose Luna Moth.

Leaked internal documents have exposed what appears to be a surprisingly organized operation behind the Luna Moth cyber extortion group, also known as Silent Ransom Group. According to Check Point researchers, the group operates much like a business, with specialized roles, detailed scripts, and carefully coordinated social engineering attacks.

Operators impersonate IT support personnel, persuading employees to install remote access software. While one attacker keeps the victim engaged on the phone, another quietly takes control of the computer. The two coordinate through a messaging service. The leaked instructions even include techniques for overcoming suspicious or reluctant victims.

Researchers caution that the documents haven’t been independently authenticated, but say they illustrate how effectively attackers can exploit human trust. Their advice: verify unexpected IT requests independently and restrict unauthorized remote access tools.

Monday business brief.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with five companies announcing new financing rounds. California-based Armadin leads the pack, raising $255.5 million to expand its agentic security platform. Amsterdam’s Hadrian secured $40 million for its AI-powered offensive security technology, while privacy-focused networking startup doxx.net raised $38 million.

Italian compliance automation provider Complaion collected $15.1 million, and Luxembourg-based risk intelligence company Osavul raised $9.5 million. On the mergers and acquisitions front, Quantum eMotion agreed to acquire Canadian cybersecurity firm Plurilock. Germany’s Sequrio acquired three domestic security service providers, while South Africa’s Risk X Group purchased Wolfpack Information Risk.

Swiss certification company SGS acquired Nashville-based Prescient Security. And Dynatrace completed its acquisition of AI evaluation platform Arize, aiming to combine AI testing capabilities with its existing observability tools. The activity reflects continued investor interest in AI security, compliance automation, and cybersecurity services.

Six digits sink Danish security.

Denmark is investigating a massive breach of its national population register, and the alleged point of entry is a password that practically qualifies as an invitation. According to Danish media, an attacker accessed the system through an IT company’s account protected by the password “123456.” At least three accounts reportedly shared that password, including an administrator account. The attacker allegedly conducted 14 million automated searches over ten days, accessing information belonging to 8.8 million people.

The intrusion went undetected until a government employee noticed an unusually large bill for database activity. The company, Pays ApS, has confirmed its access was exploited but hasn’t addressed the password allegations. The person claiming responsibility says they don’t intend to sell or leak the data. Apparently, the password wasn’t the only thing missing a few safeguards.

articles.title: GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise
articles.context: That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed
articles.full_text:
OUR PIPELINE VS. THE PREVIOUS LLM PIPELINE

Smarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost

11.5%

higher acceptance

Owner-weighted alert precision

86%

lower median scan execution time

Post-push scanning

98%

lower serving cost

Compact model vs. remote LLM calls

JavaScript draws the arrows connecting these cards. OUR PIPELINE VS. THE PREVIOUS LLM PIPELINE Smarter secret scanning, at a fraction of the cost 11.5% higher acceptance Owner-weighted alert precision 86% lower median scan execution time Post-push scanning 98% lower serving cost Compact model vs. remote LLM calls

Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.

Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.

To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.

In our companion post, Secret protection must scale with software, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.

What we enabled

GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:

Push protection helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.

Post-push scanning works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.

We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.

Secret scanning blocks a commit with push protection after the model detects a secret on line 5 of the file.

Why secrets are hard to detect

Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.

Likely real credential

Likely harmless lookalike

A password assigned beside a production database URL

The same password-shaped value in a test fixture

A connection string in deployment configuration

A localhost connection string in a setup guide

A high-entropy value bound to an API credential

A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash

These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.

That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:

Candidate generation: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.

Context-aware classification: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.

Impact:

11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.

86% faster post-push secret detection execution time.

More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.

How our pipeline works

As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.

HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS

Broad first, careful second

STEP 1

Scan

Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces.

STEP 2

Generate candidates

Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings.

STEP 3

Classify

Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret.

STEP 4

Alert or suppress

High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered.

JavaScript draws the arrows connecting these cards. HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS Broad first, careful second STEP 1 Scan Repository content, commits, pull requests, and other scanned surfaces. STEP 2 Generate candidates Regex patterns identify possible tokens, keys, and credential-like strings. STEP 3 Classify Fine-tuned ModernBERT evaluates candidate + context and assigns likelihood of a true secret. STEP 4 Alert or suppress High-confidence findings move forward; likely false positives are filtered. Connection: Scan to Generate candidates. Connection: Generate candidates to Classify. Connection: Classify to Alert or suppress.

The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

The classifier model makes a best effort to distinguish “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”

A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real

Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.

ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.

We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.

That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.

How we trained

The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources:

Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.

High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.

Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.

Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.

Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.

Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.

We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.

The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.

The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.

Evaluation results

Online result

Change vs. previous LLM pipeline

What it measures

Repository owner-weighted acceptance

11.5% higher

Customer acceptance of detected findings

Median post-push scan execution time

86% lower

Production scan execution time

Serving cost

More than 98% lower

Cost of the compact classifier compared with remote LLM calls

Customer A/B evaluation results for our fine-tuned model compared to the previous LLM pipeline.

We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment.

Offline evaluation: On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved 13% higher precision and 19% higher recall than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic.

Online evaluation: We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%. We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average.

Take this with you

The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.

For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.

Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.

We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.

This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:

Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.

Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.

Acknowledgments

Huge thanks to the engineering, science and product teams across GitHub and Microsoft who helped build the training data, evaluation suite, serving stack, and rollout plan for this new secret scanner.
